citations.supports: The construction, passage to an exact solution, and finite maximal lifespan.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: There are smooth divergence-free data on the unit torus whose classical Euler solution ceases to be smooth at a finite positive time $T_*$. The construction first produces approximate solutions with summable increments, then identifies their limit as an Euler solution and proves that its vorticity diverges at the origin, in Theorem 7.1 and Propositions 8.1–8.2. This is the existence claim that the remaining argument must establish. The formal theorem asserts the existence of one such datum and solution, representing torus fields by functions on $\mathbb R^3$ invariant under integer translations. Its stronger verdict records additional conclusions for that same solution: oddness, bounded velocity, divergent time integrals of the gradient and vorticity norms, and spatial limits away from the origin.

rows.fidelity_note: The paper’s sentence asserts finite-time blow-up from smooth periodic initial data. The formal theorem additionally chooses odd divergence-free data, proves bounded velocity and central vorticity divergence, gives both divergent time integrals, and supplies every off-origin spatial limit. These are stronger conclusions for the same selected solution; they do not apply to every smooth initial datum.

rows.name: TorusEuler.theorem11
rows.plain: Existence of a finite-time singularity for smooth periodic Euler data
rows.annotation: The odd shear $u(x,y,z)=(\sin(2\pi y),0,0)$ is zero at the origin, where its curl is $(0,0,-2\pi)$. Oddness fixes a particle at the origin and leaves room for a velocity gradient there. Theorem 1.1 constructs an unforced flow for which the curl at that fixed particle tends to infinity at a finite time.

citations.supports: The lower bound holds on successive complete activation intervals and passes to the limit.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The selected smooth Euler solution satisfies $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\to\infty$ as $t\uparrow T_*$. Proposition 8.2 proves a lower bound on each entire interval between successive activations and controls the contribution of all later increments, so the conclusion holds throughout a terminal time interval rather than only at selected times. This gives the local obstruction to a smooth continuation used in Corollary 8.3. The formal condition expresses the same full limit along $0\le t<T_*$, with the Euclidean norm on vorticity. It records the conclusion for the chosen solution and does not assert that all smooth initial data develop such a singularity.

rows.fidelity_note: For the selected solution with $T_*>0$, the formal clause is the full limit $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\to\infty$ as $t\uparrow T_*$ through $[0,T_*)$. It is not merely unboundedness along a subsequence. The pointwise vector norm is Euclidean.
rows.name: TorusEuler.EulerSingularityWitness
rows.plain: Finite lifespan, bounded velocity and central vorticity blow-up conditions
rows.annotation: Take a wave varying in the first coordinate whose velocity points along the second. Its curl points along the third, so measuring the first component ignores the wave’s curl. This is the projection used at each handoff. The lower bound has to hold between every pair of sufficiently late launches. Projecting the central curl onto the newest wave vector kills that wave’s own leading contribution $k\times a$ (see Equation (8.1) for the two projections). The preceding wave supplies a positive component in this direction that dominates the older flow and the errors. The intervals cover a full left neighborhood of $T_*$, so the lower bound holds at all sufficiently late times.

explanation.text: On the closed slab up to $T_*$, the velocity increments are uniformly bounded by $2\lambda_j^{-1}$, a summable sequence. Their uniform limit is continuous and agrees with the classical velocity for $t<T_*$. This is continuity of the velocity itself, even at the origin. The vorticity is allowed to diverge there. The formal theorem uses the conclusions of Theorem 7.1 and Proposition 8.1 for this same construction.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S678b.closedSlab_velocity_limit
rows.plain: A continuous terminal velocity
rows.annotation: If continuous increments have uniform sizes at most $2^{-j}$, the remaining tail after stage $J$ is bounded everywhere by $2^{-J}$. The stage estimates let the construction apply this uniform Cauchy argument. Every stage is defined through $T_\infty$, and both pieces of its velocity increment are bounded by $\lambda_j^{-1}$. Summing $2\lambda_j^{-1}$ on the closed time interval gives one continuous limit there, which agrees with $u$ before $T_\infty$ by uniqueness of the pointwise limit. The $C^\alpha$ range in the abstract uses the first-derivative bounds as well. Interpolation in Section 8.4 gives the power $-5/4+3\alpha/2$ of $\lambda_j$, apart from the parent-scale loss.

citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For every compact $K\subset\mathbb T^3\setminus\{0\}$ and integer $m\ge0$, both $u(t)$ and $\partial_tu(t)$ have limits in $C^m(K)$ as $t\uparrow T_*$. Proposition 8.4 uses the shrinking supports and summable corrections for $u$, then separates the pressure contribution near and far from $K$ to treat $\partial_tu$. This distinguishes the singular point from regions where every spatial derivative has a limit. The full formal condition requires these two conclusions, representing the excluded torus point by the integer lattice in $\mathbb R^3$; this is the same claim. The separate linked condition describes such convergence for a single given field, without producing either field, so that link is weaker and neither link alone asserts a smooth space-time extension through $T_*$.

citations.supports: The fundamental cell and its interpretation as the unit torus.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The unit torus is represented by the cube $[-1/2,1/2]^3$, with opposite faces describing the same spatial points. The introduction fixes this cell, and the conventions impose periodicity on the fields integrated over it. This makes the volume and spatial norms used later unambiguous. The formal domain is the same closed cube in $\mathbb R^3$, which explains the same verdict; integer-translation invariance is an additional condition on fields, not a property supplied by the cube itself. The duplicated boundary faces have zero three-dimensional Lebesgue measure and therefore do not alter integrals or essential suprema.

citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: On $\mathbb T^3\times[0,T_*)$, the velocity and pressure satisfy $\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\nabla p=0$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$. Equation (1.1) fixes the unforced incompressible equation whose smooth solution the construction must produce. The formal condition writes the convection term as $D_xu\,u$, requires $T_*>0$, and imposes smoothness and integer periodicity on both fields. Its pressure has zero spatial mean, as stipulated in the conventions, and time differentiation at zero is from the right. The same verdict concerns these equations with those conventions; the condition does not itself prove existence.

citations.supports: All conclusions and their assembly for one common initial datum and solution.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: There exist smooth odd divergence-free $u_0$ on $\mathbb T^3$ and a maximal smooth odd Euler solution on $[0,T_*)$, with $0<T_*<\infty$, bounded velocity and $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\to\infty$. Both $\int_0^{T_*}\|\nabla u\|_\infty\,dt$ and $\int_0^{T_*}\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_\infty\,dt$ diverge, while $u$ and $\partial_tu$ converge in every $C^m(K)$ for compact $K$ away from the origin. The proof is assembled from Propositions 8.1, 8.2 and 8.4 and Corollary 8.3, so all conclusions belong to the same constructed solution. Both linked formal statements retain these conclusions, use integer-periodic representatives with zero-mean pressure and one-sided time differentiation at zero, and explicitly identify the velocity and lifespan of every maximal solution from the chosen datum. The same verdict includes this explicit expression of classical uniqueness; it does not claim an Euler continuation after $T_*$.

citations.supports: Zero trace and a symmetric acceleration matrix characterize the admissible affine background.
citations.title: Craik and Criminale, Evolution of wavelike disturbances in shear flows (1986)

explanation.text: A spatially linear velocity $U(t,x)=D(t)x$ solves Euler with pressure $p_D=-x\cdot(D'+D^2)x/2$ when $\operatorname{tr}D=0$ and $D'+D^2$ is symmetric. The trace condition gives incompressibility, while symmetry makes the affine acceleration a pressure gradient, as in Craik and Criminale’s Section 2. This supplies the background on which an exact wave can be placed. The linked formal theorem goes on to verify the full wave solution when the wave equations, transversality and a primitive $P'=F$ are supplied. Its stronger verdict concerns regularity: differentiable coefficients and profile suffice for the identities, without the introductory assumption of smoothness or the profile’s oddness and periodicity.

A linear vector field is a gradient exactly when its matrix is symmetric, which gives the quadratic pressure. The trace condition handles divergence separately. The linked theorem carries both conditions into the superposition and uses a time derivative of $D$ within the interval.

explanation.text: The perturbation is $w(t,x)=\mathbf a(t)F(k(t)\cdot x)$, with $k\ne0$ and $\mathbf a\cdot k=0$. This is the plane-wave ansatz of Section 1.1 and Craik and Criminale’s Section 2; transversality makes the perturbation divergence free and eliminates its self-advection. It separates the wave’s amplitude from its transported scalar phase. One formal formula instead denotes the full velocity $u=Dx+w$ and imposes no transversality, while the theorem link uses that formula to prove Euler under the wave equations, zero trace, symmetric $D'+D^2$ and $P'=F$. Both links therefore have different scope from the sentence introducing $w$: the first adds the background, and the second proves a conditional solution theorem.

explanation.text: For $w(x)=\mathbf aF(k\cdot x)$ with $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$, the nonlinear term $(w\cdot\nabla)w$ vanishes. Differentiation gives $F(k\cdot x)F'(k\cdot x)(k\cdot\mathbf a)\mathbf a$, so the cancellation follows directly from transversality. This is why a finite-amplitude wave can satisfy the full nonlinear equation on an affine background. The formal theorem proves the same pointwise identity assuming only differentiability of $F$ at the phase in question. Its stronger verdict records that smoothness, periodicity, oddness and the time evolution equations are unnecessary for this spatial calculation.

These are the two computations establishing exact Euler evolution in Section 1.1. One formal theorem gives the acceleration formula under the phase equation and transversality; the other gives the pressure gradient for symmetric $D'+D^2$ and the stated primitive. rows.plain: The displacement energy inequalities
rows.annotation: In Equation (1.8) the displacement energy contains $-H\xi\cdot\xi$. Since $\xi(T)=0$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\xi(t)|^2\le(T-t)\int_I|\xi_t|^2$. The upper bound $H\le I$ consequently loses at most $T^2/2$ of the kinetic term, giving the lower bound $1/2$ for $T\le1$. A large negative pressure curvature increases the quadratic form. The same argument with the approximate-parent coefficient $H^\#$ gives Equation (4.8); this is why the wave construction needs a one-sided upper bound rather than smallness of the entire matrix.

citations.supports: Volume preservation and periodic integration by parts remove the pressure variation.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The pressure term in the displacement energy vanishes when $X$ preserves volume and $w=\xi\circ X^{-1}$ is divergence free. Changing variables gives $\int_{\mathbb T^3}\xi\cdot(\nabla q\circ X)\,da=\int_{\mathbb T^3}w\cdot\nabla q\,dx=0$, by periodic integration by parts. This removes the unknown pressure from (1.8) and permits an energy estimate using only the source and pressure Hessian of the parent. One formal theorem proves $\det D_aX=1$ for a jointly $C^2$ periodic divergence-free parent; another proves the vanishing gradient pairing for $C^1$ periodic $w,q$. Both are weaker than the full sentence because the change of variables and the choice $w=\xi\circ X^{-1}$ still connect the two results.

rows.annotation: For divergence it is preferable to group the same sum as $W=\sum_{p=1}^P(V_p+C_{p+1}+B_p)$. Each pair $V_p+C_{p+1}$ is a curl and each $B_p$ is solenoidal. The last pair uses $C_{P+1}$ even though there is no level-$P+1$ mean or transverse solve.

rows.fidelity_note: For $P\ge1$ and $C_1=0$, the formal theorem proves exactly the reindexing $\sum_{p=1}^P(V_p+C_{p+1}+B_p)=\sum_{p=1}^PZ_p+C_{P+1}$. It holds for arbitrary additive families. No convergence of an infinite expansion is asserted.
rows.name: TorusEuler.HierarchyProfiles.velocity_eq_sum_Z_add_completion
rows.plain: Sum of profiles with the last curl correction
rows.annotation: The sum of the $Z_p$ contains $C_1,\ldots,C_P$, whereas the sum of completed oscillations contains $C_2,\ldots,C_{P+1}$. Their difference is $C_{P+1}$ since $C_1=0$. In particular the finite expansion is a sum of curls and solenoidal means even though the individual $Z_p$ need not be solenoidal.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_5_6

rows.fidelity_note: The finite-depth existence theorem supplies the correction identity and level-dependent size estimates. The formula $C_{p+1}=C[V_p]$ and the local curl identity explain why $C_{p+1}$ completes $V_p$ to divergence-free velocity.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_5_6
rows.note: The depth estimates put the divergence completion of the transverse profile at the next level and bound the level-dependent factors.
rows.plain: Frequency decay at every level
rows.annotation: There is a distinction between the two sums in Proposition 5.4. $V_p+C_{p+1}$ is a completed curl, whereas $V_p+C_p$ groups two fields by their estimated frequency powers. The extra $\lambda^{-1}$ from $Q[V_p]$ exceeds the required level decrement $\lambda^{-2/3}$, so the completion belongs to the next size block with $1/3$ to spare. At the last level the curl is still needed for the divergence equation.

explanation.text: At fixed time and label, split the level-two error into $H_2=\langle H_2\rangle_s+(H_2-\langle H_2\rangle_s)$, where $\langle H_2\rangle_s=\int_0^1H_2(s)\,ds$. The second term has zero phase mean because the phase has period one. This separation assigns the mean to the endpoint equation and the oscillatory part to the transverse amplitude equation. The formal average is a weaker link defining only the integral, while the formal oscillatory difference is the same second term for the paper’s smooth profiles. The related mean-and-oscillation expansion in Cheverry provides context, but the sources and equations used here are those of Section 5.5.1.

ties.name: TorusEuler.phaseMean
ties.plain: Averaging over one phase period

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition gives $\langle f\rangle_s=\int_0^1f(s)\,ds$ at fixed time and label. For $f=H_2$, this is the mean in the sentence; it does not itself define the oscillatory difference. Smoothness of the paper's profiles ensures that this integral is the ordinary phase average.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. For the smooth profiles used here, integration over one phase period is exactly the paper’s average.

rows.name: TorusEuler.phaseMean
rows.plain: Averaging over one phase period
rows.annotation: A phase average is taken before evaluating the phase at its physical value. For example, the profile $b(t,x)F_h(s)$ has zero phase mean at every $x$, but the value $b(t,x)F_h(\theta(t,x))$ need not vanish or have zero spatial integral for general $b$. The operation retains the spatial dependence of the force that is to enter the mean equation.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition gives the oscillatory part $f-\int_0^1f(s)\,ds$. With $f=H_2$, it is exactly the second term in the paper's split. For an integrable period-one profile its phase mean is zero; neither integrability nor periodicity is imposed merely by the definition.

rows.plain: The oscillatory part of a profile
rows.annotation: Write $H_2=\langle H_2\rangle_s+(H_2-\langle H_2\rangle_s)$. The second summand has zero phase integral at each $(t,x)$, as required by Equation (1.12): the phase pressure derivative also has zero integral. The mean equation absorbs the first summand, for which this transverse equation alone cannot provide a centered response.

citations.supports: The level-two mean source cancels the parent residual as well as the averaged wave error.

explanation.text: At level two the mean equation is forced by $-\langle H_2\rangle_s-R_U$, so it cancels both the averaged wave error and the parent’s residual. Section 5.5.1 makes the parent residual appear only at this level. This is the step that removes the inherited forcing instead of retaining it in the limiting Euler equation. One formal expression prescribes precisely $-\langle H_p\rangle_s-\mathbf1_{p=2}R_U\circ X$, while the algebraic theorem rewrites the level-two average using $C_1=B_1=0$ and the phase-integration identity for $C_2$. Both links are weaker than the cancellation assertion because they specify or simplify the source; existence of $B_2$ with that source comes from the endpoint inverse.

ties.name: TorusEuler.HierarchyOperators.level_two_meanSource
ties.plain: Mean forcing at level two

rows.fidelity_note: At depth $P\ge2$, assume $C_1=B_1=0$, zero phase average of the linear terms in $H_2$, and $\langle(C_2\cdot\kappa)\partial_sV_1\rangle_s=\langle J\rangle_s$ for a specified profile $J$. The formal identity is $-\langle H_2\rangle_s-R=-(\langle(V_1\cdot\mathbf d)V_1\rangle_s+\langle J\rangle_s+R)$. Here $\mathbf d$ differentiates the slow coefficient at fixed phase; in the geometric application $J=(\mathbf d\cdot V_1)V_1$ and $R=R_U\circ X$. Averaging and the two advection operations are supplied linear and bilinear operations. This rewrites the forcing; it does not construct $B_2$ or prove its differential equation or divergence condition.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The mean-source formula is combined with the endpoint inverse to construct the correction.

rows.name: TorusEuler.HierarchyOperators.level_two_meanSource
rows.plain: Mean forcing at level two
rows.annotation: The part of the wave error seen by the mean equation at level two is $\mathbf d\cdot\langle V_1\otimes V_1\rangle_s$ (row divergence in labels), not the full stress of $V_1+C_2$. The fast product of $C_2$ with $V_1$ supplies the term $\langle(\mathbf d\cdot V_1)V_1\rangle_s$ needed to obtain this divergence. Since $V_1=\widetilde\chi g\mathbf a F_h$, the tensor is $\widetilde\chi^2 g^2\langle F_h^2\rangle_s\mathbf a\otimes\mathbf a$. Its negative divergence and $-R_U$ force the mean. The linked algebraic identity assumes the fast-product cancellation proved just after Equation (5.25).

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition prescribes the mean source as $-\langle H_p\rangle_s-\mathbf1_{p=2}R_U\circ X$. At $p=2$, this is precisely the force needed to cancel the averaged error and parent residual. The existence of a mean correction satisfying that equation comes from the endpoint inverse, not from this source formula.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The mean-source formula is combined with the endpoint inverse to construct the correction.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.meanSource
rows.plain: The forcing for a mean correction
rows.annotation: The residual belongs entirely to the phase-independent part: it is the same at every $s$. Even where the localized wave vanishes, the mean equation still has the inherited force $-R_U$ (or $-R_U\circ X$ in labels). It is therefore a torus-wide solve, not a correction supported only where the wave lives.

rows.name: TorusEuler.HierarchyOperators.level_two_meanSource
rows.plain: Mean forcing at level two
rows.annotation: The cancellation in Equation (5.25) is important for the size of the mean: the fast derivative $\kappa\partial_s$ can cost $\mathsf D^C\lambda^{3/2}$, but after phase integration by parts the row divergence of $\langle V_1\otimes V_1\rangle_s$ has only a slow derivative. Since $\|V_1\|_{[n]}$ is of order $\lambda^{-5/4}$ up to parent powers, the averaged quadratic source has size $\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-5/2}$ at each finite order. The parent residual is added at this level. The linked Lean lemma uses the phase integration-by-parts equality as a hypothesis.

explanation.text: For the level-two correction, $B_2(0)$ is selected so that the induced physical displacement vanishes at both time endpoints. Writing $F=D_aX$, $B_2\circ X=Fz_t$ and $\xi=Fz$ turns this into $z(0)=z(T)=0$. Theorem 4.2 supplies this endpoint solution for a smooth periodic source when $0<T\le1$ and the parent’s effective Hessian is bounded above by $I$. The first formal link only imposes the smooth label equations and endpoints, and the second proves that two existing solutions for the same parent and source have the same pulled-back physical correction. Both are weaker than selection with existence: the inverse theorem is also needed, and the preserved final positions are only a first-order statement.

ties.name: TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution
ties.plain: Smooth solution of the mean problem

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition imposes $z(0)=z(T)=0$ and $z_t=v$ for label fields, with $B=Fv$. Thus $\xi=Fz$ has zero physical displacement at both endpoints. This states the first-order endpoint requirement; it does not prove that a solution or an initial value realizing it exists.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The endpoint solution conditions are realized by the mean inverse theorem.

rows.name: TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution
rows.plain: Smooth solution of the mean problem
rows.annotation: For the endpoint condition we use the interval $[0,T]$ of the parent step, including the time before activation. The oscillations can vanish on that earlier interval while the mean is nonzero there. The selected initial velocity contributes to the new initial data in the iteration.

rows.fidelity_note: Under the same smooth parent and forcing on $[0,T]$, $0<T\le1$, with $H^\#\le I$, the formal theorem proves equality of the physical means of any two endpoint solutions. Consequently $B_2(0)$ is unique. It compares existing solutions and must be combined with the inverse's existence result to justify the paper's selection claim.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. Uniqueness of an existing endpoint correction complements the inverse theorem’s existence.

rows.name: TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.mean_eq_of_endpoints
rows.plain: Uniqueness of the mean correction with two zero displacement endpoints
rows.annotation: At stage $j$ the endpoint inverse selects an initial mean velocity so that the first-order displacement vanishes at time zero and at $T=S_j$. The wave may start later at $t_j$ within that interval. In `mean_eq_of_endpoints`, both `PaperSmoothMeanSolution p force` arguments share the same parent and source. The conclusion `EqOn a.mean b.mean J(T)` says their mean velocities agree throughout $[0,S_j]$, including the initial correction the inverse selects.

citations.supports: The level-two transverse equation, its supplementary source, and the order of construction.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: After solving for $B_2$, the oscillatory correction satisfies $D_tV_2+(\nabla U)V_2+\kappa\partial_s\pi_2=-(H_2-\langle H_2\rangle_s)-(B_2\cdot\kappa)\partial_s(\widetilde\chi A_1)$, with $\kappa\cdot V_2=0$, zero phase mean and zero initial value. Equation (1.12) and Section 5.5.1 include the second source because the mean correction transports the leading fast phase. The formal expansion condition gives the same equation and constraints, while the general finite-level equation is different in scope because it uses supplied algebraic operations whose geometric interpretation must be established. The fixed-label existence theorem is weaker because it treats a continuous centered source without proving smooth dependence on labels, while the separate transverse-solution condition presupposes smooth profiles on the full slab and only specifies their equation, transversality, zero initial value and normalizations. The remaining source formula is weaker again, supplying only $-(B_2\cdot\kappa)\partial_s(\widetilde\chi A_1)$ at level two.

ties.name: TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.construct_equations
ties.plain: The equations at each retained level

rows.fidelity_note: The formal theorem organizes the mean and oscillatory equations for every retained level $2\le p\le P$, assuming their linear solvers and prescribed operations. At $p=2$ its source has the algebraic form in (1.12). It does not itself identify the abstract operations with physical derivatives or assert $\kappa\cdot V_2=0$ and $\langle V_2\rangle_s=0$. Those geometric constraints come from the supplied transverse solutions.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The hierarchy equation theorem assembles solutions supplied by the analytic solvers.

rows.name: TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.construct_equations
rows.plain: The equations at each retained level
rows.annotation: The new term to cancel is the fast transport of $V_1$ by $B_2$. It is linear in the newly determined mean and in the known leading oscillation, so it can be added to the force for $V_2$. Although $B_2$ is phase independent, its advection of $V_1$ need not be small compared with the centered part of $H_2$: the derivative through the phase costs up to a parent power times $\lambda^{3/2}$. The recursion in Lean takes the two inverses as separate inputs.

rows.fidelity_note: For continuous coefficients along a single particle label, a transported initially nonzero covector and a continuous period-one zero-mean force, the formal theorem constructs a zero-initial periodic transverse solution with normalized phase pressure. It proves the differential equation at each phase. It does not insert the particular source containing $H_2,B_2$, or prove its smooth dependence on labels, as required for the displayed spatial field.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. Pathwise existence is supplemented by the smooth dependence on labels used for the localized wave.

rows.name: TorusEuler.exists_oscillatoryPhaseSolve_Icc
rows.plain: Solving the oscillatory equation
rows.annotation: Along a parent particle $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$. Enforcing $\partial_t(\kappa\cdot V)=0$ determines the phase pressure derivative, leaving a linear ODE for $V$ at each fixed phase. The existence theorem here is at a fixed label, for continuous periodic centered forcing; smooth dependence on the labels is established separately.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition requires $V_t+MV+\kappa\partial_s\pi=f$, transversality, zero phase mean and zero initial data, with normalized phase pressure. It therefore specifies the left side and constraints of (1.12) for a general source. It neither identifies the particular right side nor proves existence of such a solution.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The oscillatory equation conditions are realized by the transverse solver.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.TransverseSolution
rows.plain: The transverse correction problem
rows.annotation: The pressure here has a different role from the pressure of the mean equation: its phase derivative enforces $\kappa\cdot V_2=0$ in the moving transverse plane. The mean-zero condition fixes the constant of its periodic primitive separately at each time and label. These conditions specify the desired pair; the projected ODE gives it.

rows.fidelity_note: An admissible expansion requires the transverse equation with its oscillatory and supplementary sources, with $V_1=\widetilde\chi A_1$ and $C_1=0$. At level two these sources give exactly (1.12), and the transverse-solution condition includes perpendicularity, zero phase mean and zero initial data. This is part of the definition of an admissible finite expansion; its existence is a separate theorem.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.IsExpansion
rows.plain: Profile equations and support conditions for a finite expansion
rows.annotation: At level two, $Y_1=V_1$ because $C_1=0$. Consequently Equation (5.28) has precisely one term, $-(B_2\cdot\kappa)\partial_sV_1$. The expansion specification requires the transverse solution for this force plus $-(H_2-\langle H_2\rangle_s)$, rather than for the centered error alone.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition supplies only the supplementary forcing $-\sum_{i=2}^p(B_i\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY_{p+1-i}$. At $p=2$, $Y_1=V_1$ because $C_1=0$, so it becomes $-(B_2\cdot\kappa)\partial_s(\widetilde\chi A_1)$. The remaining source, differential equation and transverse constraints are not conclusions of this definition.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The supplementary source is one explicitly assembled term in the oscillatory equation.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.suppSource
rows.plain: The supplementary oscillatory source
rows.annotation: The transported phase is kept fixed by the parent: $D_t\theta=0$. In the flow with the mean added its material derivative would be $B_2\cdot\kappa$, since $\nabla_x\theta=\kappa$. Equation (1.12) compensates this change in the amplitude equation instead of rebuilding the phase for the perturbed flow.

citations.supports: Periodicity makes the fast transport by the mean have zero phase average.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Section 1.3 after equation (1.12); Section 5.5.1, supplementary source

explanation.text: The term $(B_2\cdot\kappa)\partial_s(\widetilde\chi A_1)$ represents transport of the leading fast phase by the phase-independent mean. Its phase average vanishes because $B_2\cdot\kappa$ is independent of $s$ and the integral over one period of a phase derivative is zero. This puts the term in the oscillatory equation, after the mean has already been found. The formal theorem proves exactly this cancellation for any period-one differentiable profile with continuous phase derivative and any phase-independent vectors $B,\kappa$. The same verdict concerns its zero average, not the separate estimate assigning the term to level two.

ties.name: TorusEuler.hierarchy_phaseMean_supplementary
ties.plain: The supplementary term has zero mean

rows.fidelity_note: At fixed time and label, the formal theorem proves $\int_0^1(B\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY\,ds=0$ when $B,\kappa$ are independent of phase and $Y$ is differentiable, period one, with continuous derivative. Taking $B=B_2$ and $Y=\widetilde\chi A_1$ gives the cancellation described here. The theorem does not provide the size estimate or level assignment of that source.
rows.name: TorusEuler.hierarchy_phaseMean_supplementary
rows.plain: The supplementary term has zero mean
rows.annotation: Since $B_2\cdot\kappa$ is independent of $s$, the phase average of its product with $\partial_sV_1$ is zero. Thus adding $B_2$ to remove the mean error does not change that mean error at level two. It changes only the force used in the subsequent transverse solve; the mean equation need not be solved again.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_5_3
ties.plain: Weighted transverse velocity and pressure estimates

rows.fidelity_note: The forced transverse system has a zero-start velocity profile in the plane perpendicular to the transported wave vector. Its associated pressure enforces the transverse constraint.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_5_3
rows.note: The forced transverse system has a zero-start velocity profile in the plane perpendicular to the transported wave vector. Its associated pressure enforces the transverse constraint.
rows.plain: Weighted transverse velocity and pressure estimates
rows.annotation: At fixed parent label and independent phase, differentiate $\kappa\cdot V_2=0$. Using $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$ gives $|\kappa|^2\partial_s\mathsf p_2=\kappa\cdot(f_2+f_2^S-2MV_2)$. The factor two comes from the time derivative of the moving transverse plane as well as the strain term of the momentum equation. Substituting this formula gives the forced seed ODE; the pressure is recovered as its centered phase primitive. The new $B_2$ is already known when forming $f_2^S$.

rows.note: Curl completion makes the full slow and fast divergence vanish. This supports the conclusion about the combined velocity and its correction.
rows.plain: Slow and fast divergence cancel in the curl-completed profile
rows.annotation: The ordinary divergence-of-curl identity can be used at any independent phase $s$ by replacing the local phase $\theta(y)$ by $\theta(y)-\theta(x)+s$. This changes its value at $x$ to $s$ but leaves its spatial derivatives unchanged. Applying the identity at $x$ proves solenoidality of the completed profile at $(x,s)$, before graph restriction, as required for the phase averaging in the hierarchy.

explanation.text: The divergence correction of $V_2$ is called $C_3$ and fits into the next level of the expansion. The hierarchy bounds show that the correction generated by level $p-1$ has exponent equal to the oscillatory exponent at level $p$ minus $1/3$. Thus $C_3$ is small enough to enter level three, where its errors are included in the next mean and oscillatory sources. The formal theorem states exactly this exponent identity for integer $p\ge1$. Its weaker verdict records that this arithmetic identity neither estimates the actual correction nor constructs the next pair of solutions; those tasks belong to Theorem 5.6 and the finite expansion.

ties.name: TorusEuler.hierarchy_completion_previous
ties.plain: Preceding curl correction gains one third of a frequency power

rows.fidelity_note: The formal theorem gives the correction exponent from level $p-1$ as the oscillatory exponent at level $p$ minus $1/3$. At $p=3$, this explains why the correction of $V_2$ fits into level three. It is an equality between powers assigned to estimates; it does not prove an estimate for $C_3$ or construct the next mean and oscillatory solutions.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The exponent identity records the bookkeeping used by the separate hierarchy estimates.

rows.name: TorusEuler.hierarchy_completion_previous
rows.plain: Preceding curl correction gains one third of a frequency power
rows.annotation: In Equation (3.5), $\kappa/|\kappa|^2$ contributes $\lambda^{-1}$ up to parent powers. The phase primitive and the slow curl introduce no positive power of $\lambda$. Consequently a completion is smaller than its generating oscillation by $\lambda^{-1}$, although passing from one level to the next requires only $\lambda^{-2/3}$. The extra $\lambda^{-1/3}$ is kept for the estimates of the fast interactions.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.TransverseSolution
ties.plain: The transverse correction problem

rows.fidelity_note: The formal transverse-solution definition sets the correction to zero at time zero for every label and phase.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.TransverseSolution
rows.note: The formal transverse-solution definition sets the correction to zero at time zero for every label and phase.
rows.plain: The transverse correction problem
rows.annotation: The initial condition $V_p(0)=0$ for $p\ge2$ belongs to the transverse ODE. The mean condition instead fixes the first variation of the final particle position: $\int_0^T(D_aX)^{-1}B_p\,dt=0$. A mean can therefore extend back to time zero, and has no fast phase. Exact vanishing before activation is propagated only for the oscillatory corrections, allowing convergence of derivatives before the accumulation time.

citations.supports: The final divergence correction remains in the finite approximate velocity.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Section 1.3, end of the expansion; Section 5.5.1, Proposition 5.4

explanation.text: The expansion stops at a finite depth $P$ but retains $C_{P+1}$, the divergence correction generated by the final oscillation $V_P$. Keeping this term ensures that the retained velocity remains divergence free without solving for a new $V_{P+1}$ or $B_{P+1}$. Section 5.5.1 and Proposition 5.4 assemble the resulting finite sum. Both formal sum expressions retain $\sum_{p=1}^P(V_p+C_{p+1}+B_p)$, with corrections stored at the index of their generating oscillation, and the expansion condition imposes the required correction identities. The same verdict concerns this finite truncation convention, not convergence of an infinite series or existence of the profiles.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.expansion
ties.plain: The retained finite expansion

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition retains $\sum_{p=1}^P(V_p+C_{p+1}+B_p)$, so $C_{P+1}$ is included as the correction generated by $V_P$. The sum is finite and empty at $P=0$. No convergence statement is involved.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.expansion
rows.plain: The retained finite expansion
rows.annotation: Truncating the sum by size alone would omit $C_{P+1}$, leaving the slow divergence of $V_P$ uncompensated. In the actual expansion all $P$ oscillations retain their own curl corrections, so divergence vanishes exactly at every finite depth (Proposition 5.4).

rows.fidelity_note: The formal expansion conditions impose $C_{p+1}=C[V_p]$ for $1\le p\le P$, while $V_{P+1}=B_{P+1}=0$. Thus the last divergence correction remains even though the next oscillation and mean are set to zero. These are conditions on an expansion, not a proof of its existence.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.IsExpansion
rows.plain: Profile equations and support conditions for a finite expansion
rows.annotation: The condition $C_{p+1}=C[V_p]$ is imposed for $1\le p\le P$, whereas the new mean and transverse equations are solved only for $2\le p\le P$. Thus the last operation is a curl completion, not another inverse problem.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal velocity sum stores each correction at the index of its generating oscillation. Therefore summing through stored index $P$ includes the paper's $C_{P+1}$. It defines the retained perturbation but does not yet add the parent or evaluate at the transported phase.
rows.name: TorusEuler.HierarchyProfiles.velocity
rows.plain: The finite velocity correction
rows.annotation: Each $V_p+C[V_p]$ is evaluated at $s=k_*\cdot a$, $x=X(t,a)$. On the lifted label space the compatible extension has $V(t,a+n,s+k_*\cdot n)=V(t,a,s)$ for $n\in\mathbb Z^3$, and the same holds for its completion. Evaluation on the graph is therefore periodic in $a$ even for nonintegral $k_*$. Vanishing near the cell faces gives a smooth extension, while the means are already periodic.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_5_6
ties.plain: Frequency decay at every level

rows.fidelity_note: The finite-depth estimates for the levels gain a factor λ⁻²⁄³ per level up to parent-dependent factors. The finite approximation still has a remainder.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_5_6
rows.note: The finite-depth estimates for the levels gain a factor λ⁻²⁄³ per level up to parent-dependent factors. The finite approximation still has a remainder.
rows.plain: Frequency decay at every level
rows.annotation: For wave $j$ the next parent must have residual on the scale of $\lambda_{j+1}$, rather than merely small compared with its own velocity. The schedule $\lambda_{j+1}=\lambda_j^{K_{j+1}}$ and depth $P=6K_{j+1}$ give $\lambda_j^{-2P/3}=\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$. Lemma 5.8 uses two scaled derivative orders to pass to physical $C^{1,1/2}$, losing at most the prefactor $C_{\rm step}\lambda_j^2$. The activation and truncation errors have separate bounds.

citations.supports: Frequency truncation and the estimates that control the discarded tail, the child residual and the pressure correction.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Section 1.3, Fourier cutoff; Proposition 5.11, equations (5.55)–(5.57); Appendix B

explanation.text: For a smooth periodic approximate velocity $V$, increasing the cutoff frequency $\Lambda$ reduces the truncation error when enough derivatives of $V$ are controlled. Proposition 5.11 gives $\|S_\Lambda V-V\|_{C_tC^{2,1/2}}\le C_P\varepsilon_\Lambda$, where $\varepsilon_\Lambda=\Lambda^{2-P}(1+\|V\|_{C_tC^{P,1/2}})^2$, $P\ge2$ and $\Lambda\ge1$. This is the error passed from the approximate velocity to the next truncated parent, together with the corresponding residual and pressure-Hessian errors. The formal theorem gives this same estimate for the prescribed smooth even cutoff symbol. Its exponent $2-P$ is signed integer subtraction, so decay with $\Lambda$ occurs for $P>2$; at $P=2$ this particular bound alone supplies no decay.

ties.name: TorusEuler.paperProposition511_physicalCutoff
ties.plain: Fourier truncation of the approximate Euler velocity

rows.fidelity_note: For $P\ge2$ and cutoff frequency $\Lambda\ge1$, the formal theorem bounds the $C_tC^{2,1/2}$ difference between the child and approximate velocities by $C_P\Lambda^{2-P}(1+\|V\|_{C_tC^{P,1/2}})^2$. It also controls the new residual and pressure-Hessian change. The exponent $2-P$ is an integer and is negative at $P>2$. This is the truncation error controlled by the frequency cutoff.
rows.name: TorusEuler.paperProposition511_physicalCutoff
rows.plain: Fourier truncation of the approximate Euler velocity
rows.annotation: Let $u=S_\Lambda V$ and $v_\Lambda=u-V$. In the projected momentum equation the new quadratic error is the divergence of $u\otimes u-S_\Lambda(V\otimes V)=v_\Lambda\otimes u+V\otimes v_\Lambda+(I-S_\Lambda)(V\otimes V)$. The first two terms contain the velocity tail; the last is the tail of the product. To estimate the new residual in $C^{1,1/2}$, all three tensors are estimated in $C^{2,1/2}$. This gives $C_P\Lambda^{2-P}\|V\|_{C^{P,1/2}}^2$, explaining the power and the square in Equation (5.55). The inherited contribution $\mathbb P S_\Lambda R_V$ is estimated separately.

citations.supports: Support propagation for the oscillatory part and its use away from the origin.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Section 1.3, final support paragraph; Proposition 5.4; Lemma 5.8; Proposition 8.4

explanation.text: The leading wave and higher oscillatory corrections vanish outside the image under $X$ of the cutoff’s label support. Proposition 5.4 preserves this support level by level, and Lemma 5.8 transfers it to the physical fields. This localization later allows smooth convergence on compact sets away from the origin. The formal theorem states that the oscillatory velocity is zero whenever the inverse-flow label lies outside the prescribed closed support set, or before activation, provided the leading and activation profiles vanish there. This is the same support assertion; the mean corrections and the subsequent Fourier-truncation difference need not be supported in that region.

ties.name: TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.PhysicalApproximationData.inactive

rows.fidelity_note: At depth $P\ge1$, suppose the leading profiles and their activation terms vanish before activation and outside one closed label set $S$. The formal theorem proves that the full oscillatory velocity vanishes at a point whenever its inverse-flow label is outside $S$ or the time precedes activation. It further identifies the residual there with interactions between means. The means themselves, and a later Fourier-truncation difference, need not have this support.
rows.name: TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.PhysicalApproximationData.inactive

For $|a|\le2\ell_*$ this confines the untruncated oscillation to radius $2\mathsf D\ell_*$. In Section 8 a compact set away from zero eventually misses this region for every time, while the global mean and Fourier tail are controlled separately.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_7_1
ties.plain: A common sequence of approximate Euler flows at separated frequencies

rows.fidelity_note: The lifetime conclusion of Theorem 7.1 states that activation times tend to a positive $T_\infty$ and that $T_\infty<S_i$ for every stage. Each $U_i$ is defined as a smooth approximate velocity on $[0,S_i]$.

rows.annotation: Each row represents an entire approximate velocity on $[0,S_i]$, not a successive segment of a single trajectory. Its oscillation vanishes through $t_i$, and its mean is defined from zero. The endpoints extend beyond the accumulation time, allowing the whole sequence to be compared on the same closed time interval.

citations.supports: The projection formula, pressure normalization, and its role in the projected Euler equation.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The Leray projection removes the gradient component of a periodic vector field: $\mathbb P=I-\nabla\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{div}$, with the scalar inverse Laplacian set to zero on the constant mode. This convention is used when writing the velocity equation without its pressure, including (7.5) and the limit argument. The main formal theorem gives the corresponding equality of Fourier coefficients for real $L^2$ vector fields, which is a different formulation from a pointwise classical identity. The scalar multiplier link supplies only $-2\pi i(k\cdot a)/(4\pi^2|k|^2)$ for $k\ne0$, and the remaining link proves that its value is zero at $k=0$, so both are weaker. Fixing the scalar zero mode normalizes the potential and does not remove the constant velocity mode.

ties.name: TorusEuler.periodicL2Coefficient_sub_realLeray
ties.plain: The Leray complement is a pressure gradient on the torus

rows.fidelity_note: The paper writes the spatial identity $\mathbb P=I-\nabla\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{div}$. The formal theorem proves its equality of Fourier coefficients for real $L^2$ vector fields on the unit torus. The inverse Laplacian’s constant mode is zero, so constant velocity modes are retained. The coefficient identity is the Fourier formulation of the projection, rather than a pointwise classical identity for arbitrary fields.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The Fourier description agrees with the usual Leray projection for the smooth periodic fields used in the proof.

rows.name: TorusEuler.periodicL2Coefficient_sub_realLeray
rows.plain: The Leray complement is a pressure gradient on the torus
rows.annotation: For a nonzero torus frequency $k$ and velocity coefficient $a$, the discarded coefficient is $k(k\cdot a)/|k|^2$. This is the longitudinal component, so the retained coefficient is perpendicular to $k$. At $k=0$ the discarded coefficient is zero. Lean checks this mode by mode for real $L^2$ fields by relating the real weak projection to its complex Fourier coefficients.

rows.fidelity_note: For a frequency $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ and vector coefficient $a$, the formal definition gives only the scalar multiplier $-2\pi i(k\cdot a)/(4\pi^2|k|^2)$ when $k\ne0$, with value zero at $k=0$. This is the scalar part $\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{div}$ of the paper’s projection formula. It neither constructs a spatial field nor states the full projection identity.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The Fourier description agrees with the usual Leray projection for the smooth periodic fields used in the proof.

rows.name: TorusEuler.pressureCorrectionMode
rows.plain: Fourier coefficient of the scalar pressure correction
rows.annotation: The scalar potential solves $\Delta q=\operatorname{div}v$ with zero mean. At $k\ne0$, divide the divergence coefficient $2\pi i\,k\cdot a$ by the Laplacian eigenvalue $-4\pi^2|k|^2$ to obtain the coefficient of $q$. Multiplying that scalar by $2\pi i k$ gives the gradient coefficient subtracted by the projection, with the two factors of $i$ accounting for the positive longitudinal multiplier.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal theorem proves that the scalar correction’s zero Fourier coefficient vanishes, fixing the mean of the potential. The paper additionally gives the full identity for the Leray projection. The single zero-mode statement does not establish that identity and does not remove the constant part of velocity.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The Fourier description agrees with the usual Leray projection for the smooth periodic fields used in the proof.

rows.name: TorusEuler.pressureCorrectionMode_zero
rows.plain: Zero Fourier mode of the scalar pressure correction vanishes
rows.annotation: The zero Fourier mode of the scalar potential is its spatial mean. Choosing it to be zero fixes the constant left undetermined by the Poisson equation. The gradient has zero constant mode for any such choice, so the Leray projection keeps the mean of a general velocity. The constructed velocities have zero mean by oddness.

citations.supports: The additive pressure freedom is fixed by a zero-mean convention.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The periodic Poisson equation determines the pressure up to a function of time. Setting its spatial mean to zero fixes that function. For the exact Euler solution the formal condition sets the pressure integral on the centered unit cell to zero at every time before $T_*$. The finite expansion in §5.6 also uses a sum of pressure profiles whose spatial mean can be subtracted after evaluation.

ties.name: TorusEuler.IsEulerSolution
ties.plain: A smooth periodic Euler solution

rows.fidelity_note: The formal Euler solution has mean-zero pressure on each time slice of its lifespan. This gives the stated normalization for the exact Euler pressure. The same convention is used in the paper for Poisson pressures of approximate velocities, which this declaration does not cover.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The constructed exact solution uses the normalized pressure in this declaration.

rows.name: TorusEuler.IsEulerSolution
rows.plain: A smooth periodic Euler solution
rows.annotation: The Poisson and endpoint constructions choose the free spatial constant in pressure by setting its mean to zero. The pressure assembled in Section 5.6 is specified directly by the profile sum. The linked Lean structure concerns the exact Euler solution and imposes zero integral on its centered unit cell at each time.

citations.supports: Translation equivariance of the flow and periodicity of its displacement.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The lifted flow satisfies $X(s,t,a+n)=X(s,t,a)+n$ for every integer vector $n$. Consequently its displacement $X(s,t,a)-a$ is periodic even though the lifted position map itself is not. The flow equation and periodicity of the velocity give this identity by uniqueness of trajectories, as used in Section 3.1. The formal theorem proves exactly the identity on a closed time interval for a periodic velocity with a uniform spatial Lipschitz bound and a supplied flow. Thus the verdict is same, with the paper’s smooth periodic parents furnishing the required bound on compact time intervals.

ties.name: TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.add_latticeVector
ties.plain: Integer translations of the flow

rows.fidelity_note: For a periodic velocity on a closed time interval, uniformly Lipschitz in space with one constant, and a flow satisfying its trajectory and initial conditions, the formal theorem states $X(s,t,x+n)=X(s,t,x)+n$ for every integer vector $n$ and times in the interval. Subtracting $x+n$ gives periodic lifted displacement. Smooth periodic parents on the compact time interval meet the regularity used for this convention.
rows.name: TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.add_latticeVector
rows.plain: Integer translations of the flow
rows.annotation: For $n\in\mathbb Z^3$, the curve $X(s,t,x)+n$ starts at $x+n$ and obeys the same lifted ODE, because the velocity is periodic. Uniform spatial Lipschitz control gives uniqueness on the time slab, so this curve is $X(s,t,x+n)$. Subtracting its own starting point shows why $X(s,t,x)-x$ is periodic and descends as a vector field on the torus.

citations.supports: The index convention for gradients and rowwise divergence, and the narrower linked scalar divergence.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The paper takes $(\nabla U)_{ij}=\partial_jU_i$ and $(\operatorname{div}A)_i=\sum_j\partial_jA_{ij}$, so the divergence of a matrix is taken row by row. These conventions fix the order of indices in convection, rank-one products and the projected momentum equation. The linked formal expression supplies only the scalar divergence of a vector field, $\operatorname{div}v=\sum_i\partial_iv_i$. It is compatible with the trace of the stated gradient convention but does not define either all gradient entries or rowwise matrix divergence, which explains the weaker verdict. Its derivative expression has a default value at nondifferentiable points, so the classical interpretation uses the separate differentiability assumptions.

ties.name: TorusEuler.divergence
ties.plain: Divergence of a vector field

rows.fidelity_note: The paper specifies the full gradient convention and rowwise divergence of a matrix field. The linked definition gives only $\operatorname{div}v=\sum_i\partial_i v_i$ for a differentiable vector field. It is compatible with the diagonal trace convention, but does not itself define all matrix-gradient entries or rowwise matrix divergence. At nondifferentiable points the derivative expression is assigned zero, so classical use requires the separate regularity assumptions.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The construction uses the classical divergence of smooth fields in the stated coordinate convention.

rows.name: TorusEuler.divergence
rows.plain: Divergence of a vector field
rows.annotation: Column $j$ of $\nabla U$ is the derivative in direction $e_j$. Lean takes the $j$th component of each such derivative and sums over $j$, giving the trace. Applying the vector formula to row $i$ of a matrix gives $(\operatorname{div}A)_i=\sum_j\partial_j A_{ij}$. In particular, the product rule gives $\operatorname{div}(U\otimes U)=(U\cdot\nabla)U$ for a divergence-free field.

citations.supports: The purpose of the frequency, order and amplification choices.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Section 1.5; Proposition 2.8; Theorem 7.1, equation (7.4); Section 8 opening

explanation.text: The schedule makes the errors summable while allowing each new wave to start at a small fraction of its later amplitude. Section 1.5 chooses increasing frequencies and slowly increasing derivative orders; Proposition 2.8 supplies the gain, and Theorem 7.1 gives oscillations and remaining increments bounded by $\lambda_j^{-1}$ in the retained norms. Section 8 then uses the convergent sum of these bounds to obtain the limiting velocity and its spatial derivatives on compact time intervals before the accumulation time. The formal existence theorem constructs a sequence with those quantitative bounds, while the other link merely specifies them for a given sequence. Both links are weaker than the full explanatory sentence because the summability deductions and attribution of errors to individual construction steps require the accompanying schedule and convergence arguments.

ties.name: TorusEuler.paperTheorem71
ties.plain: Existence of a common sequence of approximate Euler stages

rows.fidelity_note: The formal theorem constructs a scheduled sequence with residual bounds, localized oscillations of size at most $\lambda_j^{-1}$, and corrections bounded by $\lambda_j^{-1}$ through the retained orders. Fast growth of frequencies and increasing retained orders give the summability used in the introduction. Those summability deductions are not stated explicitly in this theorem, and it does not separately attribute the estimates to every individual truncation term.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. Choosing one successful construction is sufficient for the existential main theorem.

rows.name: TorusEuler.paperTheorem71
rows.plain: Existence of a common sequence of approximate Euler stages
rows.annotation: The cutoff $\Lambda_j$ supplies the derivative bounds when $U_j$ is used as a parent. The look-ahead in the order test has a different purpose: step $j$ will use depth $6K(q_{j+1})$ to make its residual small at $\lambda_{j+1}$. Hence the costs at that depth must already fit the preceding frequency $\lambda_{j-1}$ (Equation (7.8)).

rows.fidelity_note: For a given sequence, the formal conditions impose small oscillations and spatial Hölder corrections on the whole stage interval, and vanishing of later oscillations through activation. They quantify the effects described in the paper, but are assumptions on a construction rather than a proof that a chosen frequency schedule realizes them or that the resulting series converges.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The listed sequence properties are supplied by the construction theorem.

rows.name: TorusEuler.PaperTheorem71Conclusions
rows.plain: Uniform bounds and central-wave estimates along the stages
rows.annotation: The two estimates on an increment serve different purposes. The oscillation is summable in velocity, and can have a large gradient; the remaining increment is summable through order $q_j$. At time zero all oscillations except the first are absent, so the second estimate gives convergence of the initial data in every fixed derivative norm.

citations.supports: The logarithmic floor controls the gain losses in the frequency schedule.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The threshold must satisfy $\log\mathcal B(s)\ge4K(s+1)^3$ for every positive integer $s$. Appendix C uses this floor to ensure that the logarithmic gains remain below small powers of the preceding frequencies despite increasing derivative orders. It is therefore a quantitative restriction on when the schedule can increase its order. For the explicit threshold, the formal theorem obtains the same inequality from its exponential lower bound and proves it also at $s=0$, explaining the stronger verdict. The formal admissibility condition simply imposes the paper’s inequality for $s\ge1$ together with positivity, giving a same link without proving it for an arbitrary threshold.

ties.name: TorusEuler.fixedOrderThreshold_log_floor
ties.plain: The threshold’s logarithmic floor

rows.fidelity_note: For the explicitly chosen threshold, the formal theorem gives $\log\mathcal B(s)\ge4K(s+1)^3$ for every nonnegative integer $s$ and $b$. The paper uses $s\ge1$ and $b\ge1$. Positivity follows from the exponential term in that particular threshold, so no extension convention for the logarithm is involved.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The selected threshold dominates the actual analytic costs used by the construction.

rows.name: TorusEuler.fixedOrderThreshold_log_floor
rows.plain: The threshold’s logarithmic floor
rows.annotation: The future gain $L_{j+1}$ contains $\log\lambda_{j+2}=K_{j+2}K_{j+1}K_j\log\lambda_{j-1}$. We know the threshold test at $s=q_{j+1}$, not at $q_{j+2}$. The floor with $K(s+1)^3$ bounds all three exponents, even if the order increases once more.

rows.fidelity_note: The admissibility condition imposes exactly the floor (1.13) at every positive integer $s$, with a separate requirement $\mathcal B(s)>0$. It records a hypothesis on the chosen threshold; it does not prove that an arbitrary function satisfies it.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.AdmissibleThreshold
rows.plain: Admissible threshold functions
rows.annotation: The lower bound on $\mathcal B$ is imposed independently of the analytic costs. It gives $4K_{j+2}K_{j+1}K_j\le\log\mathcal B(q_{j+1})\le\log\lambda_{j-1}$. Thus the next gain is bounded by the square of a logarithm at the present parent scale.

citations.supports: The coupled schedule and the distinct roles of its frequency, cutoff, gain and ratio components.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The schedule couples $\lambda_j=\lambda_{j-1}^{K(q_j)}$ to $q_{j+1}=\max\{1\le s\le q_j+1:\mathcal B(s)\le\lambda_{j-1}\}$, with $\lambda_0=N$ and $q_1=1$. It then sets $\Lambda_j=\lambda_j^5$, $L_j=4\log\lambda_{j+1}$ and $\varepsilon_{j-1}=L_j^{-2}$, linking Fourier truncation, amplification and derivative control. The formal existence theorem constructs the frequency and order sequences for $b\ge1$, $N\ge1$ and $\mathcal B(1)\le N$, while the formal parameter condition records those recurrences and the threshold floor without constructing them. The other two links define only $L_j$ and the shifted ratio $\varepsilon_j=L_{j+1}^{-2}$, so each link is weaker than the complete display. The ratio is assigned zero if the gain is zero, but the paper’s positive frequency and threshold assumptions exclude that case.

ties.name: TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_exists
ties.plain: Existence of the frequency and derivative-order schedule

rows.fidelity_note: The formal theorem constructs $q_j,\lambda_j$ satisfying $q_1=1$, $\lambda_0=N$, the frequency recurrence and the maximum rule, assuming $b\ge1$, $N\ge1$ and $\mathcal B(1)\le N$. It does not define $\Lambda_j,L_j,\varepsilon_j$ or prove their bounds. These are separate parts of the displayed schedule.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The schedule existence and its quantitative properties are established in separate steps.

rows.name: TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_exists
rows.plain: Existence of the frequency and derivative-order schedule
rows.annotation: Given $q_j$ and $\lambda_{j-1}$, the first recurrence determines $\lambda_j$ and the maximum rule determines $q_{j+1}$. Iterating these two operations gives the whole frequency and order sequence; $\Lambda_j$, $L_j$ and $\varepsilon_j$ can then be read from it. In particular prescribing the target coupling ratio for each crossing requires no information about when the crossing will occur.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal parameter conditions record $q_1=1$, the recurrence and maximum rule, positivity and the logarithmic threshold floor. They do not contain the entire display: the cutoff frequencies, logarithmic gains and coupling ratios are defined elsewhere. They also omit threshold monotonicity and cost domination, and assert no existence by themselves.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The schedule existence and its quantitative properties are established in separate steps.

rows.name: TorusEuler.InductiveEulerParameters
rows.plain: Parameters for the common sequence
rows.annotation: The exponent of $\lambda_{j-1}$ uses $q_j$, but the expansion depth uses $q_{j+1}$. Thus the test for $q_{j+1}$ must use the same parent scale $\lambda_{j-1}$. In `InductiveEulerParameters` the corresponding index is $i=j-1$, and the tested order is $q_{i+2}$.

rows.fidelity_note: This formal definition gives exactly $L_j=4\log\lambda_{j+1}$ for a supplied real frequency sequence. It defines only the gain part of (1.14), not the recurrence or maximum rule. Under the paper’s frequencies $\lambda_j>1$, the gains are positive.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. Positive schedule frequencies make the gain and small ratio have their intended values.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Schedule.L
rows.plain: Prescribed logarithmic gain
rows.annotation: The gain parameter is the inverse square root of the ratio inherited from wave $j-1$. With the peak of wave $j$ fixed, the relative amplitude during its switch is bounded by $e^{3-L_j}$. Taking $L_j=4\log\lambda_{j+1}$ makes this $e^3\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$, which is the scale of the expansion remainder chosen in Section 7.

rows.fidelity_note: This formal definition gives $\varepsilon_j=L_{j+1}^{-2}$, which is (1.14) after shifting the index. It also assigns a value at the unused index zero and assigns zero if the gain is zero. The paper uses positive gains and $j\ge1$. The other parts of the schedule are not stated here.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. Positive schedule frequencies make the gain and small ratio have their intended values.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Schedule.ε
rows.plain: The prescribed successor ratio
rows.annotation: A small ratio reached by wave $j$ is an input to the growth problem for wave $j+1$, not a measure of the amplitude of wave $j$ at that time. The choice $\varepsilon_j=L_{j+1}^{-2}$ fixes the exponential factor $e^{-L_{j+1}}=\lambda_{j+2}^{-4}$ needed when wave $j+1$ is switched on (see Equation (7.10) for the switch-on estimate).

citations.supports: Monotone unit-step order growth, divergence of the orders, and the logarithmic estimate.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The maximum rule gives $q_j\le q_{j+1}\le q_j+1$, and the increasing frequencies eventually make every fixed order admissible, so $q_j\to\infty$. Lemma 1.3 and Appendix C prove this for $b\ge1$, $K(s)=320b(s+1)$, $q_1=1$, $\lambda_0\ge\mathcal B(1)$, the frequency recurrence, and positive thresholds with $\log\mathcal B(s)\ge4K(s+1)^3$. The slow but unbounded increase supplies every fixed derivative order while limiting the gain losses. All four formal links state or prove these arithmetic conclusions and additionally give $4\log\lambda_{j+2}\le(\log\lambda_{j-1})^2$ for $j\ge1$. Their stronger verdict records that monotonicity of the threshold and its domination of analytic constants are unnecessary for these arithmetic conclusions.

ties.name: TorusEuler.paperLemma13_slowOrders
ties.plain: Slow derivative-order growth under the frequency schedule

rows.fidelity_note: Let $b\ge1$ be an integer and $K(s)=320b(s+1)$. Assume $\mathcal B(s)>0$ and $\log\mathcal B(s)\ge4K(s+1)^3$ for $s\ge1$, $q_1=1$, $\lambda_0\ge\mathcal B(1)$, $\lambda_j=\lambda_{j-1}^{K(q_j)}$, and $q_{j+1}=\max\{1\le s\le q_j+1:\mathcal B(s)\le\lambda_{j-1}\}$ for $j\ge1$. The formal statement proves $q_j\le q_{j+1}\le q_j+1$, $q_j\to\infty$, and $4\log\lambda_{j+2}\le(\log\lambda_{j-1})^2$ for $j\ge1$. Since $L_i=4\log\lambda_{i+1}$, the last inequality is exactly (1.15). Threshold monotonicity and domination of the analytic constants, required by the paper's full parameter choice, are unnecessary for these arithmetic conclusions.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The arithmetic lemma proves the required schedule conclusions under fewer hypotheses.

rows.name: TorusEuler.paperLemma13_slowOrders
rows.plain: Slow derivative-order growth under the frequency schedule

explanation.text: For an affine velocity $u(t,x)=D(t)x$ on $\mathbb R^3$, zero trace gives incompressibility and symmetry of $D'+D^2$ makes the acceleration the gradient of the quadratic function $x\cdot(D'+D^2)x/2$. These are the background hypotheses in Lemma 2.1, which allow a transverse wave to be added with an explicit pressure. The linked formal statements retain both algebraic conditions and require the first time derivative of $D$ on an interval, with derivatives taken from within the interval at endpoints. Their stronger verdict concerns the relaxation from smooth to differentiable backgrounds; the wave equations and the conditions on the profile remain separate hypotheses.

rows.fidelity_note: Let $J$ be a time interval on which relative derivatives are uniquely determined. Suppose $D$ is differentiable, $\operatorname{tr}D=0$, $D'+D^2$ is symmetric, and $k'=-D^Tk$, $\mathbf a'=-D\mathbf a+p_{\rm w}k$, where $p_{\rm w}=2k\cdot D\mathbf a/|k|^2$. For differentiable $F$ and any $P$ with $P'=F$, transverse data give an Euler velocity $u=Dx+\mathbf aF(k\cdot x)$ on $\mathbb R^3$, with pressure $-x\cdot(D'+D^2)x/2-p_{\rm w}P(k\cdot x)$ and zero divergence. Nonzero perpendicular data at any $t_0\in J$ remain so throughout $J$, including earlier times. Unlike the paper, the formal statement requires neither a smooth odd periodic profile nor its normalization; the Euler identity also allows $k=0$, using zero for division by zero. The interval derivative includes one-sided endpoint derivatives. The paper states nonzero perpendicularity for $t\ge t_0$ in the interval of existence. The formal statement gives the same properties for every $t$ in the same interval, including $t<t_0$, assuming the wave equations, initial nonzero perpendicular data, and the stated background regularity. It makes no claim outside that interval.

These are chain-rule calculations in the proof of Lemma 2.1 and are what prevents spatial oscillation from producing an uncancelled transport term. The linked formal statement assumes the phase equation and transversality, then gives the combined acceleration of $u=Dx+w$ as $(D'+D^2)x+(\mathbf a'+D\mathbf a)F(k\cdot x)$. For $u=Dx+\mathbf aF(k\cdot x)$, the formal identity is $\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=(D'+D^2)x+(\mathbf a'+D\mathbf a)F(k\cdot x)$. This is the acceleration calculation in Lemma 2.1. It does not yet impose the amplitude equation, trace zero or symmetry of $D'+D^2$; those hypotheses are needed subsequently for the pressure cancellation and incompressibility. The paper separately asserts transport of $k\cdot x$ and of $w$ by $Dx$. The formal acceleration identity uses $k'=-D^Tk$ and gives their combined consequence for $u=Dx+w$, namely $(D'+D^2)x+(\mathbf a'+D\mathbf a)F$. rows.annotation: First solve the particle equation for the affine strain $U(x)=(x_1,-x_2,0)$. Along a particle, $x_2(t)=e^{-t}x_2(0)$, so $k(t)=e^t e_2$ keeps $k(t)\cdot x(t)$ constant. Choose amplitude $e_3$ and check that the wave velocity dotted with the phase gradient is zero. These are the two cancellations that let the paper study a single wave by ordinary differential equations before localizing it. Along $x'=Dx$, the phase has two contributions to its derivative, $k'\cdot x$ from the moving normal and $k\cdot Dx$ from the moving point. The transpose in $k'=-D^Tk$ cancels them. Thus the background carries each level of the phase along unchanged, leaving only the time derivative of the amplitude in the transported wave.

The chain rule gives the first equality, and transversality gives the second, as in Lemma 2.1. This exact cancellation is why a single transverse profile can be added without generating a quadratic self-interaction. The formal statement assumes only differentiability of $F$ at the phase in question and perpendicularity, and concludes zero directly. Its weaker verdict records the omission of the intermediate expression, rather than an additional physical restriction.

The statement gives the zero conclusion directly, while the paper also displays the intermediate expression $(k\cdot\mathbf a)FF'\mathbf a$. Under $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$ and differentiability of $F$ at $k\cdot x$, the formal statement proves the final equality $(w\cdot\nabla)w=0$. rows.fidelity_note: Let nonzero perpendicular paths $k,\mathbf a\in\mathbb R^3$ satisfy $k'=-B^Tk$ and $\mathbf a'=-B\mathbf a+2(k\cdot B\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$ on a time set $J$, with $\operatorname{tr}B=0$. Put $E_1=k/|k|$, $E_2=\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$, $E_3=E_1\times E_2$, $B_{ij}=E_i\cdot BE_j$ and $\sigma=|k||\mathbf a|$. The formal statement gives orthonormality and $E_1'=-B_{12}E_2-B_{13}E_3$, $E_2'=B_{12}E_1-B_{32}E_3$, $E_3'=B_{13}E_1+B_{32}E_2$, $(\log\sigma)'=B_{33}$. Derivatives are relative to $J$. These are (2.2), with no regularity assumption on $B$ beyond the supplied wave derivatives and no symmetry assumption on $B'+B^2$. All normalizations and the logarithm have nonzero positive denominators or arguments under the stated hypotheses. For nonzero transverse solutions of the wave equations, the formal statement assumes $\operatorname{tr}B=0$ and no symmetry of $B'+B^2$. In fact it does not require a time derivative of $B$ at all; the supplied derivatives of $k$ and $\mathbf a$ suffice for the frame calculation.

Trace zero enters only when the two logarithmic length rates are added and $-B_{11}-B_{22}$ is rewritten as $B_{33}$. Thus the prescribed gradient $B(t)$ and the wave data at $t$ suffice for the frame calculation used in the prescribed-matrix system of Section 2.2.

rows.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.frame
rows.plain: The moving orthonormal frame
rows.annotation: With $F'(0)=1$, the wave adds $k\times\mathbf a=|k|\,|\mathbf a|E_3$ to the curl at the origin. The order of the cross product therefore gives the direction of the wave's vorticity. When the successor normal is launched along $E_3$, its transverse amplitudes lie in the plane spanned by $E_1$ and $E_2$.

citations.supports: The meaning and ordering of the entries of the background matrix.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: In the orthonormal wave frame $E_1,E_2,E_3$, the scalar $B_{ij}=E_i\cdot BE_j$ is the component of $BE_j$ in the direction $E_i$. This convention in Lemma 2.2 determines which entries drive the frame motion, particularly $\nu=B_{12}$ and $\eta=B_{32}$. The formal statement uses the same Euclidean scalar product, with its three ordered positions corresponding to the paper's indices $1,2,3$. The same verdict concerns the formula; orthonormality is supplied by the nonzero perpendicular wave data, rather than asserted by the formula itself.

ties.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.entry
ties.plain: Entries in the wave frame

rows.fidelity_note: The formal entry is the Euclidean scalar product $E_i\cdot BE_j$. Its first, second and third positions correspond to the paper’s indices $1,2,3$. Orthonormality is not imposed by the definition; it is supplied by the wave-frame hypotheses when these scalar products are read as matrix entries.
rows.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.entry
rows.plain: Entries in the wave frame
rows.annotation: To read $B_{ij}$, apply $B$ to the input direction $E_j$ and take the output component along $E_i$. For example, the added shear $\sigma E_2\otimes E_1$ has its only nonzero entry at $(2,1)$ because it sends $E_1$ to $\sigma E_2$. This fixes which entry changes when the preceding wave is added to the older gradient in Section 2.2.1.

citations.supports: Wave strength and the two coupling entries.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For a nonzero transverse wave, $\sigma=|k||\mathbf a|$ measures the size of its rank-one velocity gradient, while $\nu=E_1\cdot BE_2$ and $\eta=E_3\cdot BE_2$ are the two indicated entries of the older gradient. Lemma 2.2 introduces these quantities so that the frame equations and the strength equation can be read directly in terms of the couplings. The linked formal frame statement uses these same scalar products and differentiates $\log(|k||\mathbf a|)$ under the wave equations and $\operatorname{tr}B=0$. The same verdict concerns the identification of the quantities; their positivity, except for the automatically positive strength, is not asserted at this stage.

ties.name: TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_movingFrame
ties.plain: Moving-frame derivative formulas for perpendicular wave data

rows.fidelity_note: At a time in a set $J$, assume $k,\mathbf a\in\mathbb R^3$ are nonzero and perpendicular, $\operatorname{tr}B=0$, and the relative derivatives satisfy $k'=-B^Tk$, $\mathbf a'=-B\mathbf a+2(k\cdot B\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$. Define $E_1=k/|k|$, $E_2=\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$, $E_3=E_1\times E_2$ and $B_{ij}=E_i\cdot BE_j$. The formal statement gives $E_1'=-B_{12}E_2-B_{13}E_3$, $E_2'=B_{12}E_1-B_{32}E_3$, $E_3'=B_{13}E_1+B_{32}E_2$ and $(\log(|k||\mathbf a|))'=B_{33}$. It is the pointwise calculation underlying (2.2); it assumes no time derivative of $B$ and no affine Euler compatibility. The separate logarithmic derivatives of $|k|$ and $|\mathbf a|$ are not conclusions of this declaration. The formal frame identity uses $\nu=E_1\cdot BE_2$, $\eta=E_3\cdot BE_2$ and the logarithm of $|k||\mathbf a|$, so the three quantities agree with the paper. Nonzero perpendicular data justify the normalized axes and make the strength positive.
rows.name: TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_movingFrame
rows.plain: Moving-frame derivative formulas for perpendicular wave data
rows.annotation: Dividing the pressure term $p_{\rm w}k$ in Equation (2.1) by $|\mathbf a|$ gives $2\nu E_1$. Thus $B_{12}$ contributes both through $-B\mathbf a$ and through pressure, while the $E_3$ component of $-B\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$ is $-\eta$. These two components turn the amplitude direction in the frame identities below.

citations.supports: Evolution of the wave frame and logarithmic strength.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For nonzero perpendicular solutions of (2.1) over a trace-free background $B$, the frame obeys $E_1'=-B_{12}E_2-B_{13}E_3$, $E_2'=B_{12}E_1-B_{32}E_3$, $E_3'=B_{13}E_1+B_{32}E_2$ and $(\log\sigma)'=B_{33}$. Lemma 2.2 obtains the first three identities by differentiating unit vectors and the cross product, and the last by adding the two logarithmic length derivatives. These formulas make the rotation of the preceding frame part of the next-wave calculation. The linked formal statements prove all four identities and orthonormality, with derivatives taken relative to the time set. Their stronger verdict reflects that smoothness of $B$ is unnecessary once the wave derivatives and zero trace are supplied.

ties.plain: Wave frame evolves with the flow

rows.fidelity_note: Let nonzero perpendicular paths $k,\mathbf a\in\mathbb R^3$ satisfy $k'=-B^Tk$ and $\mathbf a'=-B\mathbf a+2(k\cdot B\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$ on a time set $J$, with $\operatorname{tr}B=0$. Put $E_1=k/|k|$, $E_2=\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$, $E_3=E_1\times E_2$, $B_{ij}=E_i\cdot BE_j$ and $\sigma=|k||\mathbf a|$. These are (2.2), with no regularity assumption on $B$ beyond the supplied wave derivatives and no symmetry assumption on $B'+B^2$. All normalizations and the logarithm have nonzero positive denominators or arguments under the stated hypotheses. The formal statement gives all four identities in (2.2), and explicitly proves orthonormality. It assumes nonzero perpendicular wave data and zero trace, with derivatives relative to the time set, but does not require the smoothness of $B$ assumed in the paper. No symmetry of $B'+B^2$ is needed.
