rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_2
rows.plain: Evolution of the moving wave frame and strength
rows.annotation: At launch of the successor, put $k_+=\lambda E_3$ and take $E_c=0$. The added shear $\sigma_p E_2\otimes E_1$ annihilates $E_2$, so the wave equation gives $k_+'\cdot E_2=-\lambda B_{32}$. The moving frame contributes another $k_+\cdot E_2'=-\lambda B_{32}$. Multiplying the sum by $S/(\lambda r)$ gives $\zeta_2'=-2Sb_{32}$ at launch, the value of the term $-2Sb_{32}\zeta_3$ when $\zeta_3=1$.

citations.supports: Differentiation of normalization and logarithmic length.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Lemma 2.2, first formulas in the proof

explanation.text: For a differentiable nonzero vector $v$, differentiating $\widehat v=v/|v|$ gives $\widehat v'=(I-\widehat v\widehat v^T)v'/|v|$, while differentiating the positive length gives $(\log|v|)'=\widehat v\cdot v'/|v|$. Lemma 2.2 applies these identities to the wave vector and amplitude to separate changes of direction from changes of magnitude. The two linked formal statements write $v'=|v|w$ and prove, respectively, $\widehat v'=w-(\widehat v\cdot w)\widehat v$ and $(\log|v|)'=\widehat v\cdot w$. Each weaker verdict records that one link supplies only one of the two identities; both allow any real inner-product space and derivatives within a time set.

ties.name: TorusEuler.normalizeDerivOfScaled
ties.plain: Derivative of a unit vector

rows.fidelity_note: The paper displays both the unit-vector and logarithmic-norm derivatives. This formal statement gives the first: when $v\ne0$ and $v'=|v|w$, it proves $(v/|v|)'=w-((v/|v|)\cdot w)(v/|v|)$. Taking $w=v'/|v|$ gives the paper’s formula; the logarithmic derivative is supplied by the other link.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The two general differentiation rules specialize to the moving-frame calculation.

rows.name: TorusEuler.normalizeDerivOfScaled
rows.plain: Derivative of a unit vector
rows.annotation: Differentiate $v/|v|$ by writing it as $|v|^{-1}v$. The derivative of $v$ contributes $v'/|v|$ and that of the inverse norm subtracts $\widehat v(\widehat v\cdot v'/|v|)$. Only the component tangent to the unit sphere remains, as is needed for the derivatives of both unit axes.

rows.fidelity_note: This formal statement supplies the second displayed identity: for $v\ne0$ and $v'=|v|w$, it gives $(\log|v|)'=(v/|v|)\cdot w$. It does not state the unit-vector derivative. Both statements permit any real inner-product space and relative time derivatives.

rows.name: TorusEuler.logNormDerivOfScaled
rows.plain: Logarithmic derivative of the norm
rows.annotation: The scalar $\widehat v\cdot v'$ is the rate of change of $|v|$. Dividing by $|v|$ gives the fractional rate of change, whose integral along a smooth nonzero path is $\log(|v(t)|/|v(t_0)|)$. The same radial component that is subtracted in the unit-vector equation enters the change of length here.

explanation.text: For a nonzero wave vector satisfying $k'=-B^Tk$ in the transverse frame, differentiation of $E_1=k/|k|$ gives $E_1'=-B_{12}E_2-B_{13}E_3$, and its length satisfies $(\log|k|)'=-B_{11}$. explanation.text: For the model background with only $B_{12}=\nu>0$ and $B_{32}=\eta>0$ nonzero and $E_c=0$, the scaled amplitude equations approach (2.5) as $S\to\infty$, with $\varepsilon=\eta/\nu$ and the normalized interval $[0,T]$ fixed. Lemma 2.3 derives the finite-shear equations in the moving frame and proves uniform convergence of their coefficients after the scaled wave vector approaches $(\varepsilon\tau^2/2,-\varepsilon\tau,1)$. This supplies the explicit reference equation used in the perturbative analysis. The formal statements include the finite-shear equations, eventual nonvanishing of the third wave component and uniform convergence, and allow more general observation sets and background regularity, explaining the stronger verdict. The limiting statement concerns coefficients on a fixed interval, not uniform behavior as $T$ also tends to infinity.

explanation.text: The new wave sees $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p+E_c$, where the rank-one term acts by $v\mapsto(k_p\cdot v)\mathbf a_p$. Since $E_1=k_p/|k_p|$, $E_2=\mathbf a_p/|\mathbf a_p|$ and $\sigma_p=|k_p||\mathbf a_p|$, this term equals $\sigma_pE_2\otimes E_1$. This is the decomposition in §2.2.1 that separates the older gradient, preceding shear and remaining errors. The formal gradient gives only the first expression, whereas the other identity gives the normalized rank-one equality after division by the nonzero rate $r$ and with the base time shifted to activation. The weaker and different verdicts distinguish these two partial statements from the whole display; neither asserts that an arbitrary $M$ is a global Euler velocity gradient.

rows.fidelity_note: For a frame $(E_1,E_2,E_3)$ and an amplitude $\mathbf a(t)$, the formal coordinate is $E_2(t)\cdot\mathbf a(t)$. In (2.3) this is $\alpha_2$; it is not multiplied by the shear scale $S$. The definition imposes no equation, transversality or nonvanishing condition. Those assumptions enter the amplitude estimates separately. Together with the formal first coordinate $-S E_1\cdot\mathbf a=-\alpha_1$, it gives the pair $(-\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$ used in the intermediate calculations, rather than the pair displayed in the paper. This formal coordinate is $E_2\cdot\mathbf a=\alpha_2$, with no scaling by $S$. It gives only the second amplitude component of the two displayed expansions.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The coordinate definitions and reconstruction identities recover the same physical vectors.

rows.name: TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.V
rows.plain: Second amplitude component
rows.annotation: The unscaled amplitude coordinate is $V=\alpha_2$. For the chosen launch, Lemma 2.6 proves $V>0$ and bounds $|\alpha_1|/V$ and $|\alpha_3|/V$. Since $|\mathbf a|/V=\sqrt{1+S^{-2}[(\alpha_1/V)^2+(\alpha_3/V)^2]}$, those bounds compare the physical length with this single component. Positivity is needed before using that quotient.

citations.supports: The scaled initial condition obtained from launch in the third direction.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The launch condition $k(t_0)=\lambda E_3(t_0)$ makes the scaled wave coordinates at normalized time zero equal to $\zeta(0)=(0,0,1)$. Taking scalar products with the orthonormal frame in (2.3) gives the first two zeros and the last unit value. This initial value selects the explicit reference vector used in Lemma 2.3. The formal identity requires only orthonormality at activation, $\lambda\ne0$ and the launch equality, so its stronger verdict reflects the absence of the wave equation and the absence of a positivity requirement for $\lambda$ or $S$.

ties.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.coordinate_initial_values
ties.plain: Initial scaled wave vector

rows.fidelity_note: At the activation time $t_0$, assume an orthonormal frame, a nonzero frequency $\lambda$ and the initial wave vector $k(t_0)=\lambda E_3(t_0)$. The formal statement gives $\zeta_1(t_0)=0$, $\zeta_2(t_0)=0$, $\zeta_3(t_0)=1$, where $\zeta=(E_1\cdot k,SE_2\cdot k,E_3\cdot k)/\lambda$. Under $\tau=r(t-t_0)$ these are precisely $\zeta(0)=(0,0,1)$ after (2.3). The identity does not require $\lambda>0$, any restriction on $S$, or the wave equation. Positivity of the frequency belongs to the later amplification setting. The paper obtains $\zeta(0)=(0,0,1)$ for the launched wave. The formal identity only requires an orthonormal frame at $t_0$, nonzero $\lambda$ and $k(t_0)=\lambda E_3(t_0)$; neither $\lambda>0$ nor the wave equation nor positive $S$ is needed. Its base time is $t_0$, corresponding to $\tau=0$.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The coordinate definitions and reconstruction identities recover the same physical vectors.

rows.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.coordinate_initial_values
rows.plain: Initial scaled wave vector
rows.annotation: The initial value $\zeta=(0,0,1)$ is independent of $S$ and $\lambda$. Thus the difference of the finite and reference normal equations has zero initial data. All of its subsequent error comes from the coefficient differences.

citations.supports: The wave-vector norm factor and its role as a pressure denominator.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: §2.2.1, weighted wave-vector length after equation (2.3); Lemma 2.4

explanation.text: Orthonormality in (2.3) gives $|k|^2=\lambda^2m$, where $m=\zeta_1^2+\zeta_2^2/S^2+\zeta_3^2$. The factor $m$ is a weighted squared length of the scaled coordinates, not their ordinary Euclidean squared norm. It becomes the denominator of the reduced pressure coefficient in Lemma 2.3. The formal formula for $m$ is weaker because it only supplies that expression, while the linked norm identity proves the equality for nonzero $\lambda,S$ and an orthonormal frame. Although the standalone formula assigns zero to the middle quotient when $S=0$, the amplification hypotheses have $S>0$ and later give $m\ge1/4$.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.scaledNormSq
ties.plain: The weighted wave-vector norm

rows.fidelity_note: For a real scale $S$ and vector $\zeta\in\mathbb R^3$, the formal expression is $m=\zeta_1^2+\zeta_2^2/S^2+\zeta_3^2$. When $S\ne0$ and $k=\lambda(\zeta_1E_1+\zeta_2E_2/S+\zeta_3E_3)$ in an orthonormal frame, it satisfies $|k|^2=\lambda^2m$. This is the factor after (2.3), not the ordinary Euclidean squared norm of $\zeta$. The definition also permits $S=0$: division by zero is assigned zero, so the middle term vanishes. To use $m$ as a nonzero pressure denominator, the amplitude equations impose positive $S$ and nonzero $\zeta_3$. The formal definition gives $m=\zeta_1^2+\zeta_2^2/S^2+\zeta_3^2$, but does not state $|k|^2=\lambda^2m$. That equality additionally uses the scaled coordinates and orthonormal frame. At $S=0$, the definition assigns zero to its middle quotient.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The weighted coordinate norm equals the physical wave norm after the prescribed scaling.

rows.plain: The weighted wave-vector norm
rows.annotation: At reference inputs the squared frequency factor is $m_0=1+x^2=\cos^{-2}\varphi$, where $x=\tan\varphi$. It is not $|\zeta_0|^2=1+x^2+\varepsilon^2\tau^2$: the last term here comes from the magnified middle component and is suppressed by $S^{-2}$ in $m$. This is the length that enters the denominator of pressure.

rows.fidelity_note: Let $(E_1,E_2,E_3)$ be orthonormal at a fixed time and let $\lambda,S\ne0$. With $\zeta_1=(E_1\cdot k)/\lambda$, $\zeta_2=S(E_2\cdot k)/\lambda$ and $\zeta_3=(E_3\cdot k)/\lambda$, the formal statement proves $|k|^2=\lambda^2(\zeta_1^2+\zeta_2^2/S^2+\zeta_3^2)$. Here $|k|$ is the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^3$. This is the identity following (2.3). It is valid for arbitrary $k$, including $k=0$, and needs no wave equation or smallness assumption; the nonzero scale hypotheses justify the coordinate divisions. For an orthonormal frame and nonzero $\lambda,S$, the formal identity proves exactly $|k|^2=\lambda^2m$ with the displayed $m$. It is pointwise algebra and requires no wave equation.

rows.annotation: The denominator $m$ is positive whenever $k\ne0$, but the two-coordinate amplitude equation also requires $\zeta_3\ne0$. The latter condition concerns the chart, not the normal itself. Lemma 2.4 proves $\zeta_3\ge1/2$ on the comparison interval, and hence $m\ge1/4$ as well.

explanation.text: Transversality in (2.3) is $\zeta_1\alpha_1+\zeta_2\alpha_2+\zeta_3\alpha_3=0$, so $\zeta_3\ne0$ allows $\alpha_3=-(\zeta_1\alpha_1+\zeta_2\alpha_2)/\zeta_3$. This eliminates one component and reduces the amplitude equation to the two coordinates $\alpha_1,\alpha_2$. The formal statement reconstructs the entire transverse vector from the signed pair $(-\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$, assuming orthonormality and nonzero $\lambda,S,\zeta_3$. Its third physical projection is $-(\zeta_1\alpha_1+\zeta_2\alpha_2)/(S\zeta_3)$, so multiplication by $S$ gives the paper's formula. The different verdict concerns this reconstruction and coordinate convention, not a different transversality condition.

citations.supports: The reference angle, its branch and the explicit limiting coordinates.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Equation (2.4) and the paragraph introducing Lemma 2.3

explanation.text: For $\varepsilon\ge0$, the angle $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$ lies in $[0,\pi/2)$ and defines $\zeta_0=(\tan\varphi,-\varepsilon\tau,1)$. Equation (2.4) identifies the explicit limiting wave vector in scaled coordinates and the angle of its physical limiting direction from $E_3$ toward $E_1$. The linked formal expressions separately give the arctangent, the three-component vector and the scalar $\varepsilon\tau^2/2$, while two further statements prove the angle range and tangent identity. Each weaker verdict means that the link supplies only one part of the display. The tangent identity holds for all real inputs, but the asserted nonnegative angle range uses $\varepsilon\ge0$.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.referenceAngle
ties.plain: The reference turning angle

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition selects $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$ for all real inputs. It fixes the branch but does not itself assert the displayed range or define $\zeta_0$; those are the other linked statements.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The explicit arctangent branch and coordinate formula give the reference geometry.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.referenceAngle
rows.plain: The reference turning angle
rows.annotation: In the reference limit the normal direction is $\sin\varphi E_1+\cos\varphi E_3$ and the wave number is $\lambda/\cos\varphi$. An order-one turn occurs at $\tau\asymp\varepsilon^{-1/2}$, while the reference amplitude peak has $\cos\varphi\asymp\varepsilon$ and $\tau\asymp\varepsilon^{-1}$. Thus a large gain, a nearly complete turn, and a prescribed successor crossing are different events.

rows.fidelity_note: This definition gives only $\zeta_0=(\tan\varphi,-\varepsilon\tau,1)$ with the arctangent reference angle. The tangent identity and range in (2.4) are separate conclusions.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The explicit arctangent branch and coordinate formula give the reference geometry.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.zetaRef
rows.plain: The limiting scaled wave vector
rows.annotation: At finite shear the projected slope is $\zeta_1/\zeta_3$, not $\zeta_1$. With $x=\tan\varphi$ and $\zeta_3\ge1/2$, its error from $x$ is at most $2(|\zeta_1-x|+x|\zeta_3-1|)$. Thus even the projected slope has a polynomial comparison error; the actual normal also has the out-of-plane component $\lambda\zeta_2/S$.

rows.fidelity_note: This formal statement proves the range $0\le\varphi<\pi/2$ for $\varepsilon\ge0$. It does not state the tangent identity or define the three-component reference vector.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The explicit arctangent branch and coordinate formula give the reference geometry.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.referenceAngle_mem
rows.plain: Range of the reference angle
rows.annotation: The choice $0\le\varphi<\pi/2$ gives $\cos\varphi>0$ on every finite interval. More quantitatively $\cos\varphi\ge T^{-2}$ on $[0,T]$ under $\varepsilon\le1$ and $T\ge2$. The same lower bound controls division by $\cos\varphi$ in Equation (2.15) and converts the additive error in the third coupling into an error relative to its small reference value.

rows.fidelity_note: This formal statement proves $\tan\varphi=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$ for every real $\varepsilon,\tau$. It does not assert the nonnegative angle range, which requires $\varepsilon\ge0$, or the vector formula.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The explicit arctangent branch and coordinate formula give the reference geometry.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.tan_referenceAngle
rows.plain: Tangent of the reference angle
rows.annotation: Writing $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$, the branch choice gives $\cos^2\varphi=1/(1+x^2)$ and $\sin2\varphi=2x/(1+x^2)$. Thus the trigonometric coefficients of the reference equation can be expressed as rational functions of $x$; this is how the lower-level calculations use the tangent identity.

rows.fidelity_note: This formal scalar is $\varepsilon\tau^2/2$, the first coordinate of the reference vector after using the tangent identity. It does not define the angle, prove its range or define the other two coordinates.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The explicit arctangent branch and coordinate formula give the reference geometry.

rows.name: TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.x
rows.plain: The tangent of the reference angle
rows.annotation: Since $x=\tan\varphi=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$, a late cosine of order $\varepsilon_+$ requires $x\asymp\varepsilon_+^{-1}$ and hence $\tau\asymp(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}$. In particular the target ratio influences the required comparison horizon of the present wave even though it determines the gain of its successor.

rows.note: At fixed ε and T the scaled components converge uniformly, and the physical E₂ component has the additional factor 1/S.
rows.plain: Strong-shear limit for the wave vector and amplitude
rows.annotation: The exact finite-shear model displayed just below gives $k_3/\lambda=\cos(\varepsilon\tau/(\sqrt2 S))$ and $k_1/\lambda=((2S^2+1)/\varepsilon)(1-k_3/\lambda)$. Expanding the cosine with $\varepsilon,T$ fixed gives $k_1/\lambda\to\varepsilon\tau^2/2$, explaining the reference slope in Equation (2.4). The small middle component cannot simply be omitted in the equations: it is multiplied by the large preceding shear.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_4

rows.plain: Additive error bounds for the wave and amplitude equations
rows.annotation: The slope of the actual projected normal is $\zeta_1/\zeta_3$. Its difference from $x=\tan\varphi$ is $(\zeta_1-x+x(1-\zeta_3))/\zeta_3$, controlled polynomially by Lemma 2.4. For the full direction one must also retain $\zeta_2/S$. In particular the positive third coordinate, divided by the actual length, is the factor by which the preceding vorticity survives projection onto the new normal in Section 8.

explanation.text: The model assumes that throughout $[0,T]$ the moving-frame entries satisfy $B_{12}=\nu$, $B_{32}=\eta$ and all other entries vanish, while $E_c=0$. These are the hypotheses under which Lemma 2.3 computes the finite-shear system and its strong-shear limit. Constancy here is in the rotating preceding frame and does not mean that $B$ is constant in fixed spatial coordinates. The formal model condition imposes exactly these time-dependent requirements after $t=t_0+\tau/r$, giving the same verdict. The separate formal matrix only records the two entries, so its weaker verdict reflects the absence of an actual time-dependent background and the condition on $E_c$.

rows.fidelity_note: Let $\varepsilon\in\mathbb R$, $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$, $s=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}=\cos\varphi$ and $\varphi=\arctan x$. Suppose $Y'=s^2(1-\varepsilon x)-2\varepsilon\tau x s^2Y-Y^2$ on $[0,\infty)$. Define $V(\tau)=\exp\int_0^\tau Y$ and $U(\tau)=Y(\tau)V(\tau)$. The formal statement proves $V'=U$ and $U'=s^2(1-\varepsilon x)V-2\varepsilon\tau x s^2U$ for every $\tau\ge0$, with right derivatives at zero. These are (2.5) in the coordinates $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)=(-U,V)$. No condition $Y(0)=1$ is assumed. The reconstruction always has $V(0)=1$, while the paper’s initial pair $(-1,1)$ additionally requires $Y(0)=1$. Values at negative times are not constrained by the differential-equation hypothesis. Given a solution $Y$ of the Riccati equation on $[0,\infty)$, the formal statement proves that $U=Ya_{\rm ref}$ and $V=a_{\rm ref}$ solve the sign-adjusted linear system. Thus $(-U,V)$ solves (2.5). The premise $Y(0)=1$ from (2.12) gives the paper’s initial pair $(-1,1)$, although this derivative theorem does not require that initial value.

rows.annotation: Given the scalar solution $Y$, let $V=a_{\rm ref}$ and $U=YV$. Then $V'=U$ and $U'=(Y'+Y^2)V=cV-dU$, with $c$ the driving and $d$ the damping coefficient in Equation (2.5). The quadratic term has canceled, so this is the signed linear system. The reconstruction uses the Riccati equation; the additional condition $Y(0)=1$ selects the reference initial pair.

rows.fidelity_note: For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, let $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$ and consider $Y'=\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)Y-Y^2$, $Y(0)=1$, on $[0,\infty)$. There is a unique solution on that half-line, with $|Y|\le1$ and $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/4$ for one function $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$. Its amplitude $a_{\rm ref}=\exp\int_0^\tau Y$ equals $\sqrt{\cos\varphi}\exp\int_0^\tau(1+e)\cos\varphi$. It has its global maximum at the unique zero $\tau_m$ of $Y$, with $2\le\varepsilon\tau_m\le3$, positive $Y$ before and negative $Y$ after, and $\log a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)\ge\varepsilon^{-1/2}-1$. This declaration specifies the complete assertion of Lemma 2.5; a separate theorem proves it. The functions are defined on all real times, but the equation, bounds and uniqueness concern only $\tau\ge0$, with a right derivative at zero. Both statements assume $0<\varepsilon\le1$ for the global reference-solution assertion. The half-line is $\tau\ge0$; no negative-time existence is claimed.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal inequality is $x/(1+x^2)\le1/2$ for $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$ and arbitrary real $\varepsilon,\tau$. With $\varphi=\arctan x$, it is exactly $\sin\varphi\cos\varphi\le1/2$. It does not require the positive-parameter and nonnegative-time restrictions of the reference solution.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The elementary trigonometric bound holds in particular for the positive reference parameters.

rows.name: TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.x_mul_s_sq_le_half
rows.plain: The reference sine times cosine is at most one half
rows.annotation: The forcing in the parentheses is $(\varepsilon/2)x/(1+x^2)$ with $x=\tan\varphi$. It is at most $\varepsilon/4$, with equality at $x=1$. At $e=\varepsilon/8$ the linear term $-2e$ alone balances this upper bound, and the term $-e^2$ has the favorable sign.

citations.supports: Bounded correction existence and the subsequent reconstruction of the Riccati solution.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Lemma 2.5, global construction through the invariant correction interval

explanation.text: For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, the correction equation with $e(0)=0$ has a solution on $[0,\infty)$ remaining in $[0,\varepsilon/8]$. The endpoint signs of its vector field prevent escape, and boundedness permits continuation, as used in Lemma 2.5. Substituting this function into (2.13) then constructs the global Riccati solution needed for the reference amplitude. The auxiliary formal existence result supplies the correction, its equation and its bounds only, so its weaker verdict leaves the reconstruction of $Y$ to another step. The full numbered theorem includes that reconstruction and the bounded deviation together, giving the same verdict for the complete sentence.

ties.name: TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.deviation_exists_Ici
ties.plain: Global bounded deviation in the reference Riccati equation

rows.fidelity_note: For $0<\varepsilon\le1$ and $\varphi(\tau)=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$, the formal statement constructs a real function $e$ with $e(0)=0$, $e'=\cos\varphi[-2e-e^2+(\varepsilon/2)\sin\varphi\cos\varphi]$ on $[0,\infty)$, and $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$ there. Derivatives at zero are taken from the right. The function is defined at negative times too, but the equation and bound impose no conditions there. This is existence with an invariant interval for the deviation; uniqueness and the corresponding Riccati solution $Y$ are not conclusions of this declaration. For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, the formal statement constructs $e$ on $[0,\infty)$ with $e(0)=0$, its stated differential equation, and $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$. It does not itself construct $Y$; that requires substitution in the ansatz and the separate theorem deriving the Riccati equation.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The transformed equation and initial value construct the bounded reference deviation together.

rows.name: TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.deviation_exists_Ici
rows.plain: Global bounded deviation in the reference Riccati equation
rows.annotation: At $e=0$ the derivative is nonnegative, while at $e=\varepsilon/8$ it is strictly negative for $\varepsilon>0$ and finite $\tau$. The solution remains in this bounded interval. On every finite interval the coefficient is continuous and the vector field is locally Lipschitz in $e$, so there can be no finite-time obstruction to continuation.

rows.fidelity_note: For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, let $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$ and consider $Y'=\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)Y-Y^2$, $Y(0)=1$, on $[0,\infty)$. There is a unique solution on that half-line, with $|Y|\le1$ and $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/4$ for one function $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$. Its amplitude $a_{\rm ref}=\exp\int_0^\tau Y$ equals $\sqrt{\cos\varphi}\exp\int_0^\tau(1+e)\cos\varphi$. It has its global maximum at the unique zero $\tau_m$ of $Y$, with $2\le\varepsilon\tau_m\le3$, positive $Y$ before and negative $Y$ after, and $\log a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)\ge\varepsilon^{-1/2}-1$. The formal statement proves the whole assertion of Lemma 2.5, including uniqueness for all $\tau\ge0$. The functions have values at negative times as well, but neither the equation nor uniqueness constrains those values. At zero, the derivative is taken from within the half-line. The full formal theorem constructs the global Riccati solution and its bounded deviation together, retaining the asserted range $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$ for every nonnegative time.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_5
rows.plain: The global reference solution
rows.annotation: Solve the equation for $e$ first and define $Y$ by Equation (2.13). Then $a_{\rm ref}=\exp(\int_0^\tau Y)$ is positive, and direct substitution shows that $(-Ya_{\rm ref},a_{\rm ref})$ solves Equation (2.5) with the required data. This order avoids assuming that the second component of the reference solution never vanishes in order to derive a global equation for its quotient.

citations.supports: The bound on the reference growth rate and its domain.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Lemma 2.5, upper barrier for the reference slope

explanation.text: For the solution of (2.12) with $0<\varepsilon\le1$ and $Y(0)=1$, the inequality $Y'\le1-Y^2$ wherever $Y\ge0$ prevents $Y$ from crossing above one. Lemma 2.5 uses this scalar barrier to bound the early reference growth rate. The formal result assumes a solution already defined on $[0,\infty)$ and proves $|Y(\tau)|\le1$ for every nonnegative time. Its stronger verdict therefore adds a lower bound to the quoted upper bound. It does not by itself establish global existence, which is obtained through the correction equation.

ties.name: TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.riccati_abs_le_one
ties.plain: Uniform bound for the reference slope

rows.fidelity_note: Let $0<\varepsilon\le1$ and suppose $Y(0)=1$ and $Y$ solves $Y'=\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)Y-Y^2$ for all $\tau\ge0$, with $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$. Then $|Y(\tau)|\le1$ throughout that half-line. The formal statement is a bound for any solution already defined there; it does not itself prove existence. It supplies both signs of the absolute bound in Lemma 2.5, whereas the paper’s particular proof sentence $Y\le1$ concerns only the upper bound. For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, a global solution of (2.12) with $Y(0)=1$ satisfies $|Y|\le1$. The paper uses only $Y\le1$ in this sentence, so the formal result also supplies the lower bound $Y\ge-1$. It presupposes existence on the half-line.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The reference existence theorem supplies the hypotheses of the sign and gain estimates.

rows.name: TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.riccati_abs_le_one
rows.plain: Uniform bound for the reference slope
rows.annotation: To bound the positive part of $Y$, the equation at $Y\ge1$ gives $Y'\le1-Y^2\le0$. On the negative side Equation (2.13) gives $Y\ge-\min\{\varepsilon\tau/4,1/\tau\}\ge-\sqrt\varepsilon/2$. The paper needs only the resulting uniform bound $|Y|\le1$, which will also bound the entries of the coordinate change after the peak.

citations.supports: The pointwise sign argument at the lower turning scale.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Lemma 2.5, positivity before the turning time

explanation.text: For the reference representation $Y=\cos\varphi(1+e-\varepsilon\tau\sin\varphi/2)$ with $e\ge0$, the condition $\varepsilon\tau\le2$ makes $Y>0$. The strict inequality follows from $\cos\varphi>0$ and $\sin\varphi<1$ on the chosen arctangent branch. This supplies the lower side of the turning-time interval in Lemma 2.5. The formal statement proves positivity of the same expression under only $\varepsilon\ge0$, $\varepsilon\tau\le2$ and $e(\tau)\ge0$, even allowing negative time. Its stronger verdict concerns that algebraic generality and does not extend the reference differential equation to negative times.

ties.name: TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceY_pos
ties.plain: Reference slope is positive through 2/ε

rows.fidelity_note: Assume $\varepsilon\ge0$, $\varepsilon\tau\le2$, and $e(\tau)\ge0$. For $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$, the formal statement proves $(1+e(\tau))\cos\varphi-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/4>0$. Applied to the deviation of the reference Riccati solution for $\tau\ge0$, this is the positive sign before the reference peak in Lemma 2.5. The algebraic statement itself also permits negative $\tau$ and $\varepsilon=0$ and needs no differential equation or upper bound on $e$. Its extra domain does not extend the Riccati existence theorem to negative time. The formal statement proves positivity of the ansatz whenever $\varepsilon\ge0$, $\varepsilon\tau\le2$ and $e(\tau)\ge0$. It does not need the Riccati equation or $\varepsilon\le1$, and it permits negative $\tau$. Restricting to the reference solution on $\tau\ge0$ gives the paper’s claim.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The reference existence theorem supplies the hypotheses of the sign and gain estimates.

rows.name: TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceY_pos
rows.plain: Reference slope is positive through 2/ε
rows.annotation: The sign of the driving coefficient and the sign of $Y$ need not change at the same time: at $\tau=\sqrt2/\varepsilon$, the first term of Equation (2.12) vanishes but $Y>0$. By then the remaining effective growth time $\int_{\sqrt2/\varepsilon}^{\infty}\cos\varphi\,d\tau$ is at most $\sqrt2$. The large exponential gain has already occurred; the balance of this remaining gain with the decreasing cosine determines the peak.

citations.supports: The strict sine bound needed at the endpoint of the positive regime.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Lemma 2.5, strict positivity argument before the turning time

explanation.text: The angle $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$ has strictly positive cosine and satisfies $\sin\varphi<1$. In the proof of Lemma 2.5, the strict upper bound on the sine keeps $1+e-\varepsilon\tau\sin\varphi/2$ positive when $e\ge0$ and $\varepsilon\tau\le2$. The formal inequality is $x/\sqrt{1+x^2}<1$ with $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$. It holds for every real $x$, so its stronger verdict reflects the absence of the positive-parameter and nonnegative-time restrictions used for the reference solution.

ties.name: TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.x_mul_s_lt_one
ties.plain: Reference sine is below one

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement proves $x/\sqrt{1+x^2}<1$ for $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$ with arbitrary real parameters. Substituting $\varphi=\arctan x$ gives the paper’s strict inequality, with no need for its positive-parameter restrictions.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The elementary trigonometric bound holds in particular for the positive reference parameters.

rows.name: TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.x_mul_s_lt_one
rows.plain: Reference sine is below one
rows.annotation: For finite $x=\tan\varphi$, $1-\sin^2\varphi=(1+x^2)^{-1}>0$. The strictness, rather than just $\sin\varphi\le1$, rules out a zero at the lower endpoint $\varepsilon\tau=2$.

citations.supports: The pointwise negative sign at normalized time 3/ε.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Lemma 2.5, negativity at the upper turning scale

explanation.text: At $\varepsilon\tau=3$ with $0<\varepsilon\le1$, one has $\tan\varphi=9/(2\varepsilon)\ge9/2$, hence $\sin\varphi>3/4$. Since $e\le\varepsilon/8\le1/8$, the bracket $1+e-\varepsilon\tau\sin\varphi/2$ is then negative, giving $Y<0$. This is the upper-side sign used in Lemma 2.5 to locate a zero between the scales $2/\varepsilon$ and $3/\varepsilon$. The formal pointwise statement concludes negativity of the ansatz under these parameter and correction bounds, without needing a differential equation. Its weaker verdict records that the intermediate tangent and sine inequalities appear in the argument but are not separate conclusions.

ties.name: TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceY_neg_at_three
ties.plain: Reference slope is negative at 3/ε

rows.fidelity_note: Let $0<\varepsilon\le1$ and $\varepsilon\tau=3$. Suppose $e(\tau)\le\varepsilon/8$ and set $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$, $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/4$. The formal statement proves $Y(\tau)<0$. No differential equation or lower bound on $e$ is needed for this pointwise sign calculation. This gives the upper sign in the proof that the reference amplitude peaks between $2/\varepsilon$ and $3/\varepsilon$; existence and uniqueness of that peak require the later Riccati argument. Under $0<\varepsilon\le1$, $\varepsilon\tau=3$ and $e(\tau)\le\varepsilon/8$, the formal result states only that the ansatz for $Y$ is negative. It does not separately assert the intermediate tangent and sine estimates in the quoted sentence. Those estimates occur in its proof, not its conclusion.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The reference existence theorem supplies the hypotheses of the sign and gain estimates.

rows.name: TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceY_neg_at_three
rows.plain: Reference slope is negative at 3/ε
rows.annotation: At $\tau=3/\varepsilon$, one has $\tan\varphi=9/(2\varepsilon)\ge9/2$, hence $\sin\varphi>3/4$. The subtracted term in $Y/\cos\varphi$ is then $>9/8$, while $1+e\le9/8$. This gives the other strict endpoint sign without an asymptotic estimate.

citations.supports: Opposite endpoint signs and strictly downward crossings imply a unique zero.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Lemma 2.5, uniqueness of the turning time in the proof

explanation.text: For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, a global Riccati solution with the bounded representation (2.13) is positive through the lower turning scale and negative at the upper one. At any zero with $\varepsilon\tau\ge2$, equation (2.12) gives $Y'=\cos^2\varphi(1-(\varepsilon\tau)^2/2)<0$, so every zero is a downward crossing. Lemma 2.5 concludes that there is exactly one nonnegative zero, lying in $[2/\varepsilon,3/\varepsilon]$, with the stated signs on either side. The formal turning-time result assumes the global equation and the bounded-deviation representation, then supplies that interval and both strict sign assertions. This is the same conclusion; the existence of the global solution itself has already been established separately.

ties.name: TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.riccati_turning_time
ties.plain: The unique reference turning time

rows.fidelity_note: Let $0<\varepsilon\le1$, $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$ and $s=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}=\cos(\arctan x)$. Suppose $Y'=s^2(1-\varepsilon x)-2\varepsilon\tau x s^2Y-Y^2$ on $[0,\infty)$ and $Y=s(1+e)-\varepsilon\tau x s^2/2$, with $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$ there. The formal statement supplies $\tau_m\in[2/\varepsilon,3/\varepsilon]$ such that $Y(\tau_m)=0$, $Y>0$ on $[0,\tau_m)$, and $Y<0$ on $(\tau_m,\infty)$. Consequently this is the unique nonnegative zero. The global solution and its representation are hypotheses; this statement does not construct them or prove an amplitude bound. It does not separately require $Y(0)=1$. Derivatives at zero are taken from within the half-line. Given the global Riccati equation and the bounded-deviation representation, the formal statement gives a zero in $[2/\varepsilon,3/\varepsilon]$, strict positivity before it on $[0,\tau_m)$ and strict negativity afterwards. Those signs imply the claimed unique zero on $[0,\infty)$.
rows.name: TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.riccati_turning_time
rows.plain: The unique reference turning time
rows.annotation: All zeros must occur with $\varepsilon\tau>2$, where the differential equation at $Y=0$ gives $Y'<0$. At every zero the function therefore crosses from positive to negative values. Together with the opposite signs at $2/\varepsilon$ and $3/\varepsilon$, this proves existence, uniqueness and the signs on the two sides.

citations.supports: Integration before the peak gives the lower bound on logarithmic amplification.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Lemma 2.5, final gain calculation in the proof

explanation.text: On $0\le\tau\le\sqrt{2/\varepsilon}$, one has $\tan\varphi\le1$ and $\cos\varphi\ge1/\sqrt2$, and this interval ends before $\tau_m\ge2/\varepsilon$. Using $e\ge0$ in (2.14) and the reference amplitude's increase up to its peak gives the displayed logarithmic gain chain in Lemma 2.5. The formal estimate assumes continuity, the bounded-deviation representation, $Y\ge0$ up to $\tau_m$ and $\tau_m\ge2/\varepsilon$, then proves $\int_0^{\tau_m}Y\ge1/\sqrt\varepsilon-1$. This equals the final bound for $\log a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)$ by the exponential definition. Its weaker verdict reflects that the intermediate time and inequalities are not separately conclusions, and it does not require $\tau_m$ to be the unique zero.

ties.name: TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.riccati_gain_bound
ties.plain: Logarithmic bound for the reference amplitude gain

rows.fidelity_note: Let $0<\varepsilon\le1$ and $\tau_m\ge2/\varepsilon$. Suppose $Y$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$, nonnegative on $[0,\tau_m]$, and has the form $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/4$, with $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$ and $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$. The formal statement gives $\int_0^{\tau_m}Y\ge1/\sqrt\varepsilon-1$. Since $a_{\rm ref}=\exp\int_0^\tau Y$, this is $\log a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)\ge\varepsilon^{-1/2}-1$. The theorem assumes the sign and representation and does not require that $\tau_m$ be the unique zero. It records the final gain, rather than the intermediate inequalities in the paper’s proof. The paper displays a chain through the time $\sqrt{2/\varepsilon}$. The formal statement concludes only $\int_0^{\tau_m}Y\ge1/\sqrt\varepsilon-1$, assuming the bounded-deviation representation, continuity, $\tau_m\ge2/\varepsilon$ and $Y\ge0$ up to $\tau_m$. This equals the final logarithmic gain because $a_{\rm ref}=\exp\int Y$; the intermediate inequalities are not conclusions.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The reference existence theorem supplies the hypotheses of the sign and gain estimates.

rows.name: TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.riccati_gain_bound
rows.plain: Logarithmic bound for the reference amplitude gain
rows.annotation: At $b=\sqrt{2/\varepsilon}$, $\tan\varphi(b)=1$. The integral in $\log a_{\rm ref}(b)$ is at least $b/\sqrt2=\varepsilon^{-1/2}$, since $e\ge0$, and the logarithm of the prefactor is $-\tfrac14\log2$. The maximum is no smaller than this value.

citations.supports: The normalized coordinates that separate amplitude size from ratio error.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For a solution of the reference amplitude equation, (2.15) defines $h=\alpha_2/a_{\rm ref}$ and $l=-(\alpha_1+Y\alpha_2)/(a_{\rm ref}\cos\varphi)$. Dividing by $a_{\rm ref}$ removes the common growth, while $l$ measures the deviation from the reference component ratio. The formal pair is $(V/a_{\rm ref},(U-YV)/(a_{\rm ref}s))$ with $U=-\alpha_1$, $V=\alpha_2$ and $s=\cos\varphi$, so it agrees exactly. Both denominators are positive for the reference solution; the formal pair uses the maximum norm rather than the Euclidean norm. The same verdict concerns the coordinate definition, which alone supplies neither evolution nor regularity for arbitrary choices of the input functions.

ties.name: TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.normalizedState
ties.plain: Normalized amplitude and signed deviation from the reference slope

rows.fidelity_note: For real functions $Y,U,V$, let $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$ and $s(t)=(1+\varepsilon^2t^4/4)^{-1/2}$. The formal object is $(V/a_{\rm ref},(U-YV)/(s a_{\rm ref}))$. With $U=-\alpha_1$, $V=\alpha_2$ and $s=\cos\varphi$, it is exactly $(h,l)$ from (2.15). Both denominators are strictly positive. Real pairs carry the maximum norm, so a bound on the norm of this pair is a bound on both components. The definition does not assume a reference or perturbed differential equation; such equations enter the comparison theorems. The formal integral is assigned zero when $Y$ is not integrable, so $a_{\rm ref}=1$ at such an input; no derivative formula follows there. The formal pair is $(V/a_{\rm ref},(U-YV)/(a_{\rm ref}s))$ with $U=-\alpha_1$, $V=\alpha_2$ and $s=(1+\varepsilon^2\tau^4/4)^{-1/2}=\cos\varphi$. Thus both coordinates agree with (2.15). The pair carries the maximum norm; the definition imposes no differential equation.
rows.name: TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.normalizedState
rows.plain: Normalized amplitude and signed deviation from the reference slope
rows.annotation: For a solution of the reference system, the second equation of (2.5) gives $l=(dh/d\tau)/\cos\varphi$. In the time $d\xi=\cos\varphi\,d\tau$, the coordinates are therefore $h$ and $dh/d\xi$. Neither is singular at the peak, where $Y=0$ but $a_{\rm ref}$ and $\cos\varphi$ are still positive.

citations.supports: The first normalized equation and its role in the triangular system.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For $h=\alpha_2/a_{\rm ref}$, the identities $\alpha_2'=-\alpha_1$ and $a_{\rm ref}'=Ya_{\rm ref}$ yield $h'=-(\alpha_1+Y\alpha_2)/a_{\rm ref}=l\cos\varphi$. This calculation following (2.15) is the first row of the normalized triangular system. It shows that departure in the amplitude size is driven only by the ratio-error coordinate. The formal statement assumes the reference linear equations and the Riccati equation and derives both $h'=l\cos\varphi$ and $l'=-2(1+e)l\cos\varphi$ within the closed interval. Its stronger verdict reflects that second derivative conclusion; no positivity bound on $e$ is needed for these identities.

ties.name: TorusEuler.ReferencePropagator.hasDerivWithinAt_normalized
ties.plain: The triangular normalized system

rows.fidelity_note: Put $x=\varepsilon t^2/2$, $s=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}=\cos\varphi$, $\varphi=\arctan x$, and $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$. Suppose $Y'=s^2(1-\varepsilon x)-2\varepsilon t x s^2Y-Y^2$ on $[0,T]$. Set $e=(Y+\varepsilon t x s^2/2)/s-1$, $h=V/a_{\rm ref}$ and $l=(U-YV)/(sa_{\rm ref})$. At $t\in[0,T]$, suppose $U'=-2\varepsilon t x s^2U+s^2(1-\varepsilon x)V$ and $V'=U$. The formal statement proves $h'=sl$ and $l'=-2s(1+e)l$ at that time, with derivatives taken within $[0,T]$. This is the triangular system (2.16), since $(U,V)=(-\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$. The identity requires neither $Y(0)=1$ nor positivity or smallness of $e$. The chosen arctangent makes $s>0$ for every real parameter and time, and $a_{\rm ref}>0$, so both divisions in the normalized coordinates are legitimate. Assuming the reference amplitude equations and the Riccati equation, the formal statement gives both $h\prime=l\cos\varphi$ and $l\prime=-2(1+e)l\cos\varphi$ on the closed time interval. The paper sentence states only the first derivative. Endpoint derivatives are taken within the interval.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The triangular equations, their solution formula and positivity together yield the propagator bound.

rows.name: TorusEuler.ReferencePropagator.hasDerivWithinAt_normalized
rows.plain: The triangular normalized system
rows.annotation: Differentiating $\alpha_2/a_{\rm ref}$ uses $\alpha_2'=-\alpha_1$ and $a_{\rm ref}'=Ya_{\rm ref}$. The two terms combine to $(-\alpha_1-Y\alpha_2)/a_{\rm ref}=l\cos\varphi$. The reference growth disappears from the equation for $h$.

citations.supports: The explicit normalized decay formula and its arbitrary-starting-time extension.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The second normalized equation integrates to $l(\tau)=l(0)\exp(-2\int_0^\tau(1+e)\cos\varphi)$ for the reference coefficients. The paper derives the same expression using Liouville's formula and (2.14), thereby exposing the decay that remains after the common amplitude growth has been removed. The formal statement applies to any continuous coefficients $s,e$ and solutions of $h'=sl$, $l'=-2s(1+e)l$ on $[a,b]$. It gives the formula for $l$ from any starting time $a$ and also the corresponding integrated formula for $h$. Its stronger verdict reflects that generality, while decay follows from the nonnegative $s$ and $e$ supplied by the reference solution.

ties.name: TorusEuler.ReferencePropagator.triangular_propagator_formula
ties.plain: Solution formula for the triangular reference system

rows.fidelity_note: Let $s,e$ be continuous on $[a,b]$, and let $h,l$ satisfy $h\prime=sl$, $l'=-2s(1+e)l$ there. For $t\in[a,b]$, set $d(a,t)=\exp(-\int_a^t2s(1+e))$ and $q(a,t)=\int_a^t s(u)d(a,u)\,du$. The formal statement gives $l(t)=d(a,t)l(a)$ and $h(t)=h(a)+q(a,t)l(a)$. The result uses derivatives within the closed interval and permits coefficients of either sign. Decay and contraction require the separate nonnegativity hypotheses used later. With $s=\cos\varphi$, this is the solution formula behind (2.16). For arbitrary continuous coefficients $s,e$ and solutions of $h\prime=sl$, $l\prime=-2s(1+e)l$, the formal statement gives the propagation formulas from any starting time $a$. Choosing $a=0$ and $s=\cos\varphi$ gives the displayed identity for $l$. It also gives the corresponding formula for $h$, and requires no sign assumptions on the coefficients.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The triangular equations, their solution formula and positivity together yield the propagator bound.

rows.name: TorusEuler.ReferencePropagator.triangular_propagator_formula
rows.plain: Solution formula for the triangular reference system
rows.annotation: Liouville gives $a_{\rm ref}^2l\cos\varphi$ proportional to $\cos^2\varphi$. On substituting Equation (2.14), this says that $(a_{\rm ref}/\sqrt{\cos\varphi})^2l$ is constant. In the effective time $d\xi=\cos\varphi\,d\tau$, this is the constant Wronskian of $f=a_{\rm ref}/\sqrt{\cos\varphi}$ and $\alpha_2/\sqrt{\cos\varphi}$. In particular $l$ decays like the inverse square of the growing factor $f$.

rows.plain: The triangular normalized system

explanation.text: For the triangular reference system with $s=\cos\varphi>0$ and $e\ge0$, the equation $l'=-2s(1+e)l$ makes $|l|$ nonincreasing in forward time. explanation.text: The contraction of $|h|+|l|$ implies a bound of two for the Euclidean propagator of (2.16), uniformly for $0\le\tau_1\le\tau_2$. explanation.text: For nonzero $k,\mathbf a$, the coupling $\nu_+=(k/|k|)\cdot M(\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|)$ gives $p_{\rm w}=2k\cdot M\mathbf a/|k|^2=2\nu_+|\mathbf a|/|k|$. Section 2.2.4 uses this equality to turn the positive first coupling into the pressure sign needed later in §5.1. The first formal formula contains an additional scalar cutoff, so setting that cutoff to one recovers only the first coefficient expression. The other formal identity rewrites the rank-one tensor $-p_{\rm w}k\otimes k$ with the same cutoff, rather than asserting the scalar equality directly. Its different verdict and the first link's weaker verdict require that specialization and the nonzero normalizations; neither link alone proves the coupling or pressure coefficient positive.

ties.name: TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient

rows.fidelity_note: For a real scalar $c$, phase gradient $\kappa$, amplitude $\mathbf a$ and linear map $M$ on $\mathbb R^3$, the formal expression is $2c(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2$. In the localized wave, $c=\widetilde\chi(t)g(a)$ is the product of the time cutoff and spatial envelope. At the central label $a=0$, the condition $g(0)=1$ gives $c=\widetilde\chi(t)$; it equals one only when the time cutoff equals one. The definition permits arbitrary real $c$ and imposes no evolution equation or sign condition. Division by zero is assigned zero, so the expression is zero at $\kappa=0$. For a nonzero phase gradient its sign depends on both $c$ and $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a$. The formal definition is $2\chi\,k\cdot M\mathbf a/|k|^2$ with an additional scalar cutoff $\chi$. Setting $\chi=1$ gives the first formula in the paper. The definition does not state the equality with $2\nu_+|\mathbf a|/|k|$; that also uses the new-frame definition and nonzero vectors.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. Setting the cutoff to one and using the new frame gives the scalar pressure relation.

explanation.text: For the nonzero transverse new wave, $E_{1,+}=k/|k|$, $E_{2,+}=\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$ and $E_{3,+}=E_{1,+}\times E_{2,+}$ form its oriented orthonormal frame. Lemma 2.7 expresses the full parent gradient in this frame because these entries will drive the successor wave. The linked formal triple uses exactly the same Euclidean normalization and cross product. Its same verdict applies under nonzero perpendicular data; the formula also assigns zero to a normalized zero vector, but such input would not give the required frame and is excluded in the wave application.

explanation.text: The two new couplings are $\nu_+=E_{1,+}\cdot ME_{2,+}$ and $\eta_+=E_{3,+}\cdot ME_{2,+}$ for the nonzero transverse wave and full gradient $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p+E_c$. This repeats the moving-frame convention of Lemma 2.2 with the new wave in the preceding wave's role. Lemma 2.7 estimates their signs and ratio so that the next wave can be activated with a prescribed coupling ratio. The two formal formulas separately give these scalar products, so each weaker verdict records one half of the display rather than a positivity conclusion. They also accept zero vectors by normalization to zero, whereas their orthonormal-frame interpretation requires the nonzero transverse hypotheses.

citations.supports: Propagation of wave and amplitude errors into the two coupling errors.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Lemma 2.7, physical coupling perturbation estimate after the reference bounds

explanation.text: The physical coupling formulas differ from their reference values by at most $CT^p\delta$ after the wave-vector, amplitude-ratio and normalized-gradient errors have all been inserted. Lemma 2.7 proves this by estimating finite polynomial numerators, using $\zeta_3\ge1/2$ and lower bounds for the denominator factors, then adding the $E_c$ contribution. The formal pointwise estimate gives the more explicit error $256T^8\kappa+2\delta$, with $T\ge2$, $0\le\kappa\le1/2$ and $0\le\varepsilon\le1$. Its hypotheses include oriented orthonormality, positive frequency and second amplitude component, $S\ge1$, coordinate discrepancies and $S^{-2}$ bounded by $\kappa$, the ratio-error budget $|{-\alpha_1/\alpha_2}-Y|+21T^3\delta\le\kappa$, and the normalized coefficient bounds. The weaker verdict leaves the earlier wave estimates to supply these hypotheses and to replace $\kappa$ by a polynomial multiple of $\delta$.

ties.plain: Polynomial error bounds for the normalized couplings

rows.fidelity_note: At $0\le\tau\le T$, assume $T\ge2$, $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, $|Y|\le1$, an oriented orthonormal frame, $\lambda>0$, $S\ge1$, $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$, and $\alpha_2=\mathbf a\cdot E_2>0$. Define $\zeta=(k\cdot E_1,Sk\cdot E_2,k\cdot E_3)/\lambda$, $q=S\mathbf a\cdot E_1/\alpha_2$, $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$, $s=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}$. Let $0\le\kappa\le1/2$ bound each coordinate error from $(x,-\varepsilon\tau,1)$, $S^{-2}$ and $|q+Y|+21T^3\delta$. Assume $\delta\ge0$, $\|B\|\le\delta$, $|2SB_{12}-1|,|2SB_{32}-\varepsilon|\le\delta$, $|c-1|\le2T\delta$, $\|E\|\le\delta/S$, with $B_{ij}=E_i\cdot BE_j$. For $M=B+ScE_2\otimes E_1+E$, the formal statement bounds each difference between $2S\widehat k\cdot M\widehat a$, $2S(\widehat k\times\widehat a)\cdot M\widehat a$ and, respectively, $(x+\varepsilon+2\varepsilon\tau Y)s$, $(-1+\varepsilon x+2(1+x^2)Y^2+2\varepsilon\tau xY)s$, by $256T^8\kappa+2\delta$. All matrices here are already divided by the physical rate $r$; $c$ represents $\sigma_p/\sigma$. No wave equation is assumed. The formal statement assumes pointwise coordinate errors bounded by $\kappa\le1/2$, coefficient bounds measured by $\delta$, and the geometric nonzero and orientation conditions. It concludes that each normalized coupling error is at most $256T^8\kappa+2\delta$. The paper’s $CT^C\delta$ additionally uses the earlier wave and amplitude estimates to bound $\kappa$ polynomially in $T$ times $\delta$. Here hats denote division by Euclidean length.

The denominators $\zeta_3$, $\sqrt m$ and $n$ are bounded below, and all scaled coordinates and coefficients have polynomial bounds in $T$. The linked estimate quantifies this continuity by $256T^8\kappa+2\delta$ in its scaled-gradient error variables. citations.where: Lemma 2.7, absorption of the coupling error using equation (2.7)

explanation.text: Once a coupling error is bounded by $CT^p\delta$, choosing $C_0$ sufficiently large in (2.7) makes it at most $\varepsilon/(8T^2)$. This leaves enough room to divide the late-time second coupling by $\cos\varphi\ge T^{-2}$ while keeping a small relative error. The formal arithmetic statement assumes $T\ge2$, $\delta\ge0$, nonnegative integers $p,C_0$, $p+2\le C_0$, $8C\le C_0$ and $C_0T^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$. It then proves exactly $CT^p\delta\le\varepsilon/(8T^2)$, so the same verdict makes precise the paper's phrase sufficiently large. The exponent comparison is between integer powers, not an unqualified assertion for arbitrary real exponents.

rows.fidelity_note: Assume $T\ge2$, $\delta\ge0$, and nonnegative integers $p,C_0$ with $p+2\le C_0$. Let a real coefficient $C$ satisfy $8C\le C_0$. If $C_0T^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$, then $CT^p\delta\le\varepsilon/(8T^2)$. This is the precise arithmetic step used to obtain the coupling error margin in Section 2.2.4 from (2.7). The exponents are natural numbers; the formal statement does not quantify over arbitrary real exponents. It imposes no positivity on $C$, although the application uses a nonnegative error constant. For $T\ge2$, $\delta\ge0$ and integers $p,C_0$ satisfying $p+2\le C_0$ and $8C\le C_0$, the formal statement converts $C_0T^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$ into $CT^p\delta\le\varepsilon/(8T^2)$. This makes precise how sufficiently large $C_0$ absorbs the unspecified polynomial in the paper.

rows.plain: Polynomial amplitude and wave errors bound the coupling error
rows.annotation: The perturbation must be small compared with the reference turning entry even at $\tau=T$. The two additional powers are needed when comparing the turning coupling relative to the cosine.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_7
rows.plain: The new wave’s two couplings to the successor
rows.annotation: The lower bound is relative to the central lengths: with $\mathsf D\ge2/(\nu\varepsilon)$ it gives $k\cdot M\mathbf a\ge\mathsf D^{-1}|k||\mathbf a|$. In Section 5.4, relative changes of size $d$ in $k$ and $\mathbf a$ and an absolute change of size $d$ in $M$ change this contraction by at most $4\mathsf D d|k||\mathbf a|$ (central lengths on the right). Thus $d\le(8\mathsf D^2)^{-1}$ suffices for positivity on the envelope, without needing an exponentially small radius to match the launch amplitude.

citations.where: §2.2.5, definition of a crossing and Proposition 2.8

explanation.text: A crossing is a normalized time at which the new wave's coupling ratio equals the prescribed positive successor value $\varepsilon_+$: $\eta_+/\nu_+=\varepsilon_+$. Section 2.2.5 introduces this condition because the current wave then provides the shear and frozen coupling parameters for activating the next wave. The couplings are measured in the current wave's orthonormal frame against the full gradient $M$, and Lemma 2.7 supplies $\nu_+>0$ under the amplification assumptions. The formal statement uses exactly this equation at physical time $t_0+\tau/r$, explaining the same verdict. Defining a crossing does not by itself give existence or uniqueness; Proposition 2.8 establishes existence after the reference peak.

explanation.text: Proposition 2.8 retains the growing wave launched at $k(t_0)=\lambda E_3(t_0)$ and $\mathbf a(t_0)=-E_1(t_0)/S+E_2(t_0)$, with $\lambda>0$, and satisfying the transverse amplitude and wave-vector equations. Its inherited smallness is $T\ge2$, $C_0\varepsilon\le1$ and $C_0T^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$, with $\varepsilon=\eta/\nu>0$ and sufficiently large absolute $C_0$. These are the hypotheses that make the actual amplitude close to the reference amplitude and control the couplings before a crossing is located. Both formal statements retain these conditions and allow continuous background and error gradients on a compact physical observation set containing the active interval, with derivatives relative to that set. Their stronger verdict concerns this regularity and domain generality; if the observation set is enlarged, its error suprema must still satisfy the same smallness inequalities.

Lemma 2.7 provides the ratio whose crossing is located; Lemma 2.6 compares the physical amplitude with its reference value both at the crossing and at the maximum. The normal estimate from Lemma 2.4 then converts amplitude into retained shear.

explanation.text: The successor ratio is required to obey $0<\varepsilon_+\le\varepsilon/32$, and the available normalized duration must satisfy $T\ge2/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}$. The formal statement imposes both inequalities explicitly, so its same verdict concerns actual hypotheses rather than merely the formula for the endpoint. These conditions complement the wave and smallness assumptions; they alone do not establish a crossing.

The proof obtains the lower bound $\varepsilon/18$ at $\tau_m$ and uses $\varepsilon_+\le\varepsilon/32$ for a strict margin. Lemma 2.5 places that unique zero in $[2/\varepsilon,3/\varepsilon]$, and the coupling bounds put the endpoint ratios strictly on opposite sides of $\varepsilon_+$. The auxiliary formal theorem assumes a supplied global reference solution and places a crossing strictly inside $(\tau_m,H)$, strengthening the stated location. The two full formal statements use the closed interval and identify $\tau_m$ as the unique nonnegative zero for every reference solution, while allowing continuous backgrounds. These distinct improvements explain the stronger verdicts, and none asserts uniqueness of the crossing.

explanation.text: Under the hypotheses of Proposition 2.8, the strength is $\sigma_+(\tau)=|\mathbf a(\tau)||k(\tau)|$, and the estimate applies to every crossing in $[\tau_m,2/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}]$. The maximum $A=\max_{[0,T]}|\mathbf a|$ is fixed for the entire wave before choosing any of these crossings. This universal statement allows the later construction to select a convenient crossing without losing control of the successor strength. The formal statement has exactly that order of quantifiers and explicitly supplies an attained maximum, explaining the same verdict. It neither restricts the estimate to the crossing used in the existence proof nor requires that crossing to be unique.

rows.annotation: Fix the entire comparison slab first, so that $A=\max_{[0,T]}|\mathbf a|$ is known before choosing a crossing. Under the growing-wave hypotheses, (2.7), $0<\varepsilon_+\le\varepsilon/32$ and the required duration, the proof combines the reference amplitude ratio, the wave-vector norm and the two angle scales at the peak and crossing. This controls the shear strength passed to the successor even though the amplitude has begun decreasing. The auxiliary formal theorem gives the common constant $C=18\exp(3)$ on both sides, while the two full formal statements improve the lower coefficient to $\exp(-1)/4$ and retain the upper coefficient $18\exp(3)$. Their stronger verdicts concern these explicit universal constants, with the same attained maximum used at every crossing.

citations.supports: Why the reference turning time gives a maximum on the required interval.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Lemma 2.5, sign of the reference slope; Proposition 2.8, reference maximum in the strength proof

explanation.text: Since $a_{\rm ref}'=Ya_{\rm ref}$ and $a_{\rm ref}>0$, the signs of $Y$ in Lemma 2.5 make the reference amplitude increase up to $\tau_m$ and decrease afterwards. The crossing hypotheses ensure $\tau_m\le T$, so $a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)$ is its maximum on $[0,T]$. Proposition 2.8 uses this known reference maximum to compare the actual wave with its own, possibly differently located, maximum. The formal statement assumes only continuity of $Y$ on $[0,\infty)$ and the weak signs $Y\ge0$ before a nonnegative $\tau_m$ and $Y\le0$ afterwards, then gives $a_{\rm ref}(\tau)\le a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)$ for every $\tau\ge0$. Its stronger verdict reflects the larger time domain and weaker sign assumptions; it does not assert uniqueness of the maximum.

ties.name: TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceV_le_at_turning_time
ties.plain: Reference peak is a global maximum

rows.fidelity_note: Let $a\ge0$ and let $Y$ be continuous on $[0,\infty)$, with $Y\ge0$ on $[0,a]$ and $Y\le0$ on $[a,\infty)$. Then $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$ satisfies $a_{\rm ref}(t)\le a_{\rm ref}(a)$ for every $t\ge0$. The paper applies this with $a=\tau_m$, the unique zero of its reference slope. The formal statement requires only weak sign inequalities and does not assert uniqueness of the maximum or require a Riccati equation. The strict signs supplied by Lemma 2.5 are more than this step needs. For continuous $Y$ nonnegative on $[0,\tau_m]$ and nonpositive afterwards, the formal statement proves $a_{\rm ref}(\tau)\le a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)$ for every $\tau\ge0$. Thus it supplies the paper’s finite-interval maximum whenever $\tau_m\le T$, and gives the same bound on the whole half-line. It assumes those signs; Lemma 2.5 proves them.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The reference maximum, amplitude comparison and late-time geometry give the physical strength estimates.

explanation.text: Suppose $c\,a_{\rm ref}\le A\le C\,a_{\rm ref}$ on $[0,T]$, with $c,C>0$, the reference maximum at $\tau_m$, and an attained maximum $M$ of $A$. Then $(c/C)a_{\rm ref}(\tau)/a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)\le A(\tau)/M\le(C/c)a_{\rm ref}(\tau)/a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)$ for every $\tau\in[0,T]$. Proposition 2.8 applies this with $A=|\mathbf a|$, $c=e^{-\varepsilon}$ and $C=e^\varepsilon$, which are uniformly comparable when $\varepsilon\le1$. The formal statement gives those exact factors for arbitrary positive comparison constants, explaining its stronger verdict. It assumes both maxima and the comparison rather than proving them, and does not require the actual amplitude to peak at $\tau_m$.

The positivity assumptions ensure nonzero denominators. The formal statement assumes existence of $M$ and the reference maximum; it does not prove either. In the crossing argument, $A=|\mathbf a|$ and $c,C=\exp(\mp\varepsilon)$. The formal integral is assigned zero when $Y$ is not integrable, so $a_{\rm ref}=1$ at such an input; no derivative formula follows there. Assume $ca_{\rm ref}\le A\le Ca_{\rm ref}$ on $[0,T]$, $c,C>0$, an attained maximum $M$ of $A$, and a reference maximum at $\tau_m$. The formal statement gives explicit factors $c/C$ and $C/c$ in the ratio comparison. Set $A=|\mathbf a|$ and $c,C=\exp(\mp\varepsilon)$ to recover the paper’s absolute multiples. citations.supports: The exact ratio identity separating the angle factor and the tail integral.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: Dividing (2.14) at $\tau$ and $\tau_m$ and subtracting the two integrals gives $a_{\rm ref}(\tau)/a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)=\sqrt{\cos\varphi(\tau)/\cos\varphi(\tau_m)}\exp\int_{\tau_m}^{\tau}(1+e)\cos\varphi$. The cosine factors are strictly positive for $\varphi(t)=\arctan(\varepsilon t^2/2)$, so this identity separates geometric decay from the remaining accumulated growth. Proposition 2.8 uses it for $0\le\tau_m\le\tau$ before bounding the tail integral. One formal result derives the identity for any ordered nonnegative times from continuous $Y$ represented by $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon t\sin2\varphi/4$, while the other assumes the amplitude formula and continuity of $(1+e)\cos\varphi$. The stronger and same verdicts distinguish these two sets of premises; neither requires the earlier time to be a peak or the slope to solve the Riccati equation.

rows.fidelity_note: Let $\varphi(t)=\arctan(\varepsilon t^2/2)$ and suppose $Y$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ with $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon t\sin(2\varphi)/4$. For $0\le a\le b$, put $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$. The formal statement proves $a_{\rm ref}(b)/a_{\rm ref}(a)=\sqrt{\cos\varphi(b)/\cos\varphi(a)}\exp\int_a^b(1+e)\cos\varphi$. This is the ratio formula used after the reference peak, but the theorem applies to any ordered nonnegative times. Neither the Riccati equation, positivity of $\varepsilon$, nor bounds on $e$ are required for this identity. For continuous $Y$ on $[0,\infty)$ represented by (2.13), the formal statement gives this ratio identity for every $0\le a\le b$. Taking $a=\tau_m$, $b=\tau$ gives the display. It requires neither the Riccati equation nor that $a$ be a peak.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The general ratio identity includes both the initial-time and peak-time formulas used in the proof.

explanation.text: For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, $2/\varepsilon\le a\le b$ and $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$, the integrand $(1+e)\cos\varphi$ is nonnegative and bounded by $4/(\varepsilon t^2)$. Hence $0\le\int_a^b(1+e)\cos\varphi\,dt\le4/(\varepsilon a)\le2$. Proposition 2.8 applies this with $a=\tau_m$ and $b=\tau$, keeping the exponential part of the amplitude ratio between one and $e^2$. The formal statement proves the same integral bounds for any such ordered times, assuming continuous $Y$ and its bounded-deviation representation so that the integrand is continuous. Its stronger verdict removes the need for the starting time to be a Riccati zero or amplitude maximum.

ties.name: TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.reference_tail_integral_bounds
ties.plain: Bounds for the reference slope integral after 2/ε

rows.fidelity_note: Let $0<\varepsilon\le1$ and $2/\varepsilon\le a\le b$. Suppose $Y$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ with $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon t\sin(2\varphi)/4$, $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$, and $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon t^2/2)$. Then $0\le\int_a^b(1+e)\cos\varphi\,dt\le2$. This is the uniform tail bound used in the amplitude-ratio formula after the reference peak. It holds for any starting time at least $2/\varepsilon$, without assuming that $a$ is a zero of $Y$ or that $Y$ solves the Riccati equation. For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, $2/\varepsilon\le a\le b$, and the continuous bounded-deviation representation of $Y$, the formal statement gives $0\le\int_a^b(1+e)\cos\varphi\le2$. The paper uses $a=\tau_m$; the formal result does not require a zero or maximum at its initial time.

rows.plain: Bounds for the reference slope integral after 2/ε
rows.annotation: The remaining gain is uniformly bounded because the integral starts at the peak, where $\varepsilon\tau_m\ge2$. More precisely, for $\tau\ge\tau_m$, $\int_{\tau_m}^\tau\cos\varphi\,d\tau'\le (2/\varepsilon)(1/\tau_m-1/\tau)\le1$. The bound is uniform even when the target ratio is much smaller than the input ratio.

explanation.text: For $\varepsilon>0$, squaring $2/\varepsilon\le\tau_m\le3/\varepsilon$ and multiplying by $\varepsilon/2$ gives $2/\varepsilon\le\tan\varphi(\tau_m)\le9/(2\varepsilon)$. With $\varepsilon\le1$, the identity $\cos\varphi=(1+\tan^2\varphi)^{-1/2}$ then makes $\cos\varphi(\tau_m)$ comparable to $\varepsilon$. Proposition 2.8 combines this peak scale with the crossing scale $\cos\varphi\asymp\varepsilon_+$ to obtain (2.23). The formal theorem states exactly the tangent bounds from the positive parameter and time bracket, explaining the same verdict. It neither supplies the turning time nor separately proves the cosine comparison, whose uniform constants use the upper bound on $\varepsilon$.

rows.plain: Bounds for the reference tangent at the amplitude peak
rows.annotation: The tangent at the peak is of order $1/\varepsilon$, so the cosine there is of order $\varepsilon$. More precisely, the zero relation in (2.13) yields $\varepsilon\tau_m=2+O(\varepsilon)$ and hence $\cos\varphi(\tau_m)=(\varepsilon/2)(1+O(\varepsilon))$. explanation.text: Equation (2.10), together with the smallness in (2.7), makes $\left||k|^2\cos^2\varphi/\lambda^2-1\right|\le1/2$, so $|k|/\lambda$ is bounded above and below by absolute multiples of $1/\cos\varphi$. Proposition 2.8 uses this to combine wave-vector growth with the decaying reference amplitude. The formal statement instead gives $\tan\varphi/2\le K/\lambda\le3\tan\varphi$ from that scalar squared-norm estimate, assuming $K\ge0$, $\lambda>0$, $0<\varepsilon\le1$ and $\tau\ge2/\varepsilon$. Setting $K=|k|$ and using $\tan\varphi\le1/\cos\varphi\le2\tan\varphi$ recovers the paper's comparison. The different verdict concerns these two equivalent late-time scales, and the estimate itself does not derive its scalar premise from the wave equation.

It uses only the displayed scalar inequality and the late-time range; the wave equation and the source of the norm estimate are not hypotheses of this algebraic step. For $\tau\ge2/\varepsilon$, the formal statement deduces $(\tan\varphi)/2\le|k|/\lambda\le3\tan\varphi$ from $||k|^2\cos^2\varphi/\lambda^2-1|\le1/2$. The paper compares $|k|/\lambda$ with $1/\cos\varphi$. The paper uses the larger maximum of $A$ over $[0,T]$ on the right, so this conditional estimate is sharper. The application has $\varepsilon>0$.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The reference maximum, amplitude comparison and late-time geometry give the physical strength estimates.

rows.name: TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.amplitude_initial_window_of_reference_comparison
