rows.annotation: The early bound in (2.24) compares with the maximum over the full slab. Indeed $Y\le1$ gives $a_{\rm ref}\le e$ in the first unit of time, while the reference maximum is at least $\exp(\varepsilon^{-1/2}-1)$. The two uses of Equation (2.18) add at most $2\varepsilon\le1$ to the logarithm of their ratio. This accounts for the constant three in the exponent.

citations.supports: The label-flow convention and the absence of an Euler-equation assumption on the parent.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For a smooth periodic parent velocity $U$ on $[0,T]$, $X(t,a)$ is the trajectory starting at $a$: $X(0,a)=a$ and $\partial_tX(t,a)=U(t,X(t,a))$. The paper uses this change of coordinates to follow the amplitude with each particle, without requiring $U$ to solve Euler. The formal condition encodes the same trajectory and initial-value equations for a flow from any starting time $s$, of which the paper uses $s=0$. Its matching verdict therefore concerns what it means to be this flow, not a proof of existence, smoothness, volume preservation or invertibility, which require separate hypotheses and results.

ties.name: TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn
ties.plain: Parent Lagrangian flow on a time interval

rows.fidelity_note: On a time interval $I$, the formal flow is $X_{s,t}(a)$, the position at time $t$ of a particle at label $a$ at time $s$. It requires $X_{s,s}(a)=a$ and $\partial_tX_{s,t}(a)=U(t,X_{s,t}(a))$ for $s,t\in I$, with the time derivative taken within $I$. The paper writes $X(t,a)=X_{0,t}(a)$. This condition uses the parent velocity without assuming the Euler equation. Smoothness, incompressibility, and differentiability or invertibility of the spatial maps are separate properties.
rows.name: TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn
rows.plain: Parent Lagrangian flow on a time interval
rows.annotation: Only the kinematics of the parent are used in transporting the wave. In particular, $\partial_tD_aX=MD_aX$ follows by differentiating $X_t=U\circ X$, even when $U$ has a momentum residual. This permits the same wave equations on every successive approximate solution.

citations.supports: The initial flow, material velocity gradient, deformation and pulled-back derivative.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: With $X(t,a)$ the flow of the smooth parent $U$, put $F=D_aX$, $M(t,a)=D_xU(t,X(t,a))$ and $\mathbf d=F^{-T}\nabla_a$. The initial condition $X(0,a)=a$ identifies labels with time-zero positions, and the spatial chain rule makes $\mathbf d$ the Eulerian gradient written in labels. These coefficients let (3.1) distinguish differentiation of an amplitude from differentiation of its oscillatory phase. The four formal links separately specify the initial-value flow, $M$, $F$ and the derivative of the reverse flow; each is weaker than the whole display, and identifying the last derivative with $F^{-1}$ uses the smooth inverse-flow identity.

ties.name: TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn
ties.plain: Parent Lagrangian flow on a time interval

rows.fidelity_note: The formal flow definition supplies $X(0,0,a)=a$ and the trajectory equation. It does not define $M$ or $\mathbf d$ in the same display. The other rows identify the required spatial derivatives, with the paper's $X(t,a)$ represented by the flow from time zero.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The separate flow and derivative definitions are joined by the smooth-flow theorems.

rows.name: TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn
rows.plain: Parent Lagrangian flow on a time interval
rows.annotation: The label $a$ always denotes the position at time zero, even for waves that are activated later. In particular $M(t,a)$ samples the parent at its current position, and differentiating at fixed $a$ means following the parent, not holding $x$ fixed.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition is $M(t,a)=D_xU(t,X(0,t,a))$, with matrix entries $\partial_jU_i$. It gives the middle formula in the display. Neither the initial flow condition nor the inverse-deformation derivative $\mathbf d$ is asserted by this definition.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The separate flow and derivative definitions are joined by the smooth-flow theorems.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.meanGradient
rows.plain: The velocity gradient along a path
rows.annotation: The matrix $M$ acts on physical vectors, although its argument is a label. In particular $\partial_tD_aX=D_a(U\circ X)=M D_aX$. It is $M$, not $M D_aX$, that enters the local affine amplitude equation (3.2).

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition gives $F=D_aX(0,t,a)$, the forward deformation. This is the matrix whose inverse transpose appears in $\mathbf d$, but the definition alone supplies neither its invertibility nor the differential operator. Those follow from the smooth flow and the reverse derivative.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The separate flow and derivative definitions are joined by the smooth-flow theorems.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.meanDeformation
rows.plain: The deformation of the parent flow
rows.annotation: A displacement $v$ of a label becomes $D_aXv$ in physical space. For a scalar profile at fixed phase, the label gradient is therefore $(D_aX)^T$ times the physical gradient. Solving for the latter gives precisely the inverse transpose in $\mathbf d$.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition gives $G=D_xX(t,0)|_{X(0,t,a)}$. For a smooth flow it is $F^{-1}$, so $\mathbf d=G^T\nabla_a$ as in the paper. The inverse identity requires the forward and reverse flow laws; the displayed definition does not assert it for arbitrary maps.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The separate flow and derivative definitions are joined by the smooth-flow theorems.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.meanDeformationInv
rows.plain: Inverse derivative of the parent flow
rows.annotation: Writing $G=D_xX^{-1}$ at $X(t,a)$, the identity $X^{-1}\circ X=\operatorname{Id}$ gives $G D_aX=\operatorname{Id}$. Thus the coefficient in $\mathbf d$ is $G^T$. The reverse derivative in the formal definition implements precisely the inverse in the paper.

citations.supports: The lattice-equivariance of the lifted parent flow.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Section 3.1, opening paragraph and lattice-equivariance sentence

explanation.text: For the smooth periodic parent $U$ on $[0,T]$, its lifted flow obeys $X(t,a+n)=X(t,a)+n$ for every $n\in\mathbb Z^3$. Indeed, translating a trajectory by $n$ gives another trajectory with initial value $a+n$, so uniqueness of the trajectory equation gives the identity. This permits the change to labels to descend from $\mathbb R^3$ to $\mathbb T^3$ without losing periodicity. The formal statement proves the same identity for arbitrary starting and ending times in a closed interval under periodicity and a common spatial Lipschitz bound, supplied here by the smooth periodic parent.

ties.name: TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.add_latticeVector
ties.plain: Integer translations of the flow

rows.fidelity_note: On a closed time interval, the formal theorem assumes a periodic velocity with a common spatial Lipschitz constant and a solution of its trajectory equation. It proves $X(s,t,a+n)=X(s,t,a)+n$ for every integer vector $n$ and every pair of times in that interval. The paper uses $s=0$; its smooth periodic parent on a compact interval supplies the Lipschitz condition.
rows.name: TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.add_latticeVector
rows.plain: Integer translations of the flow
rows.annotation: The fields $X(t,a+n)$ and $X(t,a)+n$ satisfy the same trajectory equation and have the same initial value. Thus $D_aX$, its inverse, and $M$ are periodic in the labels. The carrier $k_*\cdot a$ need not be periodic; the envelope will be used to handle precisely this remaining obstruction.

citations.supports: The chain-rule identification of the transported wave covector.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For $\phi(a)=k_*\cdot a$, the phase in physical coordinates is $\phi(X(t,\cdot)^{-1}(x))$, whose gradient at $x=X(t,a)$ is $\kappa=F^{-T}k_*$ with $F=D_aX$. This follows directly from the spatial chain rule and identifies the local direction and frequency of the transported oscillation. The formal covector formula uses the transpose of the derivative of the reverse flow, agreeing with the paper once the inverse-flow identity is used. The separately linked gradient theorem is stronger in scope: it applies to any differentiable inverse-label candidate, without incompressibility, periodicity or $k_*\ne0$; nonvanishing matters only when later formulas divide by $|\kappa|^2$.

ties.name: TorusEuler.labelWaveVector
ties.plain: The wave covector along a path

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition is the transpose of the reverse-flow derivative at the current position, applied to $k_*$. For the smooth parent flow, the reverse derivative equals $(D_aX)^{-1}$, giving the paper's $(D_aX)^{-T}k_*$. Nonzero $k_*$ and invertibility ensure the resulting covector is nonzero; those facts are not built into the formula itself.
rows.name: TorusEuler.labelWaveVector
rows.plain: The wave covector along a path
rows.annotation: Under the planar stretch $X(a_1,a_2)=(2a_1,a_2/2)$, the phase $a_1+a_2$ becomes $x_1/2+2x_2$. Its normal changes from $(1,1)$ to $(1/2,2)$. The inverse transpose gives this change and preserves the pairing with transported tangent vectors. `labelWaveVector` uses the same rule for the derivative of the flow at each label.

rows.fidelity_note: For any differentiable map $A$ and any $k_*$, the formal theorem proves $\nabla(k_*\cdot A)=(DA)^Tk_*$. Taking $A=X(t,\cdot)^{-1}$ gives the paper's transported phase gradient. The identity is valid without a flow equation, periodicity or the nonzero-covector assumption used later for division by $|\kappa|^2$.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The local chain rule includes the smooth transported fields used by the construction.

rows.name: TorusEuler.hasGradientAt_transportedPhase
rows.plain: The gradient of the transported phase
rows.annotation: Test the rule on a shear, where transposing the forward map gives the wrong sign. If $X(a_1,a_2)=(a_1+s a_2,a_2)$, the phase $a_1$ becomes $x_1-s x_2$ and has gradient $(1,-s)$. The forward transpose would give $(1,s)$. The example distinguishes transporting a phase gradient from multiplying by the forward transpose. Differentiating $\theta(t,X(t,a))=\phi(a)$ with respect to $a$ gives $(D_aX)^T\nabla_x\theta=k_*$. This is the inverse-transpose law for the wave vector. The local chain rule assumes the differentiable reverse map; invertibility is furnished by the flow.

citations.supports: The evaluated profile and separation of label and phase derivatives.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For a profile $f(t,a,s)$ with independent phase $s$, evaluate $f^\natural(t,X(t,a))=f(t,a,k_*\cdot a)$ and set $\kappa=F^{-T}k_*$, where $F=D_aX$. Differentiating in physical space then either differentiates the label dependence through $F^{-1}$ or differentiates the phase, giving $\widetilde{\mathbf d}=F^{-T}\nabla_a+\kappa\partial_s$. This separation is the source of the slow and fast terms in the later divergence correction. The formal evaluation formula and its trajectory identity each supply only the first part of the display, hence the weaker verdicts, while the differentiable chain-rule statement supplies the operator interpretation under the inverse-label transport equation.

ties.name: TorusEuler.transportedProfile
ties.plain: Profile evaluated along the transported phase

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition gives $f^\natural(t,x)=f(t,A(t,x),k_*\cdot A(t,x))$. Under the inverse relation $A(t,X(t,a))=a$, this yields the evaluation in the display. It does not define or prove the operator $\widetilde{\mathbf d}$; differentiability is not assumed by the formula.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The profile evaluation formula is differentiated only after the inverse-flow and smoothness hypotheses are supplied.

rows.name: TorusEuler.transportedProfile
rows.plain: Profile evaluated along the transported phase
rows.annotation: At fixed $(t,a)$ the phase mean integrates over the whole circle, whereas $f^\natural$ samples just the phase $k_*\cdot a$. A profile with zero phase mean need not have zero spatial mean after evaluation. In the expansion the mean and oscillatory equations are separated before this evaluation.

rows.fidelity_note: Assuming $A(t,X(t,a))=a$, the formal theorem proves the displayed evaluation identity at that particle. It is valid for arbitrary profiles and wave vectors, but it does not state the slow-plus-fast differentiation rule or impose any regularity.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The inverse-flow substitution proves the stated trajectory evaluation.

rows.name: TorusEuler.transportedProfile_on_trajectory
rows.plain: Evaluation on a particle trajectory
rows.annotation: The trajectory identity says that $f^\natural(t,X(t,a))$ is a function of $t$ at fixed $(a,s)=(a,k_*\cdot a)$. Thus the fast phase contributes no material time derivative even if $\kappa$ varies strongly in time. In the spatial chain rule it is the changing label that makes the phase derivative appear.

rows.plain: Material and spatial chain rules for the transported profile

citations.supports: The lattice condition for the phase modulo one and the need for localization.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The circle-valued phase $a\mapsto k_*\cdot a\pmod1$ descends to $\mathbb T^3$ exactly when $k_*\in\mathbb Z^3$. An integer translation $n$ changes it by $k_*\cdot n$, and testing the three coordinate translations gives the necessity as well as the sufficiency of integral coordinates. This explains why a general real wave vector requires localization and periodic extension instead of global evaluation of the phase alone. The formal statement has exactly this equivalence for the phase modulo one; it does not claim that the real-valued linear function $k_*\cdot a$ is periodic.

ties.name: TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_modOne_linearPhase_iff
ties.plain: Periodicity modulo one iff the phase covector is integral

rows.fidelity_note: The formal theorem states that $a\mapsto k_*\cdot a$ modulo one is invariant under all integer label translations exactly when every coordinate of $k_*$ is an integer. This is the lattice condition in the paper. It is a statement about the circle-valued phase; the real-valued linear phase itself need not be periodic.
rows.name: TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_modOne_linearPhase_iff
rows.plain: Periodicity modulo one iff the phase covector is integral
rows.annotation: The phase is measured in cycles: translation by the $j$th coordinate vector changes $s$ by $(k_*)_j$, which is invisible modulo one exactly when that component is an integer. A real normal can still be used because the wave vanishes where opposite label faces are identified.

citations.supports: Periodic extension of a localized profile and smoothness across the cell boundary.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For arbitrary $k_*\in\mathbb R^3$, evaluate $f(t,a,k_*\cdot a)$ on the centered label cell and extend the resulting label field with period one in each coordinate. If this evaluated field vanishes in a positive collar of the cell boundary, its copies meet smoothly; composition with the smooth inverse flow then gives a smooth periodic physical field. Section 3.1 uses this construction to avoid an integrality restriction on the wave vector. The formal formula and periodicity result each establish only part of the claim, whereas the regularity theorem gives the matching smoothness conclusion with an explicit boundary collar and regularity of both the evaluated label field and the inverse map.

ties.name: TorusEuler.localizedTransportedProfile
ties.plain: Periodic extension of the localized profile evaluated on the phase graph

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition evaluates the profile at $s=k_*\cdot a$, extends it periodically from the centered label cell and composes with the inverse label map. It permits arbitrary real $k_*$. The formula alone does not assert smoothness or even require vanishing near the cell boundary.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. Smoothness and transport require the support and inverse-flow hypotheses supplied for the constructed wave.

rows.name: TorusEuler.localizedTransportedProfile
rows.plain: Periodic extension of the localized profile evaluated on the phase graph
rows.annotation: On a translated cell write the label as $a+n$ with $a$ in the original cell. Continue the profile as $f(t,a+n,s)=f(t,a,s-k_*\cdot n)$, so its value at $s=k_*\cdot(a+n)$ equals $f(t,a,k_*\cdot a)$. The zero collar makes this continuation smooth and the evaluated field periodic; the real carrier itself need not be periodic.

rows.fidelity_note: For an inverse map commuting with integer translations, the formal theorem proves periodicity of the extended field for every real wave vector. No regularity or boundary vanishing is assumed. The paper's additional smoothness conclusion requires the collar and differentiability theorem in the next row.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. Periodicity and smoothness of the cell extension are proved by separate arguments.

rows.name: TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_localizedTransportedProfile
rows.plain: Periodicity after label extension
rows.annotation: In the labels, the field obtained after evaluation is periodic by construction. The inverse flow takes $x+n$ to $X(t,\cdot)^{-1}(x)+n$, so this periodicity is preserved in physical coordinates. This uses equivariance of the flow, not integrality of the wave vector.

rows.fidelity_note: Suppose the evaluated label field and inverse label map have the asserted differentiability order and the label field vanishes whenever some coordinate lies within a fixed positive collar of the cell boundary. The formal theorem preserves that regularity after periodization and composition, including smoothness. This is the seam-free extension used in the paper; no integer-coordinate restriction on $k_*$ is needed.
rows.name: TorusEuler.contDiff_localizedTransportedProfile
rows.plain: Smooth periodic extension of the localized transported profile
rows.annotation: Across a cell face the representative of the label may jump by a lattice vector, and hence the carrier may jump by a noninteger phase. The oscillatory field and all its derivatives vanish in a collar of the face. The repeated field is therefore smooth across the join before composition with $X(t,\cdot)^{-1}$.

citations.supports: The affine amplitude equation and its use along each parent trajectory.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: At each fixed label $a$, put $M=(D_xU)\circ X$ and $\kappa=(D_aX)^{-T}k_*$, with $\kappa\ne0$, and evolve the amplitude by $\mathbf a_t=-M\mathbf a+2\kappa(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2$. This is the amplitude equation (2.1) with the affine velocity gradient replaced by the gradient seen by that particle, as stated in (3.2). It supplies the growing leading wave before spatial variation and the envelope create errors requiring correction. The formal existence result matches this pathwise claim after setting its projected forcing to zero; it allows a continuous coefficient matrix and transverse initial amplitude, but does not by itself prove smooth dependence on the label.

ties.name: TorusEuler.exists_oscillatoryTransverse_Icc
ties.plain: A forced transverse amplitude

rows.fidelity_note: Let $t_0\in[l,r]$, let $M$ be continuous, and let $\kappa$ solve $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$ on $[l,r]$, with $\kappa(t_0)\ne0$. For continuous $f$ and any $V_0\perp\kappa(t_0)$, the formal statement constructs $V(t_0)=V_0$ satisfying $V_t=-MV+2\kappa(\kappa\cdot MV)/|\kappa|^2+(I-P_\kappa)f$, with $\kappa\cdot V=0$ and $\kappa\ne0$ throughout the interval. Taking $f=0$ at a fixed label gives the paper’s amplitude equation. Smooth dependence on the label is not a conclusion of this pathwise existence theorem.
rows.name: TorusEuler.exists_oscillatoryTransverse_Icc
rows.plain: A forced transverse amplitude
rows.annotation: For each fixed label replace the affine gradient by $M(t,a)$. Since the transported normal satisfies $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$, the same transverse amplitude equation applies on that trajectory. The cited ODE result permits a forcing as well; the seed uses the homogeneous case. Smooth dependence on $a$ is a separate ingredient of the localized construction.

citations.supports: Differentiation of the inverse transpose deformation and the covector evolution.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For a parent flow $X$, let $F=D_aX$, $M=D_xU\circ X$ and $\kappa=F^{-T}k_*$. Differentiating $F_t=MF$ gives $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$, the transported-covector equation from the affine system (2.1). This supplies the companion equation needed to preserve transversality of the localized seed. The formal statement proves the identity for a jointly twice-differentiable periodic parent, any initial time and any initial covector, with time derivatives within the closed interval, so it is stronger than the paper's smooth odd divergence-free setting with $k_*\ne0$.

ties.name: TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.hasDerivWithinAt_labelWaveVector
ties.plain: Transport of the wave covector

rows.fidelity_note: For a jointly $C^2$ periodic parent and its flow on $[l,r]$, $l<r$, the formal theorem proves $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$ for every starting time $s\in[l,r]$ and every initial covector. The paper uses $s=0$, a smooth divergence-free odd parent and a nonzero $k_*$. None of those extra restrictions is required for this derivative identity. Endpoint time derivatives are taken within the interval.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The local chain rule includes the smooth transported fields used by the construction.

rows.name: TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.hasDerivWithinAt_labelWaveVector
rows.plain: Transport of the wave covector
rows.annotation: Differentiating $(D_aX)^T\kappa=k_*$ at fixed $a$ gives $(D_aX)^T(\kappa_t+M^T\kappa)=0$, using $\partial_tD_aX=MD_aX$. Invertibility gives $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$. This is the affine normal equation on each particle path, regardless of how $M$ varies across paths.

citations.supports: The seed initial-value problem and its relation to the affine amplitude equation.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: At each label, prescribe a smooth amplitude $\mathbf a_*$ perpendicular to the nonzero covector $\kappa(t_0,a)$ and solve $\mathbf a_t=-M\mathbf a+2\kappa(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2$ on $[t_0,T]$. This is (2.1) along the parent trajectory and determines the seed from which the leading oscillation is built. One formal link only expands the right-hand side, and its quotient is assigned zero when $\kappa=0$, so that formula alone does not encode the intended nonvanishing assumption. The other link proves existence and transversality at a fixed label, even with an added projected force, but does not supply smooth dependence on all labels; these omissions explain the weaker verdicts for the full displayed seed prescription.

ties.name: TorusEuler.affineWaveAmplitudeOperator_apply
ties.plain: Formula for the affine wave amplitude operator

rows.fidelity_note: This formal equality expands the amplitude operator as $-M\mathbf a+2\kappa(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2$. It identifies only the right side of (3.2), without a trajectory, initial value or transversality assertion. Division by zero is assigned zero, so the formula alone does not impose the nonzero-covector hypothesis used by the wave construction.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The displayed coefficient or operator is used together with the wave equations and nonvanishing hypotheses.

rows.name: TorusEuler.affineWaveAmplitudeOperator_apply
rows.plain: Formula for the affine wave amplitude operator
rows.annotation: Write the correction to $-M\mathbf a$ as $p_{\rm w}\kappa$. Differentiating $\kappa\cdot\mathbf a$ gives $-2\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a+p_{\rm w}|\kappa|^2$. There are two equal terms because the normal itself moves by $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$. Canceling them determines the pressure coefficient in Equation (3.3).

rows.fidelity_note: Let $t_0\in[l,r]$, let $M$ be continuous, and let $\kappa$ solve $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$ on $[l,r]$, with $\kappa(t_0)\ne0$. For continuous $f$ and any $V_0\perp\kappa(t_0)$, the formal statement constructs $V(t_0)=V_0$ satisfying $V_t=-MV+2\kappa(\kappa\cdot MV)/|\kappa|^2+(I-P_\kappa)f$, with $\kappa\cdot V=0$ and $\kappa\ne0$ throughout the interval. Taking $f=0$ at a fixed label gives the paper’s amplitude equation. Smooth dependence on the label is not a conclusion of this pathwise existence theorem.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. Pathwise existence is supplemented by the smooth dependence on labels used for the localized wave.

rows.name: TorusEuler.exists_oscillatoryTransverse_Icc
rows.plain: A forced transverse amplitude
rows.annotation: At a fixed label $M(t,a)$ and the nonzero $\kappa(t,a)$ are prescribed by the parent. Equation (3.2) is then linear in $\mathbf a$, with operator $-(I-2P_\kappa)M$. The linked existence result allows a transverse source, here set to zero. The seed is assembled across labels using the smooth dependence of this ODE on its coefficients and initial data.

citations.supports: Conservation of seed transversality and its use in the divergence correction.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: Suppose $\kappa\ne0$ on $[t_0,T]$, $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$, and $\mathbf a$ solves (3.2) with $\kappa(t_0)\cdot\mathbf a(t_0)=0$. Differentiating $\kappa\cdot\mathbf a$ makes the two matrix terms cancel the pressure-projection term, so this inner product stays zero. Transversality removes the fast divergence and allows the potential construction in (3.5). The formal statement proves the same conservation on any interval and also allows forcing projected onto $\kappa^\perp$, making it stronger than the homogeneous seed claim; it assumes the two evolution equations and nonvanishing rather than constructing them.

ties.name: TorusEuler.oscillatory_transverse_of_initial
ties.plain: The amplitude stays perpendicular to the transported covector

rows.fidelity_note: On an interval $J$, suppose $\kappa(t)\ne0$, $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$, and $V_t=-MV+2\kappa(\kappa\cdot MV)/|\kappa|^2+(I-P_\kappa)f$ pointwise, with derivatives taken within $J$. If $\kappa(t_0)\cdot V(t_0)=0$ at one $t_0\in J$, then $\kappa(t)\cdot V(t)=0$ for every $t\in J$. This is preservation of transversality; existence and nonvanishing are assumptions. The formal statement permits projected forcing. The paper’s homogeneous seed equation is the case $f=0$.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The homogeneous seed equation is a special case of the proved forced transversality result.

rows.name: TorusEuler.oscillatory_transverse_of_initial
rows.plain: The amplitude stays perpendicular to the transported covector
rows.annotation: Differentiation gives $\partial_t(\kappa\cdot\mathbf a)=-\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a-\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a+2\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a=0$. A transverse forcing would also have zero pairing with $\kappa$. Thus the same calculation applies to the higher forced oscillations, not only to the seed (see Equation (5.17)).

citations.supports: The leading velocity and pressure products and their momentum cancellation.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For a transverse seed $\mathbf a$, envelope $g$, odd periodic profile $F_0$ and its zero-mean primitive $P_0$, set $A_1=g\mathbf aF_0$ and $\mathsf p[A_1]=-2g(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)|\kappa|^{-2}P_0$. Multiplying the seed equation (3.2) by $gF_0$ and using $P_0'=F_0$ shows why this pressure cancels the acceleration in the $\kappa$ direction. These are the leading velocity and pressure, before the slow divergence correction or time activation. The two formal links separately specify the products for the chosen radial envelope and family $F_h,P_h$, so each is weaker than the general display; their formulas remain assigned values at $\kappa=0$, but the pressure balance uses $\kappa\ne0$.

ties.name: TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.leading
ties.plain: The selected leading oscillation

rows.fidelity_note: The paper allows arbitrary suitable $g,F_0$ and transverse initial amplitude. The formal definition gives only the leading-velocity product for the selected seed, radial envelope and narrow family $F_h$: $A_1=g\mathbf aF_h$. It does not state the pressure identity in the same display or prove the seed equation.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The construction needs the selected smooth seed and profile family, for which the asserted identity is proved.

rows.plain: The selected leading oscillation
rows.annotation: The leading profile is obtained by multiplying the amplitude ODE by $gF_0$. This is an exact cancellation at fixed $(a,s)$. Spatial localization thus introduces no additional material time derivative, even though derivatives of $g$ and of the seed in neighboring labels remain in the spatial terms.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal pressure is $-2g(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)|\kappa|^{-2}P_h$, with the chosen radial envelope, seed and primitive $P_h$. This is the pressure part of (3.3) for that family, rather than for arbitrary suitable $P_0$. At $\kappa=0$ the quotient is assigned zero; the construction's nonzero covector is needed for the intended pressure balance.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The construction needs the selected smooth seed and profile family, for which the asserted identity is proved.

rows.name: TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.leadingPressure
rows.plain: The selected leading pressure
rows.annotation: The phase derivative of $\mathsf p[A_1]$ is $-p_{\rm w}gF_0$, so its fast gradient cancels the part of the amplitude acceleration along $\kappa$. Its slow gradient is $-P_0\mathbf d(p_{\rm w}g)$; it need not be zero when the amplitude or envelope varies between particles. This term enters the next level in Equation (5.25).

citations.supports: Evaluation of the leading profile on a parent trajectory.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: Along $x=X(t,a)$, the leading wave is $A_1^\natural(t,x)=g(a)\mathbf a(t,a)F_0(k_*\cdot a)$. This follows by inserting the product (3.3) into the profile-evaluation convention preceding (3.1), using $X(t,\cdot)^{-1}(X(t,a))=a$. The formula separates the amplitude's evolution from the phase and envelope, which are fixed to the particle label. The formal identity is stronger in scope because it holds for every profile and wave vector whenever this inverse relation holds, without requiring a seed equation, smoothness or periodicity.

ties.name: TorusEuler.transportedProfile_on_trajectory
ties.plain: Evaluation on a particle trajectory

rows.fidelity_note: Whenever $A(t,X(t,a))=a$, the formal theorem gives $f^\natural(t,X(t,a))=f(t,a,k_*\cdot a)$ for every profile $f$. Inserting $f=g\mathbf aF_0$ gives the formula in the paper. No amplitude equation, smoothness, periodicity or nonzero wave vector is required for this evaluation identity.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The inverse-flow substitution proves the stated trajectory evaluation.

rows.name: TorusEuler.transportedProfile_on_trajectory
rows.plain: Evaluation on a particle trajectory
rows.annotation: On a trajectory, $g(a)F_0(k_*\cdot a)$ is fixed while $\mathbf a(t,a)$ evolves. A particle at a zero of $F_0$ has zero leading velocity along its parent path even though the velocity gradient there may be large. The formula is for the leading profile, before curl completion.

citations.supports: The derivation and role of the leading homogeneous momentum identity.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For $t\in[t_0,T]$, let $A_1=g\mathbf aF_0$ and $\mathsf p[A_1]=-p_{\rm w}gP_0$, where $\mathbf a$ solves (3.2) and $P_0'=F_0$. Then $A_{1,t}+MA_1+\kappa\partial_s\mathsf p[A_1]=0$ because the seed acceleration in the $\kappa$ direction cancels the phase-pressure derivative. This is the leading homogeneous momentum equation before slow spatial derivatives and activation generate further errors. The formal theorem establishes it, together with transversality and zero phase means, for the selected radial envelope and $F_h,P_h$ with $0<h\le1$; the weaker verdict records that restriction of the data, despite the additional conclusions.

ties.name: TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.paper_hierarchy_leading_homogeneous
ties.plain: The leading wave equation

rows.fidelity_note: On $[t_0,T]$, $t_0<T$, the formal theorem proves (3.4) for the selected seed, radial envelope and profiles $F_h,P_h$ with $0<h\le1$. It also asserts transversality and zero phase means of the leading velocity and pressure. The paper derives the equation for arbitrary suitable $g,F_0,P_0$ and seed data; this theorem verifies the family actually used in the construction.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The construction needs the selected smooth seed and profile family, for which the asserted identity is proved.

rows.name: TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.paper_hierarchy_leading_homogeneous
rows.plain: The leading wave equation
rows.annotation: The displayed defect separates in phase as $F_0^2(b\cdot\mathbf d)b-P_0\mathbf d(p_{\rm w}g)$, with $b=g\mathbf a$. The pressure term has zero phase mean, but the quadratic term contains $\langle F_0^2\rangle_s$ rather than $\langle F_0\rangle_s$. In Equation (5.25) the curl completion adds further terms to this defect; the mean of the completed quadratic interaction must be corrected as well.

citations.supports: The slow divergence left by a transverse localized profile and its removal by a curl.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text:
Let $V(t,a,s)$ be transverse to the nonzero transported covector $\kappa$, and write $V^
atural(t,X(t,a))=V(t,a,k_*\cdot a)$. Transversality removes the fast contribution to $\operatorname{div}_x V^
atural$, but derivatives of its envelope and amplitude leave $(\mathbf d\cdot V)^
atural$. Equations (3.5)–(3.6) cancel this remainder by making $(V+C[V])^
atural$ the curl of a potential. The formal statement verifies this local divergence cancellation when the inverse label map and potential are twice differentiable and geometrically compatible; its matching verdict concerns that cancellation, while smooth periodic extension is a separate step.

ties.name: TorusEuler.divergence_completedWaveOn
ties.plain: The completed wave has zero divergence

rows.fidelity_note: For a transverse profile with a nonzero covector arising from the inverse label derivative, the formal theorem proves that adding the slow curl correction makes the evaluated field divergence free. It requires the inverse map and phase potential to be $C^2$ on the spatial region. This verifies the local cancellation described here; the smooth periodic extension is established separately.
rows.name: TorusEuler.divergence_completedWaveOn
rows.plain: The completed wave has zero divergence
rows.annotation: Taking the divergence of the leading wave gives $(F_0\,\mathbf d\cdot(g\mathbf a))^\natural$, since the term $gF_0'\,\kappa\cdot\mathbf a$ vanishes. We preserve the desired oscillation by making it the fast curl of a potential; the slow curl then cancels the displayed defect exactly, with support still in the label envelope.

citations.supports: The curl chain rule and its slow and fast parts.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text:
For a differentiable potential profile $Q(t,a,s)$, evaluate it at $a=X(t,\cdot)^{-1}(x)$ and $s=k_*\cdot a$. The spatial chain rule (3.1) gives $
abla_x	imes Q^
atural=(\mathbf d	imes Q+\kappa	imes\partial_sQ)^
atural$, with $\kappa=(D_aX)^{-T}k_*$. This splits a curl into the leading oscillation and its slow divergence correction. The formal statement proves this pointwise identity from first derivatives of the inverse map and the profile, so its stronger verdict reflects the absence of the paper's global smoothness, periodicity and nonvanishing assumptions.

ties.name: TorusEuler.curl_transportedProfile
ties.plain: Curl after phase evaluation

rows.fidelity_note: At a fixed point, the formal theorem needs only differentiability of the inverse label map and joint differentiability of $Q$ in label and phase. It gives the Eulerian curl as the slow curl of $D_aQ\,D_xA$ plus $\kappa\times\partial_sQ$, with $\kappa=(D_xA)^Tk_*$. The paper's smooth periodic setting is a special case; no transversality or nonzero covector is needed for this chain rule.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The local chain rule includes the smooth transported fields used by the construction.

rows.name: TorusEuler.curl_transportedProfile
rows.plain: Curl after phase evaluation
rows.annotation: The potential is chosen so that its fast curl is the prescribed transverse velocity. The other curl, $\mathbf d\times Q$, is then a determined correction and may have a normal component. The sum is a curl in physical space, so cancellation of its divergence is exact rather than an estimate of a small divergence.

citations.supports: The potential and divergence correction, including the nonzero-covector requirement.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For a smooth period-one profile $V$ with zero phase mean, $\kappa\cdot V=0$ and $\kappa\ne0$, choose $Q[V]=-\partial_s^{-1}(\kappa\times V/|\kappa|^2)$ and $C[V]=\mathbf d\times Q[V]$. The sign and denominator make the fast curl equal to $V$, so the completed physical field is an exact curl by (3.6). The potential link alone omits the correction and is therefore weaker, while the completion link performs the slow curl with the inverse deformation and matches that prescription. The formal potential formula also assigns zero to the quotient at $\kappa=0$, but none of the subsequent recovery identities uses that degenerate case.

ties.name: TorusEuler.wavePotential
ties.plain: The vector potential of an oscillation

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition supplies the potential $Q[V]=-\partial_s^{-1}(\kappa\times V/|\kappa|^2)$ at fixed time and label. It does not define the curl correction in the second part of the display. The quotient is assigned zero at $\kappa=0$; nonvanishing and transversality are needed for the subsequent recovery of $V$.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The potential, curl and mean identities together establish the completed-wave formulas.

rows.name: TorusEuler.wavePotential
rows.plain: The vector potential of an oscillation
rows.annotation: For $z\perp\kappa$, $\kappa\times(\kappa\times z)=-|\kappa|^2z$. Hence the inverse of the fast cross product on the transverse plane is $z\mapsto-\kappa\times z/|\kappa|^2$. One can take its periodic phase primitive because $V$ has zero mean, and the inverse cross product gains one power of $|\kappa|^{-1}$.

rows.fidelity_note: For smooth profiles on $[0,T]$, $T>0$, this definition first forms the normalized potential using $\kappa(t,a,0)\ne0$ and then takes its label curl with derivative matrix $G$. In the paper $\kappa$ is phase independent and $G=(D_aX)^{-1}$, so the result is exactly $C[V]=\mathbf d\times Q[V]$. The geometric compatibility and transversality used later are not imposed by this formula alone.
rows.name: TorusEuler.HierarchySmoothProfile.profileCompletion
rows.plain: Curl correction for the oscillatory divergence
rows.annotation: The slow curl $C[V]$ is obtained by differentiating $Q[V]$ at fixed $s$. In particular it is not the curl of the graph-evaluated potential: that curl also contains the prescribed velocity $V$. Since $Q[V]$ carries $|\kappa|^{-1}$, the slow correction in Equation (5.31) costs one label derivative but no factor $|\kappa|/h$.

citations.supports: The zero-mean periodic primitive and the normalization used for the correction.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For continuous period-one $f$ with $\int_0^1f=0$, the normalized primitive is $\partial_s^{-1}f(s)=J(s)-\int_0^1J(r)\,dr$, where $J(s)=\int_0^sf(r)\,dr$. The zero mean of $f$ makes this primitive periodic, and subtracting its own mean fixes the otherwise arbitrary additive constant. This normalization is used in (3.5) and is essential when the longitudinal component is recovered in (3.6). The formal formula and periodicity theorem match these assertions under the stated hypotheses; although the formula is defined for other inputs, it then need not be a periodic primitive, and its value at zero is not prescribed to be zero.

ties.name: TorusEuler.phasePrimitive
ties.plain: Mean-zero primitive of a periodic phase profile

rows.fidelity_note: The formal primitive is $J(s)-\int_0^1J(r)\,dr$, where $J(s)=\int_0^sf(r)\,dr$. For continuous period-one $f$ of zero mean, this is the paper's normalized periodic primitive. Its value at zero need not vanish. Outside those hypotheses, the formula is still assigned values but does not assert a periodic primitive.
rows.name: TorusEuler.phasePrimitive
rows.plain: Mean-zero primitive of a periodic phase profile
rows.annotation: For a periodic mean-zero $f$, set $J(s)=\int_0^s f(r)\,dr$. The primitive used here is $J-\int_0^1J(r)\,dr$. Subtracting a constant in phase preserves the derivative but removes a phase-independent component from the potential and hence from its slow curl.

rows.fidelity_note: For a continuous period-one input with zero phase mean, the formal theorem proves that this normalized primitive has period one. The zero mean of the input prevents drift between periods; subtracting the mean of the primitive fixes its additive constant. These are precisely the conditions needed when (3.5) applies the operation to the transverse oscillation.
rows.name: TorusEuler.periodic_phasePrimitive
rows.plain: Periodicity of the phase primitive
rows.annotation: The necessary condition for a periodic primitive is that its input have zero integral over a period. Here $J(s+1)-J(s)=\int_0^1f=0$. Zero mean of the primitive itself is a different condition: it selects one of the periodic primitives.

citations.supports: Recovery of a transverse oscillation by the fast curl.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Section 3.1, equation (3.5) and its following triple-product calculation

explanation.text: Fix a nonzero covector $\kappa$ and a continuous transverse profile $V(s)$, and form $Q[V]=-\partial_s^{-1}(\kappa\times V/|\kappa|^2)$. Differentiating in phase and using $\kappa\times(\kappa\times V)=\kappa(\kappa\cdot V)-|\kappa|^2V$ gives $\kappa\times\partial_sQ[V]=V$. This is why the potential in (3.5) reproduces the desired oscillation as the fast part of its curl. The formal theorem proves this identity without requiring phase periodicity or zero phase mean, so it is stronger in scope; those additional assumptions are needed to make the paper's potential itself periodic.

ties.name: TorusEuler.wavePotential_fast_curl
ties.plain: The fast curl recovers the wave

rows.fidelity_note: The formal theorem assumes only $\kappa\ne0$, continuity of $V$ and $\kappa\cdot V(s)=0$ for every phase, and proves $\kappa\times\partial_sQ[V]=V$. It does not require period one or zero phase mean. Those assumptions are needed separately to make the potential periodic in the paper. The recovery identity itself is the vector triple-product calculation stated here.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The potential, curl and mean identities together establish the completed-wave formulas.

rows.name: TorusEuler.wavePotential_fast_curl
rows.plain: The fast curl recovers the wave
rows.annotation: In differentiating $Q[V]$ in phase, $\kappa$ is held fixed. Hence $\kappa\times\partial_s Q=-\kappa\times(\kappa\times V)/|\kappa|^2=V$ by transversality. If $V$ had a normal component, the same formula would return only its projection onto $\kappa^\perp$.

citations.supports: The completed curl identity and the normalized longitudinal component.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For smooth transverse, zero-mean periodic $V$ and the nonzero covector $\kappa=(D_aX)^{-T}k_*$, (3.6) expresses $V+C[V]$ as a full profile curl and gives $\kappa\cdot C[V]=-\partial_s^{-1}(\mathbf d\cdot V)$. The first identity follows from the fast-curl calculation, while commuting coordinate derivatives gives $\partial_s(\kappa\cdot C[V])=-\mathbf d\cdot V$ and zero phase mean fixes the integration constant. These formulas give both exact divergence cancellation and control of how the correction differentiates another wave's phase. The three formal links prove, respectively, the evaluated curl identity, the integration step under a zero-mean hypothesis, and the differentiated longitudinal identity; each is weaker than the combined display, and none alone supplies both equalities.

ties.name: TorusEuler.curl_transportedWavePotential_eq_add_slowCurl
ties.plain: Curl of the transported potential equals the wave plus its correction

rows.fidelity_note:
The formal theorem proves the first identity after physical evaluation: $
abla_x	imes Q[V]^
atural=V^
atural+C[V]^
atural$. It assumes a differentiable inverse label map, its matching nonzero covector, continuous transverse $V$ and a jointly differentiable potential. It does not state the longitudinal component formula in the second half of (3.6).

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The potential, curl and mean identities together establish the completed-wave formulas.

rows.name: TorusEuler.curl_transportedWavePotential_eq_add_slowCurl
rows.plain: Curl of the transported potential equals the wave plus its correction
rows.annotation: The fast curl is exactly $V$, so the graph evaluation of $V+C[V]$ equals $\nabla_x\times Q[V]^\natural$. The identity is exact, irrespective of the size of $\mathbf d\cdot V$. One may therefore estimate the correction in size while preserving divergence cancellation without a residual.

rows.fidelity_note: For a fixed vector $\kappa$, let $C(s)$ and $d(s)$ be continuous, with $\int_0^1C(s)\,ds=0$, and assume $\partial_s(\kappa\cdot C)=-d$ at every phase. The formal statement gives $\kappa\cdot C(s)=-\partial_s^{-1}d(s)$, where $\partial_s^{-1}d=Jd-\int_0^1Jd$ and $Jd(s)=\int_0^sd$. Taking $d=\mathbf d\cdot V$ supplies the integration step in the paper. The derivative identity and zero mean of $C$ are premises, not conclusions; neither the completed curl formula nor the mean of $Q[V]$ is established here.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The potential, curl and mean identities together establish the completed-wave formulas.

rows.name: TorusEuler.waveCorrection_longitudinal_of_mean_zero
rows.plain: The mean-zero phase primitive gives the longitudinal curl correction
rows.annotation: For the leading wave, Equation (3.6) reads $\kappa\cdot C[A_1]=-P_0(s)\,\mathbf d\cdot(g\mathbf a)$. Thus the phase velocity introduced by the completion can be computed from the slow divergence of the envelope and seed. In particular the mean of a fast interaction satisfies $\langle(\kappa\cdot C[V])\partial_s Y\rangle_s=\langle(\mathbf d\cdot V)Y\rangle_s$ by integration by parts; this is used at Equation (5.42).

rows.fidelity_note: For a smooth transverse profile and derivative directions and covector arising from one $C^2$ coordinate map, the formal theorem proves $\partial_s(\kappa\cdot C[V])=-\mathbf d\cdot V$. It stops at the phase derivative. The second equality of (3.6) additionally requires zero phase mean and integration, and the first equality is established by the separate curl theorem.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The potential, curl and mean identities together establish the completed-wave formulas.

rows.name: TorusEuler.HierarchySmoothProfile.profileCompletion_longitudinal_derivative
rows.plain: The longitudinal phase derivative
rows.annotation: Apply the full slow-fast divergence to the completed field. The slow curl has zero slow divergence, and the transverse $V$ has zero fast divergence. Thus the remaining two terms give $\partial_s(\kappa\cdot C[V])=-\mathbf d\cdot V$. This is a derivative identity; obtaining Equation (3.6) without an additive function of the labels uses the zero phase mean of $C[V]$.

citations.supports: Commutation of coordinate derivatives and the two divergence-of-curl cancellations.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For a twice-differentiable inverse coordinate map, the slow derivatives $\mathbf d_i$ commute, and so do $\widetilde{\mathbf d}_i=\mathbf d_i+\kappa_i\partial_s$ when $\kappa_i=\mathbf d_i\phi$. Consequently both the full divergence of the full curl and the slow divergence of $C[V]=\mathbf d\times Q[V]$ vanish. Section 3.1 uses these two cancellations to reduce the divergence equation to the longitudinal phase derivative in (3.6). The ordinary formal divergence-of-curl theorem supplies the first cancellation after the chain rule, while the second link supplies only the slow cancellation for compatible coordinate derivatives; both are correctly weaker than the two-part sentence.

ties.name: TorusEuler.divergence_curl
ties.plain: Divergence of a curl

rows.fidelity_note: The formal theorem is the ordinary identity $\nabla_x\cdot(\nabla_x\times Q)=0$ at a point where $Q$ is $C^2$. The paper's first cancellation follows by applying it to the transported potential and using the chain rule. The theorem does not itself mention label-phase derivatives or prove the separate slow-divergence cancellation.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The potential, curl and mean identities together establish the completed-wave formulas.

rows.name: TorusEuler.divergence_curl
rows.plain: Divergence of a curl
rows.annotation: The linked divergence-of-curl theorem is the ordinary spatial identity, proved by symmetry of mixed second derivatives. To use it before phase evaluation, observe that $[\widetilde{\mathbf d}_i,\widetilde{\mathbf d}_j]=(\mathbf d_i\kappa_j-\mathbf d_j\kappa_i)\partial_s=0$, since $\kappa_j=\mathbf d_j\phi$ and the $\mathbf d_i$ commute. The same mixed-derivative cancellation then applies at every phase.

rows.fidelity_note: Assuming the slow derivative matrix comes from a single $C^2$ coordinate map, the formal theorem proves $\mathbf d\cdot(\mathbf d\times Q)=0$ at fixed phase. This is the second cancellation, with $Q=Q[V]$. It does not state the full slow-plus-fast divergence identity in the first half of the sentence.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The potential, curl and mean identities together establish the completed-wave formulas.

rows.name: TorusEuler.HierarchySmoothProfile.profileSlowCurl_labelDivergence_zero
rows.plain: The slow curl has zero divergence
rows.annotation: The variable coefficients in $\mathbf d$ do not introduce a commutator: $\mathbf d_i$ is $\partial_{x_i}$ conjugated by $X$ at fixed $s$. Consequently the mixed second derivatives in $\mathbf d\cdot(\mathbf d\times Q)$ cancel, even though $D_aX$ varies with $a$.

citations.supports: The longitudinal phase-derivative identity obtained from transversality and commuting derivatives.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: Let $V$ be smooth and transverse to a nonzero transported covector $\kappa$, and let $C[V]=\mathbf d\times Q[V]$ with the potential from (3.5). Taking the full divergence of $V+C[V]$ and using the two divergence-of-curl cancellations leaves $\partial_s(\kappa\cdot C[V])=-\mathbf d\cdot V$. This identifies the phase variation of the correction's longitudinal component, before a normalization determines that component itself. The formal theorem gives exactly this derivative identity when the slow derivative matrix and covector come from one twice-differentiable coordinate map; no zero-mean assertion is needed until the following integration step.

ties.name: TorusEuler.HierarchySmoothProfile.profileCompletion_longitudinal_derivative
ties.plain: The longitudinal phase derivative

rows.fidelity_note: The formal theorem proves this derivative identity for a smooth transverse profile when $G(t,A(x),s)=D_xA$ and $\kappa(t,A(x),0)=(D_xA)^Tk_*\ne0$, with $A$ a $C^2$ coordinate map. In the paper $A=X(t,\cdot)^{-1}$. Zero phase mean is not needed until this derivative is integrated; the theorem itself does not yet give the formula for $\kappa\cdot C[V]$.
rows.name: TorusEuler.HierarchySmoothProfile.profileCompletion_longitudinal_derivative
rows.plain: The longitudinal phase derivative
rows.annotation: The derivative on $Y$ in a product $(\kappa\cdot C[V])\partial_sY$ can be moved to $\kappa\cdot C[V]$ inside a phase average. Its derivative is $-\mathbf d\cdot V$, so the mean is $\langle(\mathbf d\cdot V)Y\rangle_s$. The fast interaction need not be small pointwise for this reduction to hold; it is the averaged interaction that loses the fast derivative in Equation (5.42).

citations.supports: Zero phase means and recovery of the longitudinal component without an integration constant.

explanation.text: For the smooth periodic potential and correction of (3.5), the normalized primitive gives $\langle Q[V]\rangle_s=0$, and phase-independent slow derivatives give $\langle C[V]\rangle_s=0$. Together with $\partial_s(\kappa\cdot C[V])=-\mathbf d\cdot V$, this removes the additive constant and yields the second equality in (3.6). The step matters because the differentiated identity alone would leave an undetermined longitudinal term. The formal links separately establish the zero mean of the potential, the zero mean of the correction, and integration of a prescribed derivative with a zero-mean correction; each is weaker than this entire inference, and the integration theorem assumes its derivative identity.

ties.name: TorusEuler.waveCorrection_longitudinal_of_mean_zero
ties.plain: The mean-zero phase primitive gives the longitudinal curl correction

rows.fidelity_note: For a fixed vector $\kappa$, let $C(s)$ and $d(s)$ be continuous, with $\int_0^1C(s)\,ds=0$, and assume $\partial_s(\kappa\cdot C)=-d$ at every phase. The formal statement gives $\kappa\cdot C(s)=-\partial_s^{-1}d(s)$, where $\partial_s^{-1}d=Jd-\int_0^1Jd$ and $Jd(s)=\int_0^sd$. Taking $d=\mathbf d\cdot V$ supplies the integration step in the paper. The derivative identity and zero mean of $C$ are premises, not conclusions; neither the completed curl formula nor the mean of $Q[V]$ is established here.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The potential, curl and mean identities together establish the completed-wave formulas.

rows.name: TorusEuler.waveCorrection_longitudinal_of_mean_zero
rows.plain: The mean-zero phase primitive gives the longitudinal curl correction
rows.annotation: The right side of $\partial_s(\kappa\cdot C[V])=-\mathbf d\cdot V$ has zero mean, because $\mathbf d$ commutes with the phase average and $\langle V\rangle_s=0$. The normalized potential also gives $\langle C[V]\rangle_s=0$. These two mean identities justify taking the zero-mean primitive, with no free phase-independent term.

rows.fidelity_note: For smooth $V$ and a covector nonzero at phase zero on the time slab, the formal theorem proves $\langle Q[V]\rangle_s=0$. The normalized phase primitive gives this identity even without periodicity or transversality. The zero mean of $C[V]$ and the longitudinal component formula are separate conclusions.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The potential, curl and mean identities together establish the completed-wave formulas.

rows.name: TorusEuler.HierarchySmoothProfile.profilePhaseAverage_wavePotential
rows.plain: The potential has zero phase mean
rows.annotation: The potential is normalized by its mean, not by its value at $s=0$. For instance the primitive of an odd periodic oscillation is even and need not vanish at zero. Choosing its mean to be zero avoids introducing an unintended phase-independent curl.

rows.fidelity_note: For smooth profiles with nonzero covector and derivative matrix independent of phase, the formal theorem proves $\langle C[V]\rangle_s=0$ by commuting label differentiation with phase integration. It supplies that normalization, but not the derivative identity or its integration to the second part of (3.6).

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The potential, curl and mean identities together establish the completed-wave formulas.

citations.supports: The explicit potential for a leading product profile.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Section 3.1, (3.3), (3.5) and the displayed leading potential

explanation.text: For $A_1=g\mathbf aF_0$ with $g,\mathbf a,\kappa$ independent of phase and $P_0=\partial_s^{-1}F_0$, formula (3.5) becomes $Q[A_1]=gP_0(\mathbf a\times\kappa)/|\kappa|^2$. This is linearity of the normalized primitive and reversal of the cross product, with $\kappa\ne0$ in the wave construction. It gives an explicit potential whose slow curl is the leading divergence correction. The formal link verifies the formula for the selected first-wave amplitude, radial envelope and profiles $F_h,P_h$, $0<h\le1$, so it is weaker than the paper's formula for arbitrary suitable leading data.

ties.name: TorusEuler.wavePotential_firstWaveLeadingProfile

It identifies the constructed first-wave potential, rather than quantifying over arbitrary later-wave amplitudes or arbitrary envelopes.

rows.name: TorusEuler.wavePotential_firstWaveLeadingProfile

rows.annotation: In this formula $\mathbf a$ and $\kappa$ are orthogonal, so $|Q[A_1]|=|gP_0|\,|\mathbf a|/|\kappa|$. Unlike the leading velocity, the potential uses $P_0$ and need not vanish at $s=0$. Its slow curl is therefore not required to have zero central gradient, a contribution that is estimated separately in Equation (5.50).

citations.supports: Locality of the primitive and slow curl, and preservation of label support.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: At a fixed time, if $V(t,a,s)$ vanishes for every phase on a neighborhood of a label $a$, then both $Q[V]$ and its slow curl $C[V]$ vanish there. Phase integration acts at that same label, and label differentiation is local, so (3.5) does not enlarge the closed label support. This keeps the corrected physical wave inside the transported envelope rather than spreading it over the torus. The potential link proves only the phase-integration assertion, while the completion link proves vanishing outside one common closed support set and before activation; the latter is weaker than the paper's separate assertion for every instantaneous support.

ties.name: TorusEuler.wavePotential_zero_of_profile_zero
ties.plain: The potential preserves label support

rows.fidelity_note: The formal theorem says that if $V(s)=0$ for every phase at one fixed label, then $Q[V](s)=0$ there. This proves that phase integration does not enlarge label support. It does not prove the claim for the spatial curl $C[V]$, which requires locality of differentiation outside the support.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. Phase integration preserves support, and locality of the curl supplies the remaining support step.

rows.name: TorusEuler.wavePotential_zero_of_profile_zero
rows.plain: The potential preserves label support
rows.annotation: The relevant support is the set of labels where at least one phase of $V$ is nonzero. If $V(t,a,\cdot)=0$, the entire phase primitive is zero at that label. It would not suffice to know $V(t,a,k_*\cdot a)=0$, since the primitive uses other phases at the same label.

rows.fidelity_note: The paper states support preservation at each time. The formal theorem assumes that $V$ vanishes before activation and outside one common closed label set $S$ throughout $[0,T]$, and proves the same for $C[V]$. This gives the construction's common-support conclusion under a stronger temporal support hypothesis, rather than a separate assertion for every instantaneous support.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The common support set is the localization property needed for every constructed stage.

rows.annotation: Outside the closed label support the potential is zero in a neighborhood at every phase, so its slow curl is also zero there. The same argument applies on the open interval before activation. This support statement concerns the oscillation and its completion; it does not localize the phase-independent correction found by the endpoint inverse.

citations.supports: Evenness of the transported coefficients and the seed under reflection of labels.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: If the parent velocity is odd, its flow is odd and the matrices $M=D_xU\circ X$ and covectors $\kappa=(D_aX)^{-T}k_*$ are even in the label. With an even initial amplitude, the equations (3.2) at $a$ and $-a$ are identical, so uniqueness makes the seed even for $t\in[t_0,T]$. This parity is needed to obtain an odd physical velocity from the odd phase profile. One formal link supplies only evenness of the coefficients, and the other proves seed evenness for the particular projected initial amplitude in (5.4); their weaker verdicts reflect these separate or more restricted conclusions.

ties.name: TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.even_materialGradient_and_labelWaveVector

The paper uses the smooth periodic setting, which supplies that Lipschitz condition. This establishes the first inference in the sentence, but does not state the seed's parity.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The parity of the coefficients, profile and inverse flow combines to give the odd Eulerian wave.

rows.plain: Evenness of the transported velocity gradient and wave covector
rows.annotation: Oddness of $U$ and uniqueness give $X(t,-a)=-X(t,a)$ and $X(t,0)=0$. Differentiating the two odd maps $X$ and $U$ gives even matrices $D_aX$ and $D_xU\circ X$. Hence $M$ and $\kappa=(D_aX)^{-T}k_*$ are even; the seed ODE has the same coefficients at opposite labels.

rows.fidelity_note: Assume continuous even coefficient fields $M,\kappa$ and nonvanishing of $\kappa$ throughout $[t_0,T]$. The formal theorem proves evenness of the selected seed whose initial value is the projection of the central amplitude onto $\kappa(t_0,a)^\perp$. The paper allows any even initial seed. This result also assumes, rather than derives, the coefficient evenness supplied by the preceding row.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The construction needs the selected smooth seed and profile family, for which the asserted identity is proved.

rows.name: TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.even_amplitude

rows.annotation: At activation, the center amplitude is projected onto $\kappa(t_0,a)^\perp$ at each label. Since the normal is even, the projection is the same at $a$ and $-a$. The two seed equations then have the same coefficients and initial value, so their solutions are equal by uniqueness.

citations.supports: Parity of the leading profile, potential, correction and evaluated velocity.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For an odd parent flow, an even envelope and an even seed, $A_1(t,-a,-s)=-A_1(t,a,s)$ because $F_0$ is odd. Its normalized primitive is even, and the slow curl of the corresponding even potential has the same odd joint label-and-phase parity as $A_1$. Evaluation at $s=k_*\cdot a$ and the odd inverse flow therefore gives an odd completed physical velocity, as used throughout the iteration. The formal completion theorem proves the correction's parity from smoothness, periodicity and zero phase mean, while the evaluation theorem transfers already assumed joint parity to physical space; each is weaker than the whole parity argument and the latter does not include the periodic extension across the cell boundary.

ties.name: TorusEuler.HierarchySmoothProfile.profileCompletion_reflectionOdd

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The parity of the coefficients, profile and inverse flow combines to give the odd Eulerian wave.

rows.annotation: Use joint reflection $(a,s)\mapsto(-a,-s)$. With $\kappa$ even, $Q[V]$ is even; differentiation at fixed phase by the even inverse deformation makes $\mathbf d\times Q[V]$ odd.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal theorem proves oddness of the directly evaluated field when the inverse label map is odd and the supplied profile satisfies $f(t,-a,-s)=-f(t,a,s)$. It assumes that joint parity rather than deriving it from $F_0$ and $P_0$, and the centered-cell periodic extension is not part of this particular evaluation theorem.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The parity of the coefficients, profile and inverse flow combines to give the odd Eulerian wave.

rows.annotation: The inverse flow is odd, so physical reflection sends $(a,k_*\cdot a)$ to $(-a,-k_*\cdot a)$. Joint oddness of the completed profile becomes oddness of its evaluation. The symmetric cell extension preserves this relation across the torus.

citations.supports: The activation cutoff and the constant first-wave choice.

explanation.text: On $[0,T]$, choose a smooth $\widetilde\chi$ with values in $[0,1]$ that vanishes for $t<t_0$, where $0\le t_0<T$. Multiplication by this function activates a later wave without introducing a discontinuity at its starting time; for the first wave, $t_0=0$ and $\widetilde\chi=1$ need no transition. Section 3.1 then separates the resulting cutoff derivative from the homogeneous wave equation. The formal links separately encode the admissible cutoff and choose the constant first-wave cutoff, so each is weaker than the combined sentence; the admissibility conditions alone do not require eventual equality to one.

explanation.text: For the leading profile and pressure of (3.3), a smooth time-only cutoff gives $V_1=\widetilde\chi A_1$, $\mathsf p_1=\widetilde\chi\mathsf p[A_1]$ and $C[V_1]=\widetilde\chi C[A_1]$. citations.supports: The cutoff-derivative residual and the reason for controlling the wave during activation.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For the activated completed wave $\widetilde\chi(A_1+C[A_1])$, differentiation along the parent flow produces $R_{\widetilde\chi}=\widetilde\chi'(A_1+C[A_1])$. This is the product-rule term left in addition to the unactivated profile equations; a time-only multiplier contributes no new spatial derivative. Its size is therefore controlled by the wave during activation, which explains why the later construction switches the wave on before it reaches its peak. The formal link proves the identity for the selected smooth localized seed and periodic extension with $0<h\le1$, $0<\ell_*<1/4$ and nonzero $\kappa$, so it is weaker than the general identity and supplies no size estimate by itself.

No estimate on the size of this residual follows from the identity alone. The seed regularity hypothesis requires $0\le t_0<T$, $0<h\le1$, envelope radius $0<\ell_*<1/4$, and $M$, $\kappa$ and $\mathbf a$ jointly smooth on $[t_0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$ with $\kappa\ne0$ there.

On the part of the phase circle where the slope is negative, its positive eigenvalue is at most $Chp_{\rm w}|\kappa|^2$. citations.supports: The profile estimates, their uniform quantifiers and the signed higher-derivative scaling.

explanation.text: For every $0<h\le1$, Lemma 3.1 requires $F_h'(0)=1$, $-Ch\le F_h'\le1$, $\|F_h\|_\infty\le Ch$ and $\|\partial_s^jF_h\|_\infty\le C_jh^{1-j}$ for integers $j\ge2$. The constants are selected before the width and phase, so narrowing the profile preserves the central slope while increasing higher derivatives at the stated rate. The formal existential theorem matches these bounds, and the results for the fixed bump-based family strengthen existence by identifying its witnesses; the bare property list only specifies the requirements and has a different logical role. All the formal exponents $1-j$ are signed integers, so the negative powers are retained, and bounds at every phase express the displayed supremum bounds.

explanation.text: For $0<h\le1$, the normalized slope in the proof of Lemma 3.1 is even and has zero mean over a period. Integrating it from zero makes $F_h$ odd and period one, and oddness over a centered period gives the zero mean needed for a periodic primitive $P_h$. Subtracting the mean of that primitive fixes the pressure normalization used in (3.3). The five formal links establish these pieces separately—oddness of $F_h$, its periodicity, the chosen primitive, its periodicity and its zero mean—so each is weaker than the whole sentence even though together they support it.

citations.supports: Volume preservation of the parent flow and its role in the physical divergence equation.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For a smooth divergence-free periodic parent $u$, the flow $X(t,a)$ satisfies $\det D_aX(t,a)=1$ and $X(0,a)=a$. The determinant follows from the differentiated flow equation $F_t=MF$ and $\operatorname{tr}M=\operatorname{div}u\circ X=0$. This volume preservation is later used in the Piola identity that transfers the divergence constraint from label velocity to Eulerian correction. The formal theorem is stronger in scope because it proves determinant one for any pair of times of a jointly twice-differentiable periodic incompressible flow, without the pressure bound or an Euler-equation assumption.

The formal statement proves $\det D_aX_{s,t}(a)=1$ for every pair of times and every label. With $s=0$ this is the volume preservation used in the paper. The identity requires $C^2$ regularity, whereas the paper assumes smoothness; no Euler equation or curvature bound is required.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. Volume preservation and periodic integration by parts provide the pressure cancellation together.

rows.name: TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.det_labelDerivative

rows.annotation: The deformation of a small volume element is governed by $F_t=MF$, $F=D_aX$. This gives both the change of measure and the divergence transformation used in the inverse.
