rows.plain: Kinetic coefficient derivative minus vorticity coefficient
rows.annotation: From $F_t=MF$ we get $K_t=F_t^TF+F^TF_t$ and $\Omega=F_t^TF-F^TF_t$. Hence $K_t-\Omega=2F^TF_t$, and $Kv_t+2F^TF_tv=(Kv)_t-\Omega v$. This identity permits integration of the momentum equation with no time derivative on the source or on $\Omega$.

citations.supports: The momentum residual and its role in the pressure-minus-residual-gradient identity.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Section 4, definition of the residual preceding (4.3)

explanation.text: For smooth velocity $u$ and pressure $p$ on $I=[0,T]$, set $R=u_t+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\nabla p$. This is the momentum error of the parent, so $R=0$ would mean that its momentum equation is exactly Euler. Differentiating this definition yields (4.3), which allows the endpoint argument to handle parents with nonzero residual. The formal expression matches the definition with derivatives within $I$ at its endpoints; the expression by itself imposes neither differentiability nor $R=0$, and its default derivative values outside the smooth setting must not be interpreted as a momentum equation.

ties.name: TorusEuler.momentumResidual
ties.plain: The Euler momentum residual

rows.fidelity_note: For a velocity $U(t,x)$, pressure $p(t,x)$ and specified time set $I$, the formal expression defines $R(t,x)=\partial_tU(t,x)+DU(t,x)U(t,x)+\nabla p(t,x)$. Its time derivative is taken within $I$ while the label $x$ is fixed. On the smooth closed slab of the paper, this is precisely the momentum residual, with one-sided derivatives at the endpoints. The definition itself asserts neither regularity nor $R=0$; outside differentiability hypotheses, the derivative expressions have default value zero.
rows.name: TorusEuler.momentumResidual
rows.plain: The Euler momentum residual
rows.annotation:
With the pressure convention $\Delta p_U=-\operatorname{tr}((
abla U)^2)$ in Section 5.1, $\operatorname{div}R_U=0$ since $\operatorname{div}((U\cdot
abla)U)=\operatorname{tr}((
abla U)^2)$. Thus $R_U$ is the actual defect of the projected Euler equation. Its gradient enters Equation (4.3), whereas the field itself is canceled by the first mean source.

citations.supports: The material-gradient identity and the effective tensor controlling the endpoint energy.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text:
For smooth $u,p$ and a trajectory $X$, let $M=
abla u\circ X$ and $R=u_t+u\cdot
abla u+
abla p$. Differentiating the residual in space and then following the trajectory gives $M_t+M^2+(D^2p)\circ X=(
abla R)\circ X$, hence $H^\#=(D^2p-
abla R)\circ X$. This is why the one-sided bound needed for the inverse includes the residual gradient when the parent is only approximate. The formal result proves this local identity with a twice-differentiable velocity and a differentiable pressure gradient, without incompressibility or periodicity, so it is stronger in scope than the paper's smooth torus setting.

ties.name: TorusEuler.endpointHessian_eq_pressureHessian_sub_residualGradient
ties.plain: Effective Hessian equals pressure Hessian minus residual gradient

rows.fidelity_note: Let $0<T$, $t\in[0,T]$, and let $u$ be jointly $C^2$ on the closed slab. Suppose $X_t=u(t,X)$ at the time in question and the spatial pressure gradient is differentiable at $X(t)$. With $M=Du\circ X$, $R=u_t+Du\,u+\nabla p$ and the fixed-label derivative $M_t$, the formal identity is $-(M_t+M^2)=(D^2p-DR)\circ X$. It is a local trajectory identity, so no incompressibility or actual solution of Euler is needed. Smooth $u,p$ in the paper satisfy the stated weaker regularity assumptions.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The local residual identity applies to the smooth approximate parents used in the construction.

rows.name: TorusEuler.endpointHessian_eq_pressureHessian_sub_residualGradient
rows.plain: Effective Hessian equals pressure Hessian minus residual gradient
rows.annotation: The pressure condition in Theorem 7.1 is chosen so that Equation (4.3) can be used even after truncation. If the parent has frequencies at most $2\mathsf D$, then $R_U$ has frequencies at most $4\mathsf D$ and $\|\nabla R_U\|_\infty\le C\mathsf D\|R_U\|_\infty$. In the induction the parent velocity has frequencies at most $2\mu^5$ and the preceding residual has size $\lambda^{-3}$, giving $H^\#\le(2/N+C\mu^5\lambda^{-3})I\le I$.

citations.supports: The displacement product rule, its inverse formula and the role of the Sobolev test class.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: Fix a label, take $z\in H^1_0(0,T;\mathbb R^3)$ and put $\xi=Fz$ with $F=D_aX$ and $F_t=MF$. The product rule gives $\xi_t=M\xi+Fz_t$ almost everywhere, and invertibility yields $z_t=F^{-1}(\xi_t-M\xi)$. This relates label displacement to physical first variation and leads to the norm comparison (4.6). The formal link proves only the first identity at times where the supplied derivatives exist pointwise; it does not state the inverse formula or the full Sobolev product rule, which explains the weaker verdict.

ties.name: TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_endpointDisplacement
ties.plain: Time derivative of the physical displacement after the label change

rows.fidelity_note: At a time where $F_t=MF$ and $z_t=v$ exist within the specified time set, the formal statement proves $(Fz)_t=M(Fz)+Fv$. Thus $F=D_aX$ and $\xi=Fz$ give the first identity in (4.4). The statement works in a real normed space and does not require $F$ to be invertible. It does not state $v=F^{-1}(\xi_t-M\xi)$ or the almost-everywhere product rule for arbitrary $z\in H^1_0$; these require, respectively, invertibility and the Sobolev argument.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The product rule becomes the displacement equation once the flow identities are inserted.

rows.name: TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_endpointDisplacement
rows.plain: Time derivative of the physical displacement after the label change
rows.annotation: The quantity $Fz_t=\xi_t-M\xi$ is the velocity relative to the motion of the parent: if $z$ is constant along time then the physical displacement changes by $M\xi$ alone. This is the product rule used to change variables in the energy, and it remains valid for a Sobolev path with smooth $F$.

citations.supports: The first-variation equation and identification of the pulled-back correction with label velocity.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For flows $X^\varepsilon$ of $u+\varepsilon b$ sharing the initial label $a$, the variation $\xi=\partial_\varepsilon X^\varepsilon|_0$ satisfies $\xi_t=M\xi+b\circ X$ and $\xi(0)=0$, where $M=\nabla u\circ X$. This is (1.5), obtained by differentiating the trajectory equation with respect to the velocity perturbation. Comparing it with (4.4) gives $b\circ X=Fz_t$, the relation used to construct the correction from its endpoint displacement. The formal theorem proves the parameter differentiability and this same equation under explicit uniform Lipschitz and continuity assumptions, all available for the smooth periodic fields considered here.

ties.name: TorusEuler.labelFlow_firstVariation
ties.plain: The first variation of particle motion

rows.fidelity_note: The formal theorem proves $\xi_t=M\xi+b\circ X$ and $\xi(0)=0$ by differentiating the perturbed flow. Subtracting $M\xi$ and applying $(D_aX)^{-1}$ in (4.4) gives the quoted $z_t$ identity. The formal theorem supplies (1.5), one of those two ingredients.
rows.name: TorusEuler.labelFlow_firstVariation
rows.plain: The first variation of particle motion
rows.annotation: The extra factor $F^{-1}$ is essential in Equation (4.4): a velocity at two different points of the same trajectory is compared in the same label coordinates before integration. For the solenoidal constraint, $v=F^{-1}(b\circ X)$ is a pullback under a map of determinant one; Piola gives $\operatorname{div}_a v=(\operatorname{div}_x b)\circ X=0$.

citations.supports: Invertibility of the flow deformation and equivalence of the terminal displacement constraints.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The deformation $F=D_aX(t,a)$ of a smooth parent flow is invertible, with inverse $D_xX(t,\cdot)^{-1}$ evaluated at $X(t,a)$. Differentiate the forward and reverse flow identities to obtain both $F^{-1}F=I$ and $FF^{-1}=I$. Consequently $\xi(T)=F(T)z(T)=0$ is equivalent to $z(T)=0$, so the terminal constraint can be imposed in label coordinates. The formal theorem proves both inverse identities for any pair of times of a twice-differentiable periodic flow, without incompressibility or the bound on $H^\#$, giving a stronger statement than the quoted invertibility assertion.

ties.name: TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.labelDerivative_inverse
ties.plain: Inverse of the label derivative of the flow

rows.fidelity_note: For the flow $X_{s,t}$ of a jointly $C^2$ unit-periodic velocity, the formal statement proves both inverse identities $D X_{t,s}(X_{s,t}(a))D X_{s,t}(a)=I$ and $D X_{s,t}(a)D X_{t,s}(X_{s,t}(a))=I$. Thus $D_aX$ is invertible in the paper’s smooth setting. Incompressibility and a bound on $H^\#$ are not needed for this assertion. The inverse is the derivative of the reverse flow at the transported point.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The reverse flow gives the inverse deformation used in the displacement estimates.

rows.name: TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.labelDerivative_inverse
rows.plain: Inverse of the label derivative of the flow
rows.annotation: No curvature assumption is needed to pass between the two endpoint conditions. Differentiating the inverse-flow identities gives $F^{-1}F=FF^{-1}=I$; hence $F(t,a)z(t,a)=0$ if and only if $z(t,a)=0$. In particular, a zero terminal displacement is independent of which of these two coordinate systems is used.

citations.supports: The terminal integral representation of a zero-endpoint displacement.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For $z\in H^1_0(0,T;\mathbb R^3)$, put $v=z_t\in L^2(0,T)$, so $z(t)=\int_0^tv$ and $\int_0^Tv=0$. Splitting this zero integral at $t$ gives $z(t)=-\int_t^Tv(s)\,ds$. Section 4.1 uses this terminal representation to gain the factor $T-t$ in the pointwise Poincaré bound. The formal identity matches the argument and needs only integrability and zero time mean; its integral is justified by those hypotheses rather than by any default assignment to a nonintegrable expression.

ties.name: TorusEuler.endpointPrimitive_eq_neg_terminal_integral
ties.plain: The primitive from the terminal time

rows.fidelity_note: Let $v$ be integrable on $[0,T]$ with $\int_0^T v=0$, and put $z(t)=Jv(t)=\int_0^tv$. Then $z(t)=-\int_t^Tv$ for every $t\in[0,T]$. A paper displacement $z\in H^1_0$ has $v=z_t\in L^2$, zero time integral and $z=Jv$, so the formal identity gives exactly the displayed terminal representation. Integrability is a premise; the identity does not use a default value for a nonintegrable function.
rows.name: TorusEuler.endpointPrimitive_eq_neg_terminal_integral
rows.plain: The primitive from the terminal time
rows.annotation: The map $v\mapsto Jv$ is a bijection between $L^2$ paths with zero integral and $H^1_0(I;\mathbb R^3)$ displacements. Its inverse is differentiation. In particular $Jv(t)=-\int_t^T v$ for such paths, which gives the terminal Poincaré bound and also the adjoint identity $J^*v=-Jv$ used in Appendix A.

citations.supports: The terminal Cauchy–Schwarz estimates and their exact constant.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For $z\in H^1_0(0,T;\mathbb R^3)$, Cauchy–Schwarz applied to $z(t)=-\int_t^Tz_t$ gives $|z(t)|^2\le(T-t)\int_0^T|z_t|^2$. Integrating in $t$ gives $\int_0^T|z|^2\le(T^2/2)\int_0^T|z_t|^2$, which supplies the factor $1/2$ in Lemma 4.1 when $T\le1$. The formal statements use $z=Jv$ with $v\in L^2$ of zero time mean, an exact description of these endpoint displacements. Each is labelled different because it proves only one of the two inequalities while allowing arbitrary interval length and a general complete real normed target, rather than stating the displayed pair solely in $\mathbb R^3$.

ties.name: TorusEuler.endpointPrimitive_terminal_poincare_pointwise
ties.plain: Pointwise displacement bound from the terminal endpoint

rows.fidelity_note: The paper display contains a pointwise and an integrated estimate for $z\in H^1_0([0,T];\mathbb R^3)$. The formal statement gives only $\|Jv(t)\|^2\le(T-t)\int_0^T\|v\|^2$ for a zero-mean square-integrable velocity. It permits a general real normed target and needs no upper bound $T\le1$, but the integral inequality is a separate result. Here $Jv(t)=\int_0^tv(s)\,ds$, so $z=Jv$ has both zero endpoint values.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The pointwise and integrated Sobolev estimates together provide the exact coercivity constant.

rows.name: TorusEuler.endpointPrimitive_terminal_poincare_pointwise
rows.plain: Pointwise displacement bound from the terminal endpoint
rows.annotation: Cauchy–Schwarz on the tail interval gives $|z(t)|^2\le(T-t)\int_t^T|v(s)|^2\,ds$. The displayed bound replaces the tail norm by the full $L^2$ norm. It holds for the absolutely continuous representative of an $H^1$ path, at every time and at any fixed label.

rows.fidelity_note: The paper display contains two inequalities. The formal statement gives the integrated bound $\int_0^T\|Jv\|^2\le(T^2/2)\int_0^T\|v\|^2$ for every zero-mean square-integrable velocity and $T\ge0$, in a general real normed space. It retains the exact constant and permits longer intervals, but does not also state the pointwise inequality. Here $Jv(t)=\int_0^tv(s)\,ds$, so $z=Jv$ has both zero endpoint values.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The pointwise and integrated Sobolev estimates together provide the exact coercivity constant.

rows.name: TorusEuler.endpointPrimitive_terminal_poincare_integral
rows.plain: Integral Poincaré bound for a displacement vanishing at the endpoints
rows.annotation: After bounding by the full time integral, the only factor depending on $t$ is $T-t$, whose integral is $T^2/2$. The argument applies to the physical displacement $\xi$ as well as to $z$ since $F$ preserves the two zero traces. It is the estimate for $\xi$ that bounds the curvature contribution below.

citations.supports: Conversion of the physical-displacement derivative bound into a label-velocity bound.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For $0<T\le1$, $\xi=Fz$, $z\in H^1_0$ and $\|F^{-1}\|\le D_-$, equation (4.4) gives $\|z_t\|_2\le D_-(\|\xi_t\|_2+\|M\|_\infty\|\xi\|_2)$. Applying (4.5) to $\xi$ and squaring yields (4.6) with factor $D_-^2(1+\|M\|_\infty)^2$, allowing the physical energy bound to control label velocity. The first formal helper instead assumes a continuous derivative and only the terminal endpoint, so its test class differs from the paper's full Sobolev class. The second result covers every zero-mean square-integrable velocity $v=z_t$ and even a general complete real Hilbert space, giving the stronger verdict and the required Sobolev estimate.

ties.name: TorusEuler.integral_endpointLabelVelocity_norm_sq_le
ties.plain: Physical displacement energy bounds the squared label velocity

rows.fidelity_note: Let $0\le T\le1$, $D_-,L\ge0$, $F_t=MF$, $GF=I$, $\|G\|\le D_-$ and $\|M\|\le L$, with $M$ continuous. Assume $z_t=v$ pointwise, $v$ continuous and $z(T)=0$. For $\xi=Fz$, the formal estimate is $\int_0^T|v|^2\le D_-^2(1+L)^2\int_0^T|\xi_t|^2$. The paper’s class is all $H^1_0$ displacements. This helper requires a continuous derivative but drops $z(0)=0$, so neither test class contains the other as stated. The full Sobolev result is a separate declaration.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The continuous-path helper is supplemented by the full Sobolev estimate used in the endpoint argument.

rows.name: TorusEuler.integral_endpointLabelVelocity_norm_sq_le
rows.plain: Physical displacement energy bounds the squared label velocity
rows.annotation: From Equation (4.4), $\|z_t\|_2\le D_-(\|\xi_t\|_2+\|M\|_\infty\|\xi\|_2)$. The terminal Poincaré inequality bounds $\|\xi\|_2$ by $(T/\sqrt2)\|\xi_t\|_2\le\|\xi_t\|_2$. Squaring gives Equation (4.6) for differentiable paths; the Sobolev version uses the same inequality almost everywhere.

rows.fidelity_note: Let $0<T\le1$ and let $F,G,M$ act on a complete real Hilbert space, with $F_t=MF$, $M$ continuous, $GF=I$, $\|G\|\le D_-$ and $\|M\|\le L$, where $D_-,L\ge0$. For every $v\in L^2(0,T)$ with $\int_0^Tv=0$, put $z(t)=\int_0^tv$, $\xi=Fz$ and $\xi_t=M\xi+Fv$ almost everywhere. The formal statement gives $\|v\|_{L^2}^2\le D_-^2(1+L)^2\|\xi_t\|_{L^2}^2$. This is (4.6) for every paper displacement and also allows a general complete real Hilbert space.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. Zero-mean square-integrable velocities represent exactly the paper’s zero-endpoint Sobolev displacements.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S34A.integral_norm_sq_le_displacement
rows.plain: Physical kinetic energy bounds the squared label velocity
rows.annotation: For an $L^2$ path $v$ with zero integral, take its absolutely continuous primitive $z$. Then $Fz$ has weak derivative $MFz+Fv$ by the Sobolev product rule. The same Poincaré and triangle inequalities give Equation (4.6) in this class. Thus the estimate can be used for a time-path solution of Appendix A, before recovering its continuous representative.

citations.supports: The label quadratic form is the left-hand side of the integrated physical-displacement identity.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: At a fixed label, let $F=D_aX$, $K=F^TF$, $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$ and $z(t)=\int_0^tv(s)\,ds$. The label energy is $\int_0^T(\langle Kv,v\rangle+\langle\Omega v,z\rangle)\,dt$, which is the expression to be made coercive for the endpoint inverse. Equation (4.7) converts it into the kinetic-minus-$H^\#$ energy of $\xi=Fz$ when both displacement endpoints vanish. The formal expression matches this energy for square-integrable $v$ and continuous coefficients, but its definition alone neither imposes zero time mean nor asserts positivity; those enter the later coercivity theorem.

ties.name: TorusEuler.endpointL2Energy
ties.plain: The label energy on velocities

rows.fidelity_note: For $T\ge0$, continuous operator fields $F,M$ and $v\in L^2(0,T;H)$ in a complete real Hilbert space, put $z(t)=\int_0^tv$, $K=F^TF$ and $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$. The formal expression defines $\int_0^T(\langle Kv,v\rangle+\langle\Omega v,z\rangle)\,dt$. At $H=\mathbb R^3$ and $F=D_aX$ this is the paper’s label form with $v=z_t$. The definition does not require $\int_0^Tv=0$ and asserts no positivity; those are additional hypotheses of the coercivity theorem.
rows.name: TorusEuler.endpointL2Energy
rows.plain: The label energy on velocities
rows.annotation: For a test velocity $v$ of zero time integral, $J^*v(t)=\int_t^T v=-Jv(t)$. Thus $\langle (K-J\Omega)v,v\rangle=\int_I(Kv\cdot v+\Omega v\cdot Jv)$. Appendix A inverts precisely this operator after projecting onto solenoidal paths of zero time mean; Equation (4.7) gives its lower bound.

citations.supports: The energy identity before removal of the boundary derivative.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For differentiable $F,z,M$ with $F_t=MF$, put $\xi=Fz$, $K=F^TF$, $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$ and $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)$. Expanding the two label-energy terms and applying the product rule gives $Kz_t\cdot z_t+\Omega z_t\cdot z=|\xi_t|^2-H^\#\xi\cdot\xi-\partial_t(\xi\cdot M\xi)$. The last term will disappear on integrating between zero displacement endpoints, giving (4.7). The formal link is an algebraic identity for supplied matrices and vectors, with the expanded three-term expression in place of the derivative; its different verdict records that the derivative identifications $F_t=MF$, $z_t=v$ and the supplied matrix equal to $M_t$ must still be made.

ties.name: TorusEuler.endpointLabelEnergy_eq
ties.plain: The displacement energy identity

rows.fidelity_note: The paper identifies the last term as $\partial_t(\xi\cdot M\xi)$. The formal statement is an algebraic identity for arbitrary operators $F,M,N$ and vectors $z,v$, using $\xi=Fz$ and $\eta=M\xi+Fv$. Its last term is $\eta\cdot M\xi+\xi\cdot N\xi+\xi\cdot M\eta$. To obtain the displayed derivative one must additionally know $F_t=MF$, $z_t=v$ and $N=M_t$. Those derivative facts are not proved by this identity.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The algebraic integrand identity becomes the energy identity after inserting the flow and path derivatives.

rows.name: TorusEuler.endpointLabelEnergy_eq
rows.plain: The displacement energy identity
rows.annotation: After the two $|M\xi|^2$ terms cancel, the mixed terms are $-\xi_t\cdot M\xi-\xi\cdot M\xi_t$. This is $-\partial_t(\xi\cdot M\xi)+\xi\cdot M_t\xi$. The remaining square-matrix term $\xi\cdot M^2\xi$ therefore combines with the last term into $-\xi\cdot H^\#\xi$. The identity uses neither symmetry of $M$ nor an equation for the parent.

citations.supports: Integration of the energy identity, vanishing boundary term and extension by density.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Section 4.2, equation (4.7) and its preceding calculation

explanation.text: Let $z\in H^1_0(0,T;\mathbb R^3)$ and $\xi=Fz$, with $F=D_aX$, $F_t=MF$, $K=F^TF$, $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$ and $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)$. The pointwise energy calculation leaves the boundary term $[\xi\cdot M\xi]_0^T$, which is zero because both endpoint displacements vanish. Integration and density therefore give (4.7), the equality on which the coercivity estimate rests. The linked formal identity assumes pointwise derivatives with continuous $z_t$ and $M_t$, so it proves the smooth-path step but is weaker than the paper's extension to every $H^1_0$ displacement; the full square-integrable coercivity result is supplied separately.

ties.name: TorusEuler.integral_endpointLabelEnergy_eq
ties.plain: Integrating the displacement identity

rows.fidelity_note: Let $T\ge0$, $F_t=MF$, $M_t=N$, $z_t=v$ pointwise on $[0,T]$, with $N,v$ continuous and $z(0)=z(T)=0$. Set $K=F^TF$, $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$, $H^\#=-(N+M^2)$ and $\xi=Fz$. The formal identity is $\int_0^T(\langle Kv,v\rangle+\langle\Omega v,z\rangle)=\int_0^T(|\xi_t|^2-\langle H^\#\xi,\xi\rangle)$. The boundary term vanishes because both displacement endpoints vanish. The displayed paper identity is then extended to $H^1_0$ by density; this helper states only the continuously differentiable case.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The continuously differentiable energy identity is extended to the Sobolev class in the coercivity theorem.

rows.name: TorusEuler.integral_endpointLabelEnergy_eq
rows.plain: Integrating the displacement identity
rows.annotation: The integrated boundary term is $-[\xi\cdot M\xi]_0^T$, which vanishes at both ends. To pass from smooth velocities to $L^2$ velocities of zero integral, subtract the time mean from each smooth approximant. Their primitives retain the two traces, and the operations $v\mapsto FJv$ and $v\mapsto MFJv+Fv$ are continuous in $L^2$. This gives Equation (4.7) without a classical time derivative of $v$.

citations.supports: The one-sided quadratic-form hypothesis and its use for the full Sobolev displacement class.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Section 4.2, Lemma 4.1 and its proof; equation (4.5)

explanation.text: On $I=[0,T]$, $0<T\le1$, assume $\langle H^\#(t,a)w,w\rangle\le|w|^2$ for every time, label and vector, where $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)$. This is an upper bound on a quadratic form, not a bound on the absolute matrix norm and not a consequence of incompressibility. Combined with the endpoint Poincaré estimate (4.5), it gives Lemma 4.1 and hence the positive energy needed for Theorem 4.2. The formal hypotheses encode this same one-sided condition, and represent $H^1_0$ displacements by primitives of zero-mean $L^2$ velocities, so the matching verdict does not conceal a restriction to smooth test paths.

ties.name: TorusEuler.paper_mean_hardy
ties.plain: Displacement coercivity in a real Hilbert space

rows.fidelity_note: Let $0<T\le1$ and let $F,M$ be continuously differentiable operator fields on a complete real Hilbert space, with $F_t=MF$ and $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)\le I$. For $v\in L^2(0,T)$ with $\int_0^T v=0$, put $z(t)=\int_0^t v$, $\xi=Fz$ and $\xi_t=M\xi+Fv$ almost everywhere. Then $\int_0^T\langle H^\#\xi,\xi\rangle\le\frac12\int_0^T|\xi_t|^2$, and $\int_0^T(\langle F^TFv,v\rangle+\langle F^T(M^T-M)Fv,z\rangle)\ge\frac12\int_0^T|\xi_t|^2$. Invertibility and a flow interpretation of $F$ are not assumed; this includes the paper’s three-dimensional test class.
rows.name: TorusEuler.paper_mean_hardy
rows.plain: Displacement coercivity in a real Hilbert space
rows.annotation: The hypothesis is an upper bound on the symmetric part of $H^\#$, not on $\|M_t+M^2\|$. For instance a large negative eigenvalue does not reduce the lower bound in (4.7). The construction in Section 3 exploits exactly this asymmetry: a large negative contribution to the pressure Hessian is compatible with a small upper bound.

rows.fidelity_note: On $I=[0,T]$, $0<T\le1$, let $U$ be smooth, unit-periodic and divergence free, $X$ its flow from time zero, $F=D_aX$, $M=(DU)\circ X$, $K=F^TF$, $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$, and $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)\le I$ as quadratic forms. At each label, every $z\in H^1_0(0,T;\mathbb R^3)$ is represented by $v=z_t\in L^2$ with zero time integral. With $\xi=Fz$, the formal statement gives $\int\langle H^\#\xi,\xi\rangle\le\tfrac12\int|\xi_t|^2$ and $\int(\langle Kv,v\rangle+\langle\Omega v,z\rangle)\ge\tfrac12\int|\xi_t|^2$. The upper bound on $H^\#$ is a hypothesis at every time, label and test vector, not a consequence of incompressibility. This is the pair of conclusions in Lemma 4.1.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_4_1
rows.plain: Coercive displacement energy for the parent flow
rows.annotation: The test functions in the statement are all $H^1_0$ paths at a single label. Lean expresses this class using $v\in L^2(I)$ with $\int_Iv=0$, then reconstructs the path as $Jv$. These descriptions are equivalent; neither imposes a momentum equation on the test path.

rows.fidelity_note: On $I=[0,T]$, $0<T\le1$, let $U$ be smooth, unit-periodic and divergence free, $X$ its flow from time zero, $F=D_aX$, $M=(DU)\circ X$, $K=F^TF$, $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$, and $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)\le I$ as quadratic forms. explanation.text: For a fixed smooth force and a smooth incompressible parent with $0<T\le1$ and $H^\#\le I$, the conditions $z(0)=z(T)=0$ determine the endpoint solution uniquely. Since $L(0)=0$ and $F(0)=I$, the selected initial velocity is $b(0)=c$, the constant solenoidal field in (4.9). explanation.text: For a smooth deformation $F=D_aX$ with $F_t=MF$ and a smooth label velocity $v$, put $B=Fv$. Assume $\|F^{-1}\|_\infty\le D\ge1$, $\|M\|_\infty\le L$, $\|K\|_\infty\le K_0$ and $\|D_aK\|_\infty\le K_1$. No bound on $\Omega$ is needed. Assume the spatial inverse assertion of Lemma A.2 with constants $C_2\ge0$ and $p_2\in\mathbb N$. Then at each time the map $w\mapsto\mathbb P(K(t)w)$ on solenoidal $C^{0,1/2}$ fields is invertible, and $\|(\mathbb PK(t))^{-1}\mathbb P\|\le C_2(2+D^2+K_0+2K_1)^{p_2}\|\mathbb P\|$. citations.supports: The precise Fourier convention and meaning of a frequency cutoff.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Section 5.1, opening definition of frequency support

explanation.text: On the unit torus, frequencies are the integer vectors $\xi\in\mathbb Z^3$ in the modes $e^{2\pi i\xi\cdot x}$. Saying that a continuous field is supported on frequencies at most $\Lambda$ means that its Fourier coefficient is zero whenever the Euclidean length $|\xi|$ exceeds $\Lambda$. The formal condition is the same definition, with real vector components regarded as complex when taking coefficients. This convention determines the spectral radii used in Bernstein estimates and in the later doubling of the residual's frequency bound; the radius does not include an extra factor $2\pi$.

Real vector fields are first viewed as complex vector fields componentwise for Fourier coefficients. The radius is measured in the Euclidean norm of the integer lattice vector, with no additional $2\pi$ included in that radius. This is the paper’s support convention. It is a definition of a frequency condition, not a theorem that a given field meets it.

The band is measured in the spatial variable before composition with the flow.

citations.supports: Regularity and symmetry of the approximate parent velocity.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The parent velocity $U$ is smooth, periodic, odd in space and divergence-free on the closed slab $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$, with $T\le1$. These assumptions give volume-preserving smooth transport and the symmetry used to keep the origin fixed. The linked formal parent requires exactly this selected regularity and symmetry clause, together with the quantitative hypotheses collected later in Section 5. Its pressure is allowed to be any smooth periodic pressure meeting those quantitative hypotheses, so the selected agreement does not mean that every surrounding choice of normalized Poisson pressure is also required there.

explanation.text: The parent is assumed to have no Fourier modes with $|\xi|>2\mathsf D$, uniformly in time. citations.supports: Flow symmetry and the stationary origin of an odd parent velocity.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For an odd spatially Lipschitz velocity, reflecting any trajectory through the origin gives the trajectory with the reflected initial position. Uniqueness therefore makes every flow transition odd, so in particular $X(t,0)=0$. The formal statement is stronger than the quoted fixed-point property because it proves oddness of the entire flow between any two times in the interval. This fixes the center of the localized wave without requiring the parent to solve Euler exactly.

ties.name: TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.odd
ties.plain: Oddness of the parent flow

rows.fidelity_note: For an odd velocity with a uniform spatial Lipschitz bound, the formal statement proves that every transition $X_{s,t}$ is odd. Substituting the zero label gives the claimed fixed origin, for all pairs of times in the interval.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. Oddness of the flow includes the fixed-origin statement, since an odd map sends zero to zero.

rows.name: TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.odd
rows.plain: Oddness of the parent flow
rows.annotation: The reflected curve $-X_{s,t}(a)$ solves the trajectory equation with initial point $-a$, so uniqueness gives $X_{s,t}(-a)=-X_{s,t}(a)$. At $a=0$ the trajectory is fixed. Consequently the strain in the central wave equation is simply $\nabla U(t,0)$, with no moving evaluation point.

citations.supports: The origin of the even label coefficients and the scope of the two linked parity results.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: Since $U(t,\cdot)$ and its flow are odd, their spatial derivatives are even; composing the even field $\nabla U$ with the odd map $X$ makes $M=(\nabla U)\circ X$ even in labels. Thus both $D_aX$ and $M$ have the parity needed for an even seed extension. The first formal link proves only the general fact that the derivative of an odd differentiable map is even, so it is weaker than the two asserted conclusions. The second link proves evenness of $M$ and $\kappa$, rather than of $M$ and $D_aX$, so its different verdict records an actual change of the second quantity.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The derivative parity identity is applied to the smooth odd flow, so its derivative is even and no nondifferentiable case enters the argument.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The coefficient parity statements are combined with evenness of the flow derivative to give the parity used in the expansion.

explanation.text: For a smooth periodic divergence-free parent, the pressure is chosen to satisfy $\Delta p_U=-\operatorname{tr}((\nabla U)^2)$ and to have zero spatial mean. This removes the gradient component of $U\cdot\nabla U$ and makes the remaining momentum residual divergence-free. The formal existence theorem supplies precisely such a smooth periodic pressure for a parent with finite Fourier support, together with the projected residual identity. It does not require $U$ to be an Euler solution or conclude that the residual vanishes; the normalization selects the pressure associated with the given approximate velocity.

explanation.text: For a specified parent velocity and pressure, $R_U=U_t+(\nabla U)U+\nabla p_U$ is the error in the Euler momentum equation. The linked formal definition gives the same three terms, with time differentiation taken on the closed time interval where necessary. In particular, defining $R_U$ does not assert $R_U=0$ or even impose the Poisson normalization on $p_U$. The hierarchy carries this explicit error so that its first mean correction can cancel it.

rows.fidelity_note: For a velocity $U(t,x)$, pressure $p(t,x)$ and specified time set $I$, the formal expression defines $R(t,x)=\partial_tU(t,x)+DU(t,x)U(t,x)+\nabla p(t,x)$. Its time derivative is taken within $I$ while the label $x$ is fixed. On the smooth closed slab of the paper, this is precisely the momentum residual, with one-sided derivatives at the endpoints. explanation.text: With the normalized pressure solving the parent Poisson equation, the residual can be written $R_U=U_t+\mathbb P\operatorname{div}(U\otimes U)$. The formal pressure-existence theorem establishes this identity for the smooth periodic parent, so the same verdict concerns the resulting equality. This representation gives a divergence-free residual and allows its Fourier support to be read directly from the quadratic velocity term.

explanation.text: If $U$ has frequencies at most $2\mathsf D$, then $U\cdot\nabla U$ has frequencies at most $4\mathsf D$ by convolution of Fourier supports. Time differentiation preserves the original band, while the Leray projection does not enlarge a band, so $R_U=U_t+\mathbb P(U\cdot\nabla U)$ has the asserted cutoff. The formal theorem proves exactly this implication for smooth periodic fields with the projected momentum identity supplied. It does not independently choose the pressure; the identity is the hypothesis connecting the given residual to the spectrally controlled terms.

This is why the residual has a Bernstein bound even though no separate bound on $U_t$ is imposed in Equation (5.1).

With $M=Du\circ X$, $R=u_t+Du\,u+\nabla p$ and the fixed-label derivative $M_t$, the formal identity is $-(M_t+M^2)=(D^2p-DR)\circ X$. The formal bounds are $|k_*|/\lambda\le\mathsf D$ and $\mathsf D^{-2}\le|\kappa|/\lambda\le\mathsf D^2$. They omit the lower bound $|k_*|\ge\mathsf D^{-1}\lambda$. That bound follows by applying the unnormalized comparison at $(t_0,0)$. In the normalized statement, $\lambda>0$, $|\kappa(t_0,0)|=\lambda$ and $\mathsf D\ge1$ are required. The unnormalized statement needs no activation frequency.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The transported-covector estimates combine with the activation normalization $|\kappa(t_0,0)|=\lambda$ to give the paper’s comparisons.

rows.name: TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.norm_normalizedLabelWaveVector_bounds
rows.plain: The normalized wave vector bounds
rows.annotation: If $F_0=D_aX(t_0,0)$ and $F=D_aX(t,a)$, then $\kappa(t,a)=F^{-T}F_0^T\kappa(t_0,0)$. Each of these two factors and its inverse has norm at most $\mathsf D$. This gives $\mathsf D^{-2}\le |\kappa|/\lambda\le\mathsf D^2$; the same argument with $F_0^T$ alone bounds the label vector. In particular $\lambda^2/|\kappa|^2\le\mathsf D^4$ throughout the slab.

rows.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be the flow of a jointly $C^2$ unit-periodic velocity on an interval containing $0$ and $t_0$. Suppose both forward and inverse deformation norms are at most $\mathsf D>0$, and put $\kappa(t,a)=DX_{t,0}(X_{0,t}(a))^Tk_*$. The formal statement bounds $|\kappa|$ between $|k_*|/\mathsf D$ and $\mathsf D|k_*|$. It does not mention $\lambda$ or the activation normalization. Substituting $|\kappa(t_0,0)|=\lambda$ and combining these comparisons gives all four bounds in (5.3). In the normalized statement, $\lambda>0$, $|\kappa(t_0,0)|=\lambda$ and $\mathsf D\ge1$ are required. The unnormalized statement needs no activation frequency.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The transported-covector estimates combine with the activation normalization $|\kappa(t_0,0)|=\lambda$ to give the paper’s comparisons.

rows.plain: Bounds for the transported wave vector
rows.annotation: At a fixed label, $\mathsf D^{-1}|k_*|\le|\kappa|\le\mathsf D|k_*|$ follows from the inverse transpose and its inverse. The lower inequality is as important as the upper one: it bounds the denominator in the projection and the pressure coefficient. Apply the same inequalities at launch to relate $|k_*|$ to $\lambda$.

citations.supports: The frequency-dependent width used in the leading wave.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The width of the narrow periodic profile is chosen as $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$. Since the parent frequency satisfies $\lambda\ge1$, this gives $0<h\le1$, the admissible range in the narrow-profile estimates of Section 3. The formal definition is the same real-power expression. This choice supplies the extra factor $h$ in the leading velocity size while leaving the central phase derivative normalized for the rank-one gradient.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.width
ties.plain: Width of the localized phase profile

rows.fidelity_note: The formal expression defines $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$ using a real exponent. For the parent hypothesis $\lambda\ge1$, it has its ordinary meaning $h=1/\sqrt\lambda$ and gives $0<h\le1$, exactly the range required for the phase profiles. The definition is also a function of arbitrary real $\lambda$; analytic conclusions in this section use it only in the positive-frequency range and do not infer profile properties from the definition alone.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.width
rows.plain: Width of the localized phase profile
rows.annotation: The steep portion of $F_h$ occupies a phase interval of size $h$. Since the physical phase gradient is $\kappa$, its local normal thickness at the central particle at launch is $h/\lambda=\lambda^{-3/2}$. More generally the reciprocal of $h/|\kappa|$ is the cost of a fast physical derivative. The radius $\ell_*$ controls a different scale: the extent of the envelope in labels.

citations.supports: The distinct roles of the amplitude weight and the central geometric coupling.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Section 5.1, definitions of $\gamma$ and $\nu$; Section 6, moving-frame equations

explanation.text: The scalar $\gamma(t)=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|$ measures the central amplitude relative to its prescribed peak, whereas $\nu(t,0)$ measures the coupling of its unit direction to the unit wave covector through $M$. The first formal link only defines the amplitude weight, so it is weaker than the displayed pair of definitions and gives no positivity or normalization by itself. The second proves evolution equations for the orthonormal frame formed from $\kappa$ and $\mathbf a$ and contains the stated coupling $\nu$, so its conclusion is different. A second transverse coupling appearing in those frame equations is a separate scalar and must not be confused with the amplitude weight $\gamma$ used in the hierarchy estimates.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.weight
ties.plain: The central amplitude weight

rows.fidelity_note: Given a frequency $\lambda$ and central seed $\mathbf a(t,0)$, define $\gamma(t)=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|$. This is the weight used in the active-interval profile norms: $\|f\|_{[n],\gamma}$ measures spatial and phase derivatives of $f/\gamma$ on $[t_0,T]$. Because $\gamma$ depends only on time, those derivatives do not act on it. The definition itself proves neither positivity nor an upper bound. The parent frequency $\lambda\ge1$, nonzero central seed, and normalization imposed elsewhere give $0<\gamma\le1$. It does not impose the paper’s stronger equality $\max_{[t_0,T]}\gamma=1$. The quotation defines both $\gamma$ and $\nu$. This expression defines only $\gamma$ and gives no formula for $\nu$.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The weight formula and the moving-frame normalization are separate expressions; the nonzero central seed makes the weight positive.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.weight
rows.plain: The central amplitude weight
rows.annotation: The weight is positive on $[t_0,T]$, and division by $\gamma(t)$ compares a correction with the seed at the same time. For a later wave $\gamma(t_0)$ can be very small. A bound on $V/\gamma$ implies a correspondingly small velocity during switching, which is needed for the activation error (see the cutoff term in Equation (5.48)). Only the label and phase derivatives occur in this norm, and they commute with division by $\gamma$.

rows.fidelity_note: For a trace-free matrix $M$ and nonzero perpendicular vectors $\kappa,\mathbf a$ solving $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$ and $\mathbf a_t=-(I-2P_\kappa)M\mathbf a$, set $e_1=\kappa/|\kappa|$, $e_2=\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$, $e_3=e_1\times e_2$. The formal statement proves the moving-frame differential equations using $\nu=e_1\cdot Me_2$. This is the paper’s coupling at the origin. It does not define the amplitude weight $\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a|$. A separate coefficient $e_1\cdot Me_3$ in that frame calculation has no such meaning. Thus the declaration contains the coupling as part of a different differential statement, not both displayed definitions.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The moving-frame equation supplies the normalized seed dynamics; the central weight is specified separately.

rows.name: TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_movingFrame
rows.plain: Moving-frame derivative formulas for perpendicular wave data
rows.annotation: In the moving frame $E_1=\kappa/|\kappa|$, $E_2=\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$, the first coupling is $\nu=E_1\cdot ME_2$. In particular $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a=\nu|\kappa||\mathbf a|$. This is the scalar whose positivity will give the sign of the leading pressure tensor in Equation (5.51). The amplitude weight $\gamma$ here is unrelated to the frame coefficient of the same name in the frame equations.

citations.supports: The transverse projection used to extend central initial data.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: At activation, each nearby seed is obtained by projecting the central vector onto the plane perpendicular to $\kappa(t_0,a)$: $\mathbf a(t_0,a)=(\operatorname{Id}-P_{\kappa(t_0,a)})\mathbf a(t_0,0)$. For nonzero $\kappa$, $P_\kappa=\kappa\otimes\kappa/|\kappa|^2$ is the orthogonal projection onto its span, so this initial condition is transverse and reproduces the central value. The two seed conditions retain precisely this initial-value requirement, which accounts for their same verdicts without asserting existence by themselves. The projection-only link is weaker because it supplies the algebraic operator but neither a seed solution nor its initial condition; the nonzero covector assumption is essential to the stated geometric interpretation.

ties.name: TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn
ties.plain: The localized seed and its bounds

rows.fidelity_note: For supplied $M(t,a)$, $\kappa(t,a)$ and central amplitude $c(t)$ on $[t_0,T]$, the formal seed data require $\mathbf a(t,0)=c(t)$, $\mathbf a(t_0,a)=(I-P_{\kappa(t_0,a)})c(t_0)$, $\mathbf a_t=-(I-2P_\kappa)M\mathbf a$ and $\kappa\cdot\mathbf a=0$. Thus the quoted projection is exactly a defining condition. These data also include nearby-label amplitude and positive-coupling estimates; they are not merely a record of initial data. The declaration does not assert existence of an object satisfying those conditions.
rows.name: TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn
rows.plain: The localized seed and its bounds
rows.annotation: `SeedOn` contains the comparison obtained after evolving the projected data. Its bound $|\mathbf a(t,a)-\mathbf a(t,0)|\le C|a||\mathbf a(t,0)|$ is relative at each time, with $C$ a parent-dependent constant. It also gives $\kappa(t,a)\cdot M(t,a)\mathbf a(t,a)\ge(2\mathsf D)^{-1}|\kappa(t,0)||\mathbf a(t,0)|$ on the envelope. The first estimate controls velocity; the second controls the sign of the pressure contribution.

rows.fidelity_note: This defines $I-P_\kappa$, the projection used in the displayed initial condition. It does not assert that a seed starts from that value. At $\kappa=0$ the formal expression is the identity because division by zero is zero; the paper excludes that case.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The projection agrees with orthogonal projection for the nonzero transported covector used in the construction. Its value at a zero covector is unused.

rows.name: TorusEuler.oscillatoryTransverseProjection
rows.plain: Projection perpendicular to the wave
rows.annotation: Let $v=\mathbf a(t_0,0)$. Since $v\perp\kappa(t_0,0)$, the new datum minus $v$ is $-(P_{\kappa(t_0,a)}-P_{\kappa(t_0,0)})v$. Proposition 5.1 bounds the derivative of the direction projection by a parent power. Thus the initial error is $O(\mathsf D^C|a||v|)$, small even relative to a very small $v$.

rows.fidelity_note: Let $M(t,a)=\nabla U(t,X_{0,t}(a))$ and $\kappa(t,a)=D(X_{t,0})(X_{0,t}(a))^Tk_*$. A seed is a smooth field $\mathbf a$ on $[t_0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$ which agrees with the central seed at $a=0$, starts from $(I-P_{\kappa(t_0,a)})\mathbf a(t_0,0)$, and solves $\partial_t\mathbf a=-M\mathbf a+2\kappa(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2$ while satisfying $\kappa\cdot\mathbf a=0$. The differential equation uses derivatives within $[t_0,T]$ at its endpoints. This records the seed equation and (5.4), not the amplitude and coupling estimates on nearby labels. Those are later conclusions. Nonvanishing of $\kappa$ comes from the parent flow and nonzero carrier, not from this declaration alone. The projection uses $P_\kappa=(\kappa\otimes\kappa)/|\kappa|^2$. At zero covector the quotient is defined as zero; the smooth-flow and nonzero-carrier assumptions exclude that case in this application.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.IsSeed
rows.plain: The prescribed seed equation
rows.annotation: Transversality is an invariant of the seed equation. In fact $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$ and $\mathbf a_t=-M\mathbf a+2P_\kappa M\mathbf a$ give $\partial_t(\kappa\cdot\mathbf a)=-\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a-\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a+2\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a=0$. Thus projection is needed at launch only; the ODE preserves the constraint thereafter.

citations.supports: Extension of admissible central wave data to the localized hierarchy.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The construction first fixes a transported covector and a nonzero transverse amplitude at the origin, then extends the amplitude to nearby labels by the projected initial condition (5.4) and the same linear amplitude equation. This preserves the prescribed central solution and supplies the field needed inside the spatial envelope. The first formal link only describes the required smooth extension, its transversality and agreement at the origin, so it is weaker than an existence claim. Proposition 5.4 supplies existence together with the finite correction hierarchy and is stronger, but it assumes the central stability and coupling conditions rather than deriving them from an arbitrary prescribed seed.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal condition specifies the seed extension: on $[t_0,T]$ it solves $\mathbf a_t=-M\mathbf a+2\kappa(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2$, starts from $(I-P_{\kappa(t_0,a)})\mathbf a(t_0,0)$, agrees with the prescribed central seed, is smooth and remains transverse. This condition describes the required extension; it does not assert existence.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. This specifies the seed equation and initial projection. The existence required by the construction is proved in Proposition 5.4.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.IsSeed

rows.annotation: At the central label the projection in Equation (5.4) leaves the initial vector unchanged. Both the prescribed central solution and the seed at $a=0$ then solve the same linear ODE with the same data; uniqueness gives agreement on the whole active interval. `IsSeed` includes that agreement, smoothness and the transverse constraint.

citations.supports: Evenness of the amplitude extension by uniqueness of its labelwise evolution.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Section 5.1, seed parity following (5.4); Section 3, parity of the localized wave

explanation.text: The projected initial seed is even in the label, because the transported covector is even. The amplitude equation has the same coefficients at $a$ and $-a$, so uniqueness of the linear ordinary differential equation preserves this equality for all active times. The formal parity theorem establishes this same conclusion under continuity of the coefficients, their evenness and nonvanishing of the covector. This gives the seed symmetry needed for the odd physical wave after multiplication by the odd phase profile.

ties.name: TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.even_amplitude
ties.plain: Evenness of the selected seed

rows.fidelity_note: On $[t_0,T]$, $t_0\le T$, assume $M(t,a)$ and $\kappa(t,a)$ are continuous in time for each label, even in $a$, and $\kappa$ never vanishes. Let $\mathbf a$ solve $\mathbf a_t=-(I-2P_\kappa)M\mathbf a$ with projected initial data $(I-P_{\kappa(t_0,a)})c(t_0)$. The formal statement proves $\mathbf a(t,-a)=\mathbf a(t,a)$ throughout the active interval. Evenness of the coefficients and initial data permits uniqueness of the same linear equation at $a$ and $-a$. This is the parity assertion for the paper’s localized seed.
rows.name: TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.even_amplitude
rows.plain: Evenness of the selected seed
rows.annotation: At opposite labels the initial projections agree, and the coefficients of the linear equation agree. Uniqueness gives an even seed. Since the envelope is also even and $F_h$ is odd, the evaluation $g(a)\mathbf a(t,a)F_h(k_*\cdot a)$ is odd. Composing with the odd inverse flow preserves the required physical parity.

explanation.text: The central hypotheses require every homogeneous transverse solution $\mathbf b$ to satisfy $|\mathbf b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/\gamma(t')$ for $t_0\le t'\le t\le T$, and require $\nu(t,0)\ge\mathsf D^{-1}$. Thus relative transverse growth is controlled against the chosen central solution, while its coupling has a definite positive lower bound. Both formal links contain these same hypotheses, writing the first ratio with $|\mathbf a(t,0)|$ so that the common factor $\lambda^{3/4}$ cancels. The seed-existence theorem uses them together with deformation and spatial-variation bounds to obtain estimates near the center; it does not prove them for arbitrary central data, since that verification belongs to the later central dynamics.

explanation.text: The envelope radius is chosen as $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-a}$ with one sufficiently large absolute integer $a$. This makes the region small enough for nearby-seed control and supplies a scale that absorbs the cost of taking label derivatives. The formal radius formula only defines $(\mathsf D^a)^{-1}$ for a supplied integer $a$, so it is weaker than the assertion that an absolute choice works. explanation.text: If $c(t,a)$ is independent of the phase, every derivative containing $\partial_s$ vanishes. The mixed scaled norm therefore reduces exactly to $\sum_{m\le n}\ell_*^m|c|_m$, with each label multi-index counted once and no time differentiation. The formal equality and the finite-sum definition have this same content for smooth coefficients with bounded derivatives, whereas the third link only specifies the directions $\ell_*\partial_{a_i}$ and is weaker than the full norm identity. Boundedness remains a separate analytic requirement; an equality between the specified supremum expressions does not by itself establish it.

rows.fidelity_note: For a field $c(t,a)$ smooth in $a$, with arbitrary time index set and real normed target, let $f(t,a,s)=c(t,a)$. The formal statement gives exact equality of the mixed norm using directions $\ell_*\partial_{a_i},h\partial_s$ and the label norm using $\ell_*\partial_{a_i}$. All derivatives containing $\partial_s$ vanish. Thus the common expression is $\sum_{|\alpha|\le n}\ell_*^{|\alpha|}\sup_{t,a}|\partial_a^\alpha c|$, counting each multi-index once. Boundedness is separate: unbounded derivative sets have default real supremum zero, so the equality alone does not prove finiteness in the analytic sense.

rows.plain: The norm of a phase-independent field
rows.annotation: Every derivative word containing the phase direction vanishes on a phase-independent coefficient. The surviving words are exactly the label words, including the empty word. This is an exact identity for the library word norms; the paper's coordinate sums differ only by the fixed-order multiplicities.

rows.fidelity_note: For fixed spatial directions $d_i$, the order-$n$ expression sums one term for each nondecreasing derivative word of length at most $n$. Without Hölder terms, that term is the supremum of the corresponding derivative norm over the supplied time index and spatial domain. With Hölder terms, it is the maximum of that supremum and the half-Hölder seminorm. Equal-point quotients have value zero. The set whose real supremum is taken always includes zero; if it is unbounded above, its formal supremum is zero. Consequently these expressions are norms only when boundedness has been established. For $d_i=\ell_*\partial_{a_i}$, the expression is the scaled label norm; adding $h\partial_s$ gives the mixed label and phase norm. No time derivative occurs. For bounded smooth phase-independent $c$, taking the three directions $\ell_*\partial_{a_i}$ gives exactly the paper’s sum $\sum_{m\le n}\ell_*^m|c|_m$.

rows.annotation: The term of order zero is unchanged by scaling. For $m\ge1$, if $\ell_*\mathsf D^C\le1$, then $\ell_*^m\mathsf D^{C(m+1)}\le\ell_*\mathsf D^{2C}$. This spare small factor, absent at order zero, is useful in the differentiated inverse estimates when a derivative falls on a coefficient.

rows.fidelity_note: The paper gives the entire finite norm of a phase-independent coefficient. This definition specifies only the three directions $\ell_*\partial_{a_i}$; summing their mixed derivatives and discarding phase derivatives requires the other two declarations linked here.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The three scaled label directions are the coordinate derivatives used in the norm. Their definition alone is only one part of the coefficient estimates.

explanation.text: Proposition 5.1 controls the six coefficients $F$, $F^{-1}$, $M$, $\kappa/\lambda$, $\lambda^2/|\kappa|^2$ and $P_\kappa$, where $F=D_aX$ and $M=(\nabla U)\circ X$. These are precisely the deformation, material gradient and normalized covector quantities entering the transverse equations and corrections. Both formal links contain the same list and give polynomial bounds for every label derivative. The analytic coefficient theorem obtains them from smooth-flow, deformation and velocity-derivative hypotheses directly, while the numbered proposition supplies those hypotheses through the truncated parent assumptions.

rows.fidelity_note: Let $0<T\le1$, $\mathsf D\ge1$, and let $X$ be the flow of a smooth unit-periodic $U$. Assume $\|D_aX\|,\|(D_aX)^{-1}\|\le\mathsf D$ and $\|D^jU\|_\infty\le R_n\mathsf D^j$ for every $1\le j\le n$, where the nonnegative sequence $R_n$ is fixed before the flow. Put $F=DX$, $G=F^{-1}$, $M=DU\circ X$, $\kappa=G^Tk_*$, and suppose $|\kappa(t_0,0)|=\lambda>0$ at $t_0\in[0,T]$. A sequence $C_m\ge0$, chosen before the flow, gives $\|D_a^m\Phi\|_\infty\le C_m\mathsf D^{16m+16}$ for every $m\ge0$ and every $\Phi\in\{F,G,M,\kappa/\lambda,\lambda^2/|\kappa|^2,P_\kappa\}$. Norms are multilinear operator norms, uniform in time and label. This supplies (5.6) with one explicit exponent. Unlike the numbered proposition, this analytic helper assumes the velocity derivative bounds directly and requires no pressure, residual or coercivity condition.

citations.supports: Composition estimates for transporting a spatially controlled field into labels.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: If $|f|_m\le C'_mA_f\mathsf D^m$ and the parent has the flow bounds of Proposition 5.1, composition with $X$ gives $|f\circ X|_m\le C_mA_f\mathsf D^{Cm}$. The analytic formal theorem is stronger because it proves the explicit exponent $6m$ from the flow and velocity-derivative assumptions alone, without requiring the complete parent hypotheses. The numbered statement is stronger in allowing the more general admissible parent pressure, while its conditional proof is weaker because Bernstein's inequality and Lemma D.2 remain premises. Coordinate derivative sums and multilinear operator norms change only the order-dependent constants, so the estimate transfers the physical frequency scale to controlled polynomial costs in labels.

Fix a nonnegative sequence $C'_m$ before the flow. Let $f(t,\cdot)$ be smooth with values in a real normed space and satisfy $\|D^mf(t)\|_\infty\le C'_mA_f\mathsf D^m$ for every $m\ge0$, uniformly in $t$, with $A_f\ge0$. This proves (5.7) with the explicit exponent $6m$; it requires only the displayed flow and velocity-derivative hypotheses, rather than the full truncated parent.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The composition estimate allows more input fields than the paper needs, and includes its frequency-localized fields.

explanation.text: Taking $\ell_*\le\mathsf D^{-C}$ in Proposition 5.1 yields $\|c\|_{[n]}\le C_n\mathsf D^C$ for its six coefficients and $\|f\circ X\|_{[n]}\le C_nA_f$. The general summation link is different because it only converts supplied derivative bounds into a weighted sum, and the composition summation link is weaker because it supplies only the second type of estimate after the composition bound is known. The numbered statement contains both conclusions and is stronger through its broader admissible pressure class. Its proof with Bernstein and Lemma D.2 assumed is weaker as a conditional result, while together these ingredients justify using scaled derivatives without increasing the power of $\mathsf D$ at every order.

The first estimate applies the frequency bound to the differentiated field, so it does not require a bound on the undifferentiated velocity. explanation.text: Differentiating $X_t=U\circ X$ $n\ge2$ times in labels gives $\partial_tD_a^nX=M D_a^nX+N_n$, where $N_n$ contains only lower-order derivatives of $X$. The first formal result establishes the differentiated flow equation and the requisite continuity, but does not separate its linear part, so it is weaker than the displayed equation. The second is a purely spatial chain-rule identity subtracting $DU(X)D^nX$ from $D^n(U\circ X)$, and hence is different from a time-evolution statement. Together they give the variational equation to which the bounded flow propagator can be applied.

explanation.text: For the linear equation $z_t=Mz+N$ along one parent trajectory, the propagator is $F(t)F(\sigma)^{-1}$. Bounds $|F|,|F^{-1}|\le\mathsf D$ therefore give norm at most $\mathsf D^2$, and $T\le1$ bounds the time-integration length. The formal theorem has a different conclusion: for continuous forcing with $\|N\|_\infty\le C$ and zero initial value, it proves $|z(t)|\le\mathsf D^2C$. This integrated estimate applies also to multilinear-map-valued higher derivatives and supplies the factor $\mathsf D^2$ in the recurrence (5.9).

Let $z(t)$ and $N(t)$ take values in the multilinear maps from $(\mathbb R^3)^n$ to $\mathbb R^3$, with $N$ continuous, $z(0)=0$ and $z_t=Mz+N$. The paper quotes the propagator bound alone. The formal conclusion is the resulting forced-solution estimate; the propagator bound is used in its proof.

rows.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be the flow of a $C^2$ unit-periodic velocity on $[0,T]$, $0<T\le1$. Fix a label and $n\ge2$. Assume spatial $C^n$ regularity along its trajectory, the differentiated flow equation, continuity of its right side and of $M=DU\circ X$, and $\|DX\|,\|DX^{-1}\|\le\mathsf D$. Suppose $C,\mathsf D\ge0$, $\|D^kU\|\le C\mathsf D^k$ for $2\le k\le n$, and $\|D^kX\|\le v_k$ for $1\le k<n$. The sum runs over the ordered set partitions used in the iterated chain rule; every block has size below $n$. It is a recurrence assuming the lower-order bounds, not the completed induction. The paper groups coordinate derivatives by their orders and takes suprema. Passing from the formal pointwise operator norms and ordered partitions to those sums changes only the order-dependent constant.

The formal arithmetic result proves this final inequality for the partition product, so it is weaker than the displayed chain in not separately stating the intermediate equalities. This is the exponent calculation that closes the higher-flow induction without making its coefficient of $n$ grow at each step.

rows.fidelity_note: Let $0<T\le1$, $\mathsf D\ge1$, and let $X$ be the flow of a smooth unit-periodic $U$. There are $C_n\ge0$, fixed before the flow, bounding the order-$n$ derivatives of $F$, $G$ and $G^T$, $M$, $\kappa/\lambda$, $\lambda^2/|\kappa|^2$, and $P_\kappa$ by $C_n$ times $\mathsf D^{5n+1}$, $\mathsf D^{7n+1}$, $\mathsf D^{6n+1}$, $\mathsf D^{7n+2}$, $\mathsf D^{16n+4}$, and $\mathsf D^{16n+8}$, respectively. The formal statement records their resulting bounds, rather than an assertion that particular proof rules are applicable.

explanation.text: The mean correction solves $B_t+MB+\mathbf d\bar q=\bar f$ with $B=Fz_t$, zero displacement at both endpoints and the transported divergence constraint. These conditions select a response on the entire interval, allowing nonzero initial velocity and a mean that extends before wave activation. The first formal description imposes the endpoint and momentum equations for general invertible matrix fields, so its different verdict reflects the absence of the flow geometry needed to interpret transported divergence. The second link proves only that divergence constraint from volume preservation and is weaker, while the flow-based mean condition agrees with (5.11) through the Piola identity. rows.fidelity_note: On $[0,T]$, let $F,G,M$ be smooth unit-periodic matrix fields with $GF=FG=I$, $F_t=MF$, $\|G\|\le D$, $\|M\|\le L$, and $-(M_t+M^2)\le I$. Put $K=F^TF$, $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$. For a supplied label force $f_{\rm lab}$, a smooth mean solution consists of smooth unit-periodic fields $v,z,B,\mathsf q$ satisfying $z_t=v$, $z(0)=z(T)=0$, $\operatorname{div}_av=0$, $B=Fv$ and $B_t+MB+G^T\nabla_a\mathsf q=f_{\rm lab}$ on the closed interval. These are defining conditions, not an existence assertion. No spatial mean normalization of $\mathsf q$ is imposed. An actual flow is not part of these data. Only after separately identifying $F=D_aX$, $M=DU\circ X$ and $f_{\rm lab}=f\circ X$ may one interpret $Fz$ as particle displacement and $B\circ X^{-1}$ as the Eulerian correction. The paper additionally identifies $F$ with a volume-preserving flow derivative and writes the transported divergence condition. Arbitrary matrix data in this definition do not by themselves justify that geometric interpretation.

rows.annotation: Differentiating the integrated equation (4.9) gives $Kv_t+(K_t-\Omega)v-\nabla_a\phi_t=-L_t$. Here $K_t-\Omega=2F^TF_t$, $\bar q=-\phi_t$ and $-L_t=F^T\bar f$. citations.supports: The scope of the mean estimate as an a priori bound for every endpoint solution.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: Proposition 5.2 is an estimate for every smooth periodic solution of the mean equation satisfying both displacement endpoints and the divergence constraint. Both formal links have this same universal quantifier over existing endpoint solutions, with constants chosen independently of the particular parent and solution. The analytic link assumes the needed velocity-derivative and coercivity bounds directly, while the numbered statement obtains them from the parent hypotheses. This makes the estimate available for any mean produced in the hierarchy, but does not itself construct such a mean or impose $B(0)=0$.

explanation.text: The endpoint coefficients are $K=F^TF$ and $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$, with $F=D_aX$. Proposition 5.1 controls derivatives of $F$ and $M$, and the product rule of Lemma D.2 therefore gives polynomial derivative bounds of the form (D.6) for both coefficients. The formal result is weaker as a conditional implication: it assumes those two cited results and then supplies constants and exponents before the parent, valid at every derivative order. These bounds prepare both the polynomial control of the low-order inverse and the small scaled coefficient derivatives needed to lift that inverse to higher orders.

rows.fidelity_note: Let $0<T\le1$, $\mathsf D\ge2$, $\lambda\ge1$. Let $U$ be smooth, odd, solenoidal and unit-periodic, with flow $X$ and smooth periodic pressure $p_U$. Require Fourier radii $2\mathsf D$ for $U$ and $4\mathsf D$ for the odd residual $R_U=U_t+U\cdot\nabla U+\nabla p_U$, $\|DU\|_\infty,\|DX\|_\infty,\|DX^{-1}\|_\infty\le\mathsf D$, $\|R_U\|_\infty\le\lambda^{-5/2}$, and $D^2p_U-DR_U\le I$ as quadratic forms. Write $F=D_aX$, $G=F^{-1}$, $M=(DU)\circ X$, $K=F^TF$ and $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$. Assuming Proposition 5.1 and Lemma D.2, there are nonnegative sequences $C_K(m),C_\Omega(m)$ and nonnegative integers $a_K,a_\Omega$, fixed before the parent, such that $\|D_a^mK\|_\infty\le C_K(m)\mathsf D^{a_K(m+1)}$ and $\|D_a^m\Omega\|_\infty\le C_\Omega(m)\mathsf D^{a_\Omega(m+1)}$ for every $m\ge0$. Spatial derivatives are measured in multilinear operator norm. No Poisson equation or mean normalization of $p_U$ is imposed. The implication is conditional on the two cited results; it does not itself prove Proposition 5.1 or Lemma D.2.

explanation.text: In the integrated endpoint equation, $Kv$ appears without a time integral, whereas the term containing $\Omega v$ is acted on by $Jf(t)=\int_0^tf(\sigma)\,d\sigma$. On the uniform-in-time half-Hölder norm, $J$ has norm at most $T\le1$, so differentiating the two coefficients gives comparable controlled contributions. explanation.text: For smooth phase-independent $M,\kappa$ with $\kappa\ne0$ and $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$, a smooth centered source determines a transverse pair $V,\mathsf p$ with $V(0)=0$ and $\langle\mathsf p\rangle_s=0$. The construction uses the projected equation (5.17) and the normalized primitive (5.16), preserving phase period one and compatible label translations. This is the pair to which Lemma 5.3(ii) applies. The formal existence theorem supplies such a pair with its support properties, while the separate uniqueness theorem says that two smooth pairs with these same data and normalizations coincide. Same applies to the existence link, and weaker to uniqueness considered alone because equality of two possible solutions does not construct one.

ties.name: TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.exists_transverseResult
ties.plain: Existence of a transverse solution

rows.fidelity_note: The strain and nonzero covector are smooth and phase independent, with $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$; source profiles satisfy the phase period and the coupled label-translation law. For a smooth source with zero phase mean, this result constructs a transverse solution of (5.15) with zero initial velocity and normalized pressure. It also supplies the support and reflection properties required by the finite expansion. The statement proves existence with these properties; uniqueness among all solutions is established separately. The equation is $V_t+MV+\kappa\mathsf p_s=f$, with $\kappa\cdot V=0$, $\langle V\rangle_s=\langle\mathsf p\rangle_s=0$, and $V(0)=0$.
rows.name: TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.exists_transverseResult
rows.plain: Existence of a transverse solution
rows.annotation: The existence theorem produces the normalized pair with $V(0)=0$ and keeps the prescribed support and inactive prefix. It also has the phase-shift compatibility needed when the parent phase is not a lattice vector. The subsequent estimate in (5.21) controls this pair quantitatively; existence itself is not the estimate.

rows.fidelity_note:
The fields are smooth phase-periodic profiles on $[0,T]$, compatible with the same label translations and with the same transported nonzero covector. Two transverse solutions with the same source, zero initial velocity and zero-mean pressure agree. The homogeneous ordinary differential equation eliminates their velocity difference; pressure normalization then removes the remaining phase-constant difference. This proves the uniqueness asserted in §5.4 and transfers bounds for the chosen solution to every solution covered by Lemma 5.3. The equation is $V_t+MV+\kappa\mathsf p_s=f$, with $\kappa\cdot V=0$, $\langle V\rangle_s=\langle\mathsf p\rangle_s=0$, and $V(0)=0$.

The paper refers to the solution and its pressure. This theorem proves that two smooth solutions with the same forcing, zero initial velocity and zero phase mean for the pressure coincide; the existence theorem linked here supplies the pair.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The uniqueness assertion is used together with the proved existence result; it is not being used as an existence theorem.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.TransverseSolution.unique
rows.plain: Uniqueness of the transverse solution
rows.annotation: After solving the velocity ODE there is no remaining freedom in the phase pressure. If two normalized pairs solve the same equation from zero, uniqueness for the velocity and Equation (5.16) give equality of the pressure derivatives; the average removes the integration constant. The linked result proves uniqueness, not existence.

citations.supports: The supported transverse velocity-pressure estimate.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For the zero-initial transverse solution with smooth centered forcing supported after $t_0$ and inside the envelope, (5.21) gives $\|V\|_{[n],\gamma}+\lambda\|\mathsf p\|_{[n],\gamma}\le C_n\mathsf D^C\|f\|_{[n],\gamma}$. Here $0\le t_0<T\le1$, $\lambda\ge1$, $\mathsf D\ge2$, the parent obeys the deformation and coefficient bounds, and the central seed obeys (5.5), with $\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|>0$. Equation (5.20) bounds the velocity after its zero activation value is established, and (5.16) with the product and primitive estimates bounds pressure with the gain $\lambda^{-1}$. The formal inverse theorem retains this estimate for smooth profiles with the phase and lattice compatibility, giving one explicit admissible parent exponent. The stronger verdict on the numbered formulation concerns its broader admissible pressure and central-amplitude assumptions, rather than an improved power of $\lambda$ in this bound.

ties.name: TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.exists_paper_hierarchy_inverse
ties.plain: Bounds for the transverse inverse

rows.fidelity_note: Assume $0\le t_0<T\le1$, $\mathsf D\ge2$, $\lambda=|\kappa(t_0,0)|\ge1$, smooth periodic $U$, both deformation and gradient bounds $\mathsf D$, velocity derivative bounds $R_n\mathsf D^j$, and a nonzero central seed with relative transverse growth at most $\mathsf D$ and normalized coupling at least $\mathsf D^{-1}$. For a small enough radius, $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$ and $\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|$, supported solutions satisfy $\|V\|_{[n],\gamma}\le C_n\mathsf D^{20}(\gamma(t_0)^{-1}\|V(t_0)\|_{[n]}+\|f\|_{[n],\gamma})$. If the centered forcing vanishes before activation, its zero-initial solution also satisfies $\|V\|_{[n],\gamma}+\lambda\|\mathsf p\|_{[n],\gamma}\le C_n\mathsf D^{20}\|f\|_{[n],\gamma}$. Profiles are smooth on $[0,T]$ and satisfy phase and coupled lattice periodicity; support lies within $2\ell_*$ of lattice points. The transverse stability assumption is $|\mathbf b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/\gamma(t')$ for every transverse homogeneous solution $\mathbf b$ and $t_0\le t'\le t\le T$.
rows.name: TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.exists_paper_hierarchy_inverse
rows.plain: Bounds for the transverse inverse
rows.annotation: Equation (5.16) gives $|\partial_s\mathsf p|\le |\kappa|^{-1}(|f|+2|M||V|)$. The inverse wave-vector length provides the factor $\lambda^{-1}$, while taking the normalized phase primitive is bounded at the same scaled derivative order. In particular the pressure does not have to be obtained by inverting a spatial Laplacian on the torus at this step. The full-slab helper gives Equation (5.21) with exponent $20$.

rows.fidelity_note:
Assume a smooth odd solenoidal parent and smooth periodic pressure on $0<T\le1$, bands $2\mathsf D$ for $U$ and $4\mathsf D$ for its odd residual $R_U$, bounds $\|DU\|,\|DX\|,\|DX^{-1}\|\le\mathsf D$, $\mathsf D\ge2$, $\|R_U\|\le\lambda^{-5/2}$ and $D^2p_U-DR_U\le I$. Let $0\le t_0<T$, $\lambda=|\kappa(t_0,0)|\ge1$, and a nonzero transverse central seed satisfy $0<\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|\le1$ and $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a\ge\mathsf D^{-1}|\kappa||\mathbf a|$. Every transverse homogeneous solution $\mathbf b$ must obey $|\mathbf b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/\gamma(t')$ for $t_0\le t'\le t\le T$. For small fixed $\ell_*$ and $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$, nearby seeds obey $|\mathbf a(t,a)|\le2|\mathbf a(t,0)|$ and positive coupling. Supported transverse solutions obey $\|V\|_{[n],\gamma}\le C_n\mathsf D^C(\gamma(t_0)^{-1}\|V(t_0)\|_{[n]}+\|f\|_{[n],\gamma})$. Zero-initial centered forcing gives $\|V\|_{[n],\gamma}+\lambda\|\mathsf p\|_{[n],\gamma}\le C_n\mathsf D^C\|f\|_{[n],\gamma}$; the leading wave has bound $C_n\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-5/4}$. The first estimate requires full-interval profiles; the paper permits active-interval data. Pressure and amplitude assumptions are broader; the envelope is fixed.

The formal bound retains $\|V\|_{[n],\gamma}+\lambda\|\mathsf p\|_{[n],\gamma}$ for every zero-initial transverse solution with supported, centered forcing. It allows the broader parent pressure class and any nonzero central amplitude below $\lambda^{-3/4}$, without requiring the peak normalization in the paper.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The forced transverse estimate retains the pressure factor $\lambda$ and the same derivative order; the enlarged parent class includes the paper’s parent.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_5_3
rows.plain: The transverse bounds of Lemma 5.3
rows.annotation: The pressure estimate is later used together with the equation, not by differentiating it twice in physical space. At level two, $\mathsf p_2$ has size $\lambda^{-1-23/12}$ up to parent powers; two physical derivatives could leave $\lambda^{1/12}$. But $\kappa\partial_s\mathsf p_2=P_\kappa(f_2+f_2^S-2MV_2)$ has size $\lambda^{-23/12}$. Only one physical derivative is then needed, leaving $\lambda^{-5/12}$ in the Hessian bound (Equation (5.52)). The numbered Lean estimate allows the broader parent pressure and central-amplitude hypotheses.

explanation.text: With $A_1=g\mathbf a F_h$, $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$ and $\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|>0$, Lemma 5.3(iii) bounds $\|A_1\|_{[n],\gamma}+\lambda\|\mathsf p[A_1]\|_{[n],\gamma}$ by $C_n\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-5/4}$ on $[t_0,T]$. Under the parent and central-stability assumptions of §5.1, (5.20) bounds $g\mathbf a$ by $C_n\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-3/4}$ and Lemma 3.1 gives the additional profile factor $h$. Equation (5.24) then provides the pressure estimate with the same derivative order. This is the initial size used in the finite expansion and ultimately in its physical velocity bounds. Both linked formal estimates preserve the frequency powers for a particular admissible radial envelope, which is the restriction described by weaker relative to the paper's arbitrary fixed admissible cutoff.

rows.fidelity_note:
Fix nonnegative derivative constants $R_n$. There is an integer $A\ge30$, and for each $n$ a constant $C_n\ge0$, chosen before the parent. Let $0\le t_0<T\le1$, $\mathsf D\ge2$, $0<\ell_*\le\mathsf D^{-A}$, and $\lambda=|\kappa(t_0,0)|\ge1$. Assume a smooth periodic velocity with flow $X$, both deformation bounds at most $\mathsf D$, and $\|D^jU\|_\infty\le R_n\mathsf D^j$ for $1\le j\le n$. The nonzero transverse central seed has $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a\ge\mathsf D^{-1}|\kappa||\mathbf a|$ and every transverse homogeneous solution obeys $|\mathbf b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/\gamma(t')$ for $t_0\le t'\le t\le T$, where $\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|$. For a supplied localized seed with smooth compatible continuation, the fixed radial envelope shape at every such radius gives $\|A_1\|_{[n],\gamma}+\lambda\|\mathsf p[A_1]\|_{[n],\gamma}\le C_n\mathsf D^{20}\lambda^{-5/4}$. Here $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$; the norm sums scaled label and phase derivatives before division by $\gamma$. The radius is not fixed in advance.

The paper states (5.22) for its fixed admissible radial cutoff. The formal estimate uses one chosen envelope, so it preserves the bound for that choice without quantifying over every admissible cutoff.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The leading-wave estimate is proved for the fixed admissible envelope used to construct the hierarchy.

Thus the velocity can have size $\gamma\lambda^{-5/4}$ while its central gradient has scale $\gamma\lambda^{1/4}$ up to parent powers. The formal estimate uses a fixed admissible envelope.

rows.plain: The transverse bounds of Lemma 5.3
rows.annotation: Part (iii) of Lemma 5.3 starts from a nonzero homogeneous seed, not from the zero-start inverse of part (ii) of Lemma 5.3. The bound at launch is proportional to $\gamma(t_0)$, which cancels the launch denominator in Equation (5.20); multiplication by $F_h$ contributes $h$.
