citations.supports: Norm bounds for the transported frame and its projected inverse.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: Assume the forward and inverse parent deformations have operator norms at most $\mathsf D$. Restricting $D_aX$ to the fixed transverse plane gives $\|A_\perp\|\le\mathsf D$, and applying $(D_aX)^{-1}$ after an orthogonal projection gives $\|A_\perp^\dagger\|\le\mathsf D$. These two bounds convert the central transverse growth estimate into the factor $\mathsf D^3$ in fixed-plane coordinates. The first formal statement bounds the restricted map by $\|D_aX\|$, and the second bounds the projected inverse by $\|(D_aX)^{-1}\|$, without themselves assuming either quantity is at most $\mathsf D$. Each weaker verdict therefore marks one component of the pair of bounds; inserting (5.1) and combining them gives the paper's sentence.

ties.name: TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.norm_coframeLift_le
ties.plain: Operator norm bound for the transverse frame

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $F$ be any linear map on $\mathbb R^3$, and equip $k_*^\perp$ with the inherited Euclidean norm. The norm of $A_\perp$ is at most the norm of the full deformation, because restricting a linear map to a Euclidean subspace cannot increase its operator norm. Thus (5.1) gives $\lVert A_\perp\rVert\le\mathsf D$ in §5.4. This particular inequality does not require invertibility of the deformation.

The formal statement gives $\|A_\perp\|\le\|D_aX\|$ for a restricted linear map. It treats the first bound only; inserting the parent deformation bound yields $\|A_\perp\|\le\mathsf D$.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The bound for the lift from the fixed transverse plane is one of the two coefficient estimates used in the transverse equation.

rows.name: TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.norm_coframeLift_le
rows.plain: Operator norm bound for the transverse frame
rows.annotation: Let $E$ be the constant matrix with the two initial orthonormal columns. Then $A_\perp=FE$ and $|A_\perp w|\le\mathsf D|Ew|=\mathsf D|w|$. The transported frame need not be orthogonal. The corresponding lower bound from $F^{-1}$ controls its inverse on the transverse plane.

rows.fidelity_note:
For any linear map $G$, compose $G$ with the orthogonal projections onto $(G^Tk_*)^\perp$ and $k_*^\perp$. The norm of $A_\perp^\dagger$ is bounded by that of the inverse deformation: the orthogonal projections used to define it have norm at most one. Consequently, (5.1) gives $\lVert A_\perp^\dagger\rVert\le\mathsf D$ in the proof of Lemma 5.3, without estimating the inverse Gram matrix separately.

The formal statement bounds the projected inverse by $\|(D_aX)^{-1}\|$. It treats the second inequality only; the parent inverse-deformation hypothesis gives the bound by $\mathsf D$.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The pullback bound supplies the other coefficient estimate for passing between the moving and fixed transverse planes.

rows.name: TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.norm_coframePullback_le
rows.plain: Operator norm bound for the projected inverse coframe
rows.annotation: For transverse $y$, $A_\perp^\dagger y$ consists of the coordinates of $F^{-1}y$ in the initial orthonormal basis. On general $y$ there is first an orthogonal projection, of norm at most one. This gives $|A_\perp^\dagger|\le\mathsf D$ and explains why the inverse Gram matrix has norm at most $\mathsf D^2$.

citations.supports: Deriving coefficient bounds for the transverse coordinate equation.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Proof of Lemma 5.3, first paragraph; Proposition 5.1; Lemma D.2

explanation.text: Proposition 5.1 bounds the derivatives of the parent deformation, its inverse, the strain and the wave-vector projection, and Lemma D.2 transfers those bounds to the transverse frame coefficients. This supplies the spatial coefficient control needed to compare nearby transverse equations and apply Lemma D.3. The formal result assumes smooth derivative bounds $\|D^jc\|\le W_j\mathsf D^{16(j+1)}$ for $F,G,M,P_{G^Tk_*}$, and obtains exponents $32(j+1)$ for $G(I-P_{G^Tk_*})$ and $64(j+1)$ for $-2G(I-P_{G^Tk_*})MF$. For the application $F=D_aX$ and $G=F^{-1}$, these express the projected inverse and the right-hand-side generator, but the statement itself assumes no inverse relation. Different therefore reflects both this representation and scope: it does not separately bound the forward frame or use the paper's Gram-matrix formula, though the cited parent estimate supplies that remaining input.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S53.transverseCoframe_jetPower
ties.plain: Derivative bounds for the inverse coframe on the transverse plane

rows.fidelity_note:
Assume Lemmas 3.1, D.1, D.2 and the weighted derivative recurrence supplied by Lemma D.3. Let $\mathsf D\ge1$, $W_j\ge0$, $\kappa(a)=G(a)^Tk$ and $P_\kappa=\kappa\otimes\kappa/|\kappa|^2$. Suppose $F,G,M,P_\kappa$ are smooth matrix fields on $\mathbb R^3$, each satisfying $\|D^jc(a)\|\le W_j\mathsf D^{16(j+1)}$. Then $G(I-P_\kappa)$ and $-2G(I-P_\kappa)MF$ satisfy the respective bounds $C_j\mathsf D^{32(j+1)}$ and $C'_j\mathsf D^{64(j+1)}$ for every derivative order, with constants fixed before $k,\mathsf D,F,G,M$. The product estimate of Lemma D.2 proves these bounds. No inverse relation between $F,G$ is required. For the parent deformation they encode the projected inverse and the right-hand-side coefficient in (5.18). At $\kappa=0$, division by zero makes $P_\kappa=0$.

Given Lemma D.2’s product estimate and smooth coefficient bounds $\|D^jc\|\le W_j\mathsf D^{16(j+1)}$, the formal conclusion bounds $G(I-P_\kappa)$ and $-2G(I-P_\kappa)MF$ with exponents $32(j+1)$ and $64(j+1)$. The paper uses the Gram-matrix inverse in coordinates on $\mathbb R^2$. The forward frame is not separately bounded by this declaration, and no inverse relation between $F,G$ is assumed.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The coframe estimates use ambient operator norms; restriction to the transverse plane and fixed-dimensional norm comparisons give the needed coordinate bounds.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S53.transverseCoframe_jetPower
rows.plain: Derivative bounds for the inverse coframe on the transverse plane
rows.annotation: The Gram matrix $K_\perp=A_\perp^TA_\perp$ has eigenvalues between $\mathsf D^{-2}$ and $\mathsf D^2$. Differentiating $K_\perp^{-1}K_\perp=I$ bounds the jets of the inverse, and hence those of $A_\perp^\dagger$ and $\mathcal M_\perp$. These are bounds before multiplication by the radius weights; Equation (D.7) then absorbs the cost of each positive label derivative.

citations.supports: The weighted Gronwall comparison between central and nearby equations.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: Suppose the central fixed-plane equation propagates $|v|/\gamma$ by at most $\mathsf D^3$, and the nearby coefficient differs from the central one by at most $\mathsf D^{-3}$. Variation of constants in the proof of Lemma 5.3 gives an integral inequality with coefficient one, so an interval of length at most $T\le1$ yields $|v(t)|/\gamma(t)\le e\mathsf D^3|v(t')|/\gamma(t')$. This controls homogeneous amplification uniformly throughout the envelope. The formal theorem proves the same argument for continuous linear equations in a real normed space, a positive continuously differentiable weight, any $K>0$, perturbation at most $K^{-1}$ and interval length at most one. Its stronger verdict means that substituting $K=\mathsf D^3$ gives the paper's case within this more general result, with central stability assumed for every homogeneous solution.

ties.name: TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_forward
ties.plain: Weighted forward bound for a nearby amplitude generator

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $E$ be a real normed space, $A,A_1$ continuous families of bounded linear operators on $[a,b]$, and $\gamma>0$ continuously differentiable there, with endpoint derivatives taken from within the interval. Assume $K>0$, $b-a\le1$, and $\|A_1(u)-A(u)\|\le K^{-1}$ throughout. For every solution $z_t=Az$ and all $a\le u\le v\le b$, require $|z(v)|/\gamma(v)\le K|z(u)|/\gamma(u)$. Then every solution $x_t=A_1x$ satisfies $|x(t)|/\gamma(t)\le eK|x(a)|/\gamma(a)$ for $t\in[a,b]$. The stability hypothesis quantifies over all solutions of the central homogeneous equation. Taking $K=\mathsf D^3$ gives the factor in the nearby-label estimate used for Lemma 5.3.

The formal statement treats any real normed-space homogeneous equation with a positive continuously differentiable weight, a central propagation factor $K>0$, coefficient perturbation at most $K^{-1}$ and interval length at most one. It gives factor $eK$; the paper’s application takes $K=\mathsf D^3$.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The parameter-dependent homogeneous equation estimate applies to the actual seed after its coefficient and stability bounds are supplied.

rows.name: TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_forward
rows.plain: Weighted forward bound for a nearby amplitude generator
rows.annotation: In the fixed-plane equation, write the generator at $a$ as the one at $0$ plus a perturbation. Its norm is at most $\mathsf D^{-3}$, while the weighted central propagator has norm at most $\mathsf D^3$. Their product is at most one. Variation of constants therefore gives an integral inequality for $|v(t)|/\gamma(t)$ with coefficient one, so the cost of leaving the origin is at most $e^{T-t'}\le e$.

explanation.text: For $v_t+\mathcal M_\perp(t,a)v=\psi$ on $[t_0,T]$, the nearby-label homogeneous bound gives $|v(t,a)|/\gamma(t)\le e\mathsf D^3\bigl(|v(t_0,a)|/\gamma(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^t|\psi(t',a)|/\gamma(t')\,dt'\bigr)$. This requires $T\le1$, positive $\gamma$, central propagation factor $\mathsf D^3$ and coefficient perturbation at most $\mathsf D^{-3}$, as established immediately before (5.23). The formula follows by variation of constants and is the zero-order input for the higher-derivative estimate. The formal theorem assumes continuous coefficients and forcing, a positive continuously differentiable weight and the corresponding bound for every central homogeneous solution. It is stronger because it gives the same conclusion for any real normed-space equation and factor $K>0$, with the paper obtained by setting $K=\mathsf D^3$.

ties.name: TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_forced_norm_le
ties.plain: Weighted bound for a forced amplitude with a nearby generator

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $E$ be a real normed space, $A,A_1$ continuous families of bounded linear operators on $[a,b]$ and a continuous forcing $f$, and $\gamma>0$ continuously differentiable there, with endpoint derivatives taken from within the interval. Assume $K>0$, $b-a\le1$, and $\|A_1(u)-A(u)\|\le K^{-1}$ throughout. For every solution $z_t=Az$ and all $a\le u\le v\le b$, require $|z(v)|/\gamma(v)\le K|z(u)|/\gamma(u)$. Then every solution $x_t=A_1x+f$ satisfies $|x(t)|/\gamma(t)\le eK\bigl(|x(a)|/\gamma(a)+\int_a^t|f(u)|/\gamma(u)\,du\bigr)$ for $t\in[a,b]$. The stability hypothesis quantifies over all solutions of the central homogeneous equation. Taking $K=\mathsf D^3$ gives the factor in the nearby-label estimate used for Lemma 5.3.

The formal estimate applies to a general forced linear equation with continuous coefficients and forcing, positive continuously differentiable weight and perturbation at most $K^{-1}$ of a central equation with propagation factor $K$. Setting $K=\mathsf D^3$ and the initial time to $t_0$ gives the paper’s displayed bound.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The auxiliary forced equation estimate is more general than the particular transverse problem; the construction supplies its hypotheses.

rows.name: TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_forced_norm_le
rows.plain: Weighted bound for a forced amplitude with a nearby generator
rows.annotation: Let $\Phi_a(t,t')$ denote the two-dimensional homogeneous propagator. The preceding estimate bounds $\Phi_a(t,t')$ by $e\mathsf D^3\gamma(t)/\gamma(t')$. Substituting this in the variation-of-constants formula gives Equation (5.23); the denominator in the integrand is $\gamma(t')$, not $\gamma(t)$. Thus even a very small early forcing is measured in relation to the early seed, and amplification from that time is already included.

explanation.text: Under the deformation and central-stability bounds of §5.1, the projected initial seed (5.4) satisfies $|\mathbf a(t,a)-\mathbf a(t,0)|\le C\mathsf D^C|a|\,|\mathbf a(t,0)|$ on the small envelope and active interval. The proof compares the two fixed-plane equations by (5.23), including the difference in their projected initial data. This relative estimate is what allows one radius to preserve both the central amplitude scale and the positive coupling in (5.19). The linked formal construction gives the relative bound with a coefficient depending on $\mathsf D$, while the linked condition merely records it with a supplied coefficient. Both are weaker as stated because neither exposes the required uniform polynomial dependence $C\mathsf D^C$, even though they also record useful amplitude and coupling bounds.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S5a.seedNear_of_h51
ties.plain: Near-origin seed estimates from the parent coefficient bounds

rows.fidelity_note:
Assume $0\le t_0<T\le1$, the parent coefficient, residual and coercivity bounds, and a nonzero central transverse seed with relative forward growth at most $\mathsf D$ and coupling at least $\mathsf D^{-1}$. Proposition 5.1 allows one sufficiently small envelope on which every seed with initial data (5.4) satisfies the quantitative near-origin estimates. Uniqueness identifies that seed with the separately constructed local solution. The conclusion includes more than (5.19), but its relative-error constant is only specified as a function of $\mathsf D$; this statement does not expose a polynomial bound for that constant. The transverse stability assumption is $|\mathbf b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/\gamma(t')$ for every transverse homogeneous solution $\mathbf b$ and $t_0\le t'\le t\le T$.

The paper bounds the relative seed error by $C\mathsf D^C\lVert a\rVert$. The formal conclusion gives an unspecified coefficient depending on $\mathsf D$, so its statement does not expose the uniform polynomial dependence used in this display.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The omitted polynomial bound for the intermediate error coefficient is not needed downstream: a uniform radius and the required comparability and positive coupling are supplied directly.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S5a.seedNear_of_h51
rows.plain: Near-origin seed estimates from the parent coefficient bounds
rows.annotation: In the fixed coordinates, the difference $v_a-v_0$ has initial value $(A_\perp^\dagger(t_0,a)-A_\perp^\dagger(t_0,0))\mathbf a(t_0,0)$, and force $-(\mathcal M_\perp(t,a)-\mathcal M_\perp(t,0))v_a$. Both coefficient differences are bounded by a parent power times $|a|$. After applying Equation (5.23), return to the physical vectors by writing $\mathbf a(t,a)-\mathbf a(t,0)=A_\perp(t,a)(v_a-v_0)+(A_\perp(t,a)-A_\perp(t,0))v_0$. This retains the factor $|\mathbf a(t,0)|$. The Lean conclusion records the comparison with a coefficient depending on the parent bound.

rows.fidelity_note:
Given functions $M(t,a)$, $\kappa(t,a)$, $\mathbf a_c(t)$ and $\mathbf a(t,a)$, and real parameters $t_0,T,\ell_*,\mathsf D,C$, this condition requires the following for $t\in[t_0,T]$ and $|a|\le2\ell_*$: $|\mathbf a(t,a)-\mathbf a_c(t)|\le C|a||\mathbf a_c(t)|$, $\tfrac12|\mathbf a_c(t)|\le|\mathbf a(t,a)|\le2|\mathbf a_c(t)|$, $(2\mathsf D)^{-1}|\kappa(t,0)||\mathbf a_c(t)|\le\kappa(t,a)\cdot M(t,a)\mathbf a(t,a)$, $\kappa(t,a)\cdot M(t,a)\mathbf a(t,a)>0$, and $(8\mathsf D)^{-1}\le\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a/(|\kappa||\mathbf a|)$. The constant $C$ is supplied, not chosen by this definition. No smoothness or seed equation is imposed here. The paper's application has $\mathsf D\ge2$ and positive radius; unrestricted reciprocals at zero are assigned zero. The condition includes more than (5.19), but does not require $C$ to be a uniform power of $\mathsf D$.

The paper requires the relative-error coefficient to be an absolute power of $\mathsf D$. The formal condition leaves that coefficient free, so this condition alone does not assert the displayed polynomial dependence.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The omitted polynomial bound for the intermediate error coefficient is not needed downstream: a uniform radius and the required comparability and positive coupling are supplied directly.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.SeedNear
rows.plain: Quantitative bounds near the origin
rows.annotation: The comparison is required relative to the central seed at every active time. This is what permits the initial projection and coefficient variation to be small even when the central seed is far below its terminal size. A uniform absolute error would not suffice to retain the positive coupling margin in Equation (5.5). The definition does not supply the bound on its comparison coefficient.

citations.supports: The coefficient, product and phase-primitive inputs to the pressure estimate.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: To estimate the transverse pressure, write $\lambda\mathsf p$ as the zero-mean phase primitive of coefficient products involving $M$, $\kappa/\lambda$, $\lambda^2/|\kappa|^2$, $f$ and $V$. The product estimate (D.4), phase-primitive estimate (D.5) and parent coefficient bound (5.8) then give (5.24) at the same derivative order. This recovers pressure after the velocity has been estimated. The formal result linked here supplies only rescaled derivative bounds for the three coefficients, under smooth bounds at a scale $\mathsf D_0$, $\mathsf D_0^{64}\le\mathsf D$ and $\ell_*\mathsf D^{16}\le1$. It is weaker than the whole quoted step because the source and velocity bounds and the product and primitive estimates still have to be inserted; its coefficient formula alone does not require nonzero denominators, whereas the paper has $\lambda\ge1$ and $\kappa\ne0$.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S53.rescaled_pressure_jets
ties.plain: Rescaling the pressure coefficients

rows.fidelity_note:
Fix $N\in\mathbb N$ and nonnegative constants $W_j$. Assume Lemmas 3.1, D.1, D.2 and the weighted derivative recurrence supplied by Lemma D.3. Let $\mathsf D,\mathsf D_0\ge1$, $\mathsf D_0^{64}\le\mathsf D$, $\ell_*>0$ and $\ell_*\mathsf D^{16}\le1$. Each coefficient $c=M,\kappa/\lambda,\lambda^2/|\kappa|^2$ must be smooth on $\mathbb R^3$ and satisfy $\|D^jc(a)\|\le W_j\mathsf D_0^{16(j+1)}$ for every $j,a$. There is $C\ge1$, fixed before these coefficients and scales, such that every derivative of order $0\le j\le N$ of the three rescaled coefficients $c(\ell_*a)$ is bounded respectively by $C\mathsf D$, $C\mathsf D^2$ and $C\mathsf D^4$. These are operator-norm bounds, uniform in $a$. The statement assumes neither $\lambda\ne0$ nor $\kappa\ne0$; division by zero is zero. Source and velocity estimates are still needed for (5.24).

The formal statement bounds only $M(\ell_*a)$, $\kappa(\ell_*a)/\lambda$ and $\lambda^2/|\kappa(\ell_*a)|^2$, through each fixed order, by $C\mathsf D,C\mathsf D^2,C\mathsf D^4$. It assumes smooth coefficient bounds at scale $\mathsf D_0$, $\mathsf D_0^{64}\le\mathsf D$ and $\ell_*\mathsf D^{16}\le1$. The product and phase-primitive estimates invoked in the paper are still needed to obtain the pressure bound.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The rescaled pressure coefficients are the inputs to the pressure estimate; the transverse solution and phase primitive provide the remaining factors.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S53.rescaled_pressure_jets
rows.plain: Rescaling the pressure coefficients
rows.annotation: The normalization matters when differentiating in the labels: $\kappa/\lambda$ and $|\kappa/\lambda|^{-2}$ have bounds independent of $\lambda$ in Equation (5.8). Thus all the explicit frequency gain can be kept in $\mathsf p$ as a factor $\lambda^{-1}$. The coefficient lemma supplies the jet bounds for this product; the pressure estimate also uses the phase primitive.

citations.supports: Pressure recovery from normalized coefficient and field estimates.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For centered smooth phase-periodic $f,V$ and nonzero transported $\kappa$, the normalized primitive in (5.16) satisfies $\lambda\|\mathsf p\|_{[n],\gamma}\le C_n\mathsf D^C\bigl(\|f\|_{[n],\gamma}+\|V\|_{[n],\gamma}\bigr)$ under the parent coefficient bounds (5.8). This follows from the scaled product and phase-primitive estimates (D.4)–(D.5), with the positive time weight applied after spatial differentiation. It gives the pressure half of Lemma 5.3(ii) and also estimates the leading homogeneous pressure. The formal theorem instead bounds each scaled derivative using supplied constants for the coefficient fields, source and velocity, retaining their products and a derivative-order factor explicitly. Different marks that intermediate form and its normalized carrier: substituting the parent bounds, identifying the physical carrier as $\lambda$ times the normalized one, and summing derivatives produces (5.24).

ties.name: TorusEuler.oscillatoryPhasePressure_weightedWordBound
ties.plain: Weighted derivatives of the pressure

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $t$ range over any index set. For each $t$, let $V,f$ be smooth functions of $(a,s)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, one-periodic in $s$ with zero phase mean. Define linear forms $A(a)v=-2\kappa\cdot Mv/|\kappa|^2$ and $B(a)f=\kappa\cdot f/|\kappa|^2$. Suppose these coefficient fields are smooth and every scaled derivative through order $n$ is bounded by constants $A_0,B_0$, while those of $g(t)^{-1}V,g(t)^{-1}f$ are bounded by $V_0,F_0$. Scaling uses $\ell_*\partial_{a_i},h\partial_s$. For $\lambda>0$, every such derivative of $g^{-1}\lambda\mathsf p$ is at most $2^{n+1}\binom{n+4}{4}(A_0V_0+B_0F_0)$, where $\mathsf p=\partial_s^{-1}[(\lambda\kappa)\cdot(f-2MV)/|\lambda\kappa|^2]$. The primitive has zero mean. Neither $g$ nor $t$ is differentiated. Reciprocals at zero are assigned zero; the application has positive weight and nonzero carrier. Parent coefficient estimates remain inputs to (5.24).

The formal bound controls weighted derivatives of the normalized phase primitive using supplied coefficient, velocity and source bounds, for smooth centered one-periodic fields. It retains those coefficient constants explicitly. Inserting the parent estimates and summing the derivative bounds gives $C_n\mathsf D^C$ in (5.24); this theorem alone does not derive that parent power.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The zero-mean phase-primitive estimate is one step in bounding the pressure. Its explicit constants are compatible with the allowed order-dependent constants.

rows.name: TorusEuler.oscillatoryPhasePressure_weightedWordBound
rows.plain: Weighted derivatives of the pressure
rows.annotation: For a centered periodic integrand $r$, the primitive $\int_0^s r$ is periodic, and subtracting its mean gives the normalized primitive with supremum at most $2\|r\|_\infty$. Differentiation in labels commutes with this operation; differentiation in phase does too on centered periodic profiles. Thus the same bound applies to every scaled derivative word, with no extra $h^{-1}$ beyond the derivatives already included in $\|r\|_{[n],\gamma}$.

citations.supports: The homogeneous seed estimate leading to the velocity scale in (5.22).
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The time-independent envelope makes $g\mathbf a$ a homogeneous seed solution on $[t_0,T]$, supported inside the envelope and transverse to $\kappa$. Its projected initial data (5.4) have scaled norm at most $C_n\mathsf D^C\gamma(t_0)\lambda^{-3/4}$, so (5.20) with $f=0$ yields $\|g\mathbf a\|_{[n],\gamma}\le C_n\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-3/4}$. Multiplication by the profile $F_h$, whose scaled norm is $O(h)$ with $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$, then gives the leading velocity size in (5.22). The formal implication proves Lemma 5.3 from the parent, profile and derivative estimates, but its proof uses a separate homogeneous leading-wave estimate. Thus different describes the proof route rather than a contradiction in the resulting leading-wave bound.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S53.lemma_5_3_of_leaves
ties.plain: Transverse velocity and pressure estimates from the ODE bounds

rows.fidelity_note:
Assume Proposition 5.1, Lemmas 3.1, D.1, D.2 and the weighted derivative estimate for linear ordinary differential equations supplied by Lemma D.3. The formal implication then proves Lemma 5.3. The parent on $0<T\le1$ is smooth, odd, periodic and divergence free, with $\mathsf D\ge2$, Fourier radii $2\mathsf D,4\mathsf D$ for $U,R_U$, gradient and deformation bounds $\mathsf D$, $\|R_U\|_\infty\le\lambda^{-5/2}$ and $D^2p-\nabla R_U\le I$. Require $0\le t_0<T$, $\lambda=|\kappa(t_0,0)|\ge1$, central transverse stability and coupling as in (5.5), and $0<\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|\le1$. A sufficiently small $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-a}$ gives $\|V\|_{[n],\gamma}\le C_n\mathsf D^C(\gamma(t_0)^{-1}\|V(t_0)\|_{[n]}+\|f\|_{[n],\gamma})$ for supported transverse solutions, the zero-initial velocity-pressure estimate, the leading-wave bound and $|\mathbf a(t,a)|\le2|\mathbf a(t,0)|$, $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a>0$ on $|a|\le2\ell_*$. The first estimate requires profiles smooth on all of $[0,T]$; the leading bound uses a separate homogeneous estimate. The transverse stability assumption is $|\mathbf b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/\gamma(t')$ for every transverse homogeneous solution $\mathbf b$ and $t_0\le t'\le t\le T$.

The paper obtains the leading estimate by applying (5.20) with zero forcing, followed by (5.24). The formal proof uses a separate homogeneous leading-wave estimate instead, so this step reaches the same bound without invoking those already assembled conclusions.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The proof treats the leading wave separately and obtains the same bound. It does not require an unproved extension of arbitrary active-interval data.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S53.lemma_5_3_of_leaves
rows.plain: Transverse velocity and pressure estimates from the ODE bounds
rows.annotation: At $t_0$ the initial value for the homogeneous estimate is $g(I-P_\kappa)\mathbf a(t_0,0)$. Its scaled norm contains $|\mathbf a(t_0,0)|=\gamma(t_0)\lambda^{-3/4}$, so the small denominator in Equation (5.20) cancels. The factor $F_h$ contributes a further $h$ only after estimating $g\mathbf a$; this is the origin of $\lambda^{-5/4}$ in Equation (5.22).

citations.supports: The homogeneous transverse equation for the unswitched leading wave.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For a transverse seed solving (3.2), the unswitched leading wave $A_1=g\mathbf a F_h$ satisfies $A_{1,t}+MA_1+\kappa\partial_s\mathsf p[A_1]=0$ on $[t_0,T]$. The time-independent envelope and phase profile preserve the seed equation, while the pressure formula (3.4) supplies the longitudinal term. Both velocity and pressure have zero phase mean, and $\kappa\cdot A_1=0$, so (5.24) can be applied with $f=0$. The formal statement proves these identities for the chosen radial envelope, $0<h\le1$ and a controlled seed, with time derivatives taken within the active interval. Weaker records the restriction to that selected envelope, while the paper's calculation permits any fixed admissible envelope.

ties.name: TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.paper_hierarchy_leading_homogeneous
ties.plain: The leading wave equation

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $t_0<T$, $0<h\le1$, and let the selected seed solve $\mathbf a_t=-M\mathbf a+2\kappa(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2$ with transverse initial data. With $A_1=g\mathbf a F_h$ and $\mathsf p[A_1]=-2g(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)|\kappa|^{-2}P_h$, the formal statement proves $A_{1,t}+MA_1+\kappa\partial_s\mathsf p[A_1]=0$ on $[t_0,T]$. It also gives $\kappa\cdot A_1=0$ and zero phase mean for both profiles. Time derivatives hold the label fixed and are taken within the interval at its endpoints. This verifies (3.4) for the selected radial envelope and profile family; the paper's derivation allows arbitrary suitable leading data.

The paper states the homogeneous transverse identity for any fixed admissible cutoff. The formal statement proves it for the chosen envelope, a special case of the paper's statement.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The homogeneous leading-wave theorem treats the particular envelope and phase profile used in the construction.

rows.name: TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.paper_hierarchy_leading_homogeneous
rows.plain: The leading wave equation
rows.annotation: At fixed $(a,s)$, $g(a)F_h(s)$ is constant in time. Multiplication of the seed equation by this factor produces the pressure term $-2g(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)|\kappa|^{-2}F_h\kappa$, because $P_h'=F_h$. This gives the homogeneous equation for the pair $(A_1,\mathsf p[A_1])$. Switching the wave on adds the separate time-cutoff error rather than a force in this homogeneous estimate.

citations.supports: The grouping of retained velocities, means and the final divergence correction.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: At depth $P\ge2$, the perturbation is $W=\sum_{p=1}^PZ_p+C_{P+1}$, where $Y_p=V_p+C_p$, $Z_p=Y_p+B_p$ and $C_1=0$. The correction $C_{p+1}=C[V_p]$ belongs to the completed oscillation $V_p+C_{p+1}$, so the last correction remains even when no velocity $V_{P+1}$ is retained. This grouping makes the level counting in (5.26) and the remainder in (5.30) consistent. Three linked formal expressions supply the correction index and the definitions of $Y_p,Z_p$, while the finite-sum theorem supplies the displayed regrouping under $C_1=0$. Each is weaker than the complete display on its own; formal indices are nonnegative integers with subtraction truncated at zero, but all intended levels here are positive.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.Cd

The correction attached to $V_p$ is stored alongside that oscillation, but the paper denotes it by $C_{p+1}$. The paper’s $C_p$ is stored at index $p-1$; the physical expansion sets $C_1=0$. The field $Y_p=V_p+C_p$ groups the new transverse velocity with the divergence correction produced by $V_{p-1}$. rows.annotation: In the size grouping $Y_p=V_p+C[V_{p-1}]$, so both fields can be counted as level $p$ in the quadratic terms. In the divergence calculation the two fields must instead be $V_p+C[V_p]$. The individual $Y_p$ need not be divergence free, even though the full retained sum is.

rows.fidelity_note:
For an indexed family of profiles, the formal definition gives $Z_p=V_p+C_p+B_p$ in the paper's notation. Here $C_p$ is generated by the preceding oscillation $V_{p-1}$: the stored correction index is one smaller than the paper index. The formula defines the level field used in the quadratic interactions of §1.3 and §5.5. It does not impose that $B_p$ is phase independent or that $V_p$ is transverse; these belong to the expansion equations. At index zero, subtraction is truncated to zero, so the intended mathematical use is at levels $p\ge1$.

The formal definition gives $Z_p=Y_p+B_p$. The other equalities and the convention $C_1=0$ are separate definitions or hypotheses.

rows.annotation: In $(Z_i\cdot\widetilde{\mathbf d})Z_j$, the slow derivative acts on all of $Z_j=Y_j+B_j$. The fast derivative kills $B_j$, and $V_i\cdot\kappa=0$, so only $((C_i+B_i)\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY_j$ remains. This is why the fast sum can be split into a known completion term and a term containing the new mean.

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $P\ge1$ and suppose the first correction in the paper's indexing is $C_1=0$. For arbitrary families of vectors in an additive group, the formal statement proves $\sum_{p=1}^P(V_p+C_{p+1}+B_p)=\sum_{p=1}^P Z_p+C_{P+1}$, where $Z_p=V_p+C_p+B_p$. The stored correction at index $p$ is generated by $V_p$, which accounts for the shift by one. Thus the completed final oscillation contributes $C_{P+1}$ even though there is no retained $V_{P+1}$. This is an equality of finite sums; no evolution equation, support property or norm estimate is used.

The formal equality gives $W=\sum_{p=1}^PZ_p+C_{P+1}$ for $P\ge1$, assuming $C_1=0$. The paper also lists the definitions of $Y_p,Z_p$ and states the convention; this theorem uses rather than proves that convention.

rows.name: TorusEuler.HierarchyProfiles.velocity_eq_sum_Z_add_completion
rows.plain: Sum of profiles with the last curl correction
rows.annotation: Grouping $W$ by size gives $\sum_{p=1}^P Z_p+C_{P+1}$; grouping by generating oscillation gives $\sum_{p=1}^P(V_p+C_{p+1}+B_p)$. The equality follows by shifting the correction index and using $C_1=0$. The first grouping organizes the products by level, while the second establishes divergence via the curl identity.

citations.supports: The inverse-frequency gain that places the preceding correction at the current level.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The correction $C_p=C[V_{p-1}]$ gains one inverse power of $\lambda$ from the vector potential and therefore fits beside the level-$p$ oscillation. Indeed, Lemma 5.5 gives the analytic gain $\|C[V]\|_{[n],\gamma}\le C_n\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-1}\|V\|_{[n+1],\gamma}$, and the exponents in Theorem 5.6 leave an extra $\lambda^{-1/3}$ relative to $V_p$. This is why the expansion groups $C_p$ with $V_p$ in $Y_p$. The linked formal arithmetic statement checks precisely that exponent difference for $p\ge1$, and the other expression records $Y_p=V_p+C_p$ with the shifted correction index. Both are weaker than the sentence's analytic justification: neither alone bounds an actual correction, and that bound comes from (5.31).

ties.name: TorusEuler.hierarchy_completion_previous
ties.plain: Preceding curl correction gains one third of a frequency power

rows.fidelity_note:
For an integer $p\ge1$, the formal statement proves that the exponent of the correction generated by level $p-1$ is the oscillatory exponent at level $p$ minus $1/3$. In paper notation this says that $C_p$, inherited from $V_{p-1}$, fits at level $p$ with an additional factor $\lambda^{-1/3}$. The oscillatory exponent is $-5/4-2(p-1)/3$, and a correction subtracts one further power from the generating oscillation. The assumption $p\ge1$ prevents truncation in the nonnegative-integer index $p-1$. This is arithmetic among assigned exponents; an estimate for the actual correction requires the analytic bounds.

The paper asserts a bound for $C_p$. The linked formal result checks only that the frequency exponents fit; the estimate of the correction itself is a separate step.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The exponent identity is the numerical part of the correction estimate. The curl estimate supplies the corresponding profile norm bound.

rows.plain: Preceding curl correction gains one third of a frequency power
rows.annotation: For $p\ge2$ write $S_p=\lambda^{-5/4-2(p-1)/3}$. The correction estimate gives $C_p$ the scale $\lambda^{-1}S_{p-1}=\lambda^{-1/3}S_p$. In particular it is better than the level-$p$ bound by $\lambda^{-1/3}$. The extra gain matters when $C_p$ advects the phase of another oscillation.

rows.fidelity_note:
The paper’s $C_p$ is stored at index $p-1$; the physical expansion sets $C_1=0$. The field $Y_p=V_p+C_p$ groups the new transverse velocity with the divergence correction produced by $V_{p-1}$. This is the convention at the start of §5.5, reflecting the extra frequency gain of the correction. The sum itself imposes no equation; its size and constraints follow from the expansion equations and Theorem 5.6.

The definition groups $V_p$ with the preceding curl correction as $Y_p=V_p+C_p$. It does not prove the frequency gain or the norm bound justifying that grouping; Lemma 5.5 and the exponent calculation supply those facts.

rows.annotation: The definition of $Y_p$ places the known completion $C_p$ with the new oscillation $V_p$ because their bounds fit the same level budget. It does not assert that they are of equal size or form a curl pair. The completion estimate gives the stronger gain used in the phase-advection estimates.

citations.supports: Separating activation from the level-two source.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: After setting aside the activation error, the source $H_2$ consists of the unswitched linear correction multiplied by $\widetilde\chi$, the label advection $(V_1\cdot\mathbf d)V_1$, and the phase advection $(C_2\cdot\kappa)\partial_sV_1$. Its phase average determines the forcing for the first mean correction, and its centered part contributes to the first higher oscillation. The two formal source expressions instead start with the differentiated switched correction and subtract its activation contribution; identifying them with the displayed formula requires this product rule. Their different verdicts record that representation, while the weaker finite-sum equality reconciles the two source expressions but does not itself prove the cutoff identities.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.levelSource

This defines the source for $p\ge2$ using $Y_i=V_i+C_i$ and $Z_i=Y_i+B_i$; subtraction of natural-number indices is truncated at zero outside that range. The source $H_p$ contains $(\partial_t+M)C_p+\mathbf d\mathsf p_{p-1}$ and the two interaction sums of (5.26). Here $C_p$ means the correction generated by $V_{p-1}$, although the stored correction is indexed by its generating velocity. rows.name: TorusEuler.HierarchyOperators.sourceBeforeMean
rows.plain: The source before the mean solve
rows.annotation: The abstract pre-mean source at $p=2$ contains the material derivative of the stored completion of $V_1$, the slow gradient of its pressure and the two quadratic interactions. It subtracts the completion of the activation error at that level. With the cutoff identities this gives precisely the switched linear term in Equation (5.25).

citations.supports: Cancellation of the linear contribution under phase averaging.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The linear part $\widetilde\chi[(\partial_t+M)C[A_1]+\mathbf d\mathsf p[A_1]]$ of $H_2$ has zero phase average. The correction and pressure are centered, and the strain, transported derivatives and time cutoff are independent of phase, so phase averaging commutes with these operations. Only the quadratic terms remain in $\langle H_2\rangle_s$, which is why its first bound has the square scale $\lambda^{-5/2}$. The formal statement proves the corresponding zero-average identity at any level, assuming centered correction, pressure and subtracted activation term and phase-independent coefficients. Same concerns this cancellation, with centeredness supplied as hypotheses rather than inferred merely from the expression for $H_2$.

ties.name: TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.average_relayAtLevel_eq_zero
ties.plain: Linear relay term has zero phase average

rows.fidelity_note: Let the deformation and strain coefficients be phase independent, and let the preceding correction, pressure and subtracted activation term each have zero phase average. The preceding curl correction and oscillatory pressure have zero phase average, so their linear contribution to $H_p$ averages to zero. The activation term removed at level two also has zero average. This leaves the quadratic terms, together with the separately added parent residual at level two, as the forcing of the mean equation.
rows.name: TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.average_relayAtLevel_eq_zero
rows.plain: Linear relay term has zero phase average
rows.annotation: Averaging commutes with the material operator $\partial_t+M$ and the slow gradient $\mathbf d$, since their coefficients are independent of the phase. Thus the linear relay has zero mean at every level. At level two the completion of the cutoff derivative, which is removed from the relay, has zero mean as well. No estimate on the size of a time derivative is needed for this cancellation.

citations.supports: Removing the fast phase derivative from the averaged quadratic source.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For $C_2=C[V_1]$, phase periodicity and (3.6) give $\langle(C_2\cdot\kappa)\partial_sV_1\rangle_s=\langle(\mathbf d\cdot V_1)V_1\rangle_s$. Integration by parts first moves the phase derivative onto $C_2\cdot\kappa$, and the divergence-correction identity replaces that derivative by $-\mathbf d\cdot V_1$. The mean source consequently contains a label derivative instead of the expensive fast derivative, preserving the quadratic size $\lambda^{-5/2}$. The formal statement proves $\langle(C[V]\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY\rangle_s=\langle(\mathbf d\cdot V)Y\rangle_s$ for a smooth transverse centered $V$ and any smooth periodic $Y$, in a compatible transported geometry with nonzero $\kappa$. Its stronger verdict refers to the independently chosen second factor $Y$; taking $V=Y=V_1$ gives the paper's identity.

ties.name: TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.average_phaseAdv_complete
ties.plain: Phase-averaged curl advection equals a slow divergence product

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $V,Y$ be smooth profiles on $[0,T]$, one-periodic in phase with the coupled label translation law. Suppose $G,\kappa$ are independent of phase, $\kappa\ne0$, and a surjective $C^2$ map $A(t,\cdot)$ satisfies $G(t,A(t,x))=D_xA(t,x)$ and $\kappa(t,A(t,x))=D_xA(t,x)^Tk_*$. Set $\mathbf d=G^T\nabla_a$ and $C[V]=\mathbf d\times[-\partial_s^{-1}(\kappa\times V/|\kappa|^2)]$, where the primitive has zero phase mean. If $\langle V\rangle_s=0$ and $\kappa\cdot V=0$, then $\langle(C[V]\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY\rangle_s=\langle(\mathbf d\cdot V)Y\rangle_s$. This is (5.42) with $V=V_{i-1}$. The formal statement allows any such $Y$, independently of the expansion; no zero-mean condition on $Y$ is needed.

The paper applies phase integration by parts with $C_2=C[V_1]$ and the second factor also $V_1$. The formal statement allows any transverse zero-mean $V$ and an independent profile $Y$, giving the same identity for $C[V]$ and $Y$.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The phase-average identity holds for two arbitrary profiles and therefore includes the self-interaction used in the mean equation.

rows.name: TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.average_phaseAdv_complete
rows.plain: Phase-averaged curl advection equals a slow divergence product
rows.annotation: This stress calculation extends to later levels. In Equation (5.26), averaging a fast pair with $i+j=p+1$ gives $\langle(\mathbf d\cdot V_{i-1})Y_j\rangle_s$, whose indices add to $p$. Since $C_i$ is a slow curl, $\mathbf d\cdot Y_i=\mathbf d\cdot V_i$. After reindexing, the averaged fast terms therefore complete the slow oscillatory products to row divergences of $\langle Y_j\otimes Y_i\rangle_s$. This is the identity underlying the improved mean estimate (5.35).

citations.supports: The size and exact cancellation of the parent residual in the first mean solve.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The first mean source is $-\langle H_2\rangle_s-R_U\circ X$, because both contributions are bounded by $C_n\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-5/2}$ in scaled label norms. For the parent residual, the bound follows from its Fourier radius $4\mathsf D$, its supremum bound $\lambda^{-5/2}$ and the composition estimate (5.10). Including it at this stage ensures that the final residual identity cancels the old parent residual exactly. One formal expression inserts the residual only at level two, while the other proves the composition estimate for any band-limited field of that size under the stated flow and derivative bounds. Each weaker verdict marks one half of the argument: the source expression gives no bound, and the estimate neither identifies the field as a momentum residual nor inserts it into the mean equation.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.meanSource
ties.plain: The forcing for a mean correction

rows.fidelity_note:
At level $p$, the formal definition is $\overline f_p=-\langle H_p\rangle_s-\mathbf1_{p=2}R$, where $H_p$ is the source assembled before solving for the new mean and $R$ is the supplied parent residual. In the geometric application $R=R_U\circ X$ is independent of phase. The negative sign makes the mean correction cancel the averaged error, and level two is the only place where the previous parent's residual is inserted. This is the right side of the equation described in §1.3. The definition does not solve that equation or impose the endpoint conditions selecting its initial velocity.

The definition inserts $-R_U\circ X$ at level two and nowhere else. It does not bound that residual by $C_n\lambda^{-5/2}$; the other linked estimate supplies the analytic reason for including it at this level.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The expression inserts the parent residual only at level two. Its quantitative bound and its cancellation are proved in separate steps.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.meanSource
rows.plain: The forcing for a mean correction
rows.annotation: The averaged wave force is at most a parent power times $\lambda^{-5/2}$, the square of the leading velocity scale. At each active time it even carries the square of the seed weight (up to parent powers), whereas the inherited residual is only bounded in the whole-slab unweighted norm. Equation (5.10) gives it the same frequency scale at every label order. This is why the first mean inverse can remove both errors at once without losing the improved power of $\lambda$.

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $0<T\le1$, $\mathsf D\ge1$, $\lambda\ge1$, $\ell_*\ge0$, $\ell_*\mathsf D^6\le1$, and let $X$ be the flow of a smooth unit-periodic $U$, with $\|DX\|,\|DX^{-1}\|\le\mathsf D$. Fix nonnegative $V_n$ and assume $\|D^kU\|_\infty\le V_n\mathsf D^k$ for $2\le k\le n$. For any family of continuous torus fields $R(t)$ with Fourier radius $4\mathsf D$ and $\|R(t)\|_\infty\le\lambda^{-5/2}$, every scaled label norm of $R\circ X$ is finite and $\|R\circ X\|_{[n]}\le C_n\lambda^{-5/2}$, uniformly on $[0,T]$. The constants are chosen before the fields. This need not be the momentum residual of $U$; that identification is supplied in the application.

The formal statement proves the weighted residual bound after composition, assuming its $4\mathsf D$ Fourier support and size $\lambda^{-5/2}$. It does not define the first mean equation; the linked source definition performs that insertion.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The auxiliary estimate bounds the actual parent residual after pullback; the mean-source formula determines where it enters the hierarchy.

rows.name: TorusEuler.exists_parentResidualWeightedBounds
rows.plain: Scaled derivative bounds for the parent residual in label coordinates
rows.annotation: The parent residual has Fourier support in frequencies at most $4\mathsf D$, so Bernstein controls its order-$m$ derivative by $C_m\mathsf D^m\|R_U\|_\infty$. The chain rule for composition with $X$ introduces at most a fixed power of $\mathsf D$ per derivative; the formal radius condition $\ell_*\mathsf D^6\le1$ absorbs that cost. Consequently no additional parent power is needed in the bound for the residual in label norms.

citations.supports: The two conventions for assigning quadratic interaction levels.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The expansion assigns level $i+j$ to label advection $(Z_i\cdot\mathbf d)Z_j$ and level $i+j-1$ to phase advection $(Z_i\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY_j$. The second convention accounts for the larger cost of differentiating the rapid phase and determines which terms are removed by the level-$p$ equations. These assignments are used in (5.26) and leave the two distinct index thresholds in (5.30). The formal level expression is exactly $i+j-\sigma$, with $\sigma=0$ for label advection and $\sigma=1$ for phase advection. Same refers to this indexing convention; subtraction uses nonnegative integers but agrees with ordinary subtraction on the positive indices used here, and the expression alone is not a size estimate.

ties.name: TorusEuler.hierarchyAdvectionLevel
ties.plain: Hierarchy level assigned to an advection interaction

rows.fidelity_note: The two indices and the shift are nonnegative integers, so subtraction is truncated at zero. Positive interaction indices make this agree with ordinary subtraction in the paper’s uses. Label advection of levels $i$ and $j$ is assigned level $i+j$, while phase advection is assigned level $i+j-1$. This is the counting convention before (5.26). It determines which terms are canceled at the current level and which survive in the remainder; numerical estimates for these terms are proved later.
rows.name: TorusEuler.hierarchyAdvectionLevel
rows.plain: Hierarchy level assigned to an advection interaction
rows.annotation: For a phase pair with $i+j=p+1$, use $C_i$ of scale $\lambda^{-1}S_{i-1}$, where $S_q=\lambda^{-5/4-2(q-1)/3}$. Then $\lambda^{3/2}\lambda^{-1}S_{i-1}S_j=\lambda^{-1/12}S_p$. This is the least spare power among the source estimates; the level definition records the shift, not this analytic bound.

citations.supports: The source known before the level-p mean solve, with the exceptional activation term at level two.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For $3\le p\le P$, $H_p$ collects the linear correction $(\partial_t+M)C_p+\mathbf d\mathsf p_{p-1}$, label interactions with $i+j=p$, and phase interactions by $C_i$ with $i+j=p+1$, $i\ge2$. All indices are positive and all these inputs are known before the level-$p$ mean is solved, since $C_p=C[V_{p-1}]$. This separation leaves phase transport by the means for the supplementary source (5.28), which can use the new $B_p$. Both formal source expressions give precisely this formula at retained levels $3\le p\le P$, explaining same. Their unified definition also handles $p=2$ by subtracting the activation term, so it should not be read as applying the unmodified display (5.26) at that exceptional level.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.levelSource
ties.plain: Source at a level before solving for the mean

rows.fidelity_note: This defines the source for $p\ge2$ using $Y_i=V_i+C_i$ and $Z_i=Y_i+B_i$; subtraction of natural-number indices is truncated at zero outside that range. The source $H_p$ contains $(\partial_t+M)C_p+\mathbf d\mathsf p_{p-1}$ and the two interaction sums of (5.26). At level two it subtracts the activation contribution of the curl correction, recovering (5.25). The correction $C_p$ is already known from $V_{p-1}$, so the source does not depend on the new transverse velocity. The quoted formula is the case $3\le p\le P$; the formal level-two definition additionally subtracts the activation correction.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.levelSource
rows.plain: Source at a level before solving for the mean
rows.annotation: At level three the slow products are $(Z_1\cdot\mathbf d)Z_2+(Z_2\cdot\mathbf d)Z_1$. The fast products are $(C_2\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY_2+(C_3\cdot\kappa)\partial_sV_1$. Both use only earlier oscillations and means, since $C_3=C[V_2]$. The linear terms carry the completion of $V_2$ and the slow gradient of its pressure to the next level. This is the general indexing in Equation (5.26).

rows.fidelity_note: Here a stored correction at index $p-1$ is the paper’s $C_p$; subtraction of indices is truncated at zero, and the physical use is $p\ge2$. The preliminary source $H_p$ combines the preceding curl correction and pressure with label advection and phase advection by the curl corrections. At level two, the activation contribution is removed, giving (5.25); later levels give (5.26). Transport by the means is added separately after solving for $B_p$, through $f_p^S$. The quoted formula is the case $3\le p\le P$; the formal level-two definition additionally subtracts the activation correction.
rows.name: TorusEuler.HierarchyOperators.sourceBeforeMean
rows.plain: The source before the mean solve
rows.annotation: Neither $V_p$ nor $B_p$ occurs in $H_p$. In the slow sum $i+j=p$, both indices are below $p$. In the fast sum $i+j=p+1$, $i\ge2$, the largest possible first index is $p$, but that factor is $C_p=C[V_{p-1}]$, already known. The derivative in the second factor has $j\le p-1$. These index restrictions are the reason the next mean force is prescribed.

citations.supports: The signs, phase splitting and unique level-two residual term.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: At each level, $f_p=-(H_p-\langle H_p\rangle_s)$ cancels the oscillatory part of the preliminary error, and $\bar f_p=-\langle H_p\rangle_s$ cancels its phase average. At $p=2$ the mean source also includes $-R_U\circ X$, so the first mean correction removes the parent's residual as well. These signs make the sum of the mean and transverse equations cancel $H_p$ in the proof of (5.29). The formal oscillatory-source expression gives the centered term, while the two mean-source expressions give the average and the extra residual only at level two, one for arbitrary profiles and one for the selected construction. All receive weaker individually because each supplies only part of (5.27), and none of these expressions by itself asserts that the corresponding equation is solvable.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.oscSource
ties.plain: The centered transverse forcing

rows.fidelity_note:
For an arbitrary preliminary source $H_p$, phase averaging is the integral over one period; centering is an algebraic operation, not an existence statement. The forcing $f_p=-(H_p-\langle H_p\rangle_s)$ is the centered term in (5.27). Its sign cancels the oscillatory part of $H_p$ in the momentum equation. The additional forcing $f_p^S$ is formed only after the mean solve, and the transverse equation uses their sum; centering the preliminary source alone does not include that transport.

The formal definition gives only $f_p=-(H_p-\langle H_p\rangle_s)$. The mean source and its extra level-two residual are separate definitions, linked alongside it.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The centered source is one of the two transverse forcing terms. Adding the supplementary mean-advection source gives the full equation.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.oscSource
rows.plain: The centered transverse forcing
rows.annotation: The slow quadratic source splits into mean–mean, mean–oscillation, oscillation–mean and oscillation–oscillation products. Centering removes the first group exactly. The other three groups all contain an oscillatory factor, and so vanish off the envelope and before activation; in the weighted estimate for $f_p$ one places $1/\gamma$ on such a factor. The supplementary source likewise vanishes there, since it differentiates earlier oscillations in phase.

rows.fidelity_note:
At level $p$, the formal definition is $\overline f_p=-\langle H_p\rangle_s-\mathbf1_{p=2}R$, where $H_p$ is the source assembled before solving for the new mean and $R$ is the supplied parent residual. In the geometric application $R=R_U\circ X$ is independent of phase. The negative sign makes the mean correction cancel the averaged error, and level two is the only place where the previous parent's residual is inserted. This is the right side of the equation described in §1.3. The definition does not solve that equation or impose the endpoint conditions selecting its initial velocity.

The formal definition gives the mean source $-\langle H_p\rangle_s-\mathbf1_{p=2}R_U\circ X$. It does not define the centered oscillatory source $f_p$ in the same display; that part is supplied by the separate oscillatory-source definition.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The expression supplies the phase average used in the mean equation; the centered part and supplementary term give the transverse equation.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.meanSource
rows.plain: The forcing for a mean correction
rows.annotation: Adding the prescribed mean and transverse sources gives $\bar f_p+f_p=-H_p$ for $p\ge3$ and $-H_2-R_U\circ X$ for $p=2$. These are exactly the negatives of the known errors before the new mean starts transporting the earlier phases. The supplementary source then cancels the additional phase products. This split is the cancellation of the momentum residual through level $p$ in Equation (5.29).

rows.fidelity_note:
For a fixed constructed family on $[0,T]$, $H_p$ is its preliminary source and $R_U\circ X$ its phase-independent residual. The source for the level-$p$ mean equation is $-\langle H_p\rangle_s$, with the additional term $-R_U\circ X$ only at $p=2$. This is exactly the distinction in (5.27). The source belongs to the same selected expansion as its mean correction and is the quantity estimated in the unweighted norms of Theorem 5.6.

The formal definition gives the mean source $-\langle H_p\rangle_s-\mathbf1_{p=2}R_U\circ X$. It does not define the centered oscillatory source $f_p$ in the same display; that part is supplied by the separate oscillatory-source definition.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The selected mean source includes precisely the averaged nonlinear term and the level-two parent residual. The transverse source is handled separately.

rows.name: TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.PhysicalApproximationData.paperMeanSource
rows.plain: The mean source at each level
rows.annotation: The lattice compatibility is $H_p(t,a+n,s+k_*\cdot n)=H_p(t,a,s)$. Hence $\langle H_p(t,a+n,\cdot)\rangle_s$ equals $\int_0^1 H_p(t,a,s-k_*\cdot n)\,ds$, which is the original phase integral by periodicity. In particular the mean force descends to the label torus even when the carrier is not integral. The inherited residual is also periodic in the labels.

citations.supports: The supplementary phase transport by the already computed means.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The supplementary source is $f_p^S=-\sum_{i=2}^p(B_i\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY_{p+1-i}$, the negative of all phase-advection terms by means at level $p$. It is formed after $B_p$ is known and has zero phase average because the means and $\kappa$ are phase independent. Its final summand is $-(B_p\cdot\kappa)\partial_sV_1$ when $C_1=0$, so it accounts for transport of the leading wave by the new mean. The formal source expression has the same sign and index range, with $p+1-i\ge1$ throughout the sum. The second link has verdict different because it identifies the positive advection sum, not its negative; together the two expressions give (5.28) without changing the sign convention.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.suppSource
ties.plain: The supplementary oscillatory source

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition gives $f_p^S=-\sum_{i=2}^{p}(B_i\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY_{p+1-i}$, with $Y_j=V_j+C_j$ in paper notation. In particular, at $p=2$ it is $-(B_2\cdot\kappa)\partial_sV_1$ when $C_1=0$, the extra term in (1.12). The sum is empty below level two. At every included index $p+1-i\ge1$, so nonnegative-integer subtraction agrees with ordinary subtraction. For phase-independent $B_i,\kappa$ and differentiable periodic $Y_j$, its phase average vanishes. These properties are not imposed by the formula alone; they come from the geometric profiles and expansion equations.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.suppSource
rows.plain: The supplementary oscillatory source
rows.annotation: The only new mean in Equation (5.28) occurs in $-(B_p\cdot\kappa)\partial_sV_1$; all differentiated oscillations are already known. It is important here that the mean has the improved bound. If $S_p=\lambda^{-5/4-2(p-1)/3}$, the ordinary level bound $B_p=O(S_p)$ would give a fast product of size $\lambda^{1/4}S_p$ up to parent powers. The stronger induction bound $O(\lambda^{-1/2}S_p)$ instead gives $\lambda^{-1/4}S_p$. The phase mean of the product is zero.

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $P,p$ be nonnegative integers with $p\le P$, and let $B_i,Y_i$ be arbitrary profile families. Group mean phase-advection terms by the level $i+j-1$. At level $p$ their sum is exactly $\sum_{i=2}^{p}(B_i\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY_{p+1-i}$; it is zero when $p<2$. This finite identity requires no differential equation or regularity. Its negative is the supplementary source $f_p^S$ in the paper. The final summand is $(B_p\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY_1$. Only after imposing the separate convention $C_1=0$ does $Y_1=V_1+C_1$ reduce to $V_1$, explaining why the new mean must be obtained before the transverse solve.

The formal statement gives the positive advection sum $\sum_{i=2}^p(B_i\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY_{p+1-i}$ for $p\le P$. The supplementary source in the paper is its negative. The other linked definition supplies that sign.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The positive advection sum is explicitly subtracted in the transverse source, giving the minus sign in (5.28). Its active indices avoid truncated subtraction.

rows.name: TorusEuler.HierarchyOperators.meanPhaseAdvectionAtLevel_eq_sum
rows.plain: Sum of the mean–oscillation phase interactions
rows.annotation: The indices of the fast mean interactions satisfy $i+j=p+1$, $i\ge2$, $j\ge1$. The allowed pairs can therefore be enumerated by $2\le i\le p$, with $j=p+1-i$. The endpoint $i=p$ pairs the current mean with $Y_1=V_1$; the linked equality is for the positive advection, so Equation (5.28) has a minus sign.

citations.supports: The centered source and zero-initial transverse solve at the current level.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: After computing $B_p$, the oscillatory pair solves $V_{p,t}+MV_p+\kappa\partial_s\mathsf p_p=f_p+f_p^S$ with zero initial velocity and zero phase mean for velocity and pressure. The centered part $f_p$ and the supplementary mean-advection source both have zero phase average, so they are admissible for the transverse problem of §5.4. This step cancels the remaining level-$p$ error without changing the mean just obtained. The formal selection theorem identifies the pair produced by the finite recursion with the output of a supplied transverse solver for exactly this sum. Weaker records that the theorem assumes the physical solver is available; it does not itself prove the smooth existence result behind (5.15).

ties.name: TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.construct_transverse_selected
ties.plain: The selected transverse correction

rows.fidelity_note:
Fix a depth $P\ge2$, a leading wave, a phase-independent parent residual, and solution operators for the mean and transverse equations. At $2\le p\le P$, the constructed pair $(V_p,\mathsf p_p)$ is the chosen transverse solution with source $-(H_p-\langle H_p\rangle_s)-\sum_{i=2}^p(B_i\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY_{p+1-i}$. This source has zero phase average. The statement identifies the result of the recursion after the current mean has been found; existence of the physical solution operators is a separate hypothesis here.

The formal statement identifies the recursively selected pair with the output of a supplied transverse solution operator for exactly $f_p+f_p^S$, whose average is zero. Existence of that physical operator is an input here, not a conclusion of this selection theorem.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The recursive transverse step uses the mean already constructed at that level. The transverse existence theorem supplies the solver with this full source.

rows.name: TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.construct_transverse_selected
rows.plain: The selected transverse correction
rows.annotation: The new mean enters the transverse equation only in the now known supplementary force. Both $f_p$ and $f_p^S$ are centered, and the preceding oscillations make their sum vanish outside the envelope and on the inactive prefix. Thus the zero-start transverse inverse can be applied once to the entire force, with the pressure determined afterward by Equation (5.16). There is no coupled same-level iteration.

citations.supports: Formation and indexing of the curl correction from the current transverse profile.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: After solving for the transverse centered profile $V_p$, form $Q_p=-\partial_s^{-1}(\kappa\times V_p/|\kappa|^2)$ and $C_{p+1}=\mathbf d\times Q_p$. For nonzero transported $\kappa$, identity (3.6) makes $V_p+C_{p+1}=\widetilde{\mathbf d}\times Q_p$ divergence free. The correction is also an input to the next level and must remain at the final level even when the expansion stops. The formal expansion condition explicitly requires $C_{p+1}=C[V_p]$ for $1\le p\le P$, evaluating the vector potential inside that operation rather than keeping a separate $Q_p$. Both weaker verdicts reflect partial scope: the expansion condition omits the separate assignment of $Q_p$, and the reindexing expression alone asserts neither defining equality.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.IsExpansion
ties.plain: Profile equations and support conditions for a finite expansion

rows.fidelity_note:
On $[0,T]$, profiles are smooth, one-periodic in $s$, and obey $f(t,a+n,s+k_*\cdot n)=f(t,a,s)$. Put $M=DU\circ X$, $\kappa=DX^{-T}k_*$, $\mathbf d=DX^{-T}\nabla_a$, $A_1=g\mathbf aF_h$, and $S=\widetilde\chi'A_1$ in the centered cell. The requirements include $R=R_U\circ X$, $V_1=\widetilde\chi A_1$, $\mathsf p_1=\widetilde\chi\mathsf p[A_1]$, and $C_1=B_1=\bar q_1=0$. For $1\le p\le P$, $C_{p+1}=\mathbf d\times[-\partial_s^{-1}(\kappa\times V_p/|\kappa|^2)]$. For $2\le p\le P$, require $B_{p,t}+MB_p+\mathbf d\bar q_p=-\langle H_p\rangle_s-\mathbf1_{p=2}R$ and $V_{p,t}+MV_p+\kappa\mathsf p_{p,s}=-(H_p-\langle H_p\rangle_s)+f_p^S$. Here $H_p$ is the sum of the preceding linear correction and all lower-level quadratic interactions, with the activation correction subtracted at level two; $f_p^S=-\sum_{i=2}^p(B_i\cdot\kappa)\partial_s(V_{p+1-i}+C_{p+1-i})$. Means satisfy $B_p=DX\,z_{p,t}$, $\operatorname{div}_az_{p,t}=0$, $z_p(0)=z_p(T)=0$ and zero spatial pressure mean. Transverse velocities are perpendicular to $\kappa$, centered and initially zero, with centered pressure. Finally $V_{P+1}=B_{P+1}=0$. This condition asserts no existence or estimates.

The formal condition requires $C_{p+1}=C[V_p]$ for retained levels. It does not retain $Q_p$ as a separate member of the family; the vector potential is evaluated inside the curl-correction operation. Thus the correction equality is explicit while the separate assignment of $Q_p$ is absent.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The correction condition records the curl of the zero-mean phase potential. Expanding that expression gives the displayed potential formula.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5.IsExpansion
rows.plain: Profile equations and support conditions for a finite expansion

rows.fidelity_note:
Assume a smooth odd unit-periodic solenoidal parent and smooth periodic pressure on $0<T\le1$, with bands $2\mathsf D$ for velocity and $4\mathsf D$ for its odd residual, gradient and both deformation bounds $\mathsf D\ge2$, residual bound $\lambda^{-5/2}$ and $D^2p_U-DR_U\le I$. Put $M=DU\circ X$, $\kappa=DX^{-T}k_*$, $\lambda=|\kappa(t_0,0)|\ge1$ and $0\le t_0<T$. The nonzero central seed solves $\mathbf a_t=-(I-2P_\kappa)M\mathbf a$, is transverse, has $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a\ge\mathsf D^{-1}|\kappa||\mathbf a|$, and satisfies $0<\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|\le1$. Every transverse homogeneous solution $\mathbf b$ obeys $|\mathbf b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/\gamma(t')$ for $t_0\le t'\le t\le T$. Smoothness is on the closed slab; no continuation across its endpoints is asserted.

The formal statement gives seed existence and, at every $P\ge2$, existence and uniqueness of the retained velocities, normalized pressures and corrections. The formal operation has exactly this curl-potential meaning, giving same, and applies to smooth profiles compatible with simultaneous label-phase translations. citations.supports: Differentiating the potential and canceling the parallel pressure force.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: Differentiate $Q[V]=-\partial_s^{-1}(\kappa\times V/|\kappa|^2)$ using $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$ and $V_t=f-MV-q\kappa$, where $\kappa\ne0$. The numerator gives $(M^T\kappa)\times V+\kappa\times MV-\kappa\times f$, the denominator gives $-2(\kappa\times V)(\kappa\cdot M\kappa)/|\kappa|^4$, and the pressure slope disappears because $\kappa\times(q\kappa)=0$. This proves (5.33) and removes time derivatives of the forcing and strain from the subsequent correction estimate. The same formal differentiation theorem assumes these equations and joint continuity of the integrand and its proposed derivative, including derivatives within the time interval at its endpoints; it does not need periodicity merely to differentiate the normalized primitive. explanation.text: Since $C[V]=\mathbf d\times Q[V]$ and the spatial operator depends on time, its material linear term splits into $\mathbf d\times Q_t+[\partial_t,\mathbf d\times]Q+MC[V]$. rows.fidelity_note:
Let $J,G$ be curves of linear maps on $\mathbb R^3$. At $t$ in a time set where the derivative is uniquely determined, assume $J'=J_t$ and $G'=-GM$. For a matrix $B$, write $\operatorname{curl}B$ for its antisymmetric contraction, the vector that equals $\nabla\times q$ when $B=Dq$. The formal identity is $\frac{d}{dt}\operatorname{curl}(JG)+M\operatorname{curl}(JG)=\operatorname{curl}(J_tG)-\operatorname{curl}(JGM)+M\operatorname{curl}(JG)$. It is a matrix product rule. Taking $J=D_aQ[V]$, $G=(D_aX)^{-1}$ gives the paper's curl commutator only after justifying $J_t=D_a\partial_tQ[V]$. Neither existence of those spatial derivatives nor interchange of time and label differentiation follows from this identity itself.

The formal statement differentiates the contraction defining a curl from two matrix curves $J,G$, assuming $G_t=-GM$. Taking $J=D_aQ$ and identifying its derivative with $D_aQ_t$ gives the paper’s formula. These spatial differentiability and interchange identifications are additional to the matrix identity itself.

rows.annotation: Although the phase is held fixed, the slow derivative moves with the parent: $\mathbf d_j=\sum_\alpha(D_aX)^{-1}_{\alpha j}\partial_{a_\alpha}$. Commuting time past the curl therefore costs only a first spatial derivative, with no derivative of $M$ in time.

explanation.text: The homogeneous leading estimate gives $\|A_1\|_{[n],\gamma}+\lambda\|\mathsf p[A_1]\|_{[n],\gamma}\le C_n\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-5/4}$. Applying (5.31) gives the bound $C_n\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-9/4}$ for $C[A_1]$. Multiplication by the time-only cutoff $0\le\widetilde\chi\le1$ preserves these spatial and phase norms, so they hold for $V_1,\mathsf p_1,C_2$ and initialize the induction. No derivative of the cutoff enters this step because the norms do not differentiate in time. The linked formal implication is different as a statement: it concludes the whole hierarchy theorem assuming the preceding analytic results, rather than separately exporting this leading-level argument.

rows.fidelity_note:

Under the smooth parent bounds, central transverse stability and $\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$, level-$p$ oscillations decay as $\lambda^{-5/4-2(p-1)/3}$, means as $\lambda^{-5/2-2(p-2)/3}$ and $C_{p+1}$ as $\lambda^{-9/4-2(p-1)/3}$, up to $C_{n,p}\mathsf D^C$. The remainder is bounded by $C_{m,P}\lambda^{-5/4-2P/3}$. All derivative orders apply to the same profiles; the parent exponent is independent of order, level and depth. The transverse stability assumption is $|\mathbf b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/\gamma(t')$ for every transverse homogeneous solution $\mathbf b$ and $t_0\le t'\le t\le T$.

The formal implication concludes the whole hierarchy theorem from the earlier estimates. It does not separately state this leading-level cutoff argument, although the final conclusion includes the level-one velocity, pressure and curl bounds.

explanation.text: The induction proves the stronger intermediate bound $\|f_p+f_p^S\|_{[n],\gamma}+\lambda^{1/2}\|B_p\|_{[n]}\le C_{n,p}\lambda^{e_p}$, where $e_p=-5/4-2(p-1)/3$, without a parent factor. citations.supports: Why the parent-loss exponent can be fixed before the induction parameters.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The induction bound (5.40) carries no factor of $\mathsf D$, so every later parent loss comes from a fixed number of applications of the parent, mean, transverse, correction and product estimates. The resulting exponent can therefore be chosen before the derivative order, level and depth, although numerical constants may grow with those parameters. This is what permits a single condition $\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$ to close the entire construction. The linked formal result chooses such an exponent before the parent data, finite derivative reserve and depth and supplies a recurrence for the measured profile norms. Its different verdict reflects that this quantifier statement establishes uniformity, while the paper's description as a bounded sum of earlier exponents is an account of the proof rather than a separate identity it asserts.

explanation.text: The constant said to be independent of level and depth is the exponent $C$ in $\mathsf D^C$, not the numerical constants $C_{n,p}$ or $C_{m,P}$. explanation.text: Repeated application of $\widetilde{\mathbf d}$ costs at most one factor $C\mathsf D^C\lambda^{3/2}$ per spatial derivative in the scaled norms. At the end, the definition of the weighted order-zero norm gives $|f(t,a,s)|\le\gamma(t)\|f\|_{[0],\gamma}$ for $t\in[t_0,T]$ and positive $\gamma$. ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.lemma_5_7_of
ties.plain: Bounds for physical derivatives after phase evaluation

rows.fidelity_note:
Assuming Proposition 5.1 and Lemma D.1, the formal implication proves the following. For a smooth odd divergence-free periodic parent on $0<T\le1$ with deformation and gradient bounds $\mathsf D\ge2$, velocity and residual Fourier radii $2\mathsf D,4\mathsf D$, residual size $\lambda^{-5/2}$ and coercivity $D^2p-\nabla R_U\le I$, require a transverse nonzero central solution $\mathbf a_t=-(I-2P_\kappa)M\mathbf a$, $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a\ge\mathsf D^{-1}|\kappa||\mathbf a|$, and $|\mathbf b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/\gamma(t')$ for every transverse homogeneous solution and $t_0\le t'\le t\le T$, $|\kappa(t_0,0)|=\lambda\ge1$ and $0<\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|\le1$. Take $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-a}$ sufficiently small and $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$. A smooth profile with the combined lattice translation law, independent of phase outside the envelope, satisfies $\|D^mf^\natural\|\le C_m(\mathsf D^C\lambda^{3/2})^m\gamma(t)\|f\|_{[m],\gamma}$ and the $C^{m,1/2}$ bound using $m+1$. Here the derivative norm sums ordered coordinate sequences. The weighted estimates hold on $[t_0,T]$. Both estimates hold unweighted on $[0,T]$, and phase-independent fields omit $\lambda^{3/2}$. The target is any real normed space; constants precede the parent. The profile incorporates continuation across cells.

The formal implication concludes the order-$m$ physical derivative bound and its Hölder companion. The sentence describes its proof by repeated differentiation and the weighted order-zero estimate. The conclusion is the resulting bound, not a separately stated iteration identity. Smooth global profiles, including their coupled translation law, are inputs.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.lemma_5_7_of
rows.plain: Bounds for physical derivatives after phase evaluation
rows.annotation: At each application of the one-derivative estimate, the required profile order increases by one. Thus bounding the order-zero norm of all words of length $m$ uses the estimates at orders $0,\ldots,m-1$ successively, and costs at most $(\prod_{n=0}^{m-1}C_n)(\mathsf D^C\lambda^{3/2})^m\|g_0\|_{[m],\gamma}$. The exponent $C$ is fixed throughout; only the coefficient depends on $m$.

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $T>0$ and let $f$ be a smooth profile with values in a real normed space, one-periodic in phase and obeying $f(t,a+n,s+k_*\cdot n)=f(t,a,s)$. At $t\in[t_0,T]$ let $A(t,\cdot)$ and $B$ be smooth with $B(A(t,x))=D_xA(t,x)$. Require $\ell_*>0$, $\mathsf D,L\ge1$, $\ell_*^{-1}\le\mathsf D^a$, and $\ell_*^j\|D^jB\|_\infty\le L\mathsf D$ for $j\le m+1$. Assume $\lambda\ge1$, $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$ and $|k_*|\le\mathsf D\lambda$. The weight $\gamma$ is continuous and positive on $[t_0,T]\subset[0,T]$. Put $f^\natural(t,x)=f(t,A(t,x),k_*\cdot A(t,x))$, $N_j=\|f\|_{[j],\gamma}$ and $K_j=[3\,2^j(2L)]^j4^j\mathsf D^{(\max(a,1)+1)j}\lambda^{3j/2}$. The formal statement bounds the sum over all ordered coordinate derivatives of length $m$ by $3^mK_m\gamma(t)N_m$, and gives $f^\natural(t)\in C^{m,1/2}$ with norm at most $3(m+1)K_{m+1}\gamma(t)N_{m+1}$. Here $N_j$ sums scaled label and phase derivative suprema through order $j$, each multi-index once. The explicit constants depend on $L$; they are not order-only constants.

The formal conclusion is (5.44) together with its Hölder companion, conditional on explicit scaled inverse-coefficient bounds. Its proof performs the iteration, but the passage’s appeal to the parent estimates must be supplied separately.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The graph-evaluation estimate takes explicit coefficient bounds as inputs. Proposition 5.1 supplies them for the actual parent, giving Lemma 5.7.
