rows.plain: Weighted bounds for phase evaluation
rows.annotation: The weighted norm controls a profile at time $t$ after division by $\gamma(t)$. Since each of the spatial operators acts only on $a,s$, this division can be made before the entire sequence of derivatives. The last evaluation therefore restores a single factor $\gamma(t)$, not one such factor per derivative.

citations.supports: One additional bounded derivative controls the half-Hölder seminorm.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: A bounded differentiable field satisfies $\|v\|_{C^{0,1/2}}\le C(\|v\|_\infty+\|\nabla v\|_\infty)$. The derivative bound controls differences at short distances, and the supremum bound controls them at long distances. Lemma 5.7 applies this to spatial derivatives through order $m$, explaining the extra derivative in (5.45). The formal theorem gives the broader statement that if a smooth field on $\mathbb R^3$ has all derivatives through order $m+1$ bounded by $B\ge0$, then its $C^{m,1/2}$ norm is at most $3(m+1)B$. Its stronger verdict records all derivative orders, explicit Hölder regularity and the numerical bound, without a periodicity assumption.

ties.name: TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_le_of_uniformJets
ties.plain: One more derivative gives Hölder control

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $g:\mathbb R^3\to E$ be smooth, where $E$ is a real normed space. If $B\ge0$ and every derivative of order $0\le j\le m+1$ has operator norm at most $B$ everywhere, then $g\in C^{m,1/2}$ and $\|g\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\le3(m+1)B$. Order zero includes the value of the function itself. The estimate uses the derivative bound at short distances and the supremum bound at long distances. No periodicity or bounded spatial domain is assumed. Lemma 5.7 applies this result to obtain its Hölder estimate with one additional profile derivative.

The paper uses the zero-order half-Hölder estimate. The formal result treats every derivative order $m$, proves Hölder regularity, and bounds the norm by $3(m+1)B$ when all derivatives through order $m+1$ are bounded by $B$.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The general Hölder estimate includes order zero, which is the case used in the displayed bound.

rows.name: TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_le_of_uniformJets
rows.plain: One more derivative gives Hölder control
rows.annotation: For $d=|x-y|>0$, let $B_j,B_{j+1}$ bound the derivatives of orders $j,j+1$. The difference of the order-$j$ derivatives is at most $\min(2B_j,B_{j+1}d)\le\sqrt{2B_jB_{j+1}d}$. Dividing by $\sqrt d$ gives the half-Hölder seminorm. Taking $B_j,B_{j+1}\le B$ gives the linked bound $3(m+1)B$ on the sum of the supremum norms and seminorms through $m$. This explains the one extra ordinary derivative used in Equation (5.45).

citations.supports: Repeated physical derivatives of phase-independent fields contain no phase-derivative cost.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Lemma 5.7, last sentence of proof; equation (3.1)

explanation.text: For a phase-independent profile $g_0$, every application of $\widetilde{\mathbf d}$ agrees with application of $\mathbf d$ because $\partial_sg_0=0$. The coefficients of $\mathbf d$ are themselves phase independent, so this remains true after repeated differentiation. This proves the absence of the frequency cost in the mean part of Lemma 5.7. The derivative-iteration result and weighted mean theorem are weaker links because they assume the coefficient bounds and, for the latter, a positive continuous time weight and a smooth inverse label map. The complete formal implication is different in scope because its conclusion is the full derivative-and-Hölder estimate, while the operator simplification occurs within the proof.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.S5b.words_phaseIndep
ties.plain: Derivative words for a phase-independent profile

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $f$ be independent of phase, $\ell_*,h>0$, and $\gamma>0$. Assume finite weighted profile norms at every order and finite order-$j$ coefficient bounds $N_c(j),N_k(j)$ for the label and phase parts of the derivative operator. Given the finite-norm product estimate, the sum of the weighted norms after all ordered sequences of $m$ physical coordinate derivatives is at most $\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}[C_j9N_c(j)\ell_*^{-1}]\,\|f\|_{[m],\gamma}$. The phase-coefficient bounds remain formal premises, but no $N_k(j)h^{-1}$ factor appears in the conclusion because phase derivatives vanish. This is the improved mean estimate used in Lemma 5.7. The conclusion includes finiteness of all differentiated order-zero norms.

The formal result bounds arbitrary words of physical derivatives on phase-independent profiles. The vanishing of phase derivatives is used to remove the fast cost, but the linked conclusion is a norm estimate, not the displayed first-order operator identity.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The repeated-derivative estimate records the consequence of phase independence; the absent phase derivative removes the frequency cost.

Smoothness follows from evaluation through the smooth inverse parent flow; oddness and incompressibility require separate symmetry and divergence arguments. The smoothness-only theorem and the theorem collecting already established properties are weaker links, since the former omits symmetry and divergence and the latter assumes those properties as inputs.

explanation.text: The coefficient $c_{\mathbf a}=2\widetilde\chi g(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2$ combines the time cutoff, spatial envelope and coupling of the amplitude to the parent strain. At the origin $g(0)=1$ removes the spatial cutoff, while the time cutoff remains until activation is complete.

rows.fidelity_note:
Fix a time and a lattice vector $n\in\mathbb Z^3$. Write $X_f=X_{0,t}$ and $X_r=X_{t,0}$. Assume $X_f(a+n)=X_f(a)+n$, $X_r(x+n)=X_r(x)+n$, $W(a+n,s+k_*\cdot n)=W(a,s)$, and $v$ is spatially periodic. Define $c(a,s)=DX_r(X_f(a))[W(a,s)+v(X_f(a))]$. Then $c(a+n,s+k_*\cdot n)=c(a,s)$. No differentiability or inverse relation between $X_f,X_r$ is assumed by this translation statement; a derivative at a nondifferentiable point is assigned zero. For the smooth parent flow, $DX_r(X_f(a))=(DX_f(a))^{-1}$, giving the paper's pullback. The conclusion concerns the entire field before subtracting its phase average, and does not require $k_*\in\mathbb Z^3$.

The formal conclusion gives the combined translation law for the entire pulled back field $c$. Recovering the separate statement for $c_{\rm osc}$ also uses its phase average and phase periodicity; that decomposition is not asserted by this theorem.

Let $X$ be the flow of a periodic divergence-free $C^2$ velocity $U$ on $[0,T]$, $T>0$, with a uniform spatial Lipschitz bound. explanation.text: Along the lifted equation $a'=c$, $s'=k_*\cdot c$, differentiation gives $(s-k_*\cdot a)'=0$. The formal theorem proves the same conserved quantity in scaled coordinates, namely $h\sigma-k_*\cdot(\ell_*y)$, for nonzero scales and a transition solving the lifted equation. citations.supports: The divergence identity that determines the pressure source and its matrix-square meaning.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text:
For a twice continuously differentiable divergence-free vector field $u$, differentiating the advection term gives $\operatorname{div}((u\cdot
abla)u)=\operatorname{tr}((
abla u)^2)+u\cdot
abla\operatorname{div}u$. The last term vanishes, leaving the identity used to choose the pressure in Proposition 5.11. The square here is matrix composition, so its trace is $\sum_{i,j}\partial_j u_i\,\partial_i u_j$, not the sum of the squared entries of the gradient. The same formal theorem proves this spatial identity at every point under exactly twice continuous differentiability and zero divergence. It needs neither periodicity nor an Euler evolution; those enter only when applying the identity to the cutoff field and solving its Poisson equation.

explanation.text: Apply the commuting operators $S_\Lambda$ and $\mathbb P$ to $V_t+\operatorname{div}(V\otimes V)+\nabla\Pi=R_V$, and use $u_t=S_\Lambda V_t$. Existence and uniqueness of the normalized Poisson pressure identify the constructed pressure.

rows.annotation: Proposition 5.11 propagates an upper bound on the pressure increment, not yet the complete hypothesis (5.2). The latter contains $-\nabla R_u$ as well. To apply the next endpoint inverse, Section 7 sums the pressure increments and uses the $4\Lambda$ band of the new residual to bound $\nabla R_u$ by $C\Lambda\|R_u\|_\infty$. Both the sign of the pressure estimate and the new residual band are needed.

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $p,q$ be smooth periodic scalar functions on $\mathbb R^3$ and suppose $\|D^2(p-q)\|_{C^{0,1/2}}\le B$. Then at every point and for every vector $v$, $v\cdot D^2p\,v\le v\cdot D^2q\,v+B|v|^2$. Thus $D^2p\le D^2q+BI$ as quadratic forms. Periodicity ensures the relevant Hölder norm is finite. This is the passage used in §5.7 to add the cutoff pressure error to the upper bound for the approximate pressure. The statement does not itself bound $D^2q$, choose either pressure, or assert a two-sided bound on $D^2p$.

This gives only the transfer $D^2p\le D^2\Pi+BI$ from $\|D^2(p-\Pi)\|_{C^{0,1/2}}\le B$. It does not supply the bound for $D^2(\Pi-p_U)$ or the value of $B$; those are needed to obtain (5.57).

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The quadratic-form transfer uses the cutoff Hessian error. Combining it with Lemma 5.9 gives the final pressure upper bound.

rows.annotation: If $D^2(\Pi-p_U)\le sI$ and $\|D^2(p-\Pi)\|_\infty\le e$, evaluate both on the same vector $v$. Adding gives $v\cdot D^2(p-p_U)v\le(s+e)|v|^2$. This is the stage lemma; an absolute norm bound on $D^2(\Pi-p_U)$ would be stronger than needed.

rows.fidelity_note: Fix a smooth even symbol $\psi$, equal to one on $|\xi|\le1$ and zero on $|\xi|>2$. Let $P\ge2$, $T>0$, $\Lambda\ge1$, with $V,R_V$ smooth periodic fields, $V$ odd and divergence free, and a pressure $\Pi$ smooth and periodic at each time. Assume $V_t+V\cdot\nabla V+\nabla\Pi=R_V$ and $D^2(\Pi-p_U)\le sI$, with $p_U$ spatially $C^2$. The formal statement constructs $u=S_\Lambda V$ and zero-mean pressure $p$ solving $\Delta p=-\operatorname{tr}((Du)^2)$. Both $u,R_u$ are odd and divergence free, with Fourier radii $2\Lambda,4\Lambda$. Set $\varepsilon=\Lambda^{2-P}(1+\|V\|_{C_tC^{P,1/2}})^2$ and $e=C\|R_V\|_{C_tC^{1,1/2}}+C_P\varepsilon$. Then $\|u-V\|_{C_tC^{2,1/2}}\le C_P\varepsilon$, $\|R_u\|_{C_tC^{1,1/2}}+\|D^2(p-\Pi)\|_{C_tC^{0,1/2}}\le e$, and $D^2(p-p_U)\le(s+e)I$. The exponent $2-P$ is signed integer arithmetic. Constants may depend on the fixed symbol, not the fields or $\Lambda$.

rows.annotation: For the next endpoint inverse (Theorem 4.2), write $\mu=\lambda_{j-1}$ and $\lambda=\lambda_j$. The initial shear has constant pressure, and the upper bounds on subsequent pressure increments sum to at most $2/N$. The parent residual has band $4\mu^5$ and norm at most $\lambda^{-3}$; Bernstein gives $\|\nabla R_U\|_\infty\le C\mu^5\lambda^{-3}$. Consequently $D^2p_U-\nabla R_U\le(2/N+C\mu^5\lambda^{-3})I\le I$ for large $N$, as required by the next mean inverse (Theorem 4.2).

citations.supports: The regularity of the stationary shear and its use at the base of the induction.

explanation.text: For $0<\rho\le1$, the periodic shear $U_0(x)=\sin(2\pi x_2)(e_1+\rho e_3)$ is smooth, odd under $x\mapsto-x$, and divergence free. These properties follow directly from the sine formula: its only spatial dependence is on $x_2$, and its second velocity component vanishes. They provide the regularity and incompressibility required of the base approximate solution in Theorem 7.1. The formal theorem proves these properties for every real $\rho$, on $[0,1]\times\mathbb R^3$, and additionally states periodicity and a Fourier-band bound for $\lambda_0\ge1$; “stronger” refers to that wider parameter range and those additional conclusions.

explanation.text: The Fourier support of $U_0(x)=\sin(2\pi x_2)(e_1+\rho e_3)$ is contained in $\{e_2,-e_2\}$. Expanding the sine into the two exponentials $e^{\pm2\pi i x_2}$ gives this assertion, which makes the starting velocity satisfy the frequency restriction in Theorem 7.1. The formal statement concerns complex Fourier coefficients of the real periodic velocity and proves that a coefficient is nonzero if and only if its integer frequency is $e_2$ or $-e_2$. It is stronger than containment because both coefficients are proved nonzero, and it allows every real $\rho$ since $e_1+\rho e_3$ never vanishes.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The initial shear satisfies the required regularity and Fourier support; the additional conclusions do not change the construction.

explanation.text: For $U_0(x)=\sin(2\pi x_2)(e_1+\rho e_3)$, the second velocity component is zero at every point, although the other components depend on $x_2$. This follows immediately from (6.1) because $e_1+\rho e_3$ is perpendicular to $e_2$. The observation makes the nonlinear advection vanish and keeps the second coordinate constant along particle trajectories. The formal equality is the same componentwise statement for all $x\in\mathbb R^3$ and all real $\rho$, hence stronger than its use under $0<\rho\le1$; its coordinates are numbered from zero, so its coordinate numbered one is the paper's second coordinate.

rows.name: TorusEuler.stationaryShear_second

rows.annotation: The second component of $U_0$ vanishes, so particles move in planes of constant $x_2$. As the shear depends only on $x_2$, it is constant on each of these trajectories. This gives both zero self-advection and the explicit flow (6.2).

citations.supports: Why the stationary shear has zero self-advection.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The shear $U_0(x)=\sin(2\pi x_2)(e_1+\rho e_3)$ satisfies $(U_0\cdot\nabla)U_0=0$. Its only nonzero spatial derivative is in the $x_2$ direction, whereas $(U_0)_2=0$, so the directional derivative along the velocity is zero. This removes the nonlinear term from the stationary Euler equation and permits zero pressure. The formal statement proves $D U_0(x)[U_0(x)]=0$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$ and every real $\rho$; the full derivative evaluated on the velocity is precisely the displayed advection, and the unrestricted tilt makes this stronger than the paragraph's setting.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal theorem proves $D U_0(x)[U_0(x)]=0$ for every real $\rho$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^3$, where $U_0(x)=\sin(2\pi x_2)(e_1+\rho e_3)$. This is the stated advection identity with no restriction on the shear parameter.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The construction uses a positive small tilt and positive times, which lie within the larger parameter range proved here.

rows.name: TorusEuler.stationaryShear_advection

rows.annotation: For any vector $v$, $DU_0(x)v=\cos(2\pi x_2)B_\rho v$. Taking $v=U_0(x)$ gives zero, since its second component vanishes. Thus the nonlinear term is zero without any approximation.

explanation.text: For the time-independent shear $U_0(x)=\sin(2\pi x_2)(e_1+\rho e_3)$, choose the mean-zero pressure $p=0$; then the momentum residual $R=\partial_tU_0+(U_0\cdot\nabla)U_0+\nabla p$ vanishes. This uses the preceding zero-advection calculation and starts the induction with an exact Euler solution. The formal theorem supplies a smooth, periodic, divergence-free Euler solution with this velocity and zero pressure on $[0,T)$ for every $T>0$ and every real $\rho$. It is stronger than the quoted clause through those extra regularity conclusions and the wider tilt range; the residual identity follows from its momentum equation.

Since the second velocity component vanishes, the remaining components can be integrated with $a_2$ held fixed, giving (6.2). This is the reason the parent flow and its deformation have explicit formulas. The formal equality holds for every real $t$, every $a\in\mathbb R^3$ and every real $\rho$, so it is stronger than the assertion on the construction interval with $0<\rho\le1$; it is equality of lifted coordinates, before passing to the torus.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal data require positivity of $\nu=E_1(t_0)\cdot B(t_0)E_2(t_0)$ and $\eta=E_3(t_0)\cdot B(t_0)E_2(t_0)$. They are frozen entries of the older gradient in the preceding wave's normalized frame, not the couplings of the newly chosen wave.
rows.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmplification
rows.plain: Data for a physical amplification step
rows.annotation: In the reference covector equations the term $-\varepsilon\zeta_3$ turns the new wave vector away from $E_3$, with $\varepsilon=\eta/\nu$. A smaller positive ratio delays the turning and permits a larger amplification of the growing mode. The physical growth time is set independently by $r^{-1}=(2\sigma\nu)^{-1/2}$. Thus the crossing must supply both a small ratio and a large strength; a small ratio alone gives no short physical time scale.

citations.supports: The positive growth scale and its distinction from the exact frozen rate.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: §6.2, definitions following (6.5); §2.2.1, discussion of the growth rate

explanation.text:
With frozen strength $\sigma=|\kappa_p(t_0)||\mathbf a_p(t_0)|>0$ and first coupling $
u>0$, the growth scale is $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}>0$. As §2.2.1 explains, the exact frozen growing-mode rate is $\sqrt{2
u(\sigma-
u)}$ when $\sigma>
u$, so $r$ supplies the leading strong-shear scale rather than that exact eigenvalue. It converts physical elapsed time into the normalized variable used in the comparison. The formal rate has the same positive square root, as also expressed by $r^2=2\sigma
u$ and $r>0$ in the formal comparison calculations; no zero-denominator convention enters the later use of $r^{-1}$.

ties.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmplification.rate
ties.plain: The frozen growth scale

rows.fidelity_note:
At activation $t_0$, freeze the preceding strength $\sigma=|\kappa_p(t_0)||\mathbf a_p(t_0)|>0$ and first coupling $
u=E_1(t_0)\cdot B(t_0)E_2(t_0)>0$. The formal definition sets $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}$, exactly as in the quoted clause. This is the positive scale for normalized time. The exact frozen growth rate discussed in §2.2.1 is $\sqrt{2
u(\sigma-
u)}$ when $\sigma>
u$; it equals $r\sqrt{1-
u/\sigma}$.
rows.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmplification.rate
rows.plain: The frozen growth scale
rows.annotation:
With zero tilt in the ideal rotating frame the transverse amplitude components satisfy $\dot a_1=-2
u a_2$, $\dot a_2=-(\sigma-
u)a_1$. Eliminating $a_1$ gives $\ddot a_2=2
u(\sigma-
u)a_2$. Thus $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}$ is the limiting growth rate when $
u/\sigma$ is small, and $r^{-1}$ is the time unit used in the comparison.

citations.supports: The normalized shear scale and its role in the component coordinates.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text:
The dimensionless shear parameter is $S=\sigma/r=\sqrt{\sigma/(2
u)}$, where $\sigma>0$, $
u>0$ and $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}$. This is the ratio of the preceding shear strength to the growth scale introduced in §2.2.1. In (2.3), its reciprocal weights selected components of the new covector and amplitude, allowing the strong-shear limit to be compared with a fixed reference system. The formal definition is the same quotient of the frozen strength and positive rate, so the division is ordinary positive division; a quantitative lower bound on $S$ requires the subsequent comparison assumptions.

ties.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmplification.shear
ties.plain: The dimensionless preceding shear

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition is $S=\sigma/r$, with $\sigma>0$ and $r=\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}>0$ supplied by the preceding wave at activation. No zero-denominator convention affects this quantity in the stated setting.
rows.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmplification.shear
rows.plain: The dimensionless preceding shear
rows.annotation: The factors $S^{-1}$ in (2.3) occur in complementary coordinates of $k$ and $\mathbf a$, so that $k\cdot\mathbf a=(\lambda/S)\zeta\cdot\alpha$. The scaled transverse variables have comparable components at launch, although the growing physical amplitude has an $E_1$ component of order $S^{-1}$ times its $E_2$ component. Here $S$ is a dimensionless shear parameter, not the final time $S_j$ of §7.

citations.supports: The frozen amplification ratio and the distinction from the next wave’s evolving ratio.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text:
The amplification parameter is the frozen ratio $\varepsilon=\eta/
u>0$, with $
u=E_1(t_0)\cdot B(t_0)E_2(t_0)$ and $\eta=E_3(t_0)\cdot B(t_0)E_2(t_0)$. It is constant during the comparison because both couplings are evaluated at activation. Through the reference system of §2.2, this ratio sets the long normalized time needed for amplification and for the next prescribed crossing. The formal definition is exactly the same ratio with a strictly positive denominator; it must not be confused with the evolving successor ratio $\eta_+(t)/
u_+(t)$.

ties.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmplification.ratio
ties.plain: The frozen coupling ratio

rows.fidelity_note: The ratio is $\varepsilon=\eta/\nu$ for the two positive frozen couplings of the older gradient. This is ordinary division by a strictly positive number, not a ratio evaluated at a later crossing.
rows.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmplification.ratio
rows.plain: The frozen coupling ratio
rows.annotation: The input $\varepsilon$ is the ratio of the older gradient in the preceding wave's frame at launch; it is not the ratio of the new wave at launch. The target $\varepsilon_+$ is instead measured in the new frame, against $M$. At the crossing this second ratio becomes the input for the next amplification problem. In §7 these are $\varepsilon_{j-1}=L_j^{-2}$ and $\varepsilon_j=L_{j+1}^{-2}$.

citations.supports: The conversion between physical and normalized time intervals.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: Normalized time is $\tau=r(t-t_0)$, with the positive rate $r=\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}$ frozen at activation. Therefore $[t_0,T]$ becomes $[0,r(T-t_0)]$, and physical time is recovered by $t=t_0+\tau/r$. This lets the central equations use the comparison lemmas of §2.2 on their stated normalized interval. The formal formula makes exactly this affine change of variable for every real $t$; outside the construction interval it remains a formula, without asserting that the wave equations hold there.

ties.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmplification.elapsed
ties.plain: Normalized elapsed time

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition is $\tau=r(t-t_0)$ for real time $t$. Here $r>0$ is fixed at activation, so $[t_0,T]$ is converted to a normalized interval of length $r(T-t_0)$.
rows.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmplification.elapsed
rows.plain: Normalized elapsed time
rows.annotation: The derivative in normalized time is $r^{-1}$ times the physical time derivative. In particular a crossing at normalized time $\tau_*$ lies at $t_0+\tau_*/r$. This conversion is needed before comparing the bracket with the time allowance $\tau_j$ of §7 (which is a physical time).

citations.supports: The label covector chosen to prescribe the physical covector at activation.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: To make the new covector equal $\lambda E_3(t_0)$ at activation, choose the constant label covector $k_*=\lambda(D_aX(t_0,0))^TE_3(t_0)$. The transport law $\kappa=(D_aX)^{-T}k_*$ in (3.1) then gives the required orthogonality to the preceding covector and amplitude. This is the launch geometry used by the normalized amplification system. The formal theorem proves the general identity $F^{-T}(\lambda F^TE_3)=\lambda E_3$ for any invertible real linear map $F$, scalar $\lambda$ and vector $E_3$; “different” means it verifies the consequence of the choice without identifying $F$ with the parent deformation or constructing the new wave.

ties.name: TorusEuler.inverseAdjoint_activationWaveVector
ties.plain: The inverse transpose sends the launch covector to λE₃

rows.fidelity_note: The paper chooses $k_*=\lambda(D_aX(t_0,0))^TE_3(t_0)$. The formal theorem instead proves $F^{-T}(\lambda F^TE_3)=\lambda E_3$ for any invertible linear map $F$, real $\lambda$ and vector $E_3$. It verifies the required consequence of the choice; identifying $F$ with the parent deformation is not part of this theorem.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. This is the linear-algebra consequence of the activation covector choice, and neither main proof uses this particular result.

rows.name: TorusEuler.inverseAdjoint_activationWaveVector
rows.plain: The inverse transpose sends the launch covector to λE₃
rows.annotation: Write $F=D_aX(t_0,0)$. From $\kappa=F^{-T}k_*$ the prescription is $k_*=\lambda F^TE_3(t_0)$, which gives the desired normal in physical space. The vector $k_*$ need not be an integer vector: the oscillatory profiles vanish near the boundary of the label cell before periodic extension, as in §3.1.

citations.supports: The initial direction corresponding to the growing reference solution.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The new amplitude initially points along $-E_1(t_0)/S+E_2(t_0)$, with $S=\sigma/\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}>0$ from the preceding wave. In the scaled coordinates (2.3), this is $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)=(-1,1)$, the growing reference direction identified in §2.2.2. Choosing it allows the seed to acquire the gain needed for a small activation error. The formal growing-wave data prescribe a positive multiple of exactly this direction, alongside initial covector $\lambda E_3$ and the transverse wave equations on $[t_0,t_0+\Theta/r]$; “same” concerns the initial direction, while existence and the choice of its scale are separate assertions.

ties.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmplification.GrowingCrossing
ties.plain: Data at the growing wave’s selected crossing

rows.fidelity_note: The formal condition prescribes the new initial amplitude as a positive scalar multiple of $-E_1(t_0)/S+E_2(t_0)$. The frame and $S>0$ come from the preceding wave. This specifies the direction of a proposed growing wave; existence is a separate theorem.
rows.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmplification.GrowingCrossing
rows.plain: Data at the growing wave’s selected crossing
rows.annotation: In the strong-shear system at $\tau=0$, $\alpha_1'=-\alpha_2$ and $\alpha_2'=-\alpha_1$. The vector $(-1,1)$ belongs to the growing eigendirection. Undoing the scaling in Equation (2.3) gives $-E_1/S+E_2$, which is perpendicular to the chosen launch normal $E_3$.

citations.supports: Positive rescaling of the growing seed and its attained amplitude maximum.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For the growing seed on $[t_0,T]$, choose a positive scalar multiple so that its attained maximum is $\lambda^{-3/4}$, with $\lambda>0$. The linear amplitude equation preserves its direction and ratios of its lengths under this rescaling, as used in §6.2. This fixes the normalized weight $\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a|$ while retaining the amplification estimates. The formal growing-wave data instead require an independently prescribed attained maximum $U_*$ on $[t_0,t_0+\Theta/r]$; the paper's normalization is recovered by $U_*=\lambda^{-3/4}$ and $\Theta=r(T-t_0)$. Thus the verdict “different” identifies a parameter substitution, and the data requirements alone do not establish that such a seed exists.

ties.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmplification.GrowingCrossing
ties.plain: Data at the growing wave’s selected crossing

rows.fidelity_note: The paper fixes the attained peak at $\lambda^{-3/4}$. The formal condition instead has an independent prescribed peak $U_*$ and requires the maximum on $[t_0,t_0+\Theta/r]$ to equal $U_*$. Recovering this normalization requires setting $U_*=\lambda^{-3/4}$ and $\Theta=r(T-t_0)$; that substitution is not made by this declaration itself.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The constructed crossing specializes the independent peak to $U_*=\lambda^{-3/4}$ on the required physical interval.

rows.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmplification.GrowingCrossing
rows.plain: Data at the growing wave’s selected crossing
rows.annotation: The covector equation determines the normal without reference to the seed. Once the normal is fixed, the seed equation is homogeneous and linear. If the unscaled seed has maximum length $A$ on $[t_0,T]$, the positive factor $\lambda^{-3/4}/A$ makes its maximum $\lambda^{-3/4}$ while leaving its frame, and hence the crossing time, unchanged. Fixing the peak rather than the initial length makes the amplitude during the switch exponentially small relative to a prescribed later velocity scale.

citations.title: this paper

citations.supports: The formal comparison error is the four-term quantity (2.6), with the same frame, frozen couplings and rate.
citations.title: The authors' Lean formalization at fd3a158
citations.where: definition of the comparison error of the central amplification and of the preceding-wave frame

explanation.text:
For a nonzero transverse preceding wave over differentiable trace-free $B$ on $[t_0,T]$, with $r>0$ and $0<\eta\le
u$, equation (6.6) bounds $\delta$ by an absolute multiple of $(T-t_0)(\|B\|_\infty^2+\|B_t\|_\infty)/\eta+\|B\|_\infty/r+\|E_c\|_\infty/
u$. Differentiating the frame entries gives $|\partial_tB_{ij}|\le4\|B\|_\infty^2+\|B_t\|_\infty$, and integrating this controls the two relative coupling variations in (2.6); the last two terms of (2.6) already have the displayed form. The formalization defines the comparison error as exactly the four terms of (2.6): the suprema over the comparison window of $|B_{12}/
u-1|$ and $|B_{32}/\eta-1|$, with $B_{12}=E_1\cdot BE_2$ and $B_{32}=E_3\cdot BE_2$ in the moving frame $E_1=\kappa_p/|\kappa_p|$, $E_2=\mathbf a_p/|\mathbf a_p|$, $E_3=E_1	imes E_2$, plus $\sup\|B\|/r$ and $\sup\|E_c\|/
u$, where $
u$ and $\eta$ are the couplings frozen at $t_0$ and $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}$. The formal inequality has the explicit factor $8$ and accepts any uniform upper bounds for $\|B\|_\infty$, $\|B_t\|_\infty$ and $\|E_c\|_\infty$, which is why its verdict is stronger.

ties.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificationPhysicalError_le_movingFrame
ties.plain: Physical error bound in terms of moving-frame errors

rows.fidelity_note:
For a differentiable trace-free $B$ and a nonzero transverse preceding wave on $[t_0,T]$, the formal inequality bounds the comparison error by $8 igl((T-t_0)(M^2+D)/\eta+M/r+E/
u igr)$ for any uniform bounds $M\ge\|B\|_\infty$, $D\ge\|B_t\|_\infty$ and $E\ge\|E_c\|_\infty$, with $r>0$ and $0<\eta\le
u$. The quantity on the left is defined in the formalization as the four suprema of (2.6) in the frame of the preceding wave, with $
u,\eta$ frozen at $t_0$. The explicit constant and the arbitrary upper bounds make this a stronger form of (6.6).

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The explicit constant and arbitrary upper bounds preserve the comparison estimate; the error is exactly the four-term quantity in (2.6).

rows.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificationPhysicalError_le_movingFrame
rows.plain: Physical error bound in terms of moving-frame errors
rows.annotation:
The four terms of (2.6) are the relative changes of $B_{12}$ and $B_{32}$, $\|B\|_\infty/r$, and $\|E_c\|_\infty/
u$. Differentiate the entries in the moving frame: their derivatives have norm at most $4\|B\|_\infty^2+\|B_t\|_\infty$. Integrating this bound and dividing by the smaller entry $\eta$ controls both relative changes. The denominator $
u$ for $E_c$ comes from the scaling of the amplitude equations ($S/r=1/(2
u)$), so smallness merely relative to the shear strength would not suffice.

citations.supports: The frame derivative estimate used to control changing couplings.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For a nonzero perpendicular pair solving the wave equations over trace-free $B(t)$, every vector of its orthonormal frame satisfies $|\partial_tE_i(t)|\le2\|B\|_\infty$ on the interval. This follows from the frame equations (2.2), which express each frame derivative using entries of $B$. It is used in §6.2 to estimate the derivative of $B_{ij}=E_i\cdot BE_j$ and hence the comparison error. The formal result is stronger because it provides a derivative vector with norm at most $2\|B(t)\|$ at each time; derivatives are taken within the supplied time set, and the interval supremum gives the paper's bound.

ties.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.movingFrame_axis_derivative_bound
ties.plain: Derivative bounds for the moving frame axes

rows.fidelity_note: For nonzero perpendicular vectors solving the wave equations over trace-free $B$ at a time in any time set, the formal result gives $|E_i^{\prime}(t)|\le2\|B(t)\|$ for each of the three frame vectors, with derivatives taken within that set. Bounding the pointwise norm by its interval supremum gives the quoted estimate.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. A pointwise frame-speed bound gives the interval bound by taking a supremum; this separate result is outside both main proofs.

rows.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.movingFrame_axis_derivative_bound
rows.plain: Derivative bounds for the moving frame axes
rows.annotation: Each frame equation in (2.2) contains two entries of $B$. Their absolute values are at most $\|B\|_\infty$, so $|E_i'|\le2\|B\|_\infty$. In $B_{ij}'=E_i'\cdot BE_j+E_i\cdot B_tE_j+E_i\cdot BE_j'$ this gives $4\|B\|_\infty^2+\|B_t\|_\infty$. The time derivative of the moving matrix entry is therefore different from that of $B$ in a fixed frame.

explanation.text:
For a growing transverse seed over $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes\kappa_p+E_c$, with positive frozen couplings $
u,\eta$, put $\varepsilon=\eta/
u$, $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}$, $S=\sigma/r$ and $\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a|>0$. Under (2.7) on a normalized interval of length at least two, Lemmas 2.6–2.7 give $|\mathbf b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le CS|\mathbf b(t')|/\gamma(t')$ for every transverse amplitude solution and ordered times, and $
u_+(t)\ge
u\varepsilon/2$. The first formal link proves the propagation part with $C=252e$ and denominators $|\mathbf a|$, equivalent after the same positive rescaling on both sides; the second requires the coupling bound as part of the supplied growing-wave data, so each link alone covers less than the combined display. The comparison error in their hypothesis $C_0\Theta^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$ is defined in the formalization as the four-term quantity (2.6) in the preceding wave's frame, so these are the estimates obtained under (2.7) itself.

ties.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmplification.exists_physical_growth_bound_threshold
ties.plain: Weighted transverse amplitude propagation on the physical interval

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $(\kappa,\mathbf a)$ be a supplied growing transverse wave over $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes\kappa_p+E_c$ on $[t_0,t_0+\Theta/r]$, initially with $\kappa=\lambda E_3$ and amplitude in the positive direction $-E_1/S+E_2$. In the preceding wave's orthonormal frame freeze $\sigma=|\kappa_p||\mathbf a_p|$, $
u=E_1\cdot BE_2>0$ and $\eta=E_3\cdot BE_2>0$; put $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}$, $S=\sigma/r$ and $\varepsilon=\eta/
u$. The preceding pair solves the wave equations over continuous trace-free $B$, with continuous $E_c$ on a compact set containing the interval. For every sufficiently large integer $C_0$, assume $\lambda
e0$, $\Theta\ge2$, $C_0\varepsilon\le1$ and $C_0\Theta^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$. For every solution $\mathbf b_t=-(I-2P_\kappa)M\mathbf b$ with $\mathbf b\perp\kappa$, the conclusion is $|\mathbf b(t)|/|\mathbf a(t)|\le252eS|\mathbf b(t')|/|\mathbf a(t')|$ for ordered times in the interval. Here $P_\kappa$ projects onto $\mathbb R\kappa$, and the seed never vanishes. This is the propagation estimate in (6.7), without its coupling conclusion. The defining source for the formal comparison quantity $\delta$ is absent; exact agreement with (2.6) remains unchecked. To use the paper's $\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a|$, take $\lambda>0$ and multiply both amplitude denominators by this same positive factor. The coupling inequality in the quoted display is a separate conclusion.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. Multiplying both amplitude denominators by $\lambda^{3/4}>0$ gives the paper's normalization; positive coupling is supplied separately.

rows.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmplification.exists_physical_growth_bound_threshold
rows.plain: Weighted transverse amplitude propagation on the physical interval
rows.annotation: Write $G(t,s)$ for the propagator of the homogeneous transverse equation. The displayed inequality gives $\|G(t,s)\|\le CS\gamma(t)/\gamma(s)$. A solution forced by $f$ and starting with zero data thus has size after division by $\gamma(t)$ bounded by $CS\int_{t_0}^t |f(s)|/\gamma(s)\,ds$ (with the transverse projection of $f$). This is the reason for measuring the corrections in the seed weight in §5.

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes\kappa_p+E_c$, where a nonzero transverse preceding wave over $B$ supplies the frame $E_1=\kappa_p/|\kappa_p|$, $E_2=\mathbf a_p/|\mathbf a_p|$, $E_3=E_1	imes E_2$. At $t_0$ freeze $\sigma=|\kappa_p||\mathbf a_p|$, $
u=E_1\cdot BE_2>0$, $\eta=E_3\cdot BE_2>0$, and put $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}$, $\varepsilon=\eta/
u$. For proposed growing-wave data on $[t_0,t_0+\Theta/r]$, the formal condition requires nonzero transverse vectors $\kappa,\mathbf a$ and $
u_+(t)=(\kappa/|\kappa|)\cdot M(\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|)\ge
u\varepsilon/2$ throughout that interval. It does not require the propagation estimate for every transverse solution in the same display. It specifies properties of supplied data; the existence of data satisfying them is proved separately.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The selected growing wave has the paper's prescribed peak and positive frequency; its more general formulation does not change that wave.

rows.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmplification.GrowingCrossing
rows.plain: Data at the growing wave’s selected crossing
rows.annotation: The coupling bound holds on the entire active interval: $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a=|\kappa||\mathbf a|\nu_+>0$. In the leading pressure Hessian this quantity multiplies $-F_h'$ in the direction $\kappa$. Localization must preserve the sign for all these times, not merely at the crossing where the next wave is selected.

With positive frozen parameters $
u,\eta,\sigma$, set $\varepsilon=\eta/

u}$ and $S=\sigma/r$, and assume the growing-wave comparison on $[t_0,T]$ satisfies (2.7). Choosing $\mathsf D\ge CS$ and $\mathsf D\ge2/(

ties.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmplification.exists_localized_center_estimates_threshold
ties.plain: Forward amplitude and coupling bounds at the origin

rows.fidelity_note:
On $[t_0,t_0+\Theta/r]$, consider a supplied growing transverse wave $(\kappa,\mathbf a)$ over $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes\kappa_p+E_c$, starting with covector $\lambda E_3$ and amplitude in the positive direction $-E_1/S+E_2$. The nonzero preceding pair defines its orthonormal frame; freeze $\sigma=|\kappa_p||\mathbf a_p|$ and $
u=E_1\cdot BE_2$, $\eta=E_3\cdot BE_2>0$, with $
u>0$. Put $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}$, $S=\sigma/r$, $\varepsilon=\eta/
u$. The preceding pair solves the wave equations over continuous trace-free $B$, with continuous $E_c$ on a compact set containing the interval. For all sufficiently large integers $C_0$, assume $\Theta\ge2$, $\lambda
e0$, $C_0\varepsilon\le1$ and $C_0\Theta^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$. If $\mathsf D\ge252eS$ and $\mathsf D\ge2/(
u\varepsilon)$, every transverse amplitude solution satisfies $|\mathbf b(t)|/|\mathbf a(t)|\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/|\mathbf a(t')|$ for ordered times, and $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a\ge\mathsf D^{-1}|\kappa||\mathbf a|$. The seed is nonzero. Scaling both denominators by a positive constant gives (5.5). The defining source for the formal comparison quantity $\delta$ is absent, so its exact correspondence with (2.6) remains unchecked. The constant $252e$ is explicit and independent of the wave data, whereas the paper writes an unspecified absolute $C$. Dividing the second inequality by $|\kappa||\mathbf a|>0$ gives the stated coupling bound.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The explicit universal constant and positive normalization give the same central estimates at the construction's chosen parameters.

rows.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmplification.exists_localized_center_estimates_threshold
rows.plain: Forward amplitude and coupling bounds at the origin
rows.annotation: The common bound $\mathsf D$ has to cover both $CS$ and $2/(\nu\varepsilon)$. At step $j$ the first is at most $C\mu^{1/8}L_j$, and the second at most $2L_j^2/\pi$. The logarithmic bound (1.15) allows even the smaller allowance $\mu$ for these two quantities; $\mathsf D=\mu^9$ is already needed for the parent coefficients.

citations.supports: The two branches of the activation cutoff and the switching interval.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For $r>0$, the new wave is switched on by $\widetilde\chi(t)=1-\chi(1+r(t-t_0))$ for $t\ge t_0$ and by zero before activation. The cutoff $\chi$ from §5.1 is constant near the ends of its transition, so the change occurs only during the first unit of normalized time. This places the switching error where the growing seed is still exponentially smaller than its eventual maximum. One formal identity gives $\widetilde\chi(t)=1-\chi(1+r(t-t_0))$ for all real parameters using a fixed smooth transition, and the other proves $\widetilde\chi=0$ for $t\le t_0$ when $r\ge0$; each is weaker than the whole displayed piecewise prescription, and together they give it for the positive rate used here.

ties.name: TorusEuler.waveSwitch_eq_one_sub_envelopeCutoff
ties.plain: The formula for the time cutoff

rows.fidelity_note: Let $\theta:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$ be the fixed smooth transition, zero on $(-\infty,0]$ and one on $[1,\infty)$, and put $\chi(s)=1-\theta(s-1)$ and $\widetilde\chi(t)=\theta(r(t-t_0))$. For every real $r,t_0,t$, the formal statement gives $\widetilde\chi(t)=1-\chi(1+r(t-t_0))$. This is the formula on the positive-time branch in the display. The assertion that it is zero before activation follows separately from the transition's zero region when $r\ge0$; that assertion is not this identity's conclusion.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The two branches of the time cutoff are separate identities for one smooth switch.

rows.name: TorusEuler.waveSwitch_eq_one_sub_envelopeCutoff
rows.plain: The formula for the time cutoff
rows.annotation: The transition is a function of $\tau=r(t-t_0)$: it is zero for $\tau\le0$ and is $1-\chi(1+\tau)$ for $\tau\ge0$. Since the fixed profile equals one through argument $1$ and zero from argument $2$, the transition is confined to the first unit of normalized time.

rows.fidelity_note: Let $\theta:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$ be the fixed smooth transition, zero for nonpositive arguments, and set $\widetilde\chi(t)=\theta(r(t-t_0))$. For every $r\ge0$, $t_0\in\mathbb R$ and $t\le t_0$, the formal statement gives $\widetilde\chi(t)=0$. It includes the activation time and the degenerate rate $r=0$. This supplies only the zero branch of the paper's displayed formula; the other branch is a separate identity.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The two branches of the time cutoff are separate identities for one smooth switch.

rows.name: TorusEuler.waveSwitch_eq_zero_of_le
rows.plain: The wave cutoff is zero at and before launch
rows.annotation: Since $r>0$, every $t\le t_0$ has $r(t-t_0)\le0$. The fixed transition vanishes there, including at the activation time. This ensures that the oscillation is still zero at launch while the central seed itself is nonzero.

citations.supports: Smoothness of the activation transition across its endpoints.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The activation cutoff is smooth even at $t=t_0$, where its displayed formula changes from zero to $1-\chi(1+r(t-t_0))$. The cutoff chosen in §5.1 is constant on the adjoining intervals, so the transition joins smoothly. This prevents activation from introducing a time-regularity defect into the approximate velocity. The formal theorem writes the same cutoff as a fixed smooth transition evaluated at $r(t-t_0)$ and proves smoothness on all real times for every real $r,t_0$; that extends the paper's positive-rate setting, although only $r>0$ describes switching on.

ties.plain: Smoothness of the time cutoff

rows.fidelity_note: Let $\theta:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$ be the fixed smooth transition, zero on $(-\infty,0]$ and one on $[1,\infty)$. For every real $r,t_0$, the formal statement proves that $\widetilde\chi(t)=\theta(r(t-t_0))$ is smooth on all of $\mathbb R$. The paper's positive-rate activation cutoff is this same function, with $\chi(s)=1-\theta(s-1)$. Nonpositive rates are also allowed by the smoothness assertion; only positive rates have the paper's switching-on interpretation.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The stronger smoothness and weighted derivative estimates apply in particular at the positive switching rates used by the construction.

citations.supports: Completion of activation after one unit of normalized time.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For $r>0$, the cutoff is fully on whenever the normalized elapsed time $\tau=r(t-t_0)$ is at least one. The transition function defining $\chi$ has reached its constant region by then, so $\widetilde\chi(t)=1$ for $t\ge t_0+1/r$. This ensures that the complete rank-one shear is present when the following wave is activated. The formal statement uses exactly the equivalent physical-time condition $t\ge t_0+1/r$ and includes the endpoint, so the verdict is “same”.

ties.plain: The wave cutoff is one after the activation interval

rows.fidelity_note: Let $r>0$ and $\widetilde\chi(t)=\theta(r(t-t_0))$, where the fixed smooth transition $\theta$ equals one on $[1,\infty)$. If $t\ge t_0+1/r$, then the formal statement gives $\widetilde\chi(t)=1$. Since $\tau=r(t-t_0)$, the time hypothesis is exactly $\tau\ge1$. The endpoint $t=t_0+1/r$ is included. This matches the quoted assertion for the paper's activation cutoff.
rows.name: TorusEuler.waveSwitch_eq_one_of_activation
rows.plain: The wave cutoff is one after the activation interval
rows.annotation: At $t=t_0+1/r$ the argument of $\chi$ is $2$, so $\widetilde\chi$ equals one from then on. The permissible crossing bracket begins at normalized time $\tau_m\ge2/\varepsilon>1$. Hence every such crossing occurs with the entire preceding shear already switched on.

citations.supports: The cutoff derivative estimate and its residual contribution.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For the fixed smooth cutoff and positive rate $r$, the derivative obeys $|\widetilde\chi'(t)|\le Cr$, where $C$ depends only on the cutoff. The chain rule supplies the factor $r$, and the derivative vanishes outside $[t_0,t_0+1/r]$. This controls the activation contribution to the residual in (5.48). The formal theorem is stronger: one constant works for every weight with $|\gamma|\le G$ on the switching interval and gives $|\widetilde\chi'\gamma|\le CrG$ at all real times; taking $\gamma=1$ and $G=1$ recovers the quoted estimate.

ties.name: TorusEuler.waveSwitch_weighted_derivative_bound
ties.plain: The weighted cutoff derivative

rows.fidelity_note: For the fixed smooth transition $\theta$, set $\widetilde\chi(t)=\theta(r(t-t_0))$. One constant $C\ge0$ is chosen before $t_0$, $r$, $G$ and the weight. Whenever $r>0$, $G\ge0$ and $|\gamma(t)|\le G$ on $[t_0,t_0+1/r]$, the formal statement gives $|\widetilde\chi'(t)\gamma(t)|\le CrG$ for every real $t$. The derivative of the cutoff vanishes outside that interval, so no regularity or bound on the weight there is needed. Choosing $\gamma\equiv1$ and $G=1$ gives the paper's bound $|\widetilde\chi'|\le Cr$.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The stronger smoothness and weighted derivative estimates apply in particular at the positive switching rates used by the construction.

citations.supports: The intended identification of the central wave with the localized construction.

explanation.text: For wave $j$, the paper denotes its central seed by $\mathbf a_j$, its transported covector by $\kappa_j$, and their product of lengths by $\sigma_j=|\mathbf a_j||\kappa_j|$. This notation connects the localized expansion of Section 5 with the moving-frame amplification and central gradient splitting used in (7.1)–(7.3). The formal step requirements identify the central amplitude with the localized seed on $[t_j,S_j]$. They do not also require $\kappa_j(t)=(D_aX_{j-1}(t,0))^{-T}k_*$ or record the first wave's initial directions and attained normalization, so the weaker verdict identifies a missing equality between the central covector and the covector of that expansion. These omissions concern what the displayed conditions establish, not a demonstrated inequality between the two covectors.

citations.supports: The residual frequency band derived from the projected momentum equation.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: At stage $j$, the momentum residual $R_j$ has Fourier support in $|\xi|\le4\Lambda_j$, whereas $U_j$ has support in $|\xi|\le2\Lambda_j$. The projected equation (7.5) writes $R_j=\partial_tU_j+\mathbb P\operatorname{div}(U_j\otimes U_j)$; time differentiation keeps the same fixed band, and multiplication adds the two velocity bands. This permits a Bernstein estimate for $\nabla R_j$ when checking the next endpoint problem. The formal theorem proves the same residual-band conclusion for a jointly smooth periodic velocity on a closed time interval, assuming its band, the projected momentum identity and the stated spatial Hölder representative of advection; it does not assign this band to an arbitrary unrelated residual.

ties.name: TorusEuler.parentResidualFourierBand_of_projectedMomentum
ties.plain: The Fourier support of the residual

rows.fidelity_note: For a smooth velocity with Fourier support at most $2\Lambda_j$ on the entire closed interval, the formal theorem assumes the projected momentum identity with a continuous residual and the advective term represented in the spatial one-half Hölder space. It then proves that residual has support at most $4\Lambda_j$. This is the stated conclusion under the stage equation, not a bound for an arbitrary independently chosen residual.
rows.name: TorusEuler.parentResidualFourierBand_of_projectedMomentum
rows.plain: The Fourier support of the residual
rows.annotation: Apply the Leray projection before using Bernstein. In Fourier variables the quadratic product of two fields in the band $2\Lambda_j$ has band $4\Lambda_j$; projection, divergence and the time derivative do not enlarge this band. Thus $R_j$ is itself band-limited, and $\|\nabla R_j\|_\infty\le C\Lambda_j\|R_j\|_\infty$. This retains the smallness of the momentum defect, which would be lost by separately bounding its large summands.

citations.supports: The two applications of Bernstein’s estimate to the current velocity and residual.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: §7.1, paragraph following (7.5); Appendix B, Lemma B.1, (B.1); Theorem 7.1 (T1)–(T2)

explanation.text: Using $\|U_j\|_\infty\le\lambda_j$, $\|R_j\|_\infty\le\lambda_{j+1}^{-3}$ and the bands $2\Lambda_j$ and $4\Lambda_j$, Bernstein's estimate gives $\|\nabla U_j\|_\infty\le C\Lambda_j\lambda_j$ and $\|\nabla R_j\|_\infty\le C\Lambda_j\lambda_{j+1}^{-3}$. Equation (B.1) supplies one factor of the frequency radius per derivative; the fixed factors two and four enter the absolute constant. These estimates control the parent gradient and the residual derivative in the endpoint coercivity inequality. The linked formal Lemma B.1 gives the general Bernstein estimate, so the weaker verdict concerns the missing substitutions of the actual stage fields, their bands and their (T2) sizes, rather than a different differentiation exponent.

explanation.text: For sufficiently large $N$, each stage satisfies $\|\nabla U_j\|_\infty\le\lambda_j^9$ and $\|\partial_t\nabla U_j\|_\infty\le\lambda_j^{18}$ throughout $[0,S_j]$. The first bound follows from the velocity band $2\lambda_j^5$ and size $\lambda_j$; the second uses (7.5), Bernstein's estimate and boundedness of the Leray projection on $C^{0,1/2}$, with room to absorb fixed constants. These deliberately generous powers furnish uniform parent and older-gradient bounds for the next amplification. The formal theorem gives exactly the two pointwise operator-norm bounds from joint smoothness, the velocity and residual sizes, the band and the projected equation, with one threshold for $\lambda_j$ and only $\lambda_{j+1}\ge1$. At the endpoints its time derivatives are taken within the closed interval, agreeing with the slab interpretation of (7.6).

rows.name: TorusEuler.exists_parentDerivedLowBounds
rows.plain: Gradient bounds for the Fourier-truncated parent
rows.annotation: The spatial Bernstein bound costs one power of $\Lambda_j=\lambda_j^5$ and gives $C\lambda_j^6$ for the gradient. To estimate $\partial_t\nabla U_j$, take one spatial derivative in Equation (7.5). The quadratic term now contains two derivatives and the Leray projection is bounded in $C^{0,1/2}$; using a third ordinary derivative to control this Hölder norm costs $C\Lambda_j^3\lambda_j^2=C\lambda_j^{17}$. Together with the small differentiated residual this fits $\lambda_j^{18}$. The Hölder step avoids using an $L^\infty$ operator bound for the projection.

These substitutions put the induction into the hypotheses and notation of Section 5. explanation.text: The half-lengths $\tau_j=\lambda_{j-1}^{-1/8}L_{j+1}^3$ satisfy $0<\tau_j\le\lambda_{j-1}^{-1/16}$ and $4\tau_{j+1}\le\tau_j$ once $N$ is sufficiently large. Equation (1.15) makes the logarithmic factor smaller than a small power of the parent frequency, and the rapid frequency growth then gives the factor-four decay. These bounds keep the endpoint intervals nested and the remaining activation gaps summable. The formal theorem proves both inequalities and positivity uniformly in the stage from the recurrence, greatest-order choice, positive thresholds and logarithmic floor; it is stronger in that it does not need $\mathcal B$ to be nondecreasing or to majorize the analytic constants.

citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: With $\mu=\lambda_{j-1}\ge1$, $\mathsf D=\mu^9$, $\lambda=\mu^{320b(q_j+1)}$ and integer $b\ge1$, the admissibility bound $\mathcal B(q_{j+1})\le\mu$ gives $\mathcal B(q_{j+1})\mathsf D^b\le\mu^{10b}\le\lambda^{1/32}$. This is the scalar calculation (7.8), after the schedule has placed every required fixed-order constant below the parent frequency. It ensures the finite expansion's coefficient loss is small relative to the new frequency gain. The formal theorem proves the same calculation for any real upper-bound quantity $A\le\mu$ in place of $\mathcal B(q_{j+1})$ and additionally gives $A\mathsf D^b\mu\le\lambda^{1/16}$, which explains the stronger verdict.

citations.supports: The initial verification of the induction hypotheses.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: For sufficiently large $N$, the explicit shear $U_0$ satisfies (T1)–(T3): smoothness, oddness and incompressibility with two Fourier modes, velocity and deformation bounds, zero residual, and zero pressure Hessian. The first paragraph of §7.2 derives these from (6.1)–(6.2), with $S_0=1$ and $\rho=\varepsilon_1$. This starts the induction that constructs all later approximate velocities. The linked formal proof assumes the numbered preceding results and concludes the whole common-sequence theorem, whose clauses include these base properties at $j=0$; it is a location of the assembly argument rather than a separate statement of the elementary shear calculation. The supplied weaker label is misleading if read as a missing base conclusion, since the theorem explicitly includes that conclusion; omitted first-wave direction identities are irrelevant to this particular base-stage clause.

The formal conclusions of Theorem 7.1 state that the stage-zero field is the stationary shear at $\rho=\varepsilon_1$, that $S_0=1$, and that (T1)–(T3) hold at every stage $j\ge0$, including $j=0$, for every sufficiently large initial frequency; at $j=0$ this includes smoothness, oddness, zero divergence, the frequency band, $\|U_0\|_\infty\le\lambda_0$, the deformation bounds by $\lambda_0$, the residual bound and the pressure condition. The proof obtains this inside the whole construction rather than as a separate lemma, which is a matter of where the argument sits and does not weaken the conclusion. The first-wave direction identities are not part of this sentence.

explanation.text: With $\varepsilon=L_j^{-2}$ and $\mu=\lambda_{j-1}$, substituting the parent estimates into (6.6) gives $\delta\le C(\varepsilon^{-1}L_{j+1}^3\mu^{-1/16}+\mu^{-3/32}+\mu^{-1/4})$. The three terms respectively arise from variation of the older gradient over the interval, the ratio $\|B\|_\infty/r$, and the correction ratio $\|E_c\|_\infty/\nu$. This decaying bound is then compared with the logarithmic growth of the normalized time window. The formal theorem makes the same scalar implication with coefficient $A(5+c^{-1})$, assuming $\mu\ge1$, $\nu\ge1$, $r\ge c\mu^{1/8}$ for $c>0$, the stated gradient and correction bounds, and a physical-error estimate with nonnegative coefficient $A$. It treats $\delta$ as a real number satisfying that estimate, so it does not itself identify or prove the underlying comparison-error formula.

The older gradient divided by $r$ costs $C\mu^{-3/32}$, and the central error divided by $\nu$ costs $C\mu^{-1/4}$. Both latter denominators are bounded below by the inherited crossing values.

citations.supports: The decrease of successive coupling ratios and the associated crossing horizon.

explanation.text: The scheduled coupling ratios satisfy $\varepsilon_j=(L_j/L_{j+1})^2\varepsilon_{j-1}\le\varepsilon_{j-1}/32$, with $\varepsilon_{j-1}=L_j^{-2}$ and $\varepsilon_j=L_{j+1}^{-2}$. The recurrence gives $L_{j+1}/L_j=K_{j+2}\ge640$, so the displayed factor-thirty-two decrease is a generous consequence of the squared ratio. It makes the next target ratio admissible in Proposition 2.8 and makes the cumulative coupling errors summable. The formal theorem gives the same identity and inequality for positive $L_j$ and $L_{j+1}\ge640L_j$, additionally recording $(\varepsilon_{j-1}\varepsilon_j)^{-1/2}=L_jL_{j+1}\le L_{j+1}^2$; all inverses here have positive denominators.

explanation.text: For a later wave with $\varepsilon=L_j^{-2}$, $\varepsilon_j=L_{j+1}^{-2}$ and $r\ge c\mu^{1/8}$, the crossing bracket ends within physical time $\tau_j=\mu^{-1/8}L_{j+1}^3$ after activation. Indeed, $(\varepsilon\varepsilon_j)^{-1/2}=L_jL_{j+1}\le L_{j+1}^2$, so $2(\varepsilon\varepsilon_j)^{-1/2}/r\le(2/c)\mu^{-1/8}L_{j+1}^2\le\tau_j$ once $L_{j+1}\ge2/c$. This leaves room in the second half of the endpoint interval for subsequent waves. The formal theorem assumes $\mu,c,L_j>0$, $L_{j+1}\ge640L_j$ and the stated rate and size bounds, and concludes the final inequality; its weaker verdict concerns the absent intermediate displayed bound, not existence of the crossing itself, which comes from Proposition 2.8.

citations.supports: Summation of the relative coupling errors across the activation sequence.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: At successive crossings, $|\log(\nu_j(t_{j+1})/(2\pi))|\le4\varepsilon_1\le4(\log N)^{-2}$. Equation (2.19) bounds each logarithmic change by twice the preceding ratio, and (7.9) makes those ratios decrease by at least a factor of thirty-two, so the logarithms telescope and their errors sum. This keeps the first coupling uniformly close to its initial value despite infinitely many waves. The formal theorem proves the accumulated bound by four times the initial ratio for any positive coupling sequence satisfying those local bounds and ratio decay; setting its initial coupling to $2\pi$ gives the first inequality. Its weaker verdict refers to the additional schedule estimate $\varepsilon_1\le(\log N)^{-2}$, which is not part of that scalar theorem.

At wave $j$ the frozen first coupling is $
u_{j-1}(t_j)$ and the first coupling at its crossing is $
u_j(t_{j+1})$. The comparison gives a bound $2\varepsilon_{j-1}$ for the absolute logarithm of their ratio. Summing from $
u_1(t_2)=2\pi$ telescopes the logarithms, with total error at most $2\varepsilon_1/(1-1/32)<4\varepsilon_1$.

citations.supports: The uniform first-coupling interval derived from accumulated logarithmic control.

explanation.text: For every crossing, $\pi\le\nu_j(t_{j+1})\le4\pi$ once the initial frequency is large enough. The preceding telescoping estimate gives $|\log(\nu_j(t_{j+1})/(2\pi))|\le4\varepsilon_1$, and $4\varepsilon_1\le\log2$ puts the ratio between $1/2$ and $2$. This uniform positive interval lets the amplification constants remain independent of the step. The formal theorem proves exactly these bounds for positive crossing couplings starting at $2\pi$, nonnegative ratios decreasing by a factor of at least thirty-two, local logarithmic errors at most twice those ratios, and the explicit initial smallness $4\varepsilon_1\le\log2$.

explanation.text: At step $j$, the activation contribution obeys $\|\widetilde\chi'\gamma\|_\infty\le\mu\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$, where $\mu=\lambda_{j-1}$. On the switching interval, (6.8) and $L_j=4\log\lambda_{j+1}$ give $\gamma\le e^{3-L_j}=e^3\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$, while the derivative bound gives the remaining factor $Cr\le\mu e^{-3}$ for large $N$. This matches the expansion remainder's next-frequency decay in the residual estimate. The formal result chooses one cutoff constant and proves the same bound for all real times from $r,\lambda_{j+1}>0$, that local weight bound and $Cre^3\le\mu$, using that the cutoff derivative vanishes elsewhere.

explanation.text: At the current step, the parent and growing seed satisfy §5.1, and the coefficient loss obeys $C_{\rm step}=\Gamma_P\mathsf D^b\le\mu^{10b}\le\lambda^{1/32}$. The threshold choice bounds $\Gamma_P$ by $\mu$, and (7.8) then verifies the smallness requirement (5.43). This licenses the expansion estimates and subsequent Fourier truncation instead of treating them as automatic consequences of the wave choice. The linked formal assembly proof assumes the numbered Section 5 results and supplies their parent and numerical inputs before constructing the common sequence, but its conclusion does not separately state the displayed bound on $C_{\rm step}$. Thus the weaker verdict identifies a proof-location link; the scalar absorption calculation is the direct justification for the numerical inequality.

explanation.text: For the parent $U=U_{j-1}$, the full-order bound is $\|U\|_{C_tC^{P,1/2}}\le C_P\mu^{5(P+1)+1}\le\lambda^{P+2}$. Its Fourier band $2\mu^5$ and size $\mu$ give the first estimate by Bernstein's inequality, including the extra derivative used to control the half-Hölder part. The resulting bound is needed to estimate the tail when $V=U+W^{\natural}$ is truncated. The formal scalar theorem proves the second inequality under $\mu\ge1$, $C_P\le\mu$ and integer $b\ge1$ with $\lambda=\mu^{320b(q_j+1)}$; its weaker verdict concerns the actual parent's norm estimate, which is not among its conclusions.

rows.annotation: The parent has cutoff $\Lambda_{j-1}=\mu^5$ and velocity norm at most $\mu$. To bound its $C^{P,1/2}$ norm, Bernstein through order $P+1$ costs at most $C_P\mu^{5(P+1)+1}$. Since $C_P\le\mu$, this is at most $\mu^{5P+7}\le\lambda^{P+2}$. Thus the parent norm is estimated at the new frequency without differentiating its previous expansion.

citations.supports: Absorption of the high-order wave coefficient loss into the current frequency.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: At depth and derivative order $P$, the coefficient factor in (5.48) obeys $C_{P,P}\mathsf D^{b(P+2)}\le\lambda^{(P+2)/32}$. The schedule places $C_{P,P}$ below $\mu$, while $\mathsf D=\mu^9$ and $\lambda=\mu^{320b(q_j+1)}$ convert the old-parent loss into a small fraction of the current-frequency exponent. This allows the oscillatory and mean contributions to be bounded together in $C^{P,1/2}$ before truncation. The formal scalar theorem gives exactly this inequality for $\mu\ge1$, $C_{P,P}\le\mu$ and nonnegative integer orders with $b\ge1$; the exponent $(P+2)/32$ is real division, not integer division.

ties.name: TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_fullOrder_wave_budget
ties.plain: Frequency separation dominates wave coefficient constants

rows.fidelity_note: For $\mu\ge1$, $C_{P,P}\le\mu$, integers $b\ge1$ and $P,q_j\ge0$, the theorem gives $C_{P,P}(\mu^9)^{b(P+2)}\le(\mu^{320b(q_j+1)})^{(P+2)/32}$. These are exactly the paper's coefficient and frequency after $\mathsf D=\mu^9$ and $\lambda=\mu^{K_j}$ are substituted.
rows.name: TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_fullOrder_wave_budget
rows.plain: Frequency separation dominates wave coefficient constants
rows.annotation: A derivative in physical space may differentiate the phase, at cost $|\kappa|/h\lesssim\mathsf D^2\lambda^{3/2}$. The oscillatory $C^{P,1/2}$ estimate in (5.48) uses $P+1$ derivatives at this scale and starts at size $\lambda^{-5/4}$. Including the coefficient bound gives exponent $3(P+1)/2-5/4+(P+2)/32=(49P+10)/32<2(P+1)$. The mean estimate is smaller, so both fit the full-depth bound used for truncation.

citations.supports: The full-order Fourier-tail estimate and its numerical absorption.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: The Fourier-tail budget satisfies $\mu\varepsilon_\Lambda\le9\mu\lambda^{5(2-P)+4(P+1)}\le\lambda^{15-P}=\lambda^{15}\lambda_{j+1}^{-6}\le\lambda_{j+1}^{-5}$ for $P=6K_{j+1}$. The bound $1+\|V\|_{C_tC^{P,1/2}}\le3\lambda^{2(P+1)}$ and cutoff scale $\Lambda=\lambda^5$ yield the first term, while $9\mu\le\lambda$ and the depth choice give the remaining absorption. This makes truncation errors smaller than the residual already required on the next-frequency scale. The formal theorem proves the scalar inequality from $9\mu\lambda^{5(2-P)+4(P+1)}$ directly to $\lambda_{j+1}^{-5}$ for $\mu\ge2$, integer $b\ge1$ and the stated frequency powers; it does not estimate the actual tail or separately state every intermediate bound. Its weaker verdict concerns those missing analytic and intermediate claims, and the exponent $2-P$ uses real subtraction even when $P>2$.

ties.plain: Fourier cutoff tail bound from the frequency schedule

rows.fidelity_note: With $\mu\ge2$, integer $b\ge1$, $\lambda=\mu^{K_j}$, $P=6K_{j+1}$ and $\lambda_{j+1}=\lambda^{K_{j+1}}$, the theorem proves $9\mu\lambda^{5(2-P)+4(P+1)}\le\lambda_{j+1}^{-5}$. It does not estimate the actual Fourier tail $\varepsilon_\Lambda$ or state each intermediate inequality in the display. Here $2-P$ is real subtraction, not subtraction truncated at zero.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The numerical bound absorbs the actual Fourier-tail estimate after the cutoff scale and expansion depth have been inserted.

rows.name: TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_tail_absorption
rows.plain: Fourier cutoff tail bound from the frequency schedule
rows.annotation: The cutoff residual contains a divergence of quadratic tensors. To estimate that residual in $C^{1,1/2}$ one needs the tensors in $C^{2,1/2}$, hence $\Lambda^{2-P}(1+\|V\|_{C_tC^{P,1/2}})^2$. Substituting $\Lambda=\lambda^5$ and the full-depth estimate gives $9\lambda^{14-P}$. Multiplication by $\mu$ gives at most $\lambda^{15-P}=\lambda^{15}\lambda_{j+1}^{-6}\le\lambda_{j+1}^{-5}$. The factor five in the cutoff exponent outweighs the factor four from the squared velocity norm.

citations.supports: The definition of the new approximate velocity by Fourier truncation.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: §7.2, item 5, opening sentence; Proposition 5.11; Appendix B

explanation.text: The next approximate velocity is $U_j=S_{\Lambda_j}V$, with $V=U_{j-1}+W^{\natural}$ and $\Lambda_j=\lambda_j^5$. Proposition 5.11 applies the smooth Fourier multiplier from Appendix B to retain oddness and incompressibility while imposing the new finite frequency band. Its pressure is the zero-mean periodic pressure associated with the truncated velocity. The linked step condition requires this exact identity on $[0,S_j]$ for the chosen cutoff symbol, and the numbered formal theorem proves existence of expansion data satisfying it at every stage, so both same verdicts refer to the actual truncation identity rather than an arbitrary nearby velocity.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Theorem71StepData

rows.fidelity_note: The step condition requires $U_j=S_{\lambda_j^5}(U_{j-1}+W^{\natural})$ on $[0,S_j]$, with the chosen Fourier symbol and the zero-mean pressure of the truncated field. This is precisely the displayed choice, as a required identity for proposed step data.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Theorem71StepData
rows.plain: Wave, expansion and cutoff data for one induction step
rows.annotation: The velocity $V$ is the exactly divergence-free field obtained from the finite expansion. The new parent is $U_j=S_{\Lambda_j}V$, and its pressure is computed afresh from $\Delta\pi_j=-\operatorname{tr}((\nabla U_j)^2)$. If $v_\Lambda=U_j-V$, then $U_j-U_{j-1}=O_j+\bar W^\natural+v_\Lambda$. The last two terms, rather than the oscillation itself, will have small high-order norms. This is the decomposition used in Equation (7.4).

rows.fidelity_note: The numbered theorem supplies expansion data at every $j\ge1$ and requires their truncation to equal $U_j$. Thus it proves that the actual common construction has the identity $U_j=S_{\Lambda_j}V$, with $\Lambda_j=\lambda_j^5$, rather than merely postulating that identity.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_7_1
rows.plain: A common sequence of approximate Euler flows at separated frequencies
rows.annotation: The cutoff is scalar and even, preserving divergence freedom and oddness. It also commutes with the Leray projection, so the new projected residual consists of the projected cutoff of $R_V$ and the divergence of the error in cutting off $V\otimes V$. Proposition 5.11 bounds both, giving the required small residual for the following wave.

citations.supports: The application of the flow estimate to the Fourier-truncated child velocity.

explanation.text: Write $U_j=V+v_\Lambda$, where the truncation error is smooth, divergence free and has derivatives through order two bounded by $\lambda_{j+1}^{-5}\le\lambda^{-5/2}$. Lemma 5.10 therefore gives $\sup\|(D_aX_j)^{\pm1}\|\le C_{\rm step}\lambda^{1/4}\le\lambda$, using $C_{\rm step}\le\lambda^{1/32}$ and $\lambda\ge1$. This ensures that the new velocity has a controlled label flow for the next endpoint problem. The linked formal assembly proof assumes Lemma 5.10 and concludes the final forward and inverse deformation bounds for the common construction. Its weaker verdict concerns the intermediate bound omitted from the conclusion and explicit perturbation test for $v_\Lambda$, not a different final deformation estimate.

ties.plain: Inductive construction of a common sequence of Euler stages

rows.fidelity_note: Assuming the preceding results, including Lemma 5.10, this proof builds the common sequence with flow and inverse-flow derivatives bounded by $\lambda_j$. Its statement does not retain the intermediate bound $C_{\rm step}\lambda_j^{1/4}$ or the separate perturbation test for the Fourier tail. That lemma states that if $v$ is smooth and divergence free with derivatives through order two bounded by $\lambda^{-5/2}$, the flow $Y$ of $V+v$ satisfies $\sup|(D_aY)^{\pm1}|\le C_{\rm step}\lambda^{1/4}$.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The full construction proves the child flow bounds using the perturbation criterion and tail estimate; their intermediate numerical bounds are separate.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.theorem_7_1_of
rows.plain: Inductive construction of a common sequence of Euler stages
rows.annotation: The flow estimate of Lemma 5.10 avoids applying Gronwall directly to the large physical gradient. In parent labels set $c=(D_aX)^{-1}(W+v_\Lambda\circ X)$. Solenoidality gives $k_*\cdot c_{\rm osc}=-\partial_s^{-1}\operatorname{div}_a c_{\rm osc}$; thus the phase velocity is controlled without the full factor $|k_*|$. The flow of $(c,k_*\cdot c)$ has bounded derivative in the scaled label and phase coordinates. Returning to the graph $s=k_*\cdot a$ costs $|k_*|/h\le\mathsf D\lambda^{3/2}$, giving the factor $\lambda^{3/2-5/4}=\lambda^{1/4}$ in the deformation estimate. The perturbation $v_\Lambda$ is allowed because it is divergence free and $C_tC^2$-small.

explanation.text: The oscillatory profile has label support $|a|\le2\ell_*$, so its physical evaluation $O_j=W_{\rm osc}^{\natural}$ is supported in the image of that ball under the parent flow. Proposition 5.4 gives the label support, and the flow fixes zero with deformation bounded by $\mathsf D$, giving physical radius at most $2\mathsf D\ell_*\le2\mathsf D^{-2}\le\mu^{-1}$ when $\ell_*\le\mathsf D^{-3}$ and $\mathsf D=\mu^9$. This is the spatial localization used to isolate the terminal singularity at the origin. The formal conclusion condition only requires support within distance $\lambda_{j-1}^{-1}$ of the integer lattice, representing the torus origin, and leaves the expansion identity to separate step data. Its weaker verdict identifies the omitted label-support, transport and intermediate radius estimates, although the final required support radius agrees.

explanation.text: For compact $K\subset\mathbb T^3\setminus\{0\}$, choose a smooth cutoff $\chi$ equal to one on a neighborhood of $K$ and zero near the origin. This separates the pressure source into a part supported where all spatial derivatives converge and a distant part whose effect on $K$ is governed by a smooth kernel. These additional separation and range properties make the statement stronger than the quoted choice. They matter because distance on the torus must exclude coincidence modulo the lattice, not merely equality in a chosen Euclidean cell.

explanation.text: The common sequence selected in Section 8 yields smooth odd divergence-free initial data and a smooth odd periodic Euler solution by Proposition 8.1, bounded velocity and central vorticity blow-up by Proposition 8.2, finite maximal lifespan and both divergent integrals by Corollary 8.3, and terminal spatial limits away from the origin by Proposition 8.4. These conclusions together are precisely Theorem 1.1. The linked formal theorem assumes those four results and the existence of the common sequence and assembles a single solution satisfying them all, with pressure normalized to zero mean. It also retains equality of lifespan and velocity for every other maximal solution of finite lifespan from the same data. The “same” verdict concerns this assembly; the input results remain hypotheses of this theorem and are established separately.

explanation.text: For an integrable time-dependent field $f$, $Jf(t)=\int_0^t f(s)\,\mathrm ds$ is its primitive with zero initial value. In the endpoint problem, $z=Jv$ changes the final condition $z(1)=0$ into the zero-time-mean condition $\int_0^1v=0$, which permits projection onto the appropriate time-path space. The formal expression is the same oriented vector-valued integral and is defined for every real time, with negative time reversing the integration direction. Outside the integrable complete-space setting the integral expression is assigned zero, so its mere definition supplies no derivative theorem. The continuous curves and complete Hölder spaces used in Theorem A.1 give it its ordinary integral meaning on $[0,1]$.

Thus negative $t$ reverses the integration direction, and $Jv(0)=0$. The integral expression is assigned zero when the integrand is not integrable; the integral in a noncomplete target is also assigned zero. These defaults do not assert differentiability or recover a displacement. On a positive finite interval, an $L^2$ velocity with values in a real Hilbert space has an absolutely continuous primitive with derivative $v$ almost everywhere, and zero time mean gives $Jv(T)=0$. explanation.text: For a zero-mean path $w\in L^2([0,1];\mathbb R^3)$, the adjoint primitive satisfies $J^*w(t)=\int_t^1w(s)\,\mathrm ds=-Jw(t)$. The first equality comes from interchanging the two time integrals, and the second uses $\int_0^1w=0$. It changes the term $-\langle J(\Omega w),w\rangle$ into $\langle\Omega w,Jw\rangle$, giving the displacement energy used in (A.2). The formal result states the corresponding pairing identity $\langle Ju,v\rangle=-\langle u,Jv\rangle$ whenever $v$ has zero mean, for Hilbert-valued paths on any $[0,T]$ with $T\ge0$. Thus weaker identifies the absence of the displayed pointwise adjoint formula; the integral identity is exactly what the energy calculation needs.

explanation.text: For $B_0=B(a_0)$ coercive on the projected directions, (A.6) bounds the frozen inverse on $C^{0,1/2}(\mathbb T^3;H)$ by a fixed polynomial in $2+\mu^{-1}+\|B\|_\infty$. explanation.text: For the annular kernel $G_j$ associated with the frozen inverse symbol, five integrations by parts give $\|\nabla^dG_j(y)\|\le CC_0\,2^{(3+d)j}(1+2^j|y|)^{-5}$ for $d=0,1$. The formal result supplies the same decay shape at every scale $\Lambda>0$, but retains the symbol quantity $M=\sum_{i=0}^1\sum_{q=0}^5\int|\xi|^i\|D^q\sigma(\xi)\|\,\mathrm d\xi$ explicitly. ties.name: TorusEuler.scaledMultiplierKernel_decay
ties.plain: Decay of a rescaled Fourier kernel

rows.fidelity_note: Let $\sigma$ be a rapidly decreasing smooth symbol on $\mathbb R^3$ with values in a complex Banach space, and let $G$ be its inverse Fourier kernel. Define $M=\sum_{i=0}^1\sum_{j=0}^5\int|\xi|^i\|D^j\sigma(\xi)\|\,d\xi$. For $\Lambda>0$ and integer $d\in\{0,1\}$, the formal statement gives $(1+\Lambda|y|)^5\|D^dG_\Lambda(y)\|\le32(1+2\pi)4^5M\Lambda^{3+d}$, where $G_\Lambda(y)=\Lambda^3G(\Lambda y)$. The paper has already incorporated the symbol derivative bounds into $CC_0$. The formal kernel estimate retains those derivative integrals explicitly, so the stated dyadic bound follows after supplying their uniform control and choosing scale $2^j$.

rows.annotation: The cancellation of the annular symbol at frequency zero gives $\int G_j=0$. Thus $G_j*f(a)=\int G_j(y)(f(a-y)-f(a))\,dy$, so its supremum norm is bounded by $[f]_{1/2}\int\|G_j(y)\||y|^{1/2}dy\le CC_0 2^{-j/2}[f]_{1/2}$. explanation.text: The cutoff separates the coefficient error $B(a_0)-B(a)$ into a small part near $a_0$ and a part whose source stays away from that label. rows.annotation: The cutoff leaves the modes $|\xi|\le\Lambda$ unchanged and removes those with $|\xi|>2\Lambda$. The intervening smooth transition gives an integrable rescaled kernel with uniform mass. Thus one can prescribe a Fourier band for the next parent without a norm bound that grows with the number of retained modes.
