explanation.text: For a smooth periodic velocity $f$, the cutoff of Appendix B retains its even or odd parity, retains $\operatorname{div}f=0$, and has no Fourier coefficients at $|\xi|>2\Lambda$. Evenness of $\psi$ preserves the relation between opposite frequencies, its scalar action commutes with the divergence multiplier, and its support gives the frequency restriction. These properties ensure that truncation in §5.7 preserves the symmetry and incompressibility required of each parent. The three individual formal results supply, respectively, oddness with divergence and support for real velocities, parity with support for complex Banach-valued fields, and parity for real velocities; each is “weaker” because it states only part of the quoted conjunction. The full formal assertion includes all three properties for even symbols and every $\Lambda>0$, extending the radial-symbol and $\Lambda\ge1$ assumptions of the paper, which explains “stronger”.

explanation.text: For the smooth radial cutoff of Appendix B, $\|S_\Lambda f\|_{L^\infty}\le\|\check\psi\|_{L^1}\|f\|_{L^\infty}$ and the same kernel constant bounds its action on $C^{0,1/2}$, independently of $\Lambda\ge1$. The proof applies the convolution estimate separately to values and spatial increments, following the kernel method in Tao’s Appendix A; this controls the next parent without a frequency-dependent loss at order zero. The individual formal results give the essential-supremum estimate for strongly measurable complex inputs, real velocities, and real normed-space inputs, and give the Hölder estimate separately for complex Banach-valued fields, so each is “weaker” than the conjunction. The real normed-space construction agrees with the stated multiplier for even symbols in a Banach target; without evenness it symmetrizes the symbol, and the versions lacking completeness use an integral assigned zero in incomplete targets. The combined formal assertion treats complex Banach-valued measurable inputs and continuous real velocities separately, allows even symbols and $\Lambda>0$, and thus has the “different” scope recorded here.

explanation.text: If a continuous periodic field $f$ has Fourier support in $|\xi|\le4\Lambda$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ equation (B.1) bounds $\sum_{|\beta|=m}\|\partial^\beta f\|_\infty$ by $C_m\Lambda^m\|f\|_\infty$. Since $S_{4\Lambda}f=f$, differentiating its convolution kernel and using its $L^1$ scaling proves this Bernstein estimate, following the method in Tao’s Appendix A. The frequency $4\Lambda$ also covers the quadratic term in the truncated Euler equation, so the bound controls derivatives of both the velocity and its residual. The real normed-space formal result counts every multi-index once and imposes Fourier support through all continuous linear scalar measurements, giving the “same” estimate; the complex Banach-valued result instead sums all ordered coordinate differentiations, including repetitions of the same multi-index, hence its “different” target and counting conventions. The full formal assertion restores the single-counted multi-index sum for arbitrary real normed targets and permits every $\Lambda>0$ and even symbols, which explains its “stronger” scope.

explanation.text: For integers $0\le s\le M$ and a periodic field $f\in C^{M,1/2}$, equation (B.2) gives $\|(I-S_\Lambda)f\|_{C^{s,1/2}}\le C_M\Lambda^{s-M}\|f\|_{C^{M,1/2}}$. With $k=M-s$, unit kernel mass and vanishing positive moments cancel the Taylor polynomial, leaving a remainder controlled by the $k$th kernel moment; this makes the truncation error small in §5.7. The complex Banach-valued formal result supplies that estimate and output regularity for $\Lambda\ge1$, while the real three-dimensional result supplies both for every $\Lambda>0$ without requiring radiality, accounting for their “weaker” and “stronger” comparisons. The formal norms sum the supremum and half-Hölder seminorm of the full spatial derivative tensor at each order through $s$ or $M$, and the exponent $s-M$ is an integer subtraction, so a negative exponent retains the required decay. The combined assertion explicitly covers these two target classes rather than every real normed target, which is the scope distinction behind “different”.

explanation.text: Because $\psi$ is smooth and compactly supported in $\mathbb R^3$, its inverse Fourier transform $K=\check\psi$ is a Schwartz function. Appendix B uses the resulting integrability of $K$, all its derivatives and all polynomially weighted absolute values to prove the operator, Bernstein and tail bounds. The Fourier transform convention is the one compatible with the torus modes $e^{2\pi i\xi\cdot x}$, so the kernel represents the stated multiplier. The formal construction produces this complex-valued Schwartz kernel from smoothness and vanishing outside radius two, without using radiality, positivity or the unit plateau. Its “same” comparison concerns the kernel $K$ under the paper’s assumptions; it does not yet assert any estimate for $S_\Lambda$.

explanation.text: For a positive frequency scale $\Lambda$, Appendix B rescales $K=\check\psi$ by $K_\Lambda(y)=\Lambda^3K(\Lambda y)$. The factor $\Lambda^3$ compensates for three-dimensional volume under $z=\Lambda y$, making the $L^1$ norm independent of scale and giving the Fourier multiplier $\psi(\xi/\Lambda)$. This separates the fixed kernel constants from the variable frequency in the proof of Lemma B.1. The formal expression is exactly this formula, so “same” refers to equality of the kernels in the positive-scale setting. Although the expression also accepts zero or negative scales and is zero at $\Lambda=0$, the analytic conclusions used here require $\Lambda>0$.

rows.name: TorusEuler.scaledLiftKernel
rows.plain: Dilation of a spatial kernel
rows.annotation: Under dilation the mass stays fixed, while derivatives and moments scale in opposite directions. In particular $\|\partial^\beta K_\Lambda\|_1=\Lambda^{|\beta|}\|\partial^\beta K\|_1$ and $\int |y|^k|K_\Lambda(y)|\,dy=\Lambda^{-k}\int |y|^k|K(y)|\,dy$. These are the two scale factors in (B.1) and (B.2).

The Fourier transform of $K_\Lambda$ is $\psi(\xi/\Lambda)$, so this integral has exactly the Fourier coefficients specified at the start of Appendix B. This representation supplies the real-space estimates for both values and increments, without treating a periodic lift as integrable over all of $\mathbb R^3$. The formal result proves the identity for continuous fields in a complex Banach space, smooth supported $\psi$ and every $\Lambda>0$. Its “weaker” comparison records that target class and continuity hypothesis; the real-velocity version requires the corresponding inclusion in and projection from the complex vector space.

explanation.text: For $K_\Lambda(y)=\Lambda^3K(\Lambda y)$ with $\Lambda>0$, the change of variables $z=\Lambda y$ gives $\|K_\Lambda\|_{L^1}=\|K\|_{L^1}$. Applying convolution first to $f(x)$ and then to $f(x+v)-f(x)$ bounds the uniform norm and the half-Hölder seminorm by this same constant, as in the kernel method in Tao’s Appendix A. The individual formal results give the uniform estimate for continuous complex fields, the uniform estimate for continuous real velocities, and a pointwise output bound from an integrable complex input bounded almost everywhere; each is “weaker” because it does not also estimate spatial increments. The full formal proof combines uniform and Hölder bounds, with a measurable-input essential-supremum clause for complex Banach targets and a continuous-input clause for real velocities, explaining “different”. Its statement packages the resulting bounds rather than asserting the isolated kernel-norm equality, and it permits every positive scale.

explanation.text: For an integer multi-index $\beta$ and $\Lambda>0$, differentiating $K_{4\Lambda}(y)=(4\Lambda)^3K(4\Lambda y)$ contributes $(4\Lambda)^{|\beta|}$ beyond the volume factor. Integration after $z=4\Lambda y$ therefore gives $\|\partial^\beta K_{4\Lambda}\|_{L^1}=(4\Lambda)^{|\beta|}\|\partial^\beta K\|_{L^1}$. Together with $f=S_{4\Lambda}f$ for fields supported in $|\xi|\le4\Lambda$, this proves (B.1). The kernel formal result is “stronger” because it proves the scaling identity for every complex Schwartz kernel, every positive scale and any fixed list of derivative directions, including coordinate directions. The linked proof of Lemma B.1 is “weaker” as a direct match to the displayed equality: its assertion is the Bernstein bound obtained by summing these derivative estimates, while the exact identity is supplied by the kernel result.

explanation.text: For $f\in C^{M,1/2}$ and $k=M-s\ge1$, unit mass and the vanishing moments imply that only the Taylor remainder of $f(x-y)$ after degree $k-1$ contributes to $f-S_\Lambda f$. Taylor’s formula applied to derivatives through order $s$ and to their spatial increments bounds that remainder in $C^{s,1/2}$ by $C_M|y|^k\|f\|_{C^{M,1/2}}$, giving (B.2) after integration against $|K_\Lambda|$. The first formal result proves the pointwise convolution-error bound for a bounded $C^k$ complex Banach-valued field from a uniform bound on its full $k$th derivative tensor. The second proves the corresponding translated-increment bound from a bound on $D^kf(z+v)-D^kf(z)$, so choosing that bound proportional to $|v|^{1/2}$ supplies Hölder control. Each link is “weaker” than the quoted full-norm estimate because it handles one derivative field or one increment; the derivatives through $s$ must still be combined, and $k=0$ uses the separate operator bound.

explanation.text: For the schedule $q_{j+1}=\max\{1\le s\le q_j+1:\mathcal B(s)\le\lambda_{j-1}\}$, the current order $q_j$ remains an available choice at every $j\ge1$. At the first step this follows from $q_1=1$ and $\mathcal B(1)\le\lambda_0$; later, the preceding maximum gives $\mathcal B(q_j)\le\lambda_{j-2}\le\lambda_{j-1}$. Appendix C uses this to show that the construction never loses an already available derivative order. The formal statement assumes these initial conditions, nondecreasing frequencies and the maximum rule, and concludes $q_j\le q_{j+1}\le q_j+1$. Its “different” comparison records that admissibility occurs in its proof rather than as its displayed conclusion; no monotonicity of $\mathcal B$ is needed for this step.

citations.supports: The exact threshold for advancing the derivative order and the separate admissibility argument.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: At step $j$, the order advances from $q_j$ to $q_j+1$ exactly when $\lambda_{j-1}\ge\mathcal B(q_j+1)$, and otherwise remains $q_j$. The maximum rule (1.14) permits no larger order, while current-order admissibility, proved at the start of Appendix C, rules out a decrease. This precise threshold rule makes it possible to increase regularity slowly while reserving enough frequency for each new estimate. One formal result proves the threshold equivalence assuming the stated maximum exists, and the other proves the two alternatives $q_j\le q_{j+1}\le q_j+1$ from the initialization and frequency monotonicity. Each is “weaker” in isolation: the equivalence needs admissibility to identify the non-advance case, and the order bounds need the equivalence to identify when advancement occurs.

explanation.text: For $\lambda_0=N>1$ and $\lambda_{j+1}=\lambda_j^{K(q_{j+1})}$ with $K(s)=320b(s+1)$ and integer $b\ge1$, the frequencies tend to infinity. Every exponent is at least two, so repeated exponentiation gives a growing lower bound by powers of $N$, as used in Appendix C. This guarantees that each fixed finite threshold can eventually be reached, although divergence of the derivative orders still needs their selection rule. The formal statement gives exactly this frequency-divergence conclusion for arbitrary nonnegative integer orders $q_j$, without assuming the threshold maximum rule. Thus “same” refers to the conclusion under the paper’s schedule, with the formal result isolating the recurrence assumptions actually needed.

explanation.text: The derivative orders $q_j$ tend to infinity because the frequencies eventually exceed every fixed value of $\mathcal B$. More precisely, the order is nondecreasing, and once it has reached $s$, sufficiently large $\lambda_{j-1}$ forces the next permitted order $s+1$ to be selected by (1.14). This induction over $s$ is the argument in Appendix C and ensures that one sequence eventually satisfies every fixed-order estimate. The formal theorem assumes $q_1=1$, $\mathcal B(1)\le\lambda_0$, nondecreasing frequencies tending to infinity, and the maximum rule, and proves $q_j\to\infty$. Its “same” comparison concerns that conclusion; threshold monotonicity is unnecessary, since only the finiteness of each particular threshold enters the proof.

Appendix C expands exactly these three steps because the next gain parameter must be bounded using the older frequency $\lambda_{j-1}$. The formal identity is the same after setting its starting index to $j-1$, and its recurrence uses nonnegative integer exponents. It assumes no positivity: outside the paper’s range its logarithm means $\log|x|$ for $x\ne0$ and is assigned zero at zero. The construction has $\lambda_i>1$, so this convention reduces to the ordinary logarithm and the “same” comparison is exact in the setting used here.

explanation.text: The quantity $|f|_m$ is the sum of the suprema of all coordinate derivatives $\partial^\beta f$ with $|\beta|=m$, counting each multi-index once. Appendix D takes the supremum over every variable and uses either label or physical spatial coordinates according to the field, while no time derivatives are included. This exact-order quantity builds both the finite norms (D.1) and the coefficient bounds (D.6). The two formal expressions specialize it to phase-independent functions on a chosen time set times $\mathbb R^3$, first with values in a real normed algebra and then in any real normed space, so each is “weaker” than the unrestricted notation in the sentence. Smoothness and boundedness remain separate conditions: a real-valued supremum expression by itself does not certify that the derivative family is bounded.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal expression gives the exact-order sum for a phase-independent field in an arbitrary real normed space, counting each multi-index once and taking the supremum in time and label. The paper's notation also covers phase-dependent fields and derivatives in physical position. Smoothness and boundedness are not conclusions of the expression.

rows.annotation: The exact-order quantity sums one supremum for each label multi-index $|\beta|=m$; no lower derivatives are included. This definition works for a phase-independent field in any real normed space. Smoothness and boundedness are separate hypotheses.

explanation.text: For a period-one profile $f(t,a,s)$, positive scales $\ell_*,h$ and a positive amplitude $\gamma(t)$ on $[t_0,T]$, equation (D.1) sums $\ell_*^{|\beta|}h^j\sup|\partial_a^\beta\partial_s^jf|$ over $|\beta|+j\le n$ and defines the weighted norm by replacing $f$ with $f/\gamma$. The supremum includes time, label and phase, but the differentiated variables are only label and phase; this distinguishes spatial profile control from time-derivative estimates. The general formal derivative sum, the four scaled directions and the unweighted field expression each supply only one part of this construction, which explains their “weaker” comparisons. The final expression supplies exactly the weighted norm, once per mixed multi-index, and has the “same” interpretation when the smooth normalized derivative families are bounded. It also permits other time sets and zero amplitudes, assigning the normalized field zero where $\gamma=0$, so positivity must be retained to obtain the paper’s amplitude normalization.

rows.fidelity_note: The paper specifies both the mixed finite norm and its amplitude-weighted version. This expression is a general sum of real suprema of specified successive derivatives. The scaled coordinate directions, the chosen time set, and normalization by $\gamma$ must be supplied to obtain (D.1); boundedness is also required for the usual norm interpretation.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The derivative sums and supremum conventions agree with the paper on the bounded smooth fields and positive weights used in the construction.

The scaled directions used in Lean encode these factors directly. A word sum counts different orderings of the same commuting derivatives, which can be compared with the multi-index sum using constants depending only on the order.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The weighted derivative directions are specified here; their sums, time suprema and amplitude weights are defined separately.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The construction supplies bounded derivatives and a positive amplitude weight, so the formal supremum and division conventions have their usual meanings.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.fieldNorm
rows.plain: The mixed finite norm
rows.annotation: At order $n=1$, the norm is $\sup|f|+\ell_*\sum_i\sup|\partial_{a_i}f|+h\sup|\partial_s f|$. The higher-order definition includes each mixed multi-index through total order $n$, taking the supremum of each derivative separately.

rows.fidelity_note: For positive $\ell_*,h$ and $\gamma(t)>0$ on $I=[t_0,T]$, the formal expression is exactly $\sum_{|\beta|+j\le n}\ell_*^{|\beta|}h^j\sup_{t\in I,a\in\mathbb R^3,s\in\mathbb R}|\partial_a^\beta\partial_s^j(f/\gamma)|$. Each mixed multi-index occurs once. Under smoothness and boundedness of these normalized derivatives it is the weighted norm in (D.1). The definition also permits other time sets and zero weights; at $\gamma(t)=0$ it assigns the normalized field zero. Those extra values lie outside the paper's stated positive-amplitude setting and do not change the formula there.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.weightedFieldNorm
rows.plain: The amplitude-weighted finite norm
rows.annotation: On the active interval the bound $\|f\|_{[0],\gamma}\le A$ means $|f(t,a,s)|\le A\gamma(t)$ at each time. The small amplitude on the switching interval is therefore retained when the profile is read on the graph. The definition normalizes by the actual positive weight, not by its maximum over time.

explanation.text: The weighted norm in Appendix D is taken over $t\in[t_0,T]$ after dividing the profile by the strictly positive central-wave amplitude $\gamma(t)$. This removes the known amplification from the size of the oscillatory correction, while all derivatives in (D.1) remain label or phase derivatives. The bare formal expression allows any time set and any scalar weight, and assigns the normalized field zero at a zero weight, so its “weaker” comparison does not certify the stated interval, positivity or amplitude identification. The formal assertion of Lemma D.1 does require a positive weight and positive scales, but imposes no relation to a particular wave and no time regularity, since its estimates never differentiate time. Its “different” comparison records this generality; the paper’s interval and amplitude must be supplied when applying it.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.weightedFieldNorm
ties.plain: The amplitude-weighted finite norm

rows.fidelity_note: The formal expression allows any time set and scalar function $\gamma$; it does not identify that function with a seed amplitude or require positivity. Choosing the time set $[t_0,T]$ and the positive seed amplitude gives the paper's norm. At a zero value of $\gamma$, the bare expression instead assigns the normalized field zero.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The construction supplies bounded derivatives and a positive amplitude weight, so the formal supremum and division conventions have their usual meanings.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.weightedFieldNorm
rows.plain: The amplitude-weighted finite norm
rows.annotation: The weight is the seed amplitude at the time at which the profile is evaluated. Thus a bound by $A$ in the weighted norm gives $|f(t,a,s)|\le A\gamma(t)$ throughout the active interval, including near activation. A uniform unweighted bound at the final amplitude would not give that conclusion. The mean need not vanish at activation and is estimated without this weight.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal estimates require a positive time weight on an arbitrary time set, but do not identify it with the amplitude of a particular wave. Taking the set $[t_0,T]$ and the given positive amplitude supplies the stated application. No regularity in time is needed for these purely spatial and phase derivative estimates.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The general positive weight is specialized to the seed amplitude weight used by the construction.

explanation.text: If $c(t,a)$ is independent of the phase $s$, then every derivative containing $\partial_s$ vanishes, so (D.1) reduces to $\|c\|_{[n]}=\sum_{m=0}^n\ell_*^m|c|_m$. Appendix D uses this reduction for the coefficients of the mean and transverse equations, whose variation occurs only in time and label. The formal statement proves precisely this identity for every spatially smooth $c$, every nonnegative $\ell_*$ and every phase weight $h$, by removing the zero phase-derivative terms. Its “same” comparison concerns the reduction of the norm expression, with each spatial multi-index still counted once. The identity does not establish boundedness of the remaining derivative suprema, which must be known separately in the estimates.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.fieldNorm_phaseIndependent
ties.plain: Mixed finite norm of a phase-independent field

rows.fidelity_note: For a spatially smooth phase-independent coefficient and $\ell_*\ge0$, the formal statement identifies its mixed derivative expression with $\sum_{m\le n}\ell_*^m|c|_m$ for every phase weight $h$. Every positive phase derivative is zero. As an identity of expressions it does not establish boundedness.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.fieldNorm_phaseIndependent
rows.plain: Mixed finite norm of a phase-independent field
rows.annotation: A phase-independent field $c$ has $\partial_s^j c=0$ for $j>0$. Its norm consequently contains no power of $h$, and evaluation at the physical phase introduces no fast oscillatory derivative. Only the label scale and the parent deformation enter the physical derivative bound.

explanation.text: For a phase-independent coefficient $c(t,a)$, Appendix D defines $|c|_{m,1/2}$ by summing the uniform-in-time spatial $C^{0,1/2}$ norms of derivatives with $|\beta|=m$, and then sets $\|c\|_{[n],1/2}=\sum_{m\le n}\ell_*^m|c|_{m,1/2}$. These norms are needed because the mean inverse in Theorem 4.2 is estimated in spatial Hölder spaces. The three formal expressions give the exact-order quantity, the full weighted quantity and their equality after grouping by order, for spatially smooth coefficients and nonnegative $\ell_*$. Each Hölder contribution uses the maximum of the uniform norm and half-Hölder seminorm, with coincident-point quotients assigned zero, while the paper does not specify whether those two parts are maximized or added. Thus “different” identifies a norm convention equivalent within a factor two, rather than a different regularity class; boundedness is required to interpret all the expressions as finite norms.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.holderOrderNorm
ties.plain: Exact-order Hölder norm

rows.fidelity_note: The paper denotes the exact-order half-Hölder quantity without fixing the internal norm convention. This definition uses the maximum of the uniform norm and seminorm; replacing it by their customary sum changes the norm by at most a factor two.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The maximum and sum conventions for the half-Hölder norm differ by at most a factor of two, absorbed in the allowed constants.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.holderOrderNorm
rows.plain: Exact-order Hölder norm
rows.annotation: The exact-order Hölder expression sums a $C^{0,1/2}$ quantity for each derivative of order $m$. Lean combines the uniform norm and seminorm by a maximum; their sum is between that maximum and twice it, so the unspecified constants in the paper absorb the convention.

rows.fidelity_note: The paper gives the weighted Hölder norm without fixing how its uniform and seminorm parts are combined. The formal norm uses their maximum for each derivative, equivalent within a factor two to the customary sum convention.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The maximum and sum conventions for the half-Hölder norm differ by at most a factor of two, absorbed in the allowed constants.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.holderFieldNorm
rows.plain: The finite Hölder norm
rows.annotation: The weighted Hölder norm pays $\ell_*^m$ for derivatives of order $m$, including their spatial increments. Each summand uses the maximum of its uniform and half-Hölder parts. Replacing that maximum by their sum changes the full expression by at most a factor two.

rows.fidelity_note: The paper groups the Hölder norm by derivative order. This identity gives that grouping with the maximum convention for each Hölder contribution; replacing the maximum by the customary sum costs at most a factor two, which the paper’s constants absorb.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The maximum and sum conventions for the half-Hölder norm differ by at most a factor of two, absorbed in the allowed constants.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.holderFieldNorm_eq_sum
rows.plain: Sum over spatial derivative orders in the Hölder norm
rows.annotation: Group the finite label-derivative sum by $m=|\beta|$. The weight is the same within each group, so the result is $\sum_{m\le n}\ell_*^m|c|_{m,1/2}$, with the formal maximum convention for the individual Hölder norms.

citations.supports: The two pointwise bounds, their geometric-mean interpolation and the subsequent Hölder comparison.
citations.title: this paper

explanation.text: If $v:\mathbb R^3\to E$ is differentiable with $\|v\|_\infty\le A$ and $\|Dv\|_\infty\le B$, where $A,B\ge0$, then $|v(x)-v(y)|\le\min(2A,B|x-y|)\le\sqrt{2AB}|x-y|^{1/2}$. Dividing at distinct points gives the interpolation inequality preceding (D.2), and applying it to each spatial derivative of a coefficient converts a next-derivative supremum bound into a half-Hölder bound. The direct formal result states this pointwise inequality for any real normed target, with the operator norm on $Dv$, so the “same” comparison includes coincident points without division. The other linked formal theorem proves the later finite-norm comparison (D.2), using this estimate and bounded derivatives through the next order. Its “different” comparison means that the interpolation calculation is a step in the proof, whereas its conclusion is the full weighted comparison with explicit constant four.

ties.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.SBD.norm_sub_sqrt_of_derivative'
ties.plain: Half-Hölder bound from the supremum and first derivative norms

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement proves $|v(x)-v(y)|\le\sqrt{2AB}\,|x-y|^{1/2}$ for differentiable $v$ with uniform bounds $|v|\le A$ and $\|Dv\|\le B$, $A,B\ge0$. Taking the finite supremum bounds gives the paper's seminorm inequality, including coincident points without division.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.SBD.norm_sub_sqrt_of_derivative'
rows.plain: Half-Hölder bound from the supremum and first derivative norms
rows.annotation: For $r=|a-b|$, the two bounds on the increment are $2\|v\|_\infty$ and $r\|Dv\|_\infty$. The smaller is at most their geometric mean. Dividing by $r^{1/2}$ eliminates the separation and gives a bound for the half-Hölder seminorm using just the value and first derivative bounds.

rows.fidelity_note: The paper gives the geometric-mean interpolation inequality. This formal declaration states the later finite-norm comparison (D.2), with constant four and bounded-derivative hypotheses. Its proof uses the interpolation inequality, but the declaration itself does not state that inequality as a separate conclusion.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The final weighted estimate is proved from the interpolation calculation; the intermediate interpolation bound need not be a separate conclusion.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.Text.eq_D_2
rows.plain: Half-Hölder norm between consecutive finite derivative norms
rows.annotation: Apply the geometric-mean bound to every derivative of order $m$ and sum. Cauchy–Schwarz pairs the order-$m$ supremum sum with the order-$(m+1)$ sum. This is the interpolation step used in the proof of (D.2), whose stated conclusion is the finite-norm comparison.

explanation.text: For $0<\ell_*\le1$ and a spatially smooth coefficient with bounded derivatives through order $n+1$, equation (D.2) gives $\|c\|_{[n]}\le\|c\|_{[n],1/2}\le C\ell_*^{-1/2}\|c\|_{[n+1]}$, together with its displayed exact-order version. Applying the preceding interpolation inequality to each derivative and distributing the powers of $\ell_*$ proves these bounds, so a Hölder estimate costs one derivative and $\ell_*^{-1/2}$. The individual formal comparison is “weaker” because it gives only the summed bounds and additionally assumes the Hölder quantities are finite. The full formal assertion and theorem prove finiteness from the bounded next derivatives and give both exact-order and summed inequalities, with constant four. Their “same” comparisons use the maximum of uniform norm and seminorm in each Hölder contribution; using their sum changes only the unspecified absolute constant in the paper.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The comparison assumes finite Hölder regularity, which is supplied for the constructed smooth coefficients before it is applied.

rows.annotation: The mean inverse is bounded on $C^{0,1/2}$, not merely in supremum norm. To use it at label order $n$ with supremum bounds on the source, (D.2) supplies the missing seminorm from order $n+1$. Its factor $\ell_*^{-1/2}$ is paid once in the conversion. The standalone comparison assumes the Hölder quantities finite; the full formal statement also establishes finiteness.

rows.fidelity_note: For $0<\ell_*\le1$ and smooth coefficients with derivatives bounded through the required next order, the formal statement proves both bounds in (D.2) and the necessary Hölder finiteness. Its constant is four under the maximum convention for each Hölder norm. The paper leaves that convention unspecified; choosing the customary sum merely changes the unspecified absolute constant.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.Text.eq_D_2
rows.plain: Half-Hölder norm bounded by one additional label derivative
rows.annotation: Writing $A_m=\ell_*^m|c|_m$, the weighted half-Hölder seminorm at order $m$ is bounded by $C\ell_*^{-1/2}(A_m A_{m+1})^{1/2}$. The arithmetic-geometric mean inequality and summation give (D.2). Thus a half-Hölder estimate uses one additional derivative in the supremum norm and costs half an inverse radius. Lean proves finiteness and the comparison with an explicit constant $4$ in its norm convention.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal theorem proves all of (D.2) for $0<\ell_*\le1$, using smooth coefficients with bounded next derivatives. Its Hölder norm takes the maximum of supremum and seminorm, and its explicit constant is four. The equivalent sum convention gives the same paper inequalities with an adjusted absolute constant; the lower norm comparison is included.

rows.annotation: The lower comparison follows by dropping the increment part. For the upper comparison, a half derivative is paid for by the geometric mean of adjacent derivative orders and costs at most $\ell_*^{-1/2}$ in the scaled norm. Lean proves finiteness as well as the two inequalities.

citations.supports: Derivative-index shifts, the product rule and the bounded normalized derivatives required by the weighted estimates.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Appendix D, Lemma D.1, (D.3)–(D.4), and first paragraph of its proof

explanation.text: For positive $\ell_*,h,\gamma(t)$, equations (D.3)–(D.4) bound one extra label derivative by $3\ell_*^{-1}$ times the next finite norm, one phase derivative by $h^{-1}$ times that norm, and a product by $C_n\|f\|_{[n]}\|g\|_{[n],\gamma}$. The first two bounds shift the derivative index, and the product bound follows from Leibniz’ rule applied to $f(g/\gamma)$ because $\gamma$ depends only on time. These estimates control differentiated products throughout the finite expansion, with all right-hand derivative families assumed uniformly bounded over the chosen time set, labels and phases. The unweighted derivative result and the separate bilinear product result each supply only part of the display, hence “weaker”; the derivative result is applied to $f/\gamma$, while the product result bounds $B(f,g)$ with an additional factor $\|B\|$ and also permits zero weights under a zero-division convention. The full formal assertion and theorem require positivity, establish bounded output derivatives, and allow every continuous bilinear product, which is the extension described by “stronger”.

rows.fidelity_note: Let $\ell_*,h>0$ and let $f(t,a,s)$ be spatially and phase smooth, with bounded mixed derivatives through order $n+1$ over a specified time set, all labels and phases. The formal statement proves $\sum_i\|\partial_{a_i}f\|_{[n]}\le3\ell_*^{-1}\|f\|_{[n+1]}$ and $\|\partial_sf\|_{[n]}\le h^{-1}\|f\|_{[n+1]}$, counting each multi-index once. Applying it to $f/\gamma(t)$ gives (D.3) when those normalized derivative families are bounded; positivity alone does not supply that boundedness. The product estimate (D.4) is not a conclusion here.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. A derivative component of the weighted estimate is separated from the product estimate; the complete lemma supplies both.

rows.annotation: When one additional label derivative is removed from the norm at order $n+1$, it costs $\ell_*^{-1}$. Each resulting multi-index was counted at most three times, once for each possible final label direction. The phase index has only one such predecessor and costs exactly $h^{-1}$.

rows.fidelity_note: Let $B$ be a continuous bilinear map and let $f,g$ be spatially smooth fields. Choose smooth differentiation directions, a time weight $\gamma$, and an order $n$; assume bounded derivative families through order $n$ for $f$ and $g/\gamma$. The formal statement gives $\|B(f,g)/\gamma\|_{[n]}\le2^{n+1}N_n\|B\|\|f\|_{[n]}\|g/\gamma\|_{[n]}$, where $N_n$ counts the nondecreasing derivative sequences through order $n$. With the scaled label and phase directions this yields (D.4). The derivative estimates in (D.3) are separate. This helper also permits zero weights, using zero for division by zero; the paper assumes positivity.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The general bilinear product estimates include the paper's products; positive scales and weights are used in the actual application.

rows.plain: The weighted bilinear product bound
rows.annotation: In a Leibniz term the label and phase weights split exactly: $\ell_*^{|\beta|}h^j=(\ell_*^{|\beta'|}h^{j'})(\ell_*^{|\beta-\beta'|}h^{j-j'})$. Normalize only the second factor by $\gamma(t)$. Each input is needed through at most order $n$, with no additional derivative. The operator norm of the bilinear action is included in the bound.

rows.fidelity_note: For $\ell_*,h>0$, a positive time weight $\gamma$ and fields smooth in $(a,s)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, assume uniformly bounded normalized derivatives of $f/\gamma$ through $n+1$ for (D.3), and of $f$ and $g/\gamma$ through $n$ for (D.4). The formal statement gives the displayed derivative inequalities with label constant three and extends the product to every continuous bilinear $B$, multiplying the bound by $\|B\|$. It also establishes boundedness of each output derivative family. The finite norm counts each mixed multi-index once over the chosen time set.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The general bilinear product estimates include the paper's products; positive scales and weights are used in the actual application.

rows.annotation: The derivative estimates spend one order and one inverse length. The formal lemma assumes positive scales and weight, bounded normalized derivatives at the indicated orders, and allows continuous bilinear products.

The fields are smooth in label and phase. Required bounds are on $f/\gamma$ through order $n+1$ for differentiation, and on $f$ and $g/\gamma$ through order $n$ for products; they are uniform over the chosen time set, labels and phases. In (D.4), the product keeps its full derivative budget, because the weight and every derivative split between the factors. citations.supports: The phase operations, their commutation with profile derivatives and the zero-mean condition for the primitive.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Appendix D, (D.5) and second paragraph of the proof of Lemma D.1

explanation.text: For a smooth period-one profile with bounded mixed derivatives after division by $\gamma(t)>0$, equation (D.5) bounds phase averaging by one, subtraction of the average by two, and the zero-mean periodic primitive by an absolute constant in $\|\cdot\|_{[n],\gamma}$. The primitive clause requires $\langle f\rangle_s=0$ at every time and label; its value is $\int_0^sf$ minus the phase average of that integral. Averaging and this normalization commute with label and phase differentiation, so their zero-order estimates yield the finite-order bounds used in the oscillatory equations. The two separate formal results prove the unweighted averaging and primitive estimates for real Banach-valued profiles and constant derivative directions; applying them to $f/\gamma$ yields the weighted bounds, but each alone is “weaker” than the conjunction. The full formal assertion and theorem give all three bounds and finite output derivative families for positive scales, with primitive constant two, explaining “stronger”.

ties.name: TorusEuler.paperLemmaD1_phaseAverage
ties.plain: Averaging in finite derivative norms

rows.fidelity_note: Let $f:I\times\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to E$ be smooth in label and phase, period-one in phase, with $E$ a real Banach space. Assume uniformly bounded derivatives through order $n$ along a chosen finite family of constant directions. The formal statement proves contraction of the phase average and the factor-two bound for subtracting it in the corresponding derivative sum. Choosing the scaled coordinate directions and applying it to $f/\gamma(t)$ gives the first two inequalities in (D.5), provided those normalized derivatives are bounded. It contains no primitive estimate.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. Phase averaging and the zero-mean primitive have separate norm and derivative estimates, which are combined in Lemma D.1.

rows.name: TorusEuler.paperLemmaD1_phaseAverage
rows.plain: Averaging in finite derivative norms
rows.annotation: Averaging commutes with label derivatives, and the average of a positive phase derivative is zero by periodicity. Hence the average has no greater finite norm than the profile. Removing it costs at most two and gives the zero-mean forcing required for the periodic primitive. The linked statement is unweighted; apply it to $f/\gamma(t)$ for the weighted version.

rows.fidelity_note: For a real Banach-valued field smooth in label and phase, period-one in phase and of zero phase mean, assume bounded derivatives through order $n$ along a finite family of constant directions, uniformly over all times, labels and phases. The formal statement bounds its zero-mean periodic primitive by twice the input in that derivative sum. Applying it to $f/\gamma(t)$ with the scaled coordinate directions yields the last inequality in (D.5), provided the normalized derivatives are bounded. Averaging and subtraction of the mean are treated separately.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. Phase averaging and the zero-mean primitive have separate norm and derivative estimates, which are combined in Lemma D.1.

rows.name: TorusEuler.paperLemmaD1_phasePrimitive
rows.plain: Finite derivative norm bound for the phase primitive
rows.annotation: The integral from zero is periodic because a full-period integral of $f$ vanishes. Subtracting its average fixes its constant and does not change its derivative. On a period the integral and its average are each bounded by $\sup|f|$, giving constant two independently of $h$. The operation therefore solves for an oscillatory primitive without a derivative loss.

rows.fidelity_note: Let $\ell_*,h>0$, let $\gamma(t)>0$ on a specified time set, and let $f$ be smooth in label and phase, period-one in phase, with values in a real Banach space. Assume the mixed derivatives of $f/\gamma$ through order $n$ are uniformly bounded. The formal statement gives all three bounds in (D.5), with primitive constant two, and proves boundedness of the corresponding output derivative families. The primitive clause additionally assumes zero phase mean at each time and label. Thus positivity of the weight and periodicity do not replace the boundedness and zero-mean hypotheses.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. Phase averaging and the zero-mean primitive have separate norm and derivative estimates, which are combined in Lemma D.1.

rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_D_1

explanation.text: For fixed $m,q\ge0$ and all sufficiently large $j$, the correction after removing the oscillation satisfies $\sup_{0\le t\le S_j}\|\partial_t^q(U_j-U_{j-1}-O_j)(t)\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\le\lambda_j^{-1}$, with continuity in time in that norm. Here the spatial norm sums the supremum and half-Hölder seminorm of each full derivative tensor through order $m$, and the time derivatives hold the physical spatial point fixed. Summability of $\lambda_j^{-1}$ later turns these bounds into convergence of all mixed derivatives wherever the late oscillations vanish. The proved formal lemma supplies the selected construction and this eventual continuous-norm estimate; the formal fixed-stage condition expresses the same bound and continuity but leaves eventuality to its surrounding quantifiers. The time-independent Leray projection commutes with these derivatives, and Leibniz's rule distributes them between the two velocity factors. Thus the new velocity derivative uses only velocity and residual derivatives already controlled at time orders at most $q-1$. The formal identity has the same content, writing the new order as $r+1$ and expressing the nonlinear term as advection; incompressibility identifies this with the divergence of the tensor product. It holds for the smooth stage on a positive closed time interval, with endpoint derivatives taken from within that interval and $r=q-1$.

To reach the paper's finite label norms one must insert the weights $\ell_*^m$, use $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-a}$ with $a\ge16$, and sum the finitely many derivatives. explanation.text: The coefficient estimate says that fixed-label time derivatives through order $q$ of the flow matrices, transported covector, reciprocal covector length, and the mean coefficients $K$ and $\mathcal D$ have finite label norms bounded by $C_q\mu^{a_q}$. explanation.text: For a profile $f(t,a,s)$, time differentiation keeps both the flow label $a$ and the independent phase $s$ fixed. The formal derivative matches this convention by differentiating in the time direction alone on the closed stage interval, with the other two variables unchanged. Repetition gives the higher time derivatives entering $\mathcal J_q$. After evaluating the profile in physical coordinates, this derivative becomes the material derivative $\partial_t+U\cdot\nabla_x$, rather than the Eulerian derivative at a fixed physical point. The distinction is why a later conversion is needed before applying the increment estimate to physical velocity fields.

Thus profile time differentiation corresponds to the material derivative $D_t$ (see Equation (M.3.1)), not the Eulerian derivative $\partial_t$. explanation.text: For an oscillatory profile, the time derivative is formed first and its amplitude is then measured relative to the central strength $\gamma$. Thus the relevant quantity contains $\gamma^{-1}\partial_t^if$, rather than $\partial_t^i(\gamma^{-1}f)$, on the interval where the amplitude norm is used. The linked formal definition applies the amplitude seminorm to each already differentiated profile inside the factorially weighted time sum, matching this order of operations. This prevents derivatives of the normalizing weight from being introduced merely by the choice of norm. The exact spatial normalization of that formal seminorm is not displayed, but it is not needed to verify the quoted ordering of differentiation and amplitude weighting.

explanation.text: Mean profiles are measured without division by the central amplitude $\gamma$, using the unweighted spatial profile norm. citations.supports: Factorial weights turn time differentiation of products into a scalar convolution compatible with the spatial product bound.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Auxiliary note, Note 2, The two inverses with time derivatives; Lemma D.1

explanation.text: The key algebraic identity is $\frac{T^n}{n!}\binom ni=\frac{T^i}{i!}\frac{T^{n-i}}{(n-i)!}$ for $0\le i\le n$. Consequently the time Leibniz sum becomes a convolution of factorially weighted derivative norms, with no additional binomial factor to absorb. The first formal theorem proves exactly this identity, even without needing $T>0$. The second proves the corresponding inequality for nonnegative scalar sequences and positive $T$, bounding the truncated convolution sum by the product of the two weighted sums. It is weaker than a profile product estimate because applying it to fields still requires the spatial product inequality of Lemma D.1 and its hypotheses.

rows.fidelity_note: For $0\le i\le n$, the formal statement proves $(T^n/n!)\binom ni=(T^i/i!)(T^{n-i}/(n-i)!)$. This is the precise cancellation behind the convolution. It is algebraic and holds for every real $T$; positivity is needed only in the later estimate of norms.

rows.plain: Factorial time weights absorb the Leibniz binomial coefficient
rows.annotation: The coefficient of $(\partial_t^if)(\partial_t^{n-i}g)$ in the weighted $n$th derivative is $(T^n/n!)\binom ni=(T^i/i!)(T^{n-i}/(n-i)!)$. Hence the factorial-weighted derivative estimates multiply as ordinary finite convolution sums, without an additional binomial cost at each expansion level.

rows.fidelity_note: For positive $T$ and nonnegative sequences, this result bounds the factorially weighted Leibniz sum by the product of the two weighted sums. It is the scalar estimate resulting from the cancellation, not a product theorem for profiles. To obtain the stated profile estimates one must also apply the spatial product inequality.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The factorial convolution inequality is combined with the spatial product estimate to control derivatives of the profiles.

rows.name: TorusEuler.terminalTimeConvolution_le
rows.plain: The weighted product inequality

rows.fidelity_note: The formal theorem proves $\partial_t^q(S_{\Lambda_j}V)=S_{\Lambda_j}\partial_t^qV$ for the fixed spatial cutoff, with smooth periodic representatives of the time derivatives on the closed slab. Subtracting $\partial_t^qV$ gives the paper's formula for $v_\Lambda$. The linked conclusion itself is the cutoff-velocity identity.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. Subtracting the original velocity derivative from the cutoff commutation identity gives the stated truncation-error identity.

rows.name: TorusEuler.TruncatedChildStage.slabTimeJet_velocity
rows.plain: Time differentiation and the cutoff
rows.annotation: At step $j$ the operator $S_{\Lambda_j}$ is fixed throughout the slab. Therefore $\partial_t^q(S_{\Lambda_j}-\operatorname{Id})V=(S_{\Lambda_j}-\operatorname{Id})\partial_t^qV$. This permits direct application of (M.B.2) to each time jet of the uncut approximation; no derivative of the symbol or scale appears.

citations.supports: The spatial cutoff tail and the approximate-solution bound combine into the displayed negative power of the depth.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Auxiliary note, Note 2, The truncation difference; (2.5); Appendix B, (B.2)

explanation.text: Apply the cutoff tail estimate at spatial order $P$ to $\partial_t^qV$, then use (2.5) and the threshold bound on the tail constant to obtain $\|\partial_t^qv_\Lambda\|_{C_tC^{m,1/2}}\le\mu\Lambda_j^{m-P}\lambda^{2(P+1)+\psi'_q}$. Since $\Lambda_j=\lambda^5$, the exponent simplifies to $-3P+5m+2+\psi'_q$, giving strong decay when $P$ grows. The formal theorem supplies the weaker fixed-time tail estimate $C_P\Lambda_j^{m-P}\|\partial_t^qV(t)\|_{C^{P,1/2}}$ for $m\le P$, a positive fixed cutoff scale, and smooth periodic fields on the positive closed slab. Its exponent uses signed integer subtraction, so the negative power when $m<P$ is preserved. The substitutions $C_P\le\mu$, $\Lambda_j=\lambda^5$, and (2.5), together with time-norm continuity, are additional steps needed for the paper's full display.

ties.name: TorusEuler.TruncatedChildStage.slabTimeJet_velocityTail
ties.plain: The time-differentiated cutoff tail

rows.fidelity_note: For $m\le P$ and $\Lambda>0$, the formal theorem gives $C_P\Lambda^{m-P}\|\partial_t^qV(t)\|_{C^{P,1/2}}$ as a spatial tail bound. It has not substituted $C_P\le\mu$, $\Lambda=\lambda^5$ or the approximate-velocity estimate. Those substitutions produce the paper's displayed expression. Time continuity in the norm is also supplied separately.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The tail estimate gives the paper's rate after the scheduled cutoff scale, constant bound and approximate-velocity estimate are inserted.

rows.name: TorusEuler.TruncatedChildStage.slabTimeJet_velocityTail
rows.plain: The time-differentiated cutoff tail
rows.annotation: At order $P$ the differentiated approximate velocity grows at most as $\lambda^{2(P+1)+\psi'_q}$. The Fourier tail gains $\lambda^{5(m-P)}$, so its combined exponent is $-3P+5m+2+\psi'_q$. At fixed $(m,q)$ this tends to $-\infty$ as the scheduled depth increases. The additional cost $\mu$ for the cutoff constant is absorbed since $\mu\le\lambda$.

citations.supports: Increasing expansion depth absorbs the fixed derivative costs and gives the half-tail estimate.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Auxiliary note, Note 2, The truncation difference; Lemma 1.3 and (7.2)

explanation.text: For fixed $m,q$, the tail bound $\mu\lambda^{-3P+5m+2+\psi'_q}$ is eventually at most $\tfrac12\lambda^{-1}$ because $\mu\le\lambda$, $\lambda\ge2$, and $P\to\infty$. The formal numerical theorem makes a sufficient condition explicit: if $0\le C\le\lambda$, $\lambda\ge2$, and $5m+5+\psi'_q\le3P$, then $C(\lambda^5)^{m-P}\lambda^{2(P+1)+\psi'_q}\le\tfrac12\lambda^{-1}$. Under that condition the expression is at most $\lambda^{-2}$, and $\lambda^{-2}\le\tfrac12\lambda^{-1}$ follows from $\lambda\ge2$. The link is weaker than the eventual statement because it proves the inequality at one stage and does not choose the starting index. Growth of $P$ supplies that index separately for each fixed pair of derivative orders.

ties.name: TorusEuler.terminalTime_cutoff_tail_rate
ties.plain: Cutoff-tail frequency decay at fixed derivative order and depth

rows.fidelity_note: The formal result is a single-stage numerical implication: if $\lambda\ge2$, $C\le\lambda$ and $5m+5+\psi'_q\le3P$, then the cutoff expression is at most $\tfrac12\lambda^{-1}$. It does not itself prove that these hypotheses hold at all sufficiently large stages. That uses the schedule and the fact that $m,q$ are fixed.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The schedule makes the finite depth inequality valid eventually at each fixed derivative order.

rows.name: TorusEuler.terminalTime_cutoff_tail_rate
rows.plain: Cutoff-tail frequency decay at fixed derivative order and depth
rows.annotation: Since $\mu\le\lambda$, the cutoff tail bound is at most $\lambda^{-3P+5m+3+\psi'_q}$. For fixed $(m,q)$ eventually $3P\ge5m+5+\psi'_q$, so this is at most $\lambda^{-2}\le\tfrac12\lambda^{-1}$ for $\lambda\ge2$. The formal arithmetic lemma uses precisely this sufficient depth inequality.

citations.supports: The nonoscillatory increment is exactly the sum of the physical mean and the cutoff difference.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Auxiliary note, Note 2, The truncation difference; Subsections 5.6–5.7

explanation.text:
Before truncation, the child approximation is $V=U_{j-1}+W^
atural$, with $W=W_{m osc}+ ar W$ and $O_j=W_{m osc}^
atural$. Since $U_j=S_{\Lambda_j}V$ and $v_\Lambda=U_j-V$, cancellation gives $U_j-U_{j-1}-O_j= ar W^
atural+v_\Lambda$ exactly. The formal theorem gives this same identity for the actual selected fields at stages $j\ge2$. It is an algebraic equality of the globally defined fields, though the analytic bounds used on its two terms are asserted on the stage interval. This split isolates the mean and cutoff tail, each of which consumes half of the desired $\lambda_j^{-1}$ bound.

ties.name: TorusEuler.ScheduledEulerConstruction.selectedStep_increment_eq
ties.plain: Stage increment splits into oscillation, mean and cutoff error

rows.fidelity_note: For each selected later step, the formal equality identifies the correction with the actual mean of that step plus its actual Fourier-cutoff error. Its indexing starts with $j=2$. The equality is between the globally defined fields; the auxiliary estimates apply on the closed interval $[0,S_j]$.
rows.name: TorusEuler.ScheduledEulerConstruction.selectedStep_increment_eq
rows.plain: Stage increment splits into oscillation, mean and cutoff error
rows.annotation: Subtract the spatially localized, uncut $O_j=W_{\rm osc}^\natural$, not $S_{\Lambda_j}O_j$. Adding and subtracting $V$ leaves exactly $\bar W^\natural+(S_{\Lambda_j}-\operatorname{Id})V$. A finite Fourier sum cannot in general retain the support of the wave. The global tail estimate is what permits one to discard the uncut oscillation off the origin without discarding its cutoff error.

citations.supports: The exact split and two half-bounds yield the summable mixed correction bound.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Auxiliary note, Note 2, end of The truncation difference; (2.4) and (1.2)

explanation.text: The identity $U_j-U_{j-1}-O_j=\bar W^\natural+v_\Lambda$ combines the mean bound (2.4) and the cutoff-tail bound, each at most $\tfrac12\lambda_j^{-1}$. Applying the triangle inequality after the same fixed-physical-point time derivative gives (1.2) at every time of the stage. The formal theorem is weaker: at a chosen time it assumes the smooth decomposition, $\lambda\ge2$, $m\le P$, a cutoff-tail constant $C_P\le\lambda$, the depth condition $5m+5+\psi'\le3P$, the appropriate order-$P$ bound for $V$, and the half-bound for the mean. It then concludes finiteness of the correction's spatial Hölder norm and the bound $\lambda^{-1}$. The analytic premises, their eventual validity, and continuity in time in that norm still have to be supplied to obtain the complete auxiliary lemma.

ties.name: TorusEuler.TruncatedChildStage.slabTimeJet_increment_rate
ties.plain: Time derivative bounds for the stage increment minus the oscillation

rows.fidelity_note: Given a smooth split $V=U+O+M$, the explicit depth condition for the cutoff tail and a half-size mean bound, the formal theorem gives $\|\partial_t^q(S_\Lambda V-U-O)\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\le\lambda^{-1}$ at the chosen time. It does not provide the eventual starting stage or continuity in the spatial norm required by the full auxiliary Lemma 1.2.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The two half-size estimates give the increment bound; eventual stage selection and time continuity are supplied separately.

rows.name: TorusEuler.TruncatedChildStage.slabTimeJet_increment_rate
rows.plain: Time derivative bounds for the stage increment minus the oscillation
rows.annotation: Both terms in the exact correction identity are estimated in the same mixed norm: the mean by (2.4), without any fast phase cost, and the Fourier tail by (M.B.2) applied to the time jet. Their bounds are each $\tfrac12\lambda^{-1}$. Thus the estimate for the correction is global even though the oscillation it excludes is localized. Norm continuity on the closed slab is obtained separately.

citations.supports: The cutoff preserves the velocity time bound after one power of the frequency absorbs its constant.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Auxiliary note, Note 2, The residual and the new velocity; (2.5); Appendix B, (B.1)

explanation.text: Since $U_j=S_{\Lambda_j}V$, the spatial cutoff bound applied to $\partial_t^iV$ and (2.5) at $n=0$ gives $\|\partial_t^iU_j\|_\infty\le\lambda^{\psi'_q+3}$ for $i\le q$. The extra power of $\lambda$ absorbs the fixed cutoff constant, so the new velocity exponent is $\psi_q=\psi'_q+3$. The formal theorem matches this numerical estimate at a chosen time for smooth periodic fields on a positive slab, assuming $\lambda\ge2$, $1+C_0\le\lambda$, and $\|\partial_t^iV\|_{C^{0,1/2}}\le\lambda^{2+\psi'_q}$. Applying it at every time and every $i\le q$ gives the paper's uniform bound. Eventual satisfaction of the constant bound comes from the threshold choice, rather than from the cutoff theorem itself.

ties.name: TorusEuler.TruncatedChildStage.slabTimeJet_cutoffVelocity_rate
ties.plain: Time derivative bounds for the Fourier-truncated velocity

rows.fidelity_note: Let $V$ be smooth and periodic on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$, with $T>0$, and use the selected fixed cutoff at $\Lambda=\lambda^5$. At a specified time and order $i$, assume $\lambda\ge2$, $1+C_0\le\lambda$ for the fixed order-zero cutoff constant, and $\|\partial_t^iV\|_{C^{0,1/2}}\le\lambda^{2+\psi'_q}$. The formal statement gives $|\partial_t^iU_j(t,x)|\le\lambda^{\psi'_q+3}$ for every $x$. The derivatives are within the closed time interval. Applying the statement at every $i\le q$ and every time gives the quoted supremum bound; the needed approximate-velocity estimates remain hypotheses.
rows.name: TorusEuler.TruncatedChildStage.slabTimeJet_cutoffVelocity_rate
rows.plain: Time derivative bounds for the Fourier-truncated velocity
rows.annotation: At $n=0$, (2.5) bounds the time jet of $V$ by $\lambda^{2+\psi'_q}$. The uniform cutoff bound costs at most another factor $\lambda$ eventually. This yields $\psi_q=\psi'_q+3$ for all $i\le q$, as required in (1.3).

citations.supports: The residual identity isolates the cutoff stress, and time differentiation distributes through its quadratic factors.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Auxiliary note, Note 2, The residual and the new velocity; (5.58)

explanation.text: With $S=S_{\Lambda_j}$, $U_j=SV$, and $v=U_j-V$, the residual formula separates the truncated approximate residual from the error created by truncating the quadratic velocity term. The tensor inside the divergence can equivalently be written $U_j\otimes U_j-S(V\otimes V)$, because expanding $v$ gives $v\otimes U_j+V\otimes v+(I-S)(V\otimes V)$. The formal statement is stronger: for smooth periodic fields and their residual on a positive closed slab, it gives the identity after every time derivative, with the corresponding binomial sum over the two differentiated velocity factors. At time order zero it reduces to the displayed formula. Every additional quadratic error contains a cutoff difference, which lets the tail estimate supply the small factor needed to close the residual induction.

ties.name: TorusEuler.TruncatedChildStage.slabTimeJet_residual_eq
ties.plain: Time derivatives of the cutoff residual

rows.fidelity_note: The formal theorem gives every time derivative of the residual as the Leray projection of the differentiated cutoff residual and a binomial sum of quadratic cutoff errors. At order zero its tensor error is $U_j\otimes U_j-S(V\otimes V)$. With $v=U_j-V$, this equals the three tensors displayed in the paper. The cutoff symbol and scale are fixed in time.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. Expanding the quadratic tensor difference gives the paper's three terms, with the same time-independent cutoff.

rows.name: TorusEuler.TruncatedChildStage.slabTimeJet_residual_eq
rows.plain: Time derivatives of the cutoff residual
rows.annotation: Write $v=U_j-V$. Because time differentiation commutes with $S$, subtracting the cut and uncut projected equations, as in (M.5.58), leaves $SR_V$ and the projected divergence of $v\otimes U_j+V\otimes v+(\operatorname{Id}-S)(V\otimes V)$. Each of the three stress terms contains a cutoff tail. For the projected divergence in $C^{1,1/2}$ estimate the tensors in $C^{2,1/2}$; time differentiation distributes over the factors without removing the tail.

citations.supports: The next-frequency growth absorbs the remaining fixed velocity powers and closes the residual time estimate.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Auxiliary note, Note 2, final residual estimates; (1.3), (2.5), and (5.59)

explanation.text: After the cutoff residual identity is differentiated through order $q$, the approximate-residual term and all cutoff-stress terms are bounded by $\lambda^{15+2\psi'_q}\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$. Since $\lambda_{j+1}=\lambda^{K_{j+1}}$ and $K_{j+1}\to\infty$, the fixed factor $\lambda^{15+2\psi'_q}$ is eventually absorbed into $\lambda_{j+1}^{3/2}$, leaving the required $\lambda_{j+1}^{-5/2}$. The formal theorem is weaker: at a specified derivative order and time, it assumes the analytic residual and tail bounds, $\lambda\ge2$, $\psi'\ge0$, cost constants at most $\lambda$, and the sufficient growth condition $K\ge16+2\psi'$ with next frequency $\lambda^K$. It then proves the pointwise residual bound with exponent $-5/2$. Taking all times and orders $i\le q$, proving the analytic premises, and choosing their common eventual index complete the induction claimed in the paper.

ties.name: TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_cutoffResidual_rate
ties.plain: Time derivatives of the truncated residual decay in the next frequency

rows.fidelity_note: The formal result proves $|\partial_t^iR_j(t,x)|\le\lambda_{j+1}^{-5/2}$ from an assumed analytic residual-error bound and explicit inequalities including $\lambda_{j+1}=\lambda_j^K$ and $K\ge16+2\psi'_q$. It is a pointwise implication at a specified order and time. The eventual validity of those assumptions and continuity in the spatial supremum norm are separate parts of the full lemma.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The scalar rate implication is combined with the analytic residual estimate and the eventual schedule bounds.

rows.name: TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_cutoffResidual_rate
rows.plain: Time derivatives of the truncated residual decay in the next frequency
rows.annotation: The projected uncut residual contributes at most $\lambda^{1+\psi'_q}\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$ after bounding its operator constant by $\lambda$. The new cutoff terms contribute at most $\lambda^{15+2\psi'_q}\lambda_{j+1}^{-6}$, by $\Lambda=\lambda^5$ and $P=6K_{j+1}$. The formal rate lemma uses the sufficient condition $K_{j+1}\ge16+2\psi'_q$ to bound each term by $\lambda_{j+1}^{-3}$. Their sum is at most $\lambda_{j+1}^{-5/2}$ once $\lambda_{j+1}\ge4$.

citations.supports: Shrinking supports leave every compact subset of the punctured torus, reducing the late increments to their small corrections.
citations.title: this paper
citations.where: Auxiliary note, Note 3, opening paragraph; Theorem 7.1, spatial support assertion

explanation.text: A compact set $K\subset\mathbb T^3\setminus\{0\}$ has positive distance from the origin, while the support radius $\lambda_{j-1}^{-1}$ of $O_j$ tends to zero. Therefore some open neighborhood of $K$ misses every sufficiently late oscillation, uniformly for all times in the common closed interval. The formal theorem gives this same conclusion on the periodic lift, where the excluded set is $\mathbb Z^3$, from shrinking support radii and the common-interval hypotheses. It is stronger in generality because it applies to any sequence with those support properties, without using Euler or the detailed wave equations. On that neighborhood, the tail of the velocity increments consequently equals the nonoscillatory correction tail controlled by (1.2).

ties.name: TorusEuler.inductive_oscillations_eventually_zero_near_offOrigin_compact
ties.plain: Late oscillations vanish near a compact

rows.fidelity_note: For every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb Z^3$, the formal theorem gives an open neighborhood of $K$ on which all sufficiently late oscillations vanish for the whole common interval. It applies to any sequence supported in shrinking balls about lattice points, without an Euler equation or mixed derivative hypothesis. The paper's selected oscillations satisfy these support assumptions.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. Shrinking support alone gives the neighborhood vanishing needed for terminal limits; the constructed oscillations satisfy that stronger geometric hypothesis.

rows.name: TorusEuler.inductive_oscillations_eventually_zero_near_offOrigin_compact
rows.plain: Late oscillations vanish near a compact
rows.annotation: Let $d=\operatorname{dist}(K,0)>0$ on the torus. Once the support radius of $O_j$ is less than $d/2$, the oscillation is identically zero on the open $d/2$-neighborhood of $K$ throughout the slab. On the periodic lift the separation is from the entire integer lattice. Consequently every mixed derivative of the late oscillations vanishes there. The increment bound (1.2) for the remaining terms is global; only the starting index and the early finite sum can depend on $d$.
